title: New Neighbours for the Milky Way

sentences.text: Astronomers have long known that our galaxy, the Milky Way, does not travel through space alone.
It is accompanied by a collection of smaller systems that orbit it, rather as moons orbit a planet.
These satellites are held in place by the gravity of the much larger Milky Way.
The best known of these companions are the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, which can be seen with the naked eye from the Southern Hemisphere.
About 65 satellite galaxies have now been identified, but some estimates suggest that hundreds more have yet to be detected.
Many of them are so faint that they are extremely hard to pick out against the crowded background of stars.
A new observatory in Chile has now begun to fill some of these gaps.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory stands on Cerro Pachón, a mountain in the Chilean Andes, and is funded jointly by the US National Science Foundation and the Office of Science of the US Department of Energy.
Its main instrument, the Simonyi Survey Telescope, has an 8.4-metre primary mirror and feeds light to a camera of 3.2 gigapixels, the largest digital camera ever built.
Rather than studying one small patch of sky in great detail, Rubin photographs wide areas of the southern sky over and over again.
In this way it builds up a record not only of what the sky contains but also of how it changes.
Even before its main programme had properly started, the observatory was producing discoveries.

Researchers from Yale University, the University of Chicago and a number of other universities and research centres in North America and Europe examined preview observations collected between April 2025 and January 2026.
These early images covered only about 7 per cent of the night sky, a small fraction of the data Rubin is expected to gather.
Observations of this kind are often used to check that a new telescope and its camera are working as expected, but they can also contain genuine scientific results.
Within them, the team identified two objects that had never been recorded before.
The first, named Aquarius IV, is a tiny and extremely faint galaxy in the distant outskirts of the Milky Way, roughly 355,000 light-years from Earth.
Like many faint satellite galaxies, it is named after the constellation in which it appears, in this case Aquarius.
It was picked out by automated search programs rather than by a person examining the images, and the researchers are highly confident that it is real.
The discovery was reported in the journal Research Notes of the AAS by a team led by William Cerny, a graduate student in astronomy at Yale.
The second object, known as Rubin-GC1, is a star cluster rather than a galaxy.
It lies on the opposite side of the Milky Way, in a region filled with thick clouds of cosmic dust.
Because such dust blocks much of the light coming from behind it, objects in these areas are notoriously difficult to observe.
A paper describing the cluster, with Aashay Pai of the University of Chicago as first author and Cerny as second author, has been accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Why should astronomers care so much about such dim and distant objects?
Ultra-faint galaxies like Aquarius IV contain very few stars, yet most of their mass consists of dark matter, the invisible material that is thought to make up most of the matter in the universe.
This makes them valuable natural laboratories, since by studying their properties and the way they move, scientists can test competing models of dark matter.
Small satellites can also help researchers to reconstruct the history of how the Milky Way itself was assembled.
In addition, they offer clues about how the very smallest galaxies form and how they manage to survive.
Studying them is a challenge, however, precisely because they contain so few stars that can be observed.
For an observatory that had only just begun its work, these were encouraging results, and the two discoveries are expected to be the first of many.
Rubin has now begun its Legacy Survey of Space and Time, a project that will last ten years.
One of its major aims is to map the halo of our galaxy, the vast and thinly populated region that surrounds its main disc.
Cerny described the new findings as just the beginning for the observatory.
Marla Geha, a professor at Yale who was a co-author of both studies, said that the possibility of finding new satellites of the Milky Way in Rubin's data had excited her for most of her career.
If the estimates are correct, many of the galaxy's missing companions may soon appear in the observatory's images.

sentences.text: Ask most people to imagine the wild landscapes of Europe a hundred thousand or a million years ago, and they will probably picture an endless, gloomy forest.
The image is a powerful one, and it remains deeply rooted in the way Europeans think about their natural past.
Yet according to a major new review of the evidence, it is very probably misleading.
For most of its long history, the European landscape appears to have been a far brighter and more varied place.
The study, published in the journal Biological Conservation, was the work of 21 researchers.

It was led by Szymon Czyżewski, a PhD student at the Center for Ecological Dynamics in a Novel Biosphere (ECONOVO) at Aarhus University in Denmark, while Professor Jens-Christian Svenning of the same centre was the senior author.

Their central conclusion is that for more than 20 million years, much of Europe was covered not by continuous forest but by a shifting patchwork of scattered trees, open woodland, grassy clearings and meadows full of wildflowers.
Dense, closed-canopy forest of the kind that covers much of the continent today appears, by comparison, to be a relatively recent development.
This conclusion challenges what has been called the 'closed-forest paradigm'.
For decades, this view has held that thick forest was the natural condition of Europe before people began clearing land for farming and settlement.
If that were true, restoring nature would be a fairly simple matter: either plant trees or step back and let woodland reclaim the land.
Partly because it offers such a clear prescription, the paradigm has had a strong influence on conservation.

The new research suggests, however, that it overlooks a mixture of grassland, shrubs and woodland with differing amounts of tree cover, a mixture that supported species adapted to both open and wooded conditions.
Reconstructing landscapes that disappeared long ago is no easy task, and the team's approach stood out for its breadth in two respects.

First, the study covered an unusually long period, from the beginning of the Miocene epoch around 23 million years ago up to the pre-industrial era, whereas most earlier studies had concentrated on more recent times.
Second, it did not depend on any one type of evidence.
Since every record of the distant past is incomplete, the researchers brought together several independent lines of evidence, known as proxies.

These included fossil pollen and larger plant remains, charcoal from ancient wildfires, chemical traces in the teeth and bones of plant-eating animals, fossil insects and mammals, and environmental DNA, the genetic material that living things leave in their surroundings and that can survive in ancient sediments.
Czyżewski has explained that each proxy provides its own perspective, and that combining them gave the team more confidence in its conclusions than a study based on a single method could offer.
When these sources were put together, a consistent pattern emerged.
Time after time, the evidence pointed to shifting mosaics of trees, open ground and flowers rather than to unbroken forest.
Significantly, such mosaics were found not only under temperate conditions similar to those of modern Europe but also during warmer and colder periods.
Something other than the weather, then, seems to have been helping to keep the landscape open.
According to the researchers, that something was the activity of large plant-eating animals.
Elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs and bison grazed on grasses, browsed on shrubs and young trees, and disturbed the ground as they moved.
In doing so, they kept parts of the landscape open, creating clearings where grasses and wildflowers could flourish in conditions that a thick canopy of trees would not have allowed.
Through this continuous interaction between animals and plants, a wide variety of habitats was maintained, and these in turn supported a great many species.
Modern Europe has largely lost this influence.

Many of the large herbivores have disappeared, and according to Czyżewski the most dramatic change has occurred within the last hundred years, as traditional extensive grazing vanished from large parts of the continent.
This, the researchers say, helps to explain why today's ecosystems look so different from those of the past.
Larks, jackdaws and the European hamster are usually thought of as creatures of farmland, yet they may have evolutionary roots in ancient open woodlands.
Wild poppies, now a common sight in fields, probably also thrived wherever grazing animals disturbed the vegetation.
These findings have practical consequences at a time when European countries are expanding their forests in order to capture carbon, respond to climate change and restore biodiversity.
Svenning believes that current reforestation is 'on the wrong track'.
He points out that in Denmark, subsidies are given only for the planting of dense forest, a policy that sits uneasily with the kinds of ecosystem in which Europe's species evolved.
Planting uniform, closely packed woodland, the researchers warn, could actually reduce the variety of habitats and so harm the biodiversity it is meant to protect.

They also question the strict division between 'forest' and 'open habitat' that is commonly used in conservation planning, since in the past trees, meadows, shrubs and grazing animals formed connected parts of a single landscape.
Instead of uniform forest, the team argues, restoration should give priority to mosaics of woodland and open habitat, including the return of large wild herbivores.
The study adds to earlier work by the same group suggesting that big animals shaped European ecosystems more than was once recognised.

If the researchers are right, protecting Europe's wildlife will require more than simply planting trees: it will mean recreating the balance between woodland, meadow and the animals that once moved between them.

sentences.text: Every time a person breathes out, a small amount of carbon dioxide leaves the body.
This gas is a by-product of metabolism, the set of chemical processes through which the body turns food into the energy it needs to stay alive.
Even when sitting still, an adult breathes in and out many thousands of times a day.
The muscles, the brain and the other organs are using fuel all the time, even while we are asleep.
When these tiny breaths are multiplied by the billions of people on the planet, they add up to a surprisingly large figure.
A research team led by Professor Javier Gonzalez of the Centre for Exercise, Nutrition and Metabolism at the University of Bath has now tried to put a number on that figure.
Working with more than 60 colleagues, the researchers published their estimate in the journal The Lancet Planetary Health.
According to their calculations, human metabolism released about 1.18 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide in 1985.
By 2015, the yearly total had climbed to roughly 2.05 billion metric tons, an increase of 74 per cent in only thirty years.
To reach these figures, the scientists did not try to test every person on Earth, which would of course be impossible.
Instead, they gathered thousands of existing measurements showing how much carbon dioxide individuals produce as they go about their ordinary daily activities.
These records covered people at every stage of life, from babies to the elderly.
Many of them came from a large international database of measurements made with a method known as doubly labelled water, which has been supported by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
The team then combined this information with world population statistics and data on body weight, which allowed them to model how the total output had changed over time.
The main reason for the rise turned out to be a simple one.
More than 60 per cent of the increase could be explained by the growth of the world's population.
Changes in the amount of carbon dioxide produced by each individual played a much smaller part.
As Gonzalez put it, the total has grown mainly because there are now more of us.
Why does this matter?
Scientists who study the climate rely on carbon budgets, which are detailed accounts of where carbon comes from, where it travels and where it finally ends up.
A source of around two billion tons a year is too large to leave out when such budgets are drawn up.
Accurate figures also help experts to predict how effective different plans for cutting carbon emissions are likely to be.
According to the researchers, the effect of human breathing is easiest to see in crowded cities, where large numbers of people live and work close together.
In such places, the breathing of residents can make a noticeable difference to local measurements of carbon in the air.
Despite the size of the number, the team stresses that breathing is not a major cause of global warming.
The key difference lies in where the carbon originally came from.
The carbon in our breath comes mainly from the food we eat, and the plants at the start of every food chain removed that carbon from the atmosphere only recently.
Breathing it out simply returns it to a natural cycle in which it was already moving.
Burning coal, oil or gas is quite different, because it releases carbon that had been locked away underground for millions of years.
This adds new carbon to the atmosphere instead of recycling carbon that was already there.
For this reason, the researchers are not asking anyone to exercise less or to change their diet in order to reduce the carbon dioxide they breathe out.
Their aim is better measurement, not a change in the way people live.
Being able to separate natural carbon from living bodies and carbon from fossil fuels, they argue, is an essential part of understanding how the climate is changing.
The study therefore adds one more useful piece of information to the wider effort to follow how carbon moves around the planet and to judge which ways of reducing emissions really work.

title: Blood from the Age of Dinosaurs

sentences.text: Fossils usually preserve the shape of an ancient animal rather than its chemistry, which is why most of what we know about dinosaurs, from their size to the way they moved, has been worked out from the form of their skeletons.

Bones and teeth survive because minerals gradually fill or replace their original material, while soft tissues and the fragile molecules inside them are generally expected to break down long before the process is complete.
For this reason, many scientists have assumed that haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in the blood, could not possibly last for millions of years.
A new study led by researchers at Curtin University in Australia now challenges that assumption in a striking way, and it may change how scientists approach fossils in the future.
The team examined limb bones from Aratasaurus museunacionali, a meat-eating dinosaur belonging to the group known as theropods, whose remains were found in north-eastern Brazil.
The animal lived around 115 million years ago.
Inside the bones, the researchers found fossilised red blood cells lying within the vascular canals, the narrow channels that once held the animal's blood vessels.
More importantly, they detected heme, a molecule derived from haemoglobin, inside the cells themselves.
They also identified amino acids associated with collagen, the structural protein that gives strength to bones and connective tissues.
The results have been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
Structures that resemble blood cells have been reported in dinosaur fossils before, so the shapes alone were not a new discovery.
What earlier studies had not done was show conclusively that the molecular remains of blood were present inside those structures.

As long as that chemical evidence was missing, it remained possible that the shapes were simply mineral formations that happened to look like cells, and that no trace of the original blood had survived at all.
According to the authors, their work provides the first definitive chemical confirmation of haemoglobin-derived molecules inside fossilised dinosaur red blood cells.
The lead author, Professor Kliti Grice, who is the founding director of Curtin's WA-Organic and Isotope Geochemistry Centre, described the result as astonishing and called it a landmark discovery.
Why did these molecules survive when so many others disappear?
The researchers point to a mineral called hausmannite, which appears to have helped to stabilise the cells and protect their molecular contents.
In effect, the mineral acted as a kind of time capsule, holding delicate material in place for an immense period.
The circumstances of the animal's burial may also have been important.
The team suspects that the dinosaur was covered quickly by sediment in an environment that was low in oxygen but rich in microbial activity.
This combination of conditions, they believe, created an unusual opportunity for the chemistry of blood to be preserved rather than destroyed.
Grice argues that the findings challenge the long-held view that haemoglobin cannot survive through deep time.
She also believes they open new avenues for palaeontology at the molecular level.

If traces of blood chemistry can be recovered from fossils, researchers may be able to investigate how blood itself evolved, and even learn about the metabolism and activity levels of animals that died out long ago.
The authors add that other fossils may also hold molecular information that conventional methods of study have missed.
If so, specimens that have already been examined many times could still have more to reveal.
The implications may even extend beyond our own planet.
Astrobiology, the science that looks for signs of life elsewhere in the universe, depends heavily on knowing which biological molecules can last and under what conditions.
If such molecules can persist for more than 100 million years, scientists may need to rethink where they search for evidence of ancient life, both on Earth and beyond it.
The project was very much an international effort, bringing together specialists from several countries and fields.

As well as Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, it involved the Japan Agency for Marine-Earth Science and Technology, the Brazilian National Museum, the Regional University of Cariri and Johns Hopkins University in the United States.

Professor Martin Van Kranendonk, head of Curtin's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences, praised the coordinated efforts across institutions, continents and scientific disciplines that made the work possible.
The research was supported by an Australian Research Council Laureate Fellowship awarded to Grice in 2021.
For a field that has traditionally studied the shapes of bones, the study suggests that a great deal of chemical history may still be waiting to be read.

title: A Braided River: Homo erectus and Our Mixed Ancestry

sentences.text: For much of the twentieth century, the story of human evolution was drawn as a tree.
Each species occupied its own branch, and although branches split apart, they were never expected to grow back together.

One influential version of this picture, usually called the replacement model, held that modern humans spread out of Africa and displaced every archaic population they encountered, without interbreeding with any of them.
Over recent decades that tidy image has steadily come apart, and a new study of ancient teeth from China adds yet another complication.
Homo erectus is widely regarded as the first hominin to leave Africa.
It reached Eurasia nearly two million years ago and went on to become the most geographically widespread of all human ancestors.
Some of its best-known fossils come from Zhoukoudian in northern China, the site where the remains known as 'Peking Man' were unearthed in the early twentieth century.
Yet despite its long history and vast range, Homo erectus has been extremely hard to study at the genetic level, because DNA rarely survives for hundreds of thousands of years.
The new research, led by Qiaomei Fu of the Chinese Academy of Sciences and published in the journal Nature, avoided this problem by searching not for DNA but for proteins.
The team extracted ancient proteins from the enamel of six Homo erectus teeth recovered from three Chinese sites: Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong.
All of the specimens are roughly 400,000 years old.
Enamel is extremely hard, and the proteins sealed inside it can survive far longer than DNA.
Because proteins are built according to instructions carried in genes, small differences in the order of their amino acids can reveal genetic relationships between populations.
The analysis produced two notable results, each of which matters for a different reason.
First, all six individuals shared an amino acid variant that has never been found in any other hominin.
This unique marker places the East Asian Homo erectus in a distinct cluster, and it also helps to settle a long-running question about whether the fossils from Hexian really belong to Homo erectus.
The second variant was even more intriguing, because it also appears in the Denisovans, an archaic human group known mostly from genetic evidence.
Remarkably, the same variant is still carried by people living today, occurring at a frequency of about 21 percent in the Philippines but only about 1 percent in India.
This geographical pattern is consistent with the variant having entered modern humans by way of the Denisovans.
The researchers consider the following sequence of events to be the most likely.
Around 400,000 years ago in East Asia, Homo erectus interbred with Denisovans and passed the variant on to them.
Much later, Denisovans in turn interbred with the ancestors of present-day Southeast Asians and Oceanians, carrying the variant into our own species.
This kind of transfer of genetic material from one distinct population into another is known as introgression.
If the interpretation is correct, a small part of the ancestry of some people in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Southeast Asia can be traced back, indirectly, to Homo erectus.
What effect the variant actually has on the body, however, remains unknown, and finding out will require further research.
The finding adds to a growing body of evidence that mixing between human groups was a normal part of our past rather than a rare exception.
Non-African people today carry roughly 2 percent Neanderthal DNA, while Papuans and Aboriginal Australians carry an additional 2 to 5 percent of Denisovan ancestry.
In some West African populations, geneticists have detected signals from an archaic lineage that has not yet been identified.

A review published in 2019 documented at least three separate episodes of introgression from Denisovan-like groups into the ancestors of Southeast Asian and Oceanic peoples, the most recent only about 20,000 years ago.
Some of these inherited genes may even have been beneficial: certain Denisovan-derived variants in Papuan genomes appear to affect immune function, which suggests that adaptation played a part.
In the light of all this evidence, a strict replacement model is simply no longer tenable.
There is good reason to expect the picture to become more complicated still, because several other archaic populations have barely been studied.
Homo erectus may have survived in Indonesia until perhaps 100,000 years ago, and a separate species, Homo luzonensis, lived in what is now the Philippines.
Another, Homo floresiensis, nicknamed the 'hobbit', was still living on the island of Flores when modern humans arrived.
None of these populations has yet yielded any DNA, but protein analysis of the kind used in China could show whether they, too, contributed to later humans.
For these reasons, the tree, with its neat and separate branches, may no longer be the most helpful image for our evolutionary history.
A better metaphor might be a braided river, in which separate channels flow apart, join again and divide once more as they move downstream.
Human lineages, it now appears, behaved in a similar way, partly merging and then separating again over time instead of simply branching apart.
The six teeth from Zhoukoudian, Hexian and Sunjiadong are only a small piece of evidence, but they suggest that these connections may reach back at least 400,000 years.

title: A Hidden Enemy Beneath the Blueberries

sentences.text: For several years, blueberry growers in the American state of North Carolina have been puzzled by bushes that weakened and sometimes died without any obvious cause above the ground.
When farmers dug around the roots of these plants, they often found large, pale grubs feeding on them.
Reports of these underground larvae damaging blueberry roots go back to 2010, but for more than a decade nobody could say with confidence which insect they belonged to.
Without that knowledge, it was very difficult to decide how the problem should be handled.
A team at North Carolina State University (NC State) has now solved the mystery, and the researchers have described their findings in the Journal of Integrated Pest Management.
The culprit turns out to be a beetle called Prionus imbricornis, a member of the longhorn beetle family, which scientists know as Cerambycidae.
As the name 'longhorn' suggests, beetles in this family are known for their remarkably long antennae.
The young of the species, however, look nothing like their parents.
The larvae live entirely underground, where they feed on roots and can grow to as much as five inches in length.
A serious enough attack can kill a blueberry bush outright.
Curiously, the adult beetles do not feed at all, so all of the damage is done while the insect is still a larva.
Blueberries are not the beetle's usual home.
Normally, the female lays her eggs in the soil close to the roots of hardwood trees, and the larvae that hatch there are capable of killing those trees.
North Carolina is the first state in which this beetle has been documented feeding on blueberries.
For farmers, this means that a pest once linked mainly with trees has become a threat to a valuable fruit crop.
Identifying the pest was far harder than it might sound.
The larvae of different longhorn species are extremely similar in appearance, so it is not possible to tell them apart reliably just by looking at them.
According to Kenneth Geisert, a graduate student in NC State's College of Agriculture and Life Sciences and the lead author of the study, this is not just an academic problem.
If a pest is wrongly identified, growers may use treatments that do not work, and they may also harm other insects that were never the target.
To find the answer, the researchers carried out fieldwork at six blueberry farms in four counties: Pender, Sampson, Bladen and New Hanover.
They began by collecting adult beetles, which are much easier to identify than the larvae.
To catch them, the team set up black panel traps baited with sex pheromones, the chemical signals that the insects use to attract a mate.
Next, they turned to a technique called genetic barcoding, which looks at a short, standardised section of an organism's DNA.
Because this section differs from one species to another, it works rather like the barcode on a product in a supermarket.
When the researchers compared DNA from the root-feeding larvae with DNA from the adult Prionus beetles, they found a 98 to 99 percent match with Prionus imbricornis.
In other words, the mysterious grubs and the long-horned adults were the same species at different stages of life.
Knowing the name of the pest is only the first step.
At present, no insecticides are labelled for use against this beetle on blueberries, which leaves growers with very few options.
Lorena Lopez, an assistant extension professor in the university's Department of Entomology and Plant Pathology and a co-author of the paper, is now testing possible treatments.
Her team wants to find out not only which products work best but also when they should be applied.
The timing will be based on the beetle's reproductive cycle, with the aim of interrupting the development of the larvae before they can cause major damage to the roots.
Another author of the study, Gareth Powell, is an assistant professor at NC State and the director of the NCSU Insect Museum.
His involvement reflects the importance of expert identification in work of this kind.
The study is a useful reminder that solving a farming problem often begins with a very simple question: what exactly are we dealing with?
For North Carolina's blueberry farmers, that question finally has an answer, and the search for a practical solution can now begin.

sentences.text: Crude oil, as it comes out of the ground, is of little use until it has been separated into its many components.
These range from light fractions such as naphtha, gasoline and kerosene to much heavier substances.
For many decades, refineries have carried out this separation mainly by distillation.
The crude is heated to temperatures above 350°C so that parts of it turn into vapour, and the vapours are then cooled so that the different fractions can be collected.
The method is reliable, but it consumes enormous amounts of energy.
Worldwide, crude oil distillation uses about 1,100 terawatt-hours of energy each year, roughly the output of 130 large nuclear power stations running without a break.
Engineers have long hoped that membranes might offer a less energy-hungry alternative.
A membrane works rather like an extremely fine filter: instead of boiling the oil, it lets smaller and lighter molecules pass through its pores while holding back larger ones.
In practice, however, two difficulties have stood in the way.

First, researchers assumed that effective separation required an extremely thin, specialised coating on the membrane, and such coatings are expensive and can develop defects when they are produced on a large scale.
Second, membranes suffer from fouling, a process in which material gradually builds up inside the pores.
Fouling normally reduces the performance of a filter, which means that membranes have to be cleaned or replaced.

A team led by Professor Dong-Yeun Koh at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), working with Professor Ryan Lively's group at the Georgia Institute of Technology in the United States, has now turned the second of these problems into a solution.
In a study published in the journal Nature, the researchers used a bare membrane made of polyacrylonitrile, or PAN, with no special coating at all.
PAN is inexpensive and chemically stable, and it is already used as a support material in industrial filtration.
In other words, the team chose a material that was cheap, familiar and readily available, rather than developing a new and costly one.
When crude oil flowed through the PAN membrane, heavier hydrocarbon molecules began to collect along the inner walls of its pores.
As these deposits built up, the openings became steadily narrower until they formed channels less than two nanometres across.
Lighter fractions such as naphtha, gasoline and kerosene could still pass through these channels quickly, while heavier substances found it much harder to get through.
The fouling that engineers usually try to prevent had therefore created exactly the structure needed for separation.
Koh describes this as a new principle, in which a membrane interacts with a complex mixture and spontaneously forms its own separation channels.
The results were striking.
The uncoated membranes allowed crude oil to pass through about 23 times faster than the best crude oil separation membranes reported previously, and they performed steadily for 28 days in a row.
Importantly, the researchers did not rely only on mixtures prepared in the laboratory.
They tested real crude oil supplied by the Korean refining company HD Hyundai Oilbank; according to Koh, this showed that the method works under conditions that are relevant to industry.

Lively points out that the low productivity of membrane units has been one of the main obstacles to using membranes for crude oil, and he believes the large improvement means that industry should seriously consider the technology.
Computer simulations of the whole process suggest that the potential savings are considerable.
According to these simulations, the approach could reduce energy consumption by 31.6%, carbon dioxide emissions by 37.6%, the use of cooling water by 20.7% and operating costs by 36%.

For South Korea's refining and petrochemical industries alone, the team estimates that about 10 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions could be avoided each year, which is similar to the emissions of around four million vehicles with combustion engines.
A further advantage is that the membranes could be added as modular units in front of existing distillation equipment, so refineries would not need to replace all of their infrastructure.
These figures, however, come from computer models rather than from working refineries, and the technology has not yet been shown to work across operating plants.
The researchers' next steps are to produce the membranes over much larger areas and to confirm that they remain reliable over long periods of operation.

They also see possible uses beyond oil refining, including the treatment of oil produced when plastics are broken down by heat for recycling, the recovery of solvents used in battery manufacturing, the purification of medicines and the improvement of biofuel production.
If the approach succeeds, a problem that has frustrated filter designers for years may turn out to have been a hidden advantage.

sentences.text: For more than 35 years, the Hubble Space Telescope has circled the Earth, sending back images that have transformed both professional astronomy and the public's picture of the universe.
Launched in 1990, it was visited five times by astronauts travelling on the Space Shuttle, who repaired its instruments and replaced worn-out parts.
Since the shuttle programme came to an end in 2011, however, no one has been able to reach the telescope, and Hubble now faces a slow but steady threat to its survival.
Even at the height at which Hubble orbits, the Earth's atmosphere has not completely disappeared.
The thin traces of gas that remain in low Earth orbit create a small amount of drag, and this gradually lowers the telescope's altitude.
Many satellites carry engines that allow them to raise their orbits from time to time, but Hubble has no propulsion system that could do this.
It therefore cannot reverse the decline on its own.
According to NASA's analysis, if nothing is done, Hubble could re-enter the atmosphere at some point between 2033 and 2034, and any mission to lift it higher would need to take place by 2032.
Faced with this deadline, NASA has taken a step that would have been hard to imagine when Hubble was launched.
On 29 October, the agency issued a formal request for information, inviting private companies to describe technologies that could service Hubble while it remains in orbit.
Companies have until 30 November to respond.
In earlier decades, a mission of this kind would almost certainly have been designed by NASA itself and flown by its own astronauts.
NASA has been careful to stress that this is a way of gathering information rather than a decision.
No mission has been formally approved, and the agency simply wants to find out which technologies exist and whether any of them would offer a practical and affordable solution.
The request outlines three broad possibilities.
The first is an orbital boost, in which a visiting spacecraft would push Hubble into a higher orbit, potentially adding years to its scientific life.
The second is a servicing mission that would upgrade the telescope and improve its capabilities or performance.

The third accepts that Hubble's working life must eventually end, and concerns how that ending is managed: either by guiding the telescope through a controlled descent into the atmosphere or by arranging for it to be disposed of in orbit.
All three, it should be noted, are being explored rather than planned.
NASA's interest in commercial help reflects how quickly the space industry has changed.
Nicky Fox, who leads the agency's Science Mission Directorate, has observed that private companies have made rapid progress in servicing spacecraft in orbit.

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has gone further, arguing that Hubble still has important science ahead of it and that exploring ways to extend its life is something the agency owes to both taxpayers and the scientific community.

Several organisations share the work of running the telescope: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center oversees it, the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore manages its scientific operations, and the European Space Agency is an international partner.
There is, in my view, a strong case for at least exploring a rescue.
Hubble is not a museum piece; it is still a working observatory, and its observations in visible and ultraviolet light complement those of newer telescopes rather than simply repeating them.
Losing it early would leave a gap in astronomers' toolkit that would not be easy to fill.
Few scientific instruments have contributed to such a wide range of discoveries, and astronomers around the world still compete for the chance to use it.
It also seems likely that raising the orbit of an existing telescope would cost far less than designing, building and launching a comparable new one.
And asking industry what it can offer, before committing to any particular design, is a sensible way of discovering quickly what is realistic.
Enthusiasm, nevertheless, must be balanced by caution.
The timetable is extremely tight: any proposal would have to be evaluated, developed, tested and flown within five or six years.

Approaching and attaching a spacecraft to a large and delicate telescope, with no astronauts on hand to deal with problems, is technically demanding, and a failed attempt could damage the very instrument it was meant to save.
Moreover, companies eager to win a high-profile contract may promise more than they can deliver in the time available.
There is also the question of priorities.

Fox has made it clear that NASA wants to develop a major flagship mission to follow Hubble as well as explore ways of extending its life, and money spent on keeping an old telescope going cannot also be spent on its successor.
None of this means that NASA was wrong to ask the question.
If the responses show that a safe and affordable boost is possible, the agency would be right to pursue it.
If they do not, planning a controlled and responsible end for Hubble should not be seen as a failure, but as a fitting conclusion for one of the most productive scientific instruments ever built.
Either way, the decision should rest on evidence rather than on sentiment, however much affection the public may feel for the telescope.

sentences.text: Few stars in the night sky are as easy to recognise as Betelgeuse.
This huge red supergiant forms one shoulder of the constellation Orion, the hunter, and its orange colour can be seen without a telescope.
Between late 2019 and early 2020, however, the star surprised astronomers when its brightness fell to the lowest level recorded in more than 100 years.
The event became known as the Great Dimming, and it raised many questions about what was happening in the star's outer layers.
Scientists now think that the dimming had a fairly simple explanation.
Several months before the star faded, it threw out about a billion tons of material, and this material, which later formed dust, partly blocked our view of the star.
An earlier study led by Lynn Matthews of MIT Haystack Observatory had found that temperatures in the star's atmosphere were unusually low at radio wavelengths.
Researchers suggested that turbulent movements of gas deep inside the star had sent a shock wave outwards, and that this may have helped to push the material out into space.
In a new study published in The Astronomical Journal, Matthews and colleagues from institutions in the United States and Europe have returned to Betelgeuse to see how it has changed since then.
They used two of the world's most powerful radio facilities: the Very Large Array in the United States and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, known as ALMA, in Chile.
The team analysed observations collected between 2021 and 2026 at seven different radio frequencies, ranging from 22 to 485 gigahertz.

Each frequency reveals a different depth within a star's atmosphere, so by combining the data the researchers could build up a picture of the star's outer layers, from just above its visible surface to several times its radius.
The first finding was reassuring: the star's outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal.
At a distance of about 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas has a brightness temperature of around 3,500 kelvin, which is close to the temperature of the star's surface.
The observations also confirmed that there is a surprisingly cool layer between the visible surface and a higher layer called the chromosphere.
In this layer, temperatures fall to about 2,200 kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees lower than at the surface.
The region contains molecular gas, and in the past it had been studied mainly with infrared observations.
The new radio measurements therefore gave astronomers a more direct view of a temperature minimum that they had suspected for a long time.
The most exciting result, however, concerns a possible hidden partner.
The brightness of Betelgeuse rises and falls in a regular cycle of about 2,100 days, and in 2024 astronomers suggested that a companion star might be the cause.
This companion, which is thought to be smaller and hotter than Betelgeuse, has been named Siwarha, meaning 'her bracelet'.
The name was chosen because of its link with Betelgeuse's own name, which comes from an Arabic expression meaning 'the hand of al-Jawza'.
Siwarha is believed to orbit at a distance of only about twice the radius of Betelgeuse.
This means that it travels directly through the giant star's extended atmosphere, pushing through the gas and leaving a wake behind it, rather like a boat moving through water.
Since 2024, further images and measurements of the star's light have added support to the idea.
Siwarha itself is far too faint to be detected in the radio data; the team calculates that it is between tens and hundreds of times too dim.
Even so, the researchers found indirect signs of its presence.
At radio wavelengths, Betelgeuse sometimes looks slightly oval rather than perfectly round.
The team noticed that the star appears most stretched when Siwarha is at its greatest apparent distance from it, and rounder when the companion passes in front of or behind it.
Matthews said it was amazing that these instruments could resolve the disks of nearby stars.
The authors describe the pattern as compelling but not yet conclusive.
To confirm it, they will need observations that cover more of the companion's orbit, as well as data at radio frequencies that have so far received little attention.
They also hope that future instruments, such as the Next Generation Very Large Array, which is now being developed, will help to settle the question.

title: Darker Mornings: The Hidden Cost of Permanent Daylight Saving Time

sentences.text: Twice a year, people in most of the United States change their clocks.
In spring the clocks move forward by an hour, shifting daylight from the morning into the evening, and in autumn they move back again, returning to what is known as standard time.
Many people find the switch tiresome, and there has been growing support for ending it altogether.
One proposal is to remain on daylight saving time all year round, which would give people an extra hour of light on winter evenings.
A new study from the University of Washington, however, suggests that this extra evening light would come at a considerable price for schoolchildren.
The reason is a matter of simple arithmetic.
Under permanent daylight saving time, the sun would rise an hour later by the clock than it does now during the winter months.
From November to March, therefore, mornings would stay dark for longer.
For children who have to be at school early, this means that a much larger share of their journeys would begin before sunrise.
The question the researchers set out to answer was exactly how many additional journeys would be affected.
Rather than relying on rough national averages, the team, led by postdoctoral researcher Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, wanted figures that reflected where children actually go to school.
They focused on 14 of the 19 states that have already approved measures supporting permanent daylight saving time.
For each school, they combined enrolment figures with the school's official start time and its precise geographical position.

This allowed them to work out how often pupils would be travelling before sunrise, and to compare the total under year-round daylight saving time with the total under the present system of changing the clocks twice a year.

Because they used official start times, the researchers point out that their figures may be conservative, since pupils who arrive early for breakfast or other activities before lessons leave home even earlier.
The results were striking.
In Washington state alone, the change would add almost 35 million school journeys made in darkness.
The largest increase among the states studied was in Georgia, with around 71 million extra dark trips.
In some states, the relative change would be dramatic.

In Mississippi and Alabama, where schools begin on average before 8 a.m., there are currently about 2 million dark school journeys in each state, but under permanent daylight saving time this number would rise to more than 20 million in each.
Location within a time zone also matters: communities near the western edge of a zone, such as the town of Forks in Washington, already have a late sunrise and would be especially badly affected.
Some districts where pupils never travel in the dark at present would also begin to experience dark journeys to school.
The researchers then extended their analysis to the country as a whole.
Assuming that pupils generally leave home at around 8 a.m., they estimated that permanent daylight saving time would add well over a billion journeys to school before sunrise nationwide.
They regard this departure time as rather late, which means that the true figure is probably higher.
They also examined national traffic records and found that fatal road accidents involving pedestrians of school age were roughly twice as likely on dark mornings as after the sun had risen.
Safety on the roads is not the only concern.
Bright light early in the day plays a key role in setting the body's internal, or circadian, clock, which influences sleep, mood, appetite and many other functions.
Pupils who must follow a fixed school timetable may miss the morning light that their bodies rely on, particularly when mornings are dark.
Teenagers are a special case, because their biological clocks naturally run later than those of younger children and adults.

Later start times for high schools are often recommended for this reason, but the researchers argue that permanent daylight saving time could undo some of their benefit by reducing the amount of morning light that teenagers receive.
An obvious response would be simply to start school later in winter.
Senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a professor of biology, argues that this would not solve the problem.
If schools opened later, he points out, working hours and evening activities would soon move later as well.
Society as a whole would then be living according to the sun rather than the clock, which is essentially what standard time already provides.
People would therefore lose the extra evening light that was the main attraction of the change in the first place.
For de la Iglesia, the conclusion is clear: the additional hour of evening sunshine is not a gift but a transfer, taken directly from the morning.

title: Why Is the Brain Wired Backwards?

sentences.text: One of the oddest facts about the vertebrate nervous system is that it is crossed.
In humans, the left side of the brain receives most of its information from the right side of the body and sends commands back to it, while the right hemisphere looks after the left side.
This arrangement is so familiar to doctors and students of biology that it is easy to forget how strange it is.
After all, there is no obvious engineering reason why a signal from the right hand should have to cross the midline of the body before it reaches the part of the brain that interprets it.
For a long time, the usual assumption has been that such a peculiar design must bring some advantage, since otherwise natural selection would surely have removed it.
Explanations have therefore tended to focus on the benefit that crossing might provide.
A new paper in the journal Frontiers in Neuroanatomy takes a different view.

Its authors, Martin Wessendorf, an emeritus associate professor of neuroscience at the University of Minnesota, and Daniel Wang, a specialist in cognitive neuroscience and neurodegenerative disease, argue that the crossing may not be an adaptation at all.
Instead, they suggest it may be a historical legacy: a pattern established more than 500 million years ago in the visual systems of early fish, on which later circuits were simply built.
The story, according to this hypothesis, begins with vision.
The lens of a vertebrate eye reverses the image it forms, so that objects on the right fall on the left side of the retina and objects on the left fall on the right.

Nerve fibres leaving the eyes then meet at a junction called the optic chiasm, where they are sorted so that information about the right half of the visual world travels to the left side of the brain, and information about the left half travels to the right.
Much of this information arrives at the optic tectum, a structure known in mammals as the superior colliculus.
The tectum controls fast, reflex-like behaviour, such as turning towards a sudden movement.
Each tectum holds a map of the opposite half of the visual field, and its deeper layers also contain maps of sensations from the body.
Since every vertebrate possesses a tectum, it is regarded as one of the oldest structures in the vertebrate brain.
Wessendorf and Wang propose that once this crossed visual map was in place, it shaped the way that later systems developed.
Rather than designing new circuits from the beginning, evolution tends to modify and extend what already exists.
On this view, pathways that appeared later in the history of vertebrates may have followed the crossed layout of the older visual system instead of adopting an arrangement of their own.
The authors support this idea by comparing the pathways found in different groups of animals.
The dorsal column pathway, which carries gentle touch, vibration and information about the position of the limbs, crosses to the other side in the brainstem, after a relay just above the spinal cord.
It is found in amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals but not in fish, which suggests that it appeared early in the evolution of four-limbed animals, known as tetrapods.
Another sensory route, the spinothalamic tract, carries pain, itch and some kinds of touch.
Unlike the dorsal column pathway, it crosses within the spinal cord itself before rising to a region of the brain called the thalamus.
This crossing occurs in birds, mammals and reptiles, and also in some cartilaginous fish such as sharks and rays.
Motor pathways, which carry commands from the brain towards the muscles, show a similar pattern.
The tectospinal pathway, which produces quick orienting reactions to things that are seen, heard or felt, is present in most tetrapods and in some cartilaginous fish.
The rubrospinal pathway begins in a region of the midbrain called the red nucleus and helps to control the limbs.
It is most prominent in mammals, though it also occurs in other tetrapods and in some cartilaginous fish.
Finally, the corticospinal tract allows primates, including humans, to make delicate movements of the fingers.
In most other mammals, by contrast, this tract mainly regulates incoming sensations rather than movement.
Only mammals have a six-layered cerebral cortex, although all vertebrates have a telencephalon, the front region of the brain.
The authors suggest that the fine motor control so characteristic of human beings was not created from scratch.
Rather, evolution appears to have taken an existing pathway that originally helped to regulate sensory input and given it a new job.

If that is correct, then even our most sophisticated physical skills, such as writing or playing a musical instrument, depend on wiring whose basic layout was fixed long before such abilities existed.
In this account, the crossing has survived not because it is especially efficient but simply because it was there first.
It is important to stress that this is a hypothesis rather than a proven account.
The paper presents no new experimental data; its argument rests on comparing the anatomy of living vertebrates.
Nevertheless, the authors believe that their idea could be tested.
They suspect that the optic chiasm and optic tectum were already present in primitive jawless fish during the Cambrian Period, roughly 538 to 486 million years ago.
If so, fossilised skulls of such animals could be examined for evidence of these structures.
Whatever the outcome, the paper is a useful reminder that not every feature of a living body needs to be explained as a clever solution to a problem.
Some features may simply reflect the fact that evolution works with whatever materials happen to be available.

title: Hera's First Look at a Deflected Asteroid

sentences.text: For most of history, people could do nothing to stop a large rock from space from hitting the Earth.
Astronomers could track asteroids and calculate their paths, but if one had been found on a collision course, there would have been no tested way of pushing it aside.
That situation began to change in 2022, when the American space agency NASA carried out the first real experiment in what is now called planetary defence.
Today, a European spacecraft named Hera is arriving at the scene of that experiment to find out what it actually achieved.
The target of the original test was a small asteroid called Dimorphos.
It measures roughly 151 metres across, which makes it about the same size as the Great Pyramid of Giza.
Dimorphos does not travel through space alone; instead, it circles a much larger asteroid, Didymos, which is around 780 metres wide.
The two bodies form what astronomers call a binary system, with the smaller one orbiting its partner at an average distance of just 1.15 kilometres.
By space standards its movement is extremely slow, at only about 18 centimetres per second.
On 26 September 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft was deliberately flown into Dimorphos at a speed of about 6.1 kilometres per second.
The collision threw a vast cloud of rock and dust into space, and some of the debris travelled as far as 10,000 kilometres.
More importantly, it changed the way Dimorphos moves around Didymos.
After the impact, the small asteroid took about 33 minutes less to complete one orbit than it had done before.
This was the first clear proof that a spacecraft could alter the motion of an asteroid on purpose.
The technique, known as kinetic impact, is simple in principle: a fast-moving object strikes the asteroid and gives it a push.
Yet the experiment also produced a puzzle.
Before the impact, scientists had used computer simulations to predict how much the orbit would change, and the real effect turned out to be far larger than these models had suggested.
Several basic questions also remain unanswered.
Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on the surface or whether it changed the shape of the asteroid significantly.
They are also uncertain about the asteroid's mass, what it is made of and how it is structured inside.
Until these questions are answered, kinetic impact cannot be regarded as a fully reliable method of protecting the planet.
This is where Hera comes in.
Built by the European Space Agency (ESA), the spacecraft has been sent to carry out what its team describes as a "crash site investigation".
On the evening of 18 October, as it approached its destination, Hera used its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera to photograph the two asteroids.
At that moment it was about 1,280 kilometres from them, while the asteroids themselves were roughly 197 million kilometres from the Earth.
For the first time, the camera showed Didymos and Dimorphos as two separate objects instead of a single point of light.
The smaller asteroid took up only about one pixel, but the mission team was pleased that it was clearly separated from its larger companion.
Getting this close required careful navigation.
Earlier in October, Hera fired its thrusters twice, with a week between the two manoeuvres, reducing its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 metres per second.
Over the coming months, it will study Dimorphos with a range of scientific instruments.
It will also release two small satellites, known as CubeSats, each roughly the size of a shoebox, which will make closer observations of the asteroids.
Eventually, the mission is expected to include attempts to land on the surface.
ESA has announced that the first detailed images of Dimorphos will be made public on 25 November.
The results will matter well beyond this particular pair of asteroids.
By measuring exactly what DART did, scientists hope to improve their predictions of how future attempts to deflect an asteroid would turn out.
If a dangerous asteroid is ever found heading towards the Earth, such predictions could be extremely valuable.
In the meantime, members of the public can follow the mission as it unfolds through an interactive online platform called the Hera Space Companion.

title: The Frogs That Vanished from Boracéia

sentences.text: For more than forty years, a puzzle has hung over a patch of forest in south-eastern Brazil.
Boracéia Biological Station, in the state of São Paulo, lies within the Atlantic Forest, one of the richest regions for amphibians anywhere on the planet.
Between 1979 and 1982, many of the frogs living there declined sharply, and some species seemed to disappear altogether.
At the time, nobody could say with any confidence what had caused the losses.
Scientists had collected frogs at the station on several expeditions during the 1970s and 1980s, so there was a record of what had lived there before and after the losses.
Over the years, several explanations were put forward.
Some researchers argued that a changing climate, or a run of unusually extreme weather, might have pushed the populations into decline.
Disease was much harder to investigate, because the organism now regarded as the most likely culprit had not yet been identified by science.
The fungus Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, which causes an amphibian disease known as chytridiomycosis, was not formally described until 1999.
It attacks the skin, which frogs depend on to take in water and essential salts, and severe infections can kill them.
By the time the fungus had been named, many dramatic frog declines around the world had already taken place, and the evidence that might have explained them appeared to be lost.
A new study, led by Jack Boyette and published in the journal Molecular Ecology, has now looked back in time to solve the mystery.
Instead of relying only on modern fieldwork, the team turned to frogs that had been collected at Boracéia decades earlier and preserved in a museum.
Many of these specimens had been gathered by the herpetologist W. Ronald Heyer and are kept at the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History in Washington.
A preserved frog can still carry traces of the fungus on its skin, so it is possible to check whether an animal was infected when it was caught.
Altogether, the researchers tested more than 370 preserved frogs belonging to 17 species for signs of chytrid infection.
The results revealed a striking pattern.
None of the frogs collected before 1979 showed any trace of the fungus.
Among those collected in the 1980s, however, more than half tested positive.
This timing matches the period of the declines closely, suggesting that the arrival of the fungus coincided with the beginning of the crisis.
In Boyette's words, the findings "most directly implicate the chytrid fungus," although he acknowledged that environmental factors may also have played a part.
Because the specimens came from the same place over a long period, they offered a rare chance to compare conditions before and after the declines.
One result, however, seemed puzzling at first.
The species that suffered the heaviest declines showed no infections at all in the museum collection.
The researchers believe this is probably because these frogs died very quickly once they were infected, so that few sick individuals were ever caught and preserved.
By contrast, species whose numbers remained relatively stable often carried the fungus.
This suggests that these frogs were able to tolerate the infection and live with it, rather than being killed by it.
In other words, the absence of the fungus from a species' preserved specimens does not prove that the disease left that species untouched.
To find out what has happened since the crisis, the team made six visits to Boracéia, working together with the University of São Paulo.
Their surveys, carried out between 2022 and 2024, found 12 of the 17 species that had been recorded there in the past.
The other five have not been seen, and their fate remains unknown.
Their status is uncertain, and some of them may have disappeared from the site entirely.
Most of the surviving species have recovered, even though the fungus is still present in the forest.
According to the researchers, this suggests that the frogs have developed greater tolerance of the disease over several generations.
The study also highlights the value of museum collections, which are sometimes seen as little more than records of the past.

Michael Campana, one of the scientists involved, noted that such collections can preserve evidence of diseases that went unnoticed for decades, allowing researchers to reconstruct outbreaks long after they occurred.
Specimens gathered for one purpose may therefore answer questions that their collectors could never have imagined.
Nevertheless, the authors are careful not to overstate their conclusions.
Their findings apply to Boracéia, and they do not automatically explain the losses that have been reported in other parts of the Atlantic Forest.

title: What Really Makes a Good Reader?

sentences.text: When a child struggles to learn to read, the adults around them often reach for a simple explanation.
Some assume that the child is simply less intelligent than their classmates; others suspect a problem with the eyes, or with the way the brain handles what the eyes see.
Such explanations are understandable, but they can do real harm.
A label of low intelligence, once attached, is hard to remove, and a mistaken diagnosis can send parents and teachers in search of remedies that do not address the actual difficulty.
A large new analysis of how thinking skills relate to reading suggests that both of these popular assumptions deserve to be questioned.

The study was led by Daniel Hajovsky, an associate professor of educational psychology at Texas A&M University, working with colleagues from the University of Kansas, St John's University, Montclair State University and Temple University.
Rather than running a single new experiment, the team set out to combine the evidence that already existed.
They gathered around 50,000 correlations, drawn from 137 different batteries of cognitive and achievement tests, and merged them into one statistical model.
Their aim, as the title of their paper in the Journal of Intelligence makes clear, was to move towards a "consensus model" of how cognitive abilities and reading achievement are related.
An approach of this kind has an obvious strength: no single sample of children, however carefully chosen, can carry as much weight as tens of thousands of results pooled together.
It also has a limitation, since the conclusions can only be as good as the tests and studies on which they are based.
The first surprise concerned visual processing, the ability to perceive, analyse and think with visual patterns.
Given that reading involves looking at marks on a page, it might seem natural to expect this skill to play an important part.
Yet the analysis found no meaningful relationship between visual processing and reading ability.
This does not mean that eyesight is irrelevant, since a child who cannot see the page clearly will obviously struggle.
It does, however, cast doubt on the idea that weaknesses in handling visual information lie behind most reading problems.
General intelligence was also linked to reading, but its role turned out to be smaller than some earlier work had suggested.
Earlier studies had often given it a central place in explaining why some children read better than others.
Hajovsky described it as "less dominant than in some earlier meta-analyses".
This finding matters well beyond the research community.
If general intelligence is not the main driver of reading success, then a child's difficulty with reading cannot be taken as a reliable sign that the child is unintelligent.
The researchers themselves stress this point, and it is perhaps the most important message for families: a struggling reader is not necessarily a less able learner.
Instead, the strongest predictors of reading were two abilities that receive comparatively little public attention.
The first is auditory processing, which includes the capacity to recognise and tell apart the individual sounds that make up spoken words.
This skill supports decoding, the process of linking written letters to the sounds they represent, which forms the foundation of early reading.
Without it, a child may find it hard to work out a word that they have never seen in print before.
The second is comprehension-knowledge: the vocabulary, concepts and background information that a child builds up through learning and everyday experience.
A child may decode every word of a sentence correctly and still fail to understand it if the words and ideas are unfamiliar.
Other abilities, such as memory, reasoning and processing speed, also made a contribution, but they played supporting rather than leading roles.
For teachers, the practical implication is that reading difficulties should not all be treated in the same way.
One child may have trouble hearing the difference between similar sounds, while another decodes fluently but lacks the vocabulary to make sense of the text.
A single programme applied to the whole class is unlikely to meet the needs of both.
The researchers therefore recommend identifying the particular weakness of each struggling student and targeting support accordingly.
This is sensible advice, although putting it into practice is likely to demand more time and training than many schools currently have.
Even so, the cost of getting the diagnosis wrong, measured in years of frustration for the child, is surely greater.
Families, too, have a part to play.

None of this makes reading problems trivial, but it does replace a discouraging message with a more hopeful one.
Children who find reading hard are not held back by a fixed lack of ability; in many cases, they are missing specific skills that can be developed with the right support.

sentences.text: In September 1977, a small spacecraft called Voyager 1 was launched from Florida on a mission that was originally designed to last only a few years.
Almost half a century later, it is still working, and it has travelled farther from Earth than any other object ever built by humans.
Its twin, Voyager 2, had been launched just over two weeks earlier and followed a different route through the solar system.
After flying past Jupiter and Saturn, Voyager 1 continued outwards and eventually left the region dominated by the Sun's influence, entering interstellar space in 2012.
Today it is moving at roughly 38,000 miles per hour, and every day carries it deeper into the darkness between the stars.
In November 2026, Voyager 1 is set to pass an unusual milestone.
On 18 November, it is expected to be one light-day away from Earth, which means that a radio signal travelling at the speed of light will need a full day to reach it.
No object made by humans has ever been so far away that light needs a whole day to reach it.
That distance is approximately 25.89 billion kilometres, or a little over 16 billion miles.
Because every message must travel out and back again, engineers who send a command have to wait about 48 hours to learn whether it has been received.
The project manager, Suzanne Dodd, has pointed out that after sending any message, the team must wait two days for a response.
The milestone itself, however, is purely symbolic: crossing this invisible line will cause no physical change to the spacecraft.
A far more practical concern for the mission team is power.
Voyager 1 has no solar panels, because sunlight is far too weak at such enormous distances to be useful.
Instead, it relies on generators that turn the heat released by decaying plutonium into electricity.
As the plutonium slowly decays, the amount of power available to the spacecraft falls by about four watts every year.
When it was launched, Voyager 1 carried ten scientific instruments, and two of them have been switched off in recent years to save energy.
Every decision about what to keep running is therefore a careful balance between the value of the science and the limited electricity that remains.
In early September, engineers carried out a delicate operation that they nicknamed the "Big Bang".
They switched off three devices on board and turned to alternatives that use less power.
These three devices belonged to a group of six that help to keep the spacecraft warm, and they all had to be changed at the same moment so that heat would remain evenly spread across the craft.
The same procedure had been performed on Voyager 2, Voyager 1's twin, about six weeks earlier.
If it works as hoped, the change should allow the remaining instruments to continue operating for longer.
Without it, another instrument might have had to be shut down as early as the summer of 2027.
Only a few weeks after the operation, the team faced an unexpected scare.
On 18 and 19 October, the large antennas of NASA's Deep Space Network could not detect any signal from Voyager 1.
For two days, the engineers had no way of knowing whether the spacecraft was still working.
Contact was finally restored on 20 October.
When engineers examined the data, they discovered that one set of the small thrusters that help to control which way the spacecraft faces had stopped working.
The craft's built-in fault protection system had responded automatically by switching to a backup set.
Exactly why the first set failed is still being investigated.
The mission manager, Kareem Badaruddin, said that this was the first time the spacecraft had behaved in this way.
He added that, at such a late stage in the mission, the team has to expect the unexpected.
For now, the engineers are relieved to be in contact again, and they want to understand what happened.
Each year carries Voyager 1 further from home and leaves it with a little less energy.
Nobody knows exactly how many more years it will be able to keep in touch with Earth.
Yet the ageing spacecraft continues to send back information from farther away than any other machine has ever reached.

sentences.text: Around 30,000 years ago, Europe was a cold and difficult place to live.
Small groups of hunter-gatherers moved across a landscape shaped by the Ice Age, and the people of this period are associated by archaeologists with a way of life known as the Gravettian culture.
This culture flourished across much of the continent from roughly 34,000 to 25,000 years ago.
Evidence from archaeological sites had long suggested that Gravettian groups maintained contacts over great distances.
Studying their genes is far from easy, because human remains from this period are rare and the DNA they contain is often poorly preserved.
Yet when geneticists began to study ancient DNA from this period, the picture they produced seemed rather different.
Earlier genetic research pointed to two fairly distinct ancestral groups, one in the east of Europe and one in the west.
On this view, people in the two halves of the continent had remained largely separate from one another.
A new study, published in the journal Science Advances, now challenges that interpretation.
The work was led by researchers in the Department of Evolutionary Anthropology at the University of Vienna, with Pere Gelabert as first author and Ron Pinhasi as senior author.
By analysing new genetic material and combining it with DNA that had already been published, the team was able to look again at how these early Europeans were related.
The most important new evidence comes from Isturitz Cave in southwestern France.
There, the remains of a woman who lived about 30,000 years ago produced the oldest genome-wide dataset yet obtained from a modern human in southwestern Europe.
Most of her ancestry was western European, as might be expected from her location.
However, part of it was linked to populations in central and eastern Europe.
Using the patterns in her DNA, the researchers estimated that this mixing of eastern and western ancestry had taken place between about 32,500 and 31,500 years ago.
A second individual, from Ormesson, also in France, showed a similar genetic signature, suggesting that the Isturitz woman was not an isolated case.
The study also sheds light on what happened during the harshest part of the Ice Age.
This period, known as the Last Glacial Maximum, was the time when the great ice sheets reached their largest extent.
Evidence from Chufín Cave in northern Spain indicates that western European ancestry continued in the southwest of the continent for a long time.
Combined with other evidence from the region, the results suggest that this ancestry survived through the Last Glacial Maximum itself.
This supports the idea that the Iberian Peninsula acted as a refuge, a place where people could survive some of the coldest conditions of the Ice Age.
One of the most remarkable results did not come from a skeleton at all.
At El Mirón Cave in Cantabria, northern Spain, the team examined a layer of sediment about 22,000 years old that contained no human bones or teeth.
Even so, they were able to recover human nuclear DNA directly from the sediment.
This genetic material was sufficient to identify the ancestry of the people who had once occupied the site.
The technique, known as sedimentary DNA analysis, makes use of the fact that genetic traces left in cave floors can survive for thousands of years.
Its great advantage is that it allows researchers to connect an archaeological layer with a particular genetic ancestry even when no human remains have been found.
The researchers also studied a male fetus from southern Italy, known as Ostuni1b.
His mother had been examined in a previous study, and the new analysis showed that his father probably came from the same ancestral population.
Importantly, however, the two parents were not closely related to each other.
For small communities, choosing partners who are close relatives can lead to inbreeding, which may harm the health of later generations.
The researchers suggest that the mating patterns of these Ice Age groups may have helped them to limit this risk.
Taken together, the findings suggest that the populations of eastern and western Europe were less genetically isolated than scientists had assumed.
As first author Pere Gelabert put it, the two populations "were not as genetically isolated as previously assumed."
People, and the genes they carried, appear to have moved across the continent more often than earlier studies implied.
The team now plans to combine sedimentary DNA with proteomics, the study of ancient proteins, which can provide further clues about past life.
They hope to use these methods to investigate the earliest spread of modern humans across Europe.
They also want to learn how these people interacted with carnivores in places where organic remains are scarce.
