title: Did Apes Begin in the North?

sentences.text: Where did the apes come from?
The question matters to more than a handful of specialists, because the living apes include not only gibbons, orangutans, gorillas and chimpanzees but also ourselves.
For decades, the prevailing view has been that early apes and their close relatives were concentrated further south in Africa, with East Africa often seen as the most likely birthplace of the group.
It is worth remembering, however, that any account of where a group of animals first appeared is shaped by where its fossils happen to have been found.
A map of discoveries is not necessarily a map of history.
North Africa illustrates the problem well.
Sites there dating from the Early Miocene, a period that began around 23 million years ago, have produced fossil monkeys, but until recently not a single definitive ape.
It would be easy to conclude that apes were simply absent from the region.
In my view, though, such a gap should be treated as a question rather than an answer, since a missing fossil may reflect nothing more than the places researchers have chosen to search.
A discovery in Egypt now suggests that this caution was justified.
Researchers from the Mansoura University Vertebrate Paleontology Center, working with colleagues from the University of Southern California, spent five years looking for exactly this kind of fossil.
During expeditions in 2023 and 2024 to Wadi Moghra, a well-known fossil site in northern Egypt, they finally found it.
The new species, described in the journal Science in March 2026, has been named Masripithecus moghraensis.
The first part of the name combines Masr, the Arabic word for Egypt, with pithekos, the Greek word for ape, while the second part honours the site itself.
The animal lived around 17 to 18 million years ago, and it is the first definitive fossil ape ever recovered from North Africa.
So far, only parts of the lower jaw have been found.
The jaw is sturdy and carries large canine and premolar teeth, while the molars have rounded, textured chewing surfaces.
From these features, the team concluded that the animal mainly ate fruit but was also able to deal with harder foods such as nuts or seeds.
This flexibility may have been important.
At the time, a changing climate was making the seasons more pronounced across northern Africa and Arabia, so the food available would have varied considerably through the year.
An ape that could switch to tougher foods when fruit was scarce would have been well equipped to cope.
The fossil's real significance, however, lies in where it sits on the family tree.
The researchers used Bayesian analyses, a statistical approach that combined anatomical evidence, genetic data from living apes and the ages of fossils.
These analyses placed Masripithecus closer to the living apes than any known Early Miocene ape from East Africa.

A further biogeographic analysis, which estimates where ancestors are most likely to have lived, pointed to North Africa and the Middle East as the probable home of the common ancestor of all living apes, sometime between about 23 and 16 million years ago.

Erik Seiffert of the University of Southern California admits that he had previously considered it probable that this ancestor lived in or around East Africa, but he says the new analyses strongly challenge that idea.
The study's senior author, Hesham Sallam, puts it more simply: in his words, the early ape family tree has a missing piece, and North Africa holds it.
The geography of the time helps to make this scenario believable.
The African and Arabian plates were moving slowly northwards towards Asia, gradually altering the connections between these landmasses.
In addition, rising and falling sea levels periodically narrowed the stretches of water that separated them, making it easier at times for animals to travel between Africa and Eurasia.
According to the researchers, Masripithecus suggests that apes were already diversifying in this region before new land connections allowed them to spread into Europe and Asia.
None of this means that the Egyptian jaw belonged to one of our direct ancestors, and the researchers are careful not to make that claim.
They do not even argue that it was the direct ancestor of the living apes; rather, it offers clues about where the wider lineage may have begun.
Because only part of the jaw is known, the animal's overall appearance, its body size, the way it moved and its behaviour all remain unclear.
Seiffert himself notes that the likelihood of the North African scenario does not depend on Masripithecus, although the fossil is very much consistent with it.
I would argue that this is the most important point in the whole study.
A single jaw could never overturn decades of research by itself, but a statistical model that draws on many lines of evidence is far harder to dismiss.
The debate about the origins of later apes is still far from settled, and more fieldwork in North Africa and the Middle East will be needed before any firm conclusion can be reached.
Nevertheless, the discovery carries a lesson that goes beyond apes.
For years, the absence of fossils from one region was quietly taken as evidence that nothing important had happened there.
Masripithecus is a reminder that scientists can only find what they look for, and that the story of our origins may depend as much on where we dig as on what the ground contains.

sentences.text: Most people have had the experience of spotting a face where none exists.
We see eyes in the front of a car, a mouth in a cracked wall, or a whole human profile in a passing cloud.
Psychologists call this tendency pareidolia, and it seems to be a side effect of how strongly the human brain is tuned to recognise faces.
Satellite pictures of the Earth are no exception, and in late 2026 NASA's Earth Observatory published a striking example from one of the coldest places on the planet.
Seen from space, a small island off the coast of Antarctica looks remarkably like a grinning skull.
The island in question is Vega Island, which lies in the Weddell Sea to the east of the Antarctic Peninsula.
Viewed from above, its mixture of dark rock and pale ice forms the shape of a skull seen from the side.
Fittingly, the skull appears to be staring across the water towards a neighbouring piece of land called Devil Island.
Several natural features complete the picture.
A nunatak, which is a rocky peak that pokes up through the surrounding ice, creates the impression of an empty eye socket.
A lateral moraine, a long ridge of rock debris left along the side of a glacier, traces the line of the mouth.
Below it, Devil's Bay Glacier forms the lower jaw.
The images were captured by the Operational Land Imager, an instrument carried on the Landsat 9 satellite.
Landsat is a long-running series of satellites designed to observe the Earth's surface, and comparing its pictures over time allows scientists to track how landscapes change.
The first picture was taken on 22 March 2025, when the island was covered in snow and the skull was much harder to make out.
A second picture, taken on 10 October 2026, looks very different, because large areas of darker glacier ice had become exposed.
An attempt to photograph the island in March 2026 had failed, since clouds hid it from view.
Why had so much snow disappeared?
According to Mauri Pelto, a glaciologist at Nichols College, the answer lies in the weather.
He explained that the winter of 2026 had been unusually warm on the island, especially in the month of June.
As a result, very little fresh snow built up on the surface.
Some of the snow that did fall was lost through sublimation, the process in which ice turns directly into water vapour, while some was simply carried away by the wind.
The change matters for more than just the appearance of the island.
Bare glacier ice is darker than snow, which means it absorbs more of the sunlight that falls on it.
As a result, the exposed ice may warm up and melt more quickly once spring arrives.
A fresh fall of snow could slow this process down by covering the dark surface again.
If melting continues over many years, however, it may slowly change the shape of the skull itself, wearing away its jawline and its eye socket.
In other words, the face that people see today is only a temporary arrangement of rock and ice.
Vega Island's ice has been studied for decades.
In 1982, researchers used early Landsat data together with aerial photographs to map the island, and they counted four ice caps and 29 glaciers.
Devil's Bay Glacier has been monitored regularly since the Antarctic summer of 1998 to 1999, and over that period it has lost mass overall.
Other glaciers on the island have also retreated, leaving more of the bedrock beneath them exposed.
The island also has a place in the history of polar exploration.
Between 1901 and 1903, members of the Swedish Antarctic Expedition were stranded in the region after their ship was lost in the pack ice.
The explorers split into three separate groups, and in the spring of 1903 two of these groups found each other again at a spot near the skull's forehead.
The place was later given the cheerful name Cape Well-met.
Eventually, the explorers were rescued by an expedition from Argentina.

sentences.text: Few animals have a worse reputation on the Great Barrier Reef than the crown-of-thorns starfish.
Covered in sharp spines and able to grow wider than a dinner plate, it feeds on living coral by pushing its stomach out of its body and digesting the soft tissue of the coral beneath it.
When the starfish appear in huge numbers, they can strip large areas of reef of their living coral.
Not surprisingly, the species is usually described as one of the reef's greatest threats.
New research from the University of Sydney, however, suggests that this picture is incomplete, and that in small numbers the starfish may actually play a useful part in the life of a reef.
The study was led by Dr Shawna Foo, a Horizon Fellow in the university's School of Life and Environmental Sciences, and was published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.
The team carried out its fieldwork around the university's One Tree Island Research Station on the Great Barrier Reef.
The study sites were chosen with care.
They lay within protected areas where fish populations were healthy and where crown-of-thorns starfish were present only in relatively low numbers.
This allowed the researchers to observe how the starfish affect corals when they are part of a balanced ecosystem, rather than during a population explosion.
The scientists examined the scars that the starfish left on corals after feeding and recorded how much living tissue remained.
The results were unexpected.
In nearly three-quarters of the feeding events they observed, at least some living coral tissue survived.
This challenges the common image of the starfish as an animal that leaves nothing behind but bare coral skeletons.
According to Dr Foo, the starfish appear to eat a fairly consistent amount of coral at each meal and then move on.
As a result, patches of living tissue are frequently left behind, giving the coral a chance to recover.
What happened next depended on the type of coral.
Surviving fragments of fast-growing corals from the family Acroporidae did not grow back over the damaged areas.
By contrast, regrowth was seen mainly in slower-growing corals belonging to the groups Montipora and Porites.
In other words, feeding by the starfish had very different consequences for different kinds of coral.
This difference matters.
When fast-growing corals are left unchecked, they can spread rapidly and take over much of the available space, leaving little room for slower competitors.
By holding back these dominant species, a small population of starfish may create room for slower-growing corals, which could increase the variety of corals on a reef.
Co-author Professor Maria Byrne points out that the findings are consistent with an established idea in ecology known as the intermediate disturbance hypothesis.
This theory proposes that a moderate level of disturbance can stop any one species from dominating an ecosystem.
The idea has been used to explain patterns of diversity in a range of habitats, from tropical rainforests to coral reefs.
If disturbance is very rare, a few strong competitors tend to take over, while if it is very frequent or severe, only the hardiest species survive.
Between these extremes, the theory suggests, a wider range of species is able to live side by side.
Seen in this light, the crown-of-thorns starfish may act as a natural source of moderate disturbance, preventing a single type of coral from monopolising the reef.
None of this means that the starfish are harmless.
The Great Barrier Reef has suffered four major outbreaks since the 1960s, occurring roughly every 15 years, and these remain a serious threat to the reef.
One reason reefs have become more vulnerable is that the natural predators of the starfish, such as the triton snail and several species of reef fish, have declined.
The researchers stress that there is a clear difference between the starfish acting as a natural predator at low density and an outbreak that causes the long-term decline of a reef.
The study also has implications for how the reef is managed.
Culling has long been used to bring outbreaks of the starfish under control.
The new findings suggest that once an outbreak has been suppressed, the aim should not necessarily be to remove every last starfish.
Instead, culling should be combined with strong marine management that protects the natural predators of the starfish, so that the starfish population is kept in check.
Such an approach would treat the starfish not simply as a pest to be destroyed, but as a natural member of the reef community.
In this way, the reef might keep the benefits of a predator in moderation while avoiding the damage caused by a predator in excess.

sentences.text: In its early history, the universe was filled with a thin fog of neutral hydrogen gas.
This fog absorbed ultraviolet light so effectively that much of the radiation produced by the first stars and galaxies could not travel far.
Then, roughly 13 billion years ago, the situation began to change.
Energetic radiation gradually stripped electrons from the hydrogen atoms, a process known as ionisation, and the fog lifted, allowing light to move freely across space.
Astronomers refer to this transformation as reionisation, and it ranks among the most important events in cosmic history.
Yet, as Cody Carr, an astronomer involved in a new study, admits, scientists still do not know exactly which objects caused it or how it evolved.
For the fog to clear, two conditions had to be met.
First, something had to produce enormous quantities of ionising radiation, and young galaxies full of hot, massive stars are widely regarded as the leading candidates.
Second, that radiation had to escape from the galaxies in which it was produced.
This second step is far from simple, because galaxies are themselves surrounded by gas and dust that can absorb the radiation before it ever reaches intergalactic space.
Understanding how ionising light gets out of galaxies is therefore central to explaining how reionisation took place.
For many years, the favoured explanation has centred on supernovae, the violent explosions that end the lives of massive stars.
According to this view, the combined energy of many supernovae drives powerful winds of gas outwards through a galaxy.
Supernovae certainly seem powerful enough for such a role: a single explosion can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.
These winds were thought to clear channels through the surrounding material, rather like holes torn in a curtain, through which radiation could then stream into space.

The idea is so widely accepted that, as the astrophysicist Renyue Cen notes, supernovae play a central role in the computer simulations that cosmologists use to model how radiation escapes from galaxies.
Testing this idea directly is difficult, because the galaxies of the reionisation era are extremely distant and faint.
The new study, published in the journal Nature Astronomy, therefore took an indirect approach.

A team of nearly 30 scientists from more than a dozen institutions, including researchers at the University of Michigan, used the Hubble Space Telescope to examine nearby compact starburst galaxies, which are forming stars at an exceptional rate.
Such galaxies are considered modern stand-ins for the young galaxies of the early universe.
Because they are much closer, they can be studied in far greater detail than their ancient counterparts.
By analysing dips in the galaxies' spectra caused by absorption, the researchers were able to measure how fast their winds were moving.
They then compared these speeds with the proportion of ionising radiation escaping from each galaxy.
If the supernova model were correct, the galaxies with the fastest winds should have been the most efficient at releasing radiation.
The researchers found exactly the opposite.
The galaxies with the fastest winds allowed the smallest fraction of their ionising radiation to escape.

One possible explanation is that, instead of clearing a path, the energy from supernovae stirs up the surrounding gas and dust, spreading neutral material more widely so that it blocks more of the radiation.
If so, the radiation that does escape probably leaves earlier, released by young, massive stars before supernovae have had time to generate large winds.
In Carr's words, the observations show that the ionising photons are escaping before galactic winds form.
The findings could have significant consequences for cosmology.
Simulations that rely heavily on supernova-driven winds to release radiation may need to be revised.
The authors suggest that more attention should be paid to the period before the first supernovae explode, and to the effects of smaller winds and other activity associated with young stars.
In other words, the key stage for releasing radiation may come earlier in a galaxy's life than has generally been assumed.
At the same time, they are careful to stress that their results do not yet settle the question of what caused reionisation.
They are now seeking more observing time on Hubble to find out whether the same pattern appears in other galaxies.
In my view, this caution is entirely justified.
Nearby starbursts may resemble early galaxies in some respects, but they exist in a universe that is billions of years older, and there is no guarantee that they behave in exactly the same way.
Moreover, a pattern observed in one group of galaxies needs to be confirmed in a much larger sample before it can overturn a well-established model.
Even so, the result is valuable precisely because it contradicts expectations.

An explanation that has become a standard ingredient of computer simulations can easily be accepted without sufficient testing, and observations that challenge it force researchers to re-examine their assumptions.

Should the supernova model turn out to be wrong, the story of how the universe became transparent will need to be rewritten, with the youngest stars, rather than the dying ones, playing the leading role.
Whatever the final answer, the study is a reminder that even the most familiar explanations in science remain open to question.

sentences.text: Anyone who has walked through a forest after a strong wind will have seen trees leaning at odd angles.
Some never recover, but many young trees slowly lift themselves back towards the vertical.
For a long time, botanists explained this recovery mainly in terms of two outside signals: gravity, which tells a plant which way is down, and light, which tells it where the sky is.
A new study by researchers at INRAE, France's national research institute for agriculture, food and the environment, suggests that this explanation is incomplete.
Trees, it appears, also rely on an inner sense of their own shape.
In animals, this inner sense is called proprioception.
It is the reason a person can touch their nose with their eyes closed: sensors in the muscles and joints constantly report the position of the body to the brain.
For many years, proprioception was regarded as something that only animals possessed.
However, in 2012 a team that included INRAE scientists published evidence that plants are also able to sense how they are curved.
The latest work, which appears in the journal New Phytologist, goes further by showing how trees actually use this information to correct their posture.
The main difficulty in studying this sense in plants is that gravity and light are always present, so it is hard to tell which signal a plant is responding to.
To solve this problem, the researchers built an unusual piece of equipment.
Young poplar trees were placed on a horizontal platform that rotated inside a large sphere.
The inside of the sphere was lit equally from every direction, so the plants received no steady clue about where the light was coming from.
Because the platform kept turning, the pull of gravity on the stems kept changing direction, which meant that it could not guide their growth either.
In effect, the trees were left with only one reliable source of information: their own shape.
Before the experiment began, the poplars were grown lying on their sides for about ten days.
During this period, their stems bent upwards as the trees tried to grow towards the vertical, which left each stem with a clear curve.
Once the trees were placed in the rotating sphere, something remarkable happened.
Over several weeks, the curved stems gradually straightened, even though neither gravity nor light could have been telling them to do so.
The only reasonable explanation was that the trees were detecting their own curvature and responding to it.
When the scientists examined the wood inside the stems, they discovered how the straightening had been achieved.
Trees produce a special material called tension wood, which pulls on the stem as it forms, rather like a muscle.
Until now, it was generally believed that tension wood develops only on the upper side of a leaning stem, where it helps to lift the tree.
In the poplars, however, the tension wood on the original upper side stopped forming once the trees were inside the sphere.
Instead, the same kind of wood began to develop on the opposite side, pulling the stem in the other direction until it was almost straight.
The two sides therefore behaved like a pair of opposing muscles, similar to those that bend and straighten a human arm.
Bruno Moulia, a research director at INRAE, described the process as "a genuine sensorimotor loop" at work in the woody parts of trees.
The discovery has several possible practical uses.
Storms, landslides and a changing climate can all leave trees bent or displaced, so knowing how trees regain their posture could become increasingly important.
The findings may also be useful in agriculture, where cereal crops sometimes fall over before they can be harvested, a problem known as lodging.
If breeders understood the mechanism better, they might be able to develop crop varieties that are less likely to collapse.
Finally, the research could benefit the timber industry.
When tension wood forms in a poorly coordinated way, it can leave excessive stresses inside the wood, which can reduce the quality of the timber.
A better understanding of how trees control tension wood could therefore help foresters and breeders to produce better wood.

title: Metals That Keep Their Nerve in the Cold

sentences.text: Most people assume that cold makes materials harder, and in one sense this is true: cooling a metal generally makes it stronger.
Strength, however, is not the same as toughness.
As temperatures fall, many metals also become more brittle, which means that instead of bending under a heavy load, they snap.
A component that performs well at room temperature may therefore behave very differently when it is exposed to intense cold.
This change, known as the ductile-to-brittle transition, is a serious concern for engineers who design parts that must work in extremely cold conditions.
The problem is especially severe for metals with what is called a body-centred cubic (BCC) crystal structure, a group that includes iron, tungsten and chromium.
Close to absolute zero, a tiny crack that such a metal would normally absorb by changing shape can instead spread rapidly through the material and cause it to fracture.
According to Professor Dong Liu of the Department of Engineering Science at the University of Oxford, this transition has for decades been regarded as a fundamental limitation of BCC metals.
To understand why, it helps to know how metals normally deform.
Inside a metal, the atoms are arranged in regular layers, but the arrangement is never perfect.
It contains defects known as dislocations, which allow layers of atoms to slide past one another when the metal is put under stress.
It is this sliding that lets a metal bend or stretch rather than break.
At low temperatures, however, dislocations in BCC metals become harder to move.
With fewer ways to relieve the stress that builds up around the tip of a crack, the metal is more likely to fail suddenly.
A new study published in the journal Nature suggests that this limitation is not as fixed as once believed.
An international team, with Liu as the corresponding author and Dr David Cook as lead author, tested two experimental alloys based on niobium and titanium.
Cook carried out the research while working at the University of California, Berkeley, and has since moved to the University of Cambridge.
The researchers found that both alloys resisted cracking even at 20 kelvin, or minus 253 degrees Celsius, which is only 20 degrees above absolute zero.
The explanation lies in an unexpected way of dealing with stress.
When the alloys were strained in extreme cold, tiny regions of their crystal structure rearranged themselves into mirror-image patterns, a process called nanoscale twinning.
This took place together with a local change in the crystal structure itself.
Where these newly formed regions met the boundaries between neighbouring crystals, known as grains, they concentrated stress, and this in turn produced fresh defects.
These new defects gave the metal extra ways to deform, so that it changed shape instead of cracking.
The team compares the effect to traffic being redirected when the main roads are covered in ice: when the usual route for deformation is blocked, the material creates alternative routes of its own.
Reaching these conclusions required a wide range of techniques.

The samples were cooled using gaseous helium and then pulled from both ends in a specialised testing machine, which recorded how much force they could withstand and how far they stretched before breaking.

During the tests, beams of neutrons were sent through the materials using the Engin-X instrument at the ISIS Neutron and Muon Source in Oxfordshire, allowing the team to observe what was happening inside the metal as it deformed.
Afterwards, electron microscopes were used to examine the samples, including the areas close to cracks.
A technique called atom-probe analysis was also used to map how individual elements were distributed in the alloys.
Finally, computer simulations helped the researchers understand how the different processes worked together.
In the authors' view, the findings challenge some long-held assumptions.
Scientists have traditionally concentrated on how easily existing defects can move through a metal.
The new results suggest that the ability to create new defects at interfaces may be just as important in deciding whether a metal turns brittle.
"Our results suggest we should change how we think about what governs the transition to brittleness for these metals," says Cook.
The practical consequences could be considerable.

Liu says that the alloys remain remarkably damage tolerant even at 20 kelvin, and that materials of this kind could be useful for components that face both extremely hot and extremely cold temperatures.
The researchers point to possible uses in energy systems, transport and aerospace engineering.
For the moment, though, the niobium-titanium alloys remain experimental materials rather than commercial products.
Looking further ahead, Cook suggests that engineers might one day design materials whose internal structure allows them to create their own paths to remain ductile under extreme conditions.

sentences.text: For a long time, the story of early complex societies in Africa has been told mainly through the lens of Egypt.
The monuments of the Nile Valley are so famous that they have tended to overshadow developments elsewhere on the continent.
North Africa to the west of Egypt, in particular, has often been treated as a region on the edge of the great changes that were taking place around the Mediterranean.
Recent discoveries in the hills of north-west Morocco suggest that this picture is in serious need of revision.
The site in question, Oued Beht, overlooks the river from which it takes its name.

Archaeologists working on the Oued Beht Archaeological Project had already shown that it was home to what is probably the earliest and largest farming complex in Africa outside the Nile Valley, dating from roughly 5,400 to 4,900 years ago.
Excavations carried out in 2023, and published in 2026 in the journal Libyan Studies, have now added a new and unexpected chapter to its history.
The team uncovered what appears to be the oldest large-scale defensive structure known in North Africa beyond the Nile Valley.
The structure is not a single wall but a system built in several phases, combining a ditch, an earth rampart and a wall.
It runs across a narrow section of a ridge, between the river on one side and a ravine on the other, cutting off and protecting the southern tip of the ridge.
The site had not gone completely unnoticed in modern times.

In the 1930s, the French archaeologist Armand Ruhlmann recorded three walls there, with the fourth side guarded by the natural steep slope of the ridge, and he described the place as a 'barred spur', a type of fortified promontory.
Radiocarbon dating of deposits associated with the structure now places its construction between about 4,000 and 3,500 years ago.
This makes it, in the view of the excavators, the earliest confirmed defensive construction in North Africa outside Egypt.
Long before the wall was built, however, Oued Beht was already a substantial place.
Activity at the site covered at least ten hectares, and its first major phase belongs to the Final Neolithic, in the middle of the fourth millennium and the early third millennium BC.
The people who lived there grew barley and wheat, gathered wild plants and kept livestock.
They were also skilled craftspeople: excavators have found thousands of polished stone axes, as well as finely made pottery, some of it painted.
Even so, the exact nature of the settlement remains uncertain.
It may have been a permanent village, a seasonal centre where people gathered at certain times of the year, or something else entirely.
Over time, the focus of activity shifted.

Whereas the earlier community had spread across the larger and more open northern part of the site, later activity concentrated on the narrower southern end of the ridge, which was far easier to defend.
The construction of the defences fits this pattern.
Exactly what the inhabitants were afraid of, however, is unknown.
The researchers are careful not to imagine invading armies.
Instead, they suggest that the defences may reflect competition over land and resources, or a wish to control movement through the landscape.
This cautious interpretation is worth noting, since it is all too easy to assume that every ancient wall must have been built in response to war.
The history of the site does not end in prehistory.
Thousands of years later, between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries AD, people returned to Oued Beht.
They rebuilt the old defensive structure, established a small hamlet or farm on a nearby hilltop and buried their dead in a cemetery that lay between the two areas.
Nothing in the evidence indicates who these medieval settlers were or whether they knew anything of the people who had first fortified the ridge.
What is clear is that the location remained attractive to people living there many centuries apart.
Perhaps the most important implications of the discovery concern North Africa's place in the wider Mediterranean world.

The wall dates from the period known in the western Mediterranean as the Bronze Age, and it invites comparison with the Argaric societies of southern Iberia, which flourished between about 2200 and 1550 BC.
These societies built fortified settlements on hilltops, worked metal and were marked by clear social hierarchies.
Placing Oued Beht alongside such communities allows archaeologists to ask whether the two sides of the western Mediterranean were developing in comparable ways at the same time.

For the authors of the study, the answer points in one direction: the Maghreb, the region made up of Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, was not cut off from the rest of the Mediterranean but connected to its wider networks.
If this is correct, accounts of the ancient Mediterranean that move directly from Egypt to the civilisations of the northern shore will need to be rewritten.
Many questions remain open, from the purpose of the defences to the character of the people who built them.

Yet Oued Beht already shows how much can still be learned from regions that have received relatively little archaeological attention, and how new fieldwork can change the way that the past of an entire region is understood.

title: Ancient Ice on the Roof of the World

sentences.text: Ice cores are among the most valuable records of the Earth's past climate.
When snow falls on a glacier year after year, it is slowly pressed into ice, and each layer keeps a trace of the conditions at the time it formed.
By drilling down through an ice cap and lifting out long cylinders of ice, scientists can read this history in much the same way that geologists read layers of rock.
Most of the oldest ice cores have come from Antarctica and Greenland, but glaciers high in the mountains of other regions also contain important records.
One such glacier lies on the Guliya Plateau in north-western Tibet.

A team led by Lonnie Thompson, an earth scientist at the Byrd Polar Research Center of Ohio State University in the United States, has now reported that some of the ice there may be more than 128,000 years old.
If this is correct, it extends the known glacial history of the region by over 100,000 years, and it makes these the oldest ice cores ever recovered from this part of Tibet.
The study, which was funded by the US National Science Foundation, was published in the journal Science Advances.
Researchers from Switzerland and China also took part in the work.
The age of the Guliya ice has been a matter of debate for some time.
Earlier research had suggested that the record went back only as far as the middle of the Holocene, the relatively warm period that began almost 12,000 years ago.
The new work indicates that at least part of the ice is much older than this.
According to Thompson, the question is about more than a single number.
If Tibet held only ice that had formed during the Holocene, it would mean that the great ice masses of the last ice age had disappeared by the early part of that period.
The evidence from Guliya, he says, shows that they survived.
To build a reliable timescale, the researchers combined several kinds of evidence.
First, they compared two sets of cores that had been drilled from the ice cap 23 years apart, in 1992 and 2015.
Both showed remarkably similar patterns of oxygen isotopes, a chemical signal that reflects the climate at the time the snow fell.
Thompson believes that being able to reproduce a record in this way is essential.
Matching cores that were taken a quarter of a century apart, he explains, can reveal a great deal about how the ice has behaved over time.
Second, the team measured radioactive forms of two elements, beryllium and chlorine.
These allowed them to identify a well-known event called the Laschamp geomagnetic excursion, a disturbance in the Earth's magnetic field that took place more than 41,000 years ago.
The disturbance left a distinctive chemical mark in the ice, giving the scientists a fixed point in time against which other layers could be compared.
Finally, they compared the Guliya record with oxygen isotope data from cave deposits in nearby parts of Tibet, which helped them to push the timeline further back.
These results make Guliya unusual among mountain glaciers.
Thompson says it is the only mountaintop ice core outside the polar regions that is known to reach back this far.
By comparison, the ice cores from Huascarán, a mountain in Peru, cover only around 30,000 years.
The researchers also think that the shape of the local landscape may help the ice cap to preserve such old layers.
For climate scientists, an accurate timeline is the key to answering larger questions, such as when periods of intense glaciation in the region began and ended.
Knowing exactly when ice formed, and when it was lost, depends on having dates that can be trusted.
"Our results tell a very consistent story," Thompson says.
The team now plans to study further samples to see how other indicators of past climate and environment fit into the longer record.

title: What an Elephant's Tooth Reveals About Early Humans

sentences.text: About 700,000 years ago, a huge elephant lived and died in what is now northern Israel.
Today, a single tooth from that animal is helping scientists to reconstruct the world in which some of the region's earliest human inhabitants lived.
Fossil teeth are among the most durable parts of an animal's body, which is one reason why they so often survive when other remains have disappeared.
The study, published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews, was led by Hannah Farrell, a doctoral student at the University of Haifa.
Rather than relying on a single method, it brought together evidence from several scientific fields to build a detailed picture of an ancient landscape.
The result is a vivid portrait of the setting in which these early people made their tools and found their food.
The tooth was recovered at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, a site whose name means "Daughters of Jacob Bridge".
It lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, a short distance south of the Hula Valley.
The site was excavated by Professor Gonen Sharon of Tel-Hai University and his colleagues, who found elephant remains lying alongside stone tools made of basalt.
These tools, which include handaxes and cleavers, belong to the Acheulian tradition, one of the oldest and most widespread stone-tool technologies ever developed.
Because the tools were found right beside the bones, the site offers a valuable opportunity to study animals and early humans together.
The fossils examined by the team, a large molar and several fragments of tusk, came from a species called Palaeoloxodon antiquus.
This animal, commonly known as the straight-tusked elephant, was one of the largest mammals to walk on land during the Pleistocene epoch.
An animal of such enormous size would have needed vast quantities of food and water every day.
For this reason, its remains can reveal a great deal about the environment that was able to support it.
Studying such a species therefore offers far more than a glimpse of a single animal.
To extract as much information as possible, the researchers used a wide range of techniques.
CT scanning allowed them to look inside the tooth without damaging it, and the scans were then used to produce a three-dimensional reconstruction.
Such non-destructive methods are especially important when a fossil is rare and cannot be replaced.
They also examined the surface of the tooth under a microscope in order to study the patterns of wear left by chewing.
In addition, they carried out isotope analysis, a geochemical method that measures different forms of elements such as carbon.
Finally, specialists studied ancient pollen preserved in the sediments surrounding the fossils.
The pollen work was carried out by Minji Jin and Dafna Langgut of Tel Aviv University, while the isotope studies were led by Cheryl Makarewicz of the University of Haifa.
Nimrod Marom, also from Haifa, contributed expertise in archaeozoology, the study of animal remains from archaeological sites.
Taken together, the results describe a varied and productive landscape.
There were woodlands and open grasslands, as well as marshes, flowing rivers and areas of shallow water.
The carbon isotope measurements suggested that the elephant had access to a reliable supply of water throughout its life.
The pollen record supported this picture, revealing plants typical of wet habitats, such as reeds, sedges, willow and tamarisk, together with plants that grow in water.
Such a rich mixture of habitats could have supported large mammals and early human communities at the same time.
In short, this was far from a harsh or barren environment.
The location of the site adds to its significance.
The Hula Valley sits within the Levantine Corridor, a natural route that connects Africa with Eurasia.
Conditions in the valley may therefore have mattered not only to the groups that lived there but also to those moving between the two landmasses.
The researchers believe that the area acted as a relatively stable ecological refuge, a place that kept its key habitats and resources over long periods of time.
Dependable water, plants and animals may have helped early human groups both to survive and to travel through the region.
For Professor Sharon, the study shows why it is important to understand how humans and animals responded to changes in their surroundings.
Such knowledge, he argues, gives us a clearer view of the forces that shaped our own species.
He also stresses that the availability of water, vegetation and animal resources determined where both humans and wildlife were able to survive.
His comments highlight a theme that runs through much research on early human history: people depended heavily on the natural resources around them.
In this sense, a single fossil tooth can open a window onto an entire lost world.

title: Following the Warmth: Why Crocodiles Outlived the Dinosaurs

sentences.text: When the Chicxulub asteroid struck the Earth around 66 million years ago, the age of the dinosaurs came to an abrupt end.
Yet crocodiles, which had shared the planet with dinosaurs for tens of millions of years, came through the catastrophe and are still with us today.
Crocodiles are, after all, reptiles that rely heavily on warmth from their surroundings, which might seem to make them especially vulnerable to sudden cooling.
Why one group perished while the other endured has long been a puzzle for palaeontologists.

A new study from University College London, published in the journal Science Advances, suggests that a large part of the answer lies in a simple habit: for most of their history, crocodiles and their relatives have followed warm climates rather than adapting to new ones.
The research team, led by Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza, examined more than 7,000 fossils and records belonging to over 400 living and extinct species.
Drawing on fossils, evolutionary family trees and the present-day distribution of crocodiles, they reconstructed the temperatures and rainfall levels that each species preferred.
These preferences were then combined with computer models of climate and geography stretching back 245 million years.
This approach allowed the scientists to trace not only where crocodile relatives lived, but also why their ranges shifted over time.
Such a large dataset made it possible to look for patterns across the entire history of the group rather than in isolated species.
The picture that emerged was one of remarkable consistency, a pattern that biologists describe as climatic niche conservatism.
Across roughly 250 million years, the group tended to keep the same climatic preferences, so that when the planet changed, they moved rather than changing themselves.

During warm periods they spread towards the poles: in the early Eocene, about 50 million years ago, when global temperatures were around 10°C higher than today and there was no permanent ice at the poles, crocodile relatives lived at high latitudes in North America, Europe and even Antarctica.
When the Earth cooled again, the area of suitable habitat shrank and they retreated towards the tropics.
This conservatism is all the more striking given how varied the group once was.
The wider lineage, known as pseudosuchians, included heavily armoured plant-eaters, predators that hunted on land and animals weighing more than a tonne.
Sarcosuchus, sometimes called the "super croc", could grow to about 12 metres long, while Postosuchus was a land hunter that could walk on either two legs or four.
Some looked so unlike modern crocodiles that a casual observer might not have recognised them as relatives at all.
Despite this variety of body forms and lifestyles, the group's relationship with temperature changed surprisingly little.
There were, however, two notable exceptions.

Around 94 million years ago, during a period known as the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, temperatures rose as high as 14°C above modern levels, and one branch of the group evolved a greater tolerance of heat.
Much later, about 34 million years ago, an extinct group in Australia adapted to increasingly dry, desert-like conditions as a long period of cooling reduced rainfall.
These cases show that adaptation was possible, but they appear to have been the exception rather than the rule.
The habit of tracking warmth may explain how crocodiles survived the asteroid impact.
The team simulated the aftermath of the collision, in which dust and ash would have blocked sunlight while volcanic activity raised levels of carbon dioxide.
If sunlight was reduced by 5 or 10 per cent, regions near the equator remained suitable for crocodile relatives.
Only a 15 per cent reduction made those regions unsuitable as well, and the researchers point out that such an extreme scenario is now considered unlikely.
Higher carbon dioxide levels, meanwhile, made no difference to the availability of suitable climates.
Earlier modelling by members of the same team had found that the habitats of non-avian dinosaurs shrank far more severely after the impact.
In effect, the tropics may have acted as a warm refuge in which crocodiles could wait out the crisis.
The researchers are careful not to claim that temperature was the whole story.
Other traits probably helped as well: many crocodile relatives were small, could live partly in water, ate a wide range of foods and, as cold-blooded animals, needed relatively little energy.
It would be a mistake, therefore, to attribute their survival to a single advantage.
Rather, a strategy of following familiar conditions, combined with a flexible way of life, seems to have served them well when conditions changed suddenly.
The findings also carry a warning for the present.
For millions of years, moving to a suitable climate has been the main way in which crocodiles have coped with climate change.
Today, however, roads, farmland and cities increasingly stand in the way of such movement.
Where a river is dammed or a wetland drained, there may simply be nowhere for an animal to go.
As Professor Philip Mannion, one of the study's authors, has pointed out, living species will need room to move as the planet warms, and the loss of their habitats is making this more difficult.
The strategy that carried crocodiles through one of the greatest disasters in the Earth's history may not be enough to protect them in a world reshaped by humans.

sentences.text: Along the deep reefs of southern Australia lives a group of tiny fish that very few people have ever heard of.
At first glance, they look exactly like seahorses.
Their heads are shaped like a horse's and point downwards from the body, their tails curl round to grip objects, and the males carry their young in a closed pouch.
Yet a new study has shown that these animals are not seahorses at all.
Scientists have nicknamed them "sea muppets", and they belong to a genus called Australyichthys, a name built from the Latin word for "southern" and the Greek word for "fish".
The discovery shows how much can still be learnt from specimens that have been sitting quietly in museum collections.
The most recently described member of the group is Australyichthys aegis, which has been given the common name "helmethead sea muppet".
Like its relatives, it is no longer than a human thumb.
It owes its name to a rounded crest on top of its head that resembles a helmet.
The word aegis refers to a protective shield that appears in Greek mythology.
The genus contains two other known species: the bullneck sea muppet and the paradoxical sea muppet.
What makes these fish especially mysterious is that no one has ever seen one alive.
Only seven specimens exist, and they were collected over a period of roughly 65 years along more than 2,500 kilometres of coastline.
For an entire genus of animals, that is an extraordinarily small number of records.
Every one of them was caught by accident, brought up in trawl nets or dredges that were dragged across the seabed at depths of about 50 to 125 metres.
No new specimen has been found for almost twenty years.
The helmethead specimen has a particularly unusual history.
It was collected in 2006 near the Gambier Islands, at the entrance to Spencer Gulf in South Australia, by a dredge that was actually searching for brachiopods, small animals with shells.
After the expedition, the fish was mistakenly stored among the invertebrates at the South Australian Museum, where it sat unnoticed for years.
The other specimens are kept in several collections, including those of the Australian Museum, Museums Victoria and the national science agency CSIRO.
Because the specimens were so rare, the researchers could not cut them open.
Instead, they used micro-CT scanning to create three-dimensional models of the skeletons, which allowed them to compare each bone with those of true seahorses.
This technique uses X-rays to produce detailed images of internal structures without harming the specimen.
The differences were clear.
A true seahorse has a stiff cage of joined bony plates that supports its belly, as well as a bony crown on its head known as a coronet.
The sea muppets have neither of these features; instead, their bellies are held up by an arrangement of bones not found in any seahorse.
DNA provided further evidence, although only the helmethead specimen could be tested.
It was the only one that had been preserved in ethanol, while the others had been kept in formalin, which damages genetic material.
The genetic results placed the fish outside the seahorse group, on a neighbouring branch of the family tree.
Seahorses, sea muppets, pipefishes, pipehorses and seadragons all belong to the same family, called Syngnathidae.
The new findings suggest that the seahorse body shape evolved at least twice within this family.
This is an example of convergent evolution, in which animals that are not closely related develop similar features because they live in similar ways.

The sea muppets come from the Great Southern Reef, a network of kelp forests and rocky reefs around the southern coast of Australia that is home to many species found nowhere else, and whose deeper parts remain largely unexplored.
The scientists have labelled the fish a "lost species", but they stress that this does not mean the animals have died out.

Rather, it marks them as a priority for surveys designed to look for them deliberately instead of relying on lucky catches, and the researchers believe the fish are probably still living in deep water that people seldom visit.
Until such surveys take place, the sea muppets will remain known only from a handful of preserved bodies in museum jars.

title: Borrowing from Chips to Build Better Batteries

sentences.text: Electric cars have become far more common over the past decade, but their batteries are still heavy, bulky and expensive.
Engineers are therefore searching for designs that can store more energy in a smaller space, so that vehicles can travel further on a single charge without carrying extra weight.
One of the most promising ideas is the so-called anode-free lithium battery.

A team led by Professors Jinwoo Lee and Hee-Tae Jung at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) has now found a way to make such batteries last much longer, by borrowing techniques from the manufacture of computer chips.
A typical lithium battery contains two electrodes, and in most designs one of them, the anode, is made from a material such as graphite.
An anode-free battery leaves out this material altogether.
Instead, when the battery is charged, lithium is deposited directly onto a very thin sheet of copper foil.
Removing the graphite reduces both the weight and the size of the cell, so more energy can be packed into the same space.
For car makers, this could eventually mean smaller, lighter battery packs that still offer a longer driving range.
The difficulty is that these batteries tend to wear out quickly.
Each time the battery is charged, lithium builds up on the copper, and after many cycles it can grow into branching, needle-like structures known as dendrites.
Dendrites reduce the battery's performance, and at the same time the protective layer that forms around the lithium can become unstable.
Together, these two problems shorten the battery's working life.

Earlier attempts to solve them, such as adding extra lithium or applying thicker coatings, made the battery heavier and larger, which cancelled out the main reason for choosing an anode-free design in the first place.
The KAIST researchers took a different approach, which works on two levels.
First, they used a semiconductor technique called secondary sputtering lithography to carve a regular pattern of microscopic tubes into the surface of the copper.
Each tube measures about 300 nanometres across and 150 nanometres high.
These tiny features increase the usable surface area to about four times that of a flat sheet.
With more space available, lithium is laid down more evenly, and the dangerous spikes are less likely to develop.
Second, the team covered the patterned copper with an extremely thin layer of a two-dimensional material called MXene.
The coating is only about 10 nanometres thick, which is less than a thousandth of the thickness of a human hair.
It acts as a foundation on which a stronger and more stable protective layer can grow while the battery is operating.
In the electrolyte used in the experiments, this protective layer is rich in lithium fluoride.
It limits unwanted chemical reactions between the lithium and the electrolyte, and it also restricts the growth of dendrites.
To confirm what was happening, the researchers examined the surfaces and cross sections of their electrodes while keeping their exposure to air to a minimum.
They used several advanced instruments, including X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy, time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry and transmission electron microscopy.
These tests showed that an extremely thin protective layer forms evenly across the MXene surface, and they also revealed the process by which it forms.
According to Professor Lee, the study shows that fabrication methods developed for semiconductors can create both evenly spread sites for lithium to settle on and a stable protective layer.
Importantly, this is achieved without changing the chemical recipe of the electrolyte or adding surplus lithium.
The team believes the approach could speed up the commercial development of high-energy anode-free batteries while keeping any added weight and volume to a minimum.
The work was carried out with partners at Kyungpook National University and the National NanoFab Center, and the results were published in the journal Advanced Functional Materials.
The project is also a good example of how ideas can travel from one industry to another.
Chip makers have spent decades learning to shape materials with extraordinary precision, because smaller features allow more components to fit onto a single piece of silicon.
The KAIST team applied this same kind of precision to the inside of a battery cell.
The KAIST study was supported in part by national programmes that give scientists access to advanced semiconductor fabrication facilities and that aim to link semiconductor and battery research.
Of course, results achieved in a laboratory do not always translate easily into commercial products, and many promising battery designs never reach the market.
If the KAIST team's results can be repeated on a larger scale, the tools that made computers faster and smaller may one day help electric cars to travel further as well.

title: How Northern Ice May Have Reached the Southern Ocean

sentences.text: Over the past few million years, Earth's climate has swung repeatedly between long, cold ice ages and shorter, warmer periods like the one we are living in today.

Scientists broadly agree that these swings were set in motion by slow, natural changes in Earth's orbit around the Sun, which alter how much sunlight reaches different parts of the planet in different seasons.
Yet orbital changes are only part of the story.
Another key ingredient was carbon dioxide: during ice ages, the atmosphere contained considerably less of this greenhouse gas, because more carbon was stored in the oceans.
Much of this storage is thought to have been controlled by the Southern Ocean, the vast body of water that surrounds Antarctica.

In this region, deep water rises towards the surface and comes into contact with the atmosphere, so changes in the way the ocean circulates there can help decide whether carbon escapes into the air or remains locked away in the depths.
For this reason, research into ice-age climate has traditionally concentrated on the Southern Ocean itself.
Only recently have scientists begun to ask seriously whether distant parts of the ocean might also play a role.
This raises an awkward question.

The great ice sheets that expanded during ice ages lay mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, covering large parts of North America and northern Europe, and their growth was initially driven by the changes in Earth's orbit.
The Southern Ocean, however, lies at the opposite end of the planet, separated from those ice sheets by the entire length of the Atlantic.
How, then, could ice building up in the far north affect the amount of carbon absorbed by waters thousands of kilometres away around Antarctica?
Until this question is answered, the explanation of how ice ages deepen remains incomplete.
A study led by Madison Shankle of the University of St Andrews, published in the Journal of Climate, offers a possible answer.
The team proposes a chain of events that links the two hemispheres through the ocean.
As ice sheets spread across the north, they cool the nearby waters of the North Atlantic.
This colder water then travels southwards until it reaches the Southern Ocean.
If the cooling is strong enough, it can change the circulation around Antarctica in a way that allows more carbon dioxide to be stored below the surface.
With less of the gas in the atmosphere, the planet cools further, and this extra cooling may in turn make the ice age more severe.
To test the idea, the researchers turned to computer simulations of ocean circulation, which allow scientists to change one factor at a time and watch how the rest of the system reacts.
Rather than cooling the whole planet, they cooled only the most northerly latitudes, imitating the effect of a large ice sheet, and then observed how the Southern Ocean responded.
The result was striking.
Cooling in the north alone produced 74 per cent of the fall in carbon dioxide that occurred in a separate simulation in which the entire planet was cooled.
In other words, a change that began in one hemisphere was able to achieve most of the effect of a global one, with the ocean itself carrying the influence from north to south.
It is worth being clear about what this finding does and does not show.

Shankle herself describes the work as providing a plausible mechanism that connects northern ice sheets with changes in circulation in the south, and as demonstrating that connection in model simulations.
A computer model, however sophisticated, is a simplified version of the real ocean, and a mechanism that works in a simulation still has to be checked against evidence from the past.
Such evidence may come from sediments on the sea floor, which can preserve chemical traces of how ancient oceans behaved.
Even so, the study is valuable, because it turns a vague possibility into a specific proposal that other scientists can test.
Nor is the study merely a matter of historical curiosity.

The authors point out that understanding how the ocean took up carbon during past ice ages helps scientists to understand the natural carbon cycle, and to predict how the oceans may respond to the rising levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere today.
The ocean already absorbs a large share of the carbon dioxide released by human activity, so knowing what controls its ability to store carbon is of practical importance.
Some of the ways in which the ocean stores carbon are physical: colder water, for example, can hold more dissolved gas than warmer water.
Others depend on how water moves between the surface and the deep ocean, which is the kind of circulation change at the heart of the new study.
If a change in one region can alter such processes across the globe, then predicting the ocean's future behaviour will require models that treat the planet as a single connected system.
Perhaps the broadest lesson of the research is that the climate system is deeply interconnected.
A change in the North Atlantic, it seems, can be felt as far away as Antarctica, and that is worth remembering whether we are studying the distant past or preparing for the future.

title: What Really Happens to a Falling Meteor

sentences.text: Most people imagine that a meteor simply burns away as it races across the night sky, leaving nothing behind except a brief streak of light.
A new study led by Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames Research Center suggests that the reality is far more dramatic.
By examining video recordings and photographs of 75 meteorite falls, his team identified seven distinct stages that a rock passes through as it enters the atmosphere.
Their main conclusion is that melting and breaking apart, rather than simple evaporation, decide how much material a rock loses, how quickly it slows down and where its surviving pieces land.
The research was published in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.
The process begins high above the ground, at the point where the air first becomes thick enough for a shock wave to build up in front of the incoming rock.
Both the rock and the gas around it become extremely hot and start to glow, creating what observers call a meteor or a shooting star.
As the object pushes deeper into denser air, it grows steadily brighter.
Interestingly, its brightness often rises and falls in a regular pattern, and this flickering allows scientists to work out how fast the rock is spinning.
The fastest spinners in the study completed one rotation every 0.5 to 5 seconds.
In the third stage, the meteor turns into a fireball, and melting becomes the main way in which it loses material.
The rushing air strips away tiny drops of molten rock, which continue to evaporate after they have broken free.

In the fourth stage, at an altitude of roughly 60 kilometres, melting settles into a fairly steady state, so the fireball either keeps a nearly constant brightness or becomes brighter at an even rate.
According to the team, melting on its own can remove as much as 40 per cent of the rock's original mass.
The fifth stage is the moment when the rock begins to fall apart.
As the air pressure on its front surface increases, cracks open and fragments separate, sometimes producing a series of flashes.
Surprisingly, this break-up can start when the pressure is only about one-fifth of the strength measured in meteorites that have been recovered on the ground.
The researchers think the rock may already have been weakened by heating and by cracks left behind by earlier collisions in space.
Once fragmentation begins, the remaining body shrinks quickly and slows down sharply, and the more it breaks up, the faster it loses speed.
In the sixth stage, the rear part of the rock shatters, releasing a bright flare and scattering fragments at higher speeds.
Because the object has slowed down by this point, these final flashes are usually red, whereas the earlier light tends to look green.
Meteorites heavier than about 20 grams were generally spread over a wider area, and many of them seem to have come from near the back of the original rock.
In the seventh and final stage, melting and fragmentation continue until the pieces are moving too slowly to give off visible light.
A thin layer known as a fusion crust then forms and darkens their surfaces, and winds may push them away from their original path before they reach the ground.
The study also explains how the smallest pieces are distributed.
Darrel Robertson of NASA Ames, one of the co-authors, explains that if the back of the main body stays in one piece, it creates a region of low pressure behind it.
This wake pulls smaller fragments along with it, so that the small meteorites end up lying in a narrow strip on the ground.

Observations of real falls are especially valuable because, as co-author Eric Stern points out, laboratories cannot recreate the levels of radiation that a rock experiences when it enters the atmosphere at such high speeds.
One of the events the team studied was a fireball seen over Normandy, France, on 13 February 2023, which was caused by the small asteroid 2023 CX1 and produced meteorites that were later recovered.
The findings may also tell us something about larger objects.
Jenniskens notes that solid asteroids up to several tens of metres across tend to spin faster than bigger asteroids, which are often loose piles of rubble.
The 20-metre asteroid that exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 went through the same seven stages.
Understanding these stages could therefore help scientists to explain why objects of this size burst apart high in the air instead of reaching the ground in one piece.

title: How Jumping Genes Helped Ants Inherit the Earth

sentences.text: About 66 million years ago, an asteroid struck the Earth with catastrophic results.
The impact brought the age of the dinosaurs to an end and triggered a mass extinction in which a large proportion of the planet's species disappeared.
Yet disasters on this scale also create opportunities, because the survivors suddenly find themselves in a world full of empty ecological space.
Among the groups that took advantage of this changed world were the ants.
Today they form the largest family of social insects, with more than 15,000 species found throughout the world.
A new study suggests that the remarkable rise of the ants after the asteroid impact was helped along by an unexpected factor hidden inside their DNA.
The research was led by Dr Lukas Schrader of the Institute for Evolution and Biodiversity at the University of Münster in Germany, and it was carried out by an international team of scientists.

The idea that the asteroid cleared the way for new groups of animals is not new, but the genetic processes that allowed particular groups to take advantage of that opportunity have remained poorly understood.
The team's findings, published in the journal Science Advances, concern a class of DNA sequences known as transposable elements, or, more popularly, 'jumping genes'.
Jumping genes are stretches of DNA that are able to move from one position in a genome to another, often making copies of themselves as they do so.
In many organisms, including humans, such sequences make up a substantial share of the total DNA.
For decades, biologists regarded them mainly as 'genomic parasites': pieces of DNA that spread for their own benefit while contributing little or nothing to the organism carrying them.
There was some justification for this view, since jumping genes can disrupt important genes and are sometimes linked to disease.
More recently, however, scientists have started to see them in a more positive light.
By moving around and copying themselves, jumping genes generate genetic variation, and variation is the raw material on which evolution works.
Earlier studies of primates and bats had already found connections between bursts of jumping gene activity and the emergence of new species.
To find out whether something similar had happened in ants, Schrader and his colleagues compared the genomes of 163 ant species.
These species represented 12 of the 16 subfamilies of ants that are alive today, giving the team a broad view of the family's evolutionary tree.
Subfamilies are the major branches of that tree, and each contains many closely related groups of species.
Comparing so many genomes is a demanding task, but improvements in DNA sequencing have made studies on this scale increasingly practical.
Using the genetic data, the researchers reconstructed how the activity of jumping genes had risen and fallen over a period of roughly 100 million years.
Two clear patterns emerged from the analysis.
First, the lineages whose genomes contained the most jumping genes also tended to be those that include the largest number of species today.
Second, several major ant lineages had each experienced their own surge in jumping gene activity during the early Paleogene, the period that followed the asteroid impact.
Crucially, these surges took place shortly before the lineages concerned diversified into thousands of species.
The timing suggests that the genetic changes were not simply a consequence of diversification but may have helped to drive it.
The researchers also examined which genes had been affected.
They found that jumping genes were associated with the expansion of gene families that code for odorant receptors, the proteins that allow ants to detect smells.
This matters because ants depend heavily on their sense of smell.
Chemical signals enable them to find their way, to recognise members of their own colony and to coordinate the many tasks carried out within a nest.
One possibility is that a lineage which gained new odorant receptors was able to develop new forms of chemical communication, which could in turn have helped it to occupy new ecological niches.

According to Schrader, the asteroid had dramatic consequences for the environment, and he believes his team has now identified the genomic mechanism that links those upheavals to the rapid diversification of ants.
In this picture, the impact provided the opportunity, while jumping genes supplied the genetic raw material that allowed ants to exploit it.

It should be remembered that comparative studies of this kind reveal associations rather than direct proof of cause, and the argument rests largely on the close timing between the bursts of gene activity and the diversification that followed.
Even so, the findings add to a growing body of evidence that pieces of DNA once dismissed as useless may play a central role in shaping the diversity of life on Earth.

sentences.text: Sleep is one of the enduring puzzles of biology.
For hours at a time, a sleeping animal becomes largely unaware of its surroundings, unable to search for food and vulnerable to attack.
It is hard to imagine a behaviour that seems more costly, and yet sleep, or something very like it, appears to be remarkably widespread in the animal kingdom.
For much of the twentieth century, scientific research on sleep concentrated on mammals and birds, partly because these animals show clear changes in brain activity when they sleep.

Over recent decades, however, sleep-like states have been reported in a far wider range of creatures, including insects, and the question of how sleep evolved has become correspondingly more intriguing.
A recent study from the University of Bonn in Germany suggests that the sleep of spiders may be considerably more complex than anyone had suspected.

The researchers, whose results appeared in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, worked with Portia fimbriata, an Australian jumping spider that grows to roughly the size of a one-euro coin.
Portia spiders are unusual hunters, since they specialise in preying on other spiders.
They sometimes deceive web-building species by imitating the vibrations of an insect trapped in a web, luring the owner of the web towards them.
An animal capable of such sophisticated behaviour is an intriguing subject for anyone interested in what sleep does for small brains.
Studying sleep in a spider, however, presents particular difficulties.
In mammals, sleep is usually identified by recording electrical activity in the brain, but the Bonn team did not measure brain activity and relied entirely on what the spiders did.
Each spider was kept on its own in a plastic dish 12 centimetres across and observed under a variety of lighting conditions.
At night, infrared cameras recorded the animals without exposing them to visible light, capturing their sleeping postures, their periods of quiet rest and their bursts of movement.
Over several days and nights, the cameras produced a large collection of high-resolution video.
Simply keeping still, of course, is not the same as being asleep.

To tell the two apart, the researchers played sounds to the spiders and measured how quickly they reacted, because a sleeping animal is normally slower to respond to a disturbance than one that is merely resting.
They also deprived some spiders of sleep in order to see whether the animals would later sleep more to make up for what they had lost, a phenomenon known as sleep rebound.
Both are standard methods for establishing that a period of inactivity is genuine sleep rather than ordinary rest.
The study indicated that the spiders' sleep was not a single uniform state.
Instead, the researchers were able to distinguish two separate stages.
One of these resembled the rapid eye movement (REM) sleep seen in humans and other vertebrates, and it was accompanied by movements of the eyes and twitching of the muscles.
In people, REM sleep is the stage most closely associated with vivid dreaming, so it is tempting to conclude that the spiders, too, were dreaming.
The authors, however, are clear that their findings do not show whether spiders dream, and in my view their caution is fully justified.
Dreaming is a subjective experience, and the only reason we know that humans dream is that they can wake up and describe what they have experienced.
A spider can report nothing of the kind.
Twitching legs or moving eyes might reflect processes that have nothing to do with conscious experience, such as the maintenance of the nervous system.
To claim that a spider dreams on the basis of behaviour alone would be to read far more into the evidence than it can bear.
Yet it would be equally mistaken to dismiss the study as a mere curiosity.
Spiders and vertebrates last shared a common ancestor many hundreds of millions of years ago, and their nervous systems are organised in very different ways.

If both groups have nevertheless arrived at a sleep pattern with two distinct stages, this suggests either that such a pattern is extremely ancient or that it has evolved more than once because it serves some important purpose.

Either possibility would tell us something fundamental about the function of sleep, and the researchers themselves believe that their results may help to explain how sleep evolved in nervous systems that differ greatly from our own.
The Bonn team now plans to compare REM-like sleep across different species of spider and to find out whether spiders sleep in the same way in the wild as they do in the laboratory.
They also intend to investigate the links between sleep and cognition, including what takes place inside the brains of spiders and insects while they sleep.
Finally, they hope to examine how climate change and artificial light at night might disturb the sleep of arthropods.
This last line of enquiry may well prove the most urgent of all.

Artificial lighting now brightens the night across much of the inhabited world, and if sleep matters to small invertebrates as much as it now appears to, the cost of a world that never becomes fully dark could be greater than we have assumed.
