title: The Hidden Glow of the Fire Salamander

sentences.text: The fire salamander is one of Europe's most easily recognised amphibians.
Its glossy black body is marked with bold patches of yellow, a pattern that has long been understood as a warning to predators.
More than a hundred years ago, scientists discovered that the salamander's skin produces samandarines, a group of extremely poisonous compounds made from substances related to cholesterol.
The bright colours, in other words, are an honest advertisement: an animal that tries to eat a fire salamander is likely to regret it.
Biologists call this strategy aposematism, which means the use of eye-catching colours to signal that an animal is dangerous or unpleasant to eat.
Now researchers have found that the species has another visual trait which, until recently, nobody had noticed.
When fire salamanders are lit with ultraviolet (UV) light, parts of their bodies give off a green and cyan glow.

The discovery was made by a team led by scientists from the Museum of Natural Sciences of Barcelona and the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology in Germany, and it was reported in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
The work formed part of a conservation project for amphibians in Catalonia, which was supported by the Barcelona Zoo Foundation.
It is important to distinguish this glow from the light produced by fireflies or deep-sea fish.
Those animals are bioluminescent, which means that they generate their own light through chemical reactions inside their bodies.
Fire salamanders, by contrast, are biofluorescent: they absorb light of one colour and then release it again as a different colour.
As a result, they do not shine in complete darkness, and a human observer needs a UV lamp to see the effect at all.
For a long time, biofluorescence was thought to be almost entirely a feature of marine life, with scorpions among the few known exceptions on land.
In recent years, however, it has been recorded in a growing number of reptiles, birds and amphibians.
What makes the fire salamander unusual is where its glow comes from.
The researchers found that the fluorescence was strongest on the animals' yellow undersides and along their sides.
It originated mainly in the skin glands and in the toxic secretions that these glands release.
Remarkably, the secretions continued to fluoresce for more than 24 hours after they had left the salamander's body.
According to Andrés Brunetti of the Max Planck Institute, the team was not aware of any earlier published reports of fluorescence in the skin secretions of salamanders.
Why should a salamander glow at all?
The researchers are careful to say that they do not yet know, but they have suggested two possible explanations.
The first is communication.
Full moonlight contains a higher proportion of UV and violet light than daylight does, so at night the glow might stand out against the salamander's yellow markings.
Under these conditions, it could help individuals to recognise one another, to judge possible mates, or to find each other in dark or thickly vegetated places.
Martin Kaltenpoth, a director at the Max Planck Institute, has said that fluorescence meets several criteria which suggest that it plays a role in communication.
The second explanation is defence.
If predators can perceive the glow, it might strengthen the warning that is already given by the salamander's yellow patches.
Some animals have eyes that are more sensitive than ours, and they might be able to detect the glow faintly even without the help of a lamp.
In that case, the glowing secretions would act as an additional signal that the animal is best left alone.
Several important questions remain unanswered.

The chemical compound responsible for the glow has not yet been identified, and Salvador Carranza, a member of the team, believes that it is probably a molecule that has never before been found in this species.
The researchers are now working to isolate and describe it, which may reveal where it comes from and whether it matters for the animals' behaviour or survival.
Such knowledge could be valuable, because the fire salamander is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
Across its range, the species is threatened by the loss and fragmentation of its habitat.

sentences.text: For decades, an archaeological site called 'Ubeidiya has held a special place in the study of human prehistory.
Located in the Jordan Valley, a short distance south of the Sea of Galilee, it lies along one of the routes that early humans could have followed as they moved out of Africa.
Excavations there have produced large numbers of stone tools as well as the fossil bones of many animals.
Now a new study suggests that the site is far older than scientists had believed, a finding that could change how we picture the earliest human journeys beyond Africa.
The tools found at 'Ubeidiya belong to what archaeologists call the early Acheulean tradition.
Its best-known products are large tools that have been shaped on both sides, such as hand axes.
The site also contains the remains of numerous animal species, some associated with Africa and others with Asia, and several of these species no longer exist.
This combination of tools and fossils has made 'Ubeidiya a key reference point for researchers trying to understand when and how early humans spread into new regions.
Until recently, the site was thought to be between 1.2 and 1.6 million years old.
However, these figures did not come from direct measurements of the deposits themselves.
Instead, they were based on comparisons with other archaeological sites and with geological evidence from elsewhere.
Such indirect estimates can be useful, but they leave considerable room for error.

To obtain a more reliable date, a team led by Professor Ari Matmon of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Professor Omry Barzilai of the University of Haifa and Professor Miriam Belmaker of the University of Tulsa collected fresh samples from the site.
They then applied three independent dating techniques, each based on a different natural process.
Their results, published in the journal Quaternary Science Reviews, indicate that 'Ubeidiya is at least 1.9 million years old, hundreds of thousands of years older than earlier estimates.
The first method, cosmogenic isotope burial dating, relies on rare isotopes that form when cosmic rays strike rock at the Earth's surface.
Once the rock is buried, these isotopes decay at known rates, so measuring what remains shows how long the rock has been underground.
The second method, palaeomagnetism, makes use of the fact that sediments settling at the bottom of a lake record the direction of the Earth's magnetic field at the time.

Because the magnetic field has reversed many times in the past, the researchers could match the record at 'Ubeidiya to a known period called the Matuyama Chron, which began more than two million years ago.
The third method involved uranium-lead dating of the fossil shells of Melanopsis, a freshwater snail, which provided a minimum age for the layers containing the stone tools.
All three approaches pointed to an age much older than had previously been accepted.
The work was not without its puzzles.
Some of the first cosmogenic measurements suggested that certain rocks were around three million years old, which did not fit the other evidence.
The team traced this conflict to the complicated history of the Dead Sea rift, where sediments were repeatedly laid down, buried, exposed and moved.
In other words, some of the material had been buried long before it was carried to the shore of the ancient lake at 'Ubeidiya and deposited again.
Once this recycling of sediments was taken into account, the conflicting results could be reconciled, and they supported the new, older age.
The revised date makes 'Ubeidiya roughly as old as Dmanisi in Georgia, and the two are now among the oldest known sites of early human activity outside Africa.
This is significant because the stone tools at Dmanisi belong to the simpler Oldowan tradition, whereas those at 'Ubeidiya are of the more advanced Acheulean type.
If the two sites are of similar age, the two toolmaking traditions may have spread out of Africa during overlapping periods rather than one after the other.
It is possible that different groups of early humans carried distinct technologies into new environments at about the same time.
For researchers, the study also carries a lesson about method.
Dates that rely on comparisons with other sites can change substantially once direct measurements become available.
Combining several independent techniques, and paying close attention to the geological history of a site, can help to resolve contradictions that a single method might leave unexplained.
As more early sites are re-examined in this way, the story of how humans first left Africa may turn out to be considerably more complicated than a simple picture of one wave of migration.

title: Reading the Future of Arctic Ice in the Past

sentences.text: When people talk about the shrinking Arctic, they usually picture the summer, when vast areas of ice melt and open water stretches towards the North Pole.
The summer minimum has become a familiar symbol of climate change, and it is the season that has received most of the attention.
Yet a new study argues that winter deserves far more scrutiny than it has been given.
Winter sea ice, after all, is where climate models disagree most, and it largely determines how much heat and moisture escape from the ocean into the atmosphere.
The importance of winter ice is not merely theoretical.
Its decline has been linked to colder winters and heavier snowfall in the United Kingdom, northern Europe and North America.
In March 2025, the annual maximum extent of Arctic sea ice was the lowest in the modern record, and in 2026 the Arctic matched that low again.
Such observations make it urgent to know how winter ice will behave in the coming decades, yet the models used to answer that question produce a wide range of results.
The difficulty is a familiar one in climate science.
Dozens of climate models exist, each built by a different group with slightly different assumptions, and they rarely agree exactly.
A common response is simply to average them, treating every model as equally trustworthy.
The weakness of this approach is clear: if many models share the same bias, averaging them will not remove it.
What is needed is an independent test of which models capture the behaviour of sea ice most accurately.
A team from the University of Cambridge and Mexico's Centro de Investigación en Matemáticas (CIMAT) found such a test in the distant past.
Around 6,000 years ago, during a period known as the mid-Holocene, small changes in the Earth's orbit produced a warmer Arctic with less ice.
Evidence of conditions at that time is preserved in sediment cores taken from the seabed.

The researchers compiled the largest database of its kind on a chemical marker called IP25, which is produced by algae living in sea ice, and combined it with markers from organisms that live in open water.
Together, these records allowed them to reconstruct how much ice covered the Arctic during the mid-Holocene.
The team then compared their reconstruction with simulations of the same period from 27 climate models.
Taken together, the models produced more winter sea ice than the ancient evidence supported.
Using a statistical technique known as Bayesian weighting, the researchers gave greater influence to the models that matched the evidence well and less to those that matched it poorly.
Because the physical processes controlling sea ice are the same in different climates, the same weights could then be applied to simulations of the recent past and the future.
The results were striking.
Once the models were weighted, the excess of ice that had appeared in their simulations of the recent past disappeared.
More significantly, projections of future winter sea ice fell by roughly one million square kilometres compared with earlier estimates.
At the same time, the range of possible outcomes narrowed, by as much as 85 per cent in some projections.
In other words, the study suggests not only that the Arctic will probably lose more winter ice than expected, but also that scientists can be more confident about how much.
An obvious objection is that the mid-Holocene is a poor guide to the present, since its warmth was caused by changes in the Earth's orbit rather than by human activity.
The lead author, Crystal Fu of the Scott Polar Research Institute at Cambridge, rejects this argument.
In her view, the cause of the warming does not alter the physics: whether the warming is natural or human-made, sea ice melts when it gets warmer.
She also points out that records of past climate have been accumulating for decades, but that it has been hard to link them to projections because of uncertainty at both ends.
Her co-author Marco Aquino-López of CIMAT adds that the method produces more reliable maps of where winter ice is likely to disappear and makes clearer how much uncertainty remains.
The consequences may extend well beyond the Arctic itself.

When the researchers applied the same weighting to precipitation, they found signs that current models may underestimate future snowfall in south-eastern Greenland and rainfall across the Mediterranean.
Heavier snowfall in Greenland could affect the stability of its ice sheet, while more rain in the Mediterranean could raise the risk of flooding in southern Europe.
If so, the effects of Arctic warming may be more widespread than existing predictions indicate.
The study also carries a broader lesson for climate science.
The past is not a perfect copy of the future, but it offers something that models cannot provide on their own: a record of how the real climate system actually behaved.
Rather than treating every model as equally reliable, scientists can use such records to judge which models deserve more trust.
If this approach is extended to other parts of the climate system, it could help turn a confusing spread of projections into clearer guidance for those who must plan for a changing world.

title: Hiding Heat: A Cloak for Infrared Eyes

sentences.text: Most people associate invisibility cloaks with fantasy stories, but engineers have been working for years on a more practical version.
Instead of hiding objects from the human eye, these devices aim to conceal them from instruments that detect heat.
Every warm object gives off infrared radiation, and thermal cameras turn this radiation into images that reveal differences in temperature.
A thermal cloak tries to make an object blend into its surroundings so completely that such a camera cannot tell it is there.
A team at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has now built what it describes as the first three-dimensional cloak of this kind.
The project was led by Shelly Zhang, a professor of civil and environmental engineering, together with postdoctoral researcher Weichen Li and graduate student Yibo Wang.
They worked with Professor Ole Sigmund of the Technical University of Denmark, and their results were published in the journal Nature Communications.
Funding for the research came from the National Science Foundation, the Villum Foundation and the Air Force Office of Scientific Research.
Earlier thermal cloaks had serious limitations.
Some worked only in two dimensions, while others functioned only when heat was travelling in one particular direction.
The new device, by contrast, can conceal objects of many different shapes, and it works for heat arriving from many different directions.
This flexibility matters because, in real situations, heat rarely flows in a single neat line.
The basic idea behind the cloak is surprisingly simple.
Rather than trying to block heat, which would itself create a suspicious hot or cold spot, the cloak steers heat around the hidden object.
The heat then continues on its way as if nothing had interrupted it.
As a result, an infrared camera records the same temperature pattern that it would see if the space were empty.
To achieve this, the researchers returned to the principles of a field known as transformation thermotics, which studies how specially designed materials can redirect the flow of heat.
They asked what kind of internal structure a material would need in order to provide almost all of the thermal properties required for perfect cloaking.
Their answer was a lattice-based material whose structure can be adjusted independently in three directions.
By changing the lattice, the team could control how easily heat passed through each part of the cloak.
The new material covers a much wider range of thermal conductivities than previous designs and comes close to the ideal values predicted by theory.
Importantly, the team did not stop at computer simulations.
They used a 3D metal printer to produce an intricate aluminium lattice, which acts as a set of efficient pathways for heat.
They then cast a rubber-like material, which conducts heat poorly, into the remaining gaps.
The combination of a good conductor and a poor one allowed them to guide heat precisely where they wanted it to go.
In the laboratory, the cloak was placed between a hot region and a cold region, so that heat was forced to flow through the surrounding environment.
An infrared camera then recorded the temperature patterns around the device.
The cloak guided heat around the hidden area while leaving the surrounding pattern almost unchanged, so the camera saw nothing unusual.
At the same time, the temperature inside the cloak remained uniform, which meant that the concealed space was protected from the extreme conditions outside.

The researchers were even able to hide complex 3D shapes, including detailed forms resembling human heads, and they say that no earlier experimental cloak had combined such complicated geometry with similar performance.
The technology could have a number of practical uses.
In electronics, it might help to draw heat away from sensitive components, improve the cooling of microchips and protect devices working in harsh conditions.
In security and defence, it could potentially hide people or equipment from thermal detection, or shield valuable objects from severe temperatures.
Zhang describes the wider aim as hiding and protecting the information that heat carries.
There is, however, an obvious next challenge.
The current cloak protects objects from heat that comes from outside, but it cannot yet hide an object that produces heat itself.
Doing so would require materials that can actively gather, spread or guide thermal energy as conditions change.
The team regards this as the next step towards cloaks that do not simply shield objects but actively manipulate heat.

title: What an Ancient Eclipse Tells Us

sentences.text: On 17 July 709 BCE, observers at the court of the Lu Duchy in ancient China watched the Sun disappear completely behind the Moon.
The event was preserved in the Spring and Autumn Annals, a chronicle compiled roughly two to three centuries later, which states simply that the Sun was totally eclipsed.
More than 2,700 years afterwards, an international team of researchers has returned to this brief record.
By combining historical geography with modern astronomical calculations, they have reconstructed how the eclipse would have looked from Qufu, the capital of the Lu state.
Their study, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, provides more precise evidence about how fast Earth was spinning in ancient times.
Why did Chinese courts keep such careful records of the sky?
For many centuries, successive dynasties employed specialists whose job was to watch for unusual celestial events.
Such events were treated as omens, and the practice of interpreting signs in the heavens was closely bound up with politics.
An eclipse or an aurora, for instance, might be read as a sign that a ruler had behaved improperly.
As a result, records were kept with great care over long periods, and they are now a valuable resource for scientists who study ancient eclipses.
When the team first calculated the path of the 709 BCE eclipse, however, they ran into a problem.
When existing estimates of Earth's ancient rotation were used, the eclipse did not appear to have been total when seen from the location usually given for Qufu.
This suggested that something was wrong, either with the historical record or with the calculations.
The researchers eventually traced the mismatch to the geographical coordinates used for the city.
After checking archaeological excavation reports and other historical evidence, they found that earlier studies had placed Qufu about eight kilometres away from its real position.
Once this error was corrected, the apparent conflict between the record and the calculations disappeared.
The corrected location allowed the team to examine Earth's rotation more closely.
Our planet does not spin at a perfectly constant rate.
Tidal friction caused by the Moon's gravity has been gradually slowing it down, which means that Earth turned slightly faster 2,700 years ago than it does today.
Scientists describe the difference between Earth's actual rotation and a perfectly uniform time scale using a value called delta T.
For the 709 BCE eclipse, the team estimated delta T at between 20,264 and 21,204 seconds.

According to coauthor Mitsuru Sôma of the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan, the new data correct coordinate errors in earlier studies of Earth's rotation and will also help to date historical astronomical events more accurately.
The study also looked at a second, much later source.
The Hanshu, or Book of Han, written around seven centuries after the eclipse, adds a description in which the Sun appears entirely yellow above and below.

Lead author Hisashi Hayakawa of Nagoya University, who holds doctorates in both solar physics and oriental history, believes that this may be one of the earliest surviving written descriptions of the solar corona, the outer atmosphere of the Sun.
However, the researchers are careful to separate their two claims.
The 709 BCE event is the earliest total solar eclipse to be explicitly recorded and securely dated, and its timing is reliable enough for studying Earth's rotation.
The description of the corona, by contrast, comes from a text written centuries later and must be treated as tentative.
If the description is accurate, it could reveal something about the behaviour of the Sun at that time.
The Sun normally follows an activity cycle of about 11 years, but it occasionally enters long quiet periods called grand minima, when sunspots are rare and cycles are weak.
One of these, the Neo-Assyrian or 'Homer' Grand Minimum, lasted from roughly 808 to 717 BCE, so the eclipse took place shortly after it had ended.

The appearance of the corona described in the Hanshu suggests strong magnetic activity, possibly close to the peak of an 11-year cycle, which would be consistent with a Sun that had resumed its regular cycles.
This matters because scientists usually reconstruct past solar activity from radiocarbon stored in tree rings.
Radiocarbon is produced by cosmic rays in the atmosphere, and trees absorb it and fix it in their annual growth rings.
When the Sun is more active, its magnetic field deflects many of these cosmic rays, so radiocarbon levels act as a record of solar activity.
Coauthor Mathew Owens of the University of Reading says that the eclipse account could serve as a useful reference point for tree-ring and ice-core reconstructions.
The account agrees with earlier radiocarbon-based findings, although, given the uncertainty about the corona description, it cannot be regarded as definite proof.

Meng Jin of the Lockheed Martin Solar and Astrophysics Laboratory points out that ancient observers were highly skilled, and that combining their records with modern computational methods may reveal much more about the distant past of both Earth and the Sun.

sentences.text: Shipwrecks are among the most valuable sources an archaeologist can hope for, because each one preserves a moment frozen in time: a cargo, a route and a voyage that ended suddenly.
A wreck recently found off the coast of southern Turkey may now prove to be the oldest of them all.
On the basis of the pottery it carried, a research team has tentatively dated the ship to between about 2700 and 2400 BCE, roughly 4,500 years ago.
If that date holds, the vessel would be older than the current record holder, a wreck off the Greek island of Dokos that is around 4,200 years old.
It is worth stressing, however, that the work is unfinished and that the findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.
The wreck was located in 2024 by Hakan Öniz of Akdeniz University, an archaeologist who has spent decades studying this stretch of coast.
It lies in shallow water off Kekova, west of the city of Antalya, and Öniz was led to it by local seafarers who knew of the site.
In 2026 he invited Karin Sowada of Macquarie University, an archaeologist who normally works at desert sites, to help date the pottery.
For a specialist used to working on dry land, the underwater excavation involved unfamiliar methods and painstaking conservation.
The date the team has proposed is provisional, and further study could push it either earlier or later.
What happened to the ship can only be partly reconstructed.
It was apparently sailing along the southern coast of Turkey, although its final destination remains unknown.
The most likely explanation for its loss is that the crew, caught in a storm, tried to shelter in the calm water between two islands, and the vessel struck the rocks.
The sailors may well have come from the Levant, the region along the eastern shore of the Mediterranean.
Nothing remains of the wooden hull, but much of the cargo is still embedded in a rocky slope on the seabed.
Divers spent four months carefully prying pieces of pottery free from the barnacles that had grown over them.
In the absence of the ship itself, the pottery is the key to the whole story.
Unlike wood, fired clay can survive for thousands of years, and the forms of ancient vessels carry a great deal of information.
The cargo included large storage jars known as amphorae: egg-shaped, flat-bottomed containers with two handles, many of them circled by a raised band of clay around the middle.
Their shape and method of construction help archaeologists to date the cargo, while their style hints at where they were made and what they once held.

Some of these belted jars, or at least the clay used to make them, may have come from the Central Jordan Valley, which is consistent with the idea that the ship collected its cargo at several different ports rather than loading it all in one place.
Residues can still be seen inside some of the jars, and although chemical analyses have yet to be carried out, they may turn out to be olive oil, wine or tree resin.
In my view, however, the real importance of the Kekova wreck lies less in its record-breaking age than in what it may reveal about trade.
Commerce in the eastern Mediterranean between 3000 and 2000 BCE is far less well understood than trade in later periods.
What scholars do know comes mainly from Egyptian texts, from pottery, and from materials discovered in tombs.
It is known, for example, that at around this time, the age of the mighty pharaohs who built at Giza, Egypt traded through the port of Byblos in what is now Lebanon.
Through such contacts it imported goods it lacked at home, including cedar, tin or lead, oils, tree resins, lapis lazuli and silver.
Research also indicates that by around 2600 BCE Egypt was obtaining silver from the Lavrion mines near modern Athens.
It would be tempting to link the Kekova ship directly to Egypt, but this would go beyond the evidence.
Egyptian ships probably did not make this particular voyage.
What seems more likely is that the vessel was one part of a wider international network of exchange.

If the residues in the jars do prove to be oil, wine or resin, they would match products that appear in Egyptian texts, and the wreck would provide rare physical evidence of the kind of trade those texts describe.
This, far more than the precise date, is what could make the find a missing piece in our picture of how the early Bronze Age Mediterranean was connected.
Nonetheless, caution is needed.

A single wreck cannot reveal an entire trading system, and every conclusion drawn so far, from the date of the voyage to the origins of the jars and the nature of their contents, will remain tentative until the scientific analyses are complete and the research has been examined by other specialists.
Enthusiasm for a record-breaking discovery should not be allowed to run ahead of the evidence.
What is beyond doubt is that the southern Turkish coast is extraordinarily rich in ancient wrecks, and several of the world's best-known examples have been found there.
Since maritime archaeology is still a relatively young discipline, it seems likely that these waters hold many more surprises.

sentences.text: For most people, the word 'fungus' brings to mind a small mushroom on a lawn or a patch of mould on old bread.
Yet a discovery in the forests of Yunnan, in south-western China, shows that some fungi can reach a truly impressive size.

Scientists from the Kunming Institute of Botany, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, have described a new species whose upright reproductive structures can grow to around 50 centimetres tall and weigh as much as 2.2 kilograms.
The discovery was reported in the journal Frontiers in Fungal Biology.
The researchers named the species Dianjunus rex, although it is already better known by its nickname, 'D-rex'.
The fungus was found during surveys of several different kinds of forest in the province.
These included temperate conifer forests near Damaidi and Yipinglang, as well as a tropical rainforest near Nanbang.
At these sites, the researchers noticed large, whitish structures rising out of the ground beside Chinese cork oak trees.
On closer inspection, the structures turned out to be growing from the woody roots of the oaks, in the zone of soil around the roots that scientists call the rhizosphere.
The team suspected that they were looking at a fungus that nobody had yet identified.
D-rex belongs to the Ascomycota, the largest major group of fungi, which contains more than 64,000 known species.
Unlike typical mushrooms, ascomycetes do not form true mushroom structures.
Instead, they produce their spores inside, or on the surface of, tiny sac-like structures contained within their fruiting bodies.
In D-rex, these fruiting bodies take the form of tall, upright structures known as stromata.

Before this discovery, the tallest ascomycete fruiting bodies on record measured only about 20 to 30 centimetres, so the new species is substantially taller than any previously known member of the group.
To study the fungus properly, the team collected samples and stored reference specimens in the institute's collections.
They also grew its spores in the laboratory so that they could examine its physical features in detail.
In addition, they sequenced the fungus's genome, including the genes that carry the instructions for making proteins.

When the genetic results were combined with the physical evidence, it became clear that D-rex was so different from other fungi that it needed not only a new genus but also an entirely new family, which the researchers named Dianjunaceae.
This family belongs to a larger group, the order Xylariales.
The species name honours the ancient Dian kingdom, which once existed in the region, and also refers to the fungus's remarkable size.
Its closest known relative is a fungus called Graphostroma platystoma, which grows on dead hardwood across the Northern Hemisphere.
Members of the Xylariales are well known for producing chemical compounds and enzymes that can break down complex plant molecules.
The researchers suspect that D-rex uses similar enzymes to decompose dead wood and take nutrients from it.
Using a technique known as a molecular clock, they also compared its DNA with genetic data from hundreds of other fungi whose evolutionary histories are already understood.
This allowed them to estimate that the D-rex family first appeared around 65 million years ago.
That date falls roughly one million years after the mass extinction that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs.
The team suggests that the collapse of forests at that time may have left behind huge amounts of dead plant material, creating new opportunities for fungi that feed on decaying wood.
But why should a fungus grow so tall?
One possible explanation is that height helps it release its spores above the dense vegetation of the forest floor, where they can more easily be carried away by the wind.
However, building such a large structure requires a great deal of energy.
According to Dr Indunil Senanayake, the study's corresponding author, this strategy probably evolved only in places where the benefits of spreading spores further outweighed the cost.

The researchers believe that China's subtropical forests are particularly good places for unusual fungi to develop, thanks to their wide variety of habitats, relatively stable climate and complex interactions between species.
Even so, many fungi in the region have received little attention from scientists.
Difficult terrain makes some forests hard to explore, and fruiting bodies often appear only in certain seasons or remain hidden from view.
In the past, researchers have also tended to concentrate on species with commercial value.
The team expects that further exploration will reveal many more species, as well as evolutionary histories that nobody has yet predicted.

transcriptTranslations: 至少在美国，求职描述和面试中经常会提到“热情”一词。总的来说，人们对有热情的人持正面看法，认为他们很可能实现自己的目标。但说到预测成就时，热情的重要性是否被夸大了？
根据斯坦福大学的一项新研究，热情在某些文化中的重要性可能较低，而热情常被视为成就关键这一事实，或许反映了一种明显具有西方特色的动机模式。研究考察的主要因素是一个社会的个人主义程度。研究人员断言，在个人主义文化中，人们更容易受到追求与自身热情相关道路的激励；而集体主义文化中的人则更可能将自己视为某个社会网络的一部分。他们往往更重视履行对他人的义务，而不是专注于自身的兴趣。
研究人员考察了来自近60个国家的数据。他们发现，在科学类学科中，热情与学业成就呈正相关。更高程度的愉悦感和兴趣也会提高测试成绩。
但这种相关性的强度在不同文化之间并不相同。在美国、澳大利亚和英国等个人主义社会中，热情与成就之间的联系更为紧密。而对于哥伦比亚或泰国等更加集体主义的社会而言，热情对表现的影响则更为微妙。
数学和阅读方面的成就也呈现出同样的情况。从这些研究结果可以清楚看出，热情并不是激励人们实现目标的唯一因素。
为什么自然界会形成各种图案？图案之所以经常出现在自然界中，原因很简单：在许多形成图案的物质和生物中，相同的基本物理或化学过程会反复发生。无论是在植物和动物中，还是在岩石、泡沫和冰晶中，自然界中出现的复杂图案，归根结底都与原子和分子层面发生的事情有关。
自然界中的图案，是指形状或颜色有规律地重复排列的任何形式。其中一些最引人注目的例子包括英国巨人之路上六边形的岩石阵列，以及热带鱼身上色彩斑斓的条纹和斑点。这类图案在材料经历干燥、冻结、起皱、扩散和反应等过程时，会先在微小尺度上开始形成。随后，这些变化会在更大尺度上产生人们能够看见的复杂图案。
想象一下冬天窗户上精致的冰晶。是什么形成了这种图案？水结冰时，其中的分子开始聚集在一起。水分子具有特殊的弯曲形状，这使它们在冻结时会堆叠成团。随着团簇不断增大，包括湿度和温度在内的许多外部因素开始影响它的整体形状。例如，如果水是在窗户上结冰，玻璃表面的随机瑕疵就会影响分子的堆叠，并形成更大的图案。
但科学家并不总是知道某种图案的作用，甚至不知道它是否具有作用。相关的分子过程足够简单，因此它们可能只是偶然形成了某种图案。

transcript.text: Makeup can do more than just change your appearance—it can also alter others' perceptions of you, for better or for worse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: According to new research from the University of Stirling in Scotland, although both men and women perceive women who wear makeup as being of a higher status, men associate makeup with prestigious, positive qualities, while women view other women wearing makeup as being dominant and a potential threat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The research showed that men and women both rated the faces with cosmetics as being more attractive, but only women rated made-up faces as being more dominant, while only men rated made-up faces as being higher in prestige.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: A follow-up study investigated the root cause behind these differences in perception, and found that female-on-female jealousy seemed to be the main cause of the differences in perception.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Women rating women with makeup said they would be more jealous of them and thought they would be more attractive to men than their non-makeup wearing counterparts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Cosmetic products are good for more than just giving you a pretty face.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It can be particularly useful for women to understand how wearing makeup alters others' perceptions of them in situations where they are trying to gain others' trust and admiration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: At a job interview, knowing whether the hiring committee will consist of men or women might influence a female candidate's decision about wearing makeup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Whether the interviewers will view her as attractive, dominant and prestigious can affect the interviewers' actions and perhaps the outcome of the interview itself.

transcript.text: You may have seen advertisements trumpeting methods of changing a habit that require absolutely no willpower whatsoever.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But can you really change a bad habit or create a good one without willpower?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: To answer this question, we first have to ask: "What is willpower?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Most people, sadly, think of it only as the ability to clench their teeth and resist attractive temptations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In this view, willpower means self- denial and no fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: No wonder people hope to make changes without it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: I define willpower as "using only the thought of your motivators to control your actions."
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Let's say your motivators are "prevent diabetes" and "reach a healthy weight".
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So if you are at the all-you-can-eat buffet, you think about your motivator—avoid diabetes through weight loss—and you take small portions and avoid the dessert table.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So, amazingly enough, willpower begins with a thought—a bright idea—some way to improve your life or contribute to others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: This bright idea is your motivator.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Doctor Walter Mischel, an expert on willpower skills, uses the expressive term "a burning goal".
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Whether you call it a motivator, a burning goal, or a bright idea, this idea is the force behind your willpower.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: What sort of bright ideas—motivators—make for effective willpower?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In fact, any goal that you value strongly counts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The list may include good health, self-respect, a better future for your family, a personal mission and being a role model for your child.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: All these can certainly drive a positive change.

transcriptTranslations: 化妆不仅能改变你的外表，还能改变他人对你的看法，结果可能更好，也可能更糟。根据苏格兰斯特灵大学的一项新研究，虽然男性和女性都认为化妆的女性地位更高，但男性会将化妆与有声望、积极的品质联系起来，而女性则认为化妆的其他女性更具支配性，并可能构成威胁。
研究表明，男性和女性都认为化妆后的面孔更具吸引力，但只有女性认为化妆后的面孔更具支配性，只有男性认为化妆后的面孔具有更高的声望。
一项后续研究探究了这些认知差异背后的根本原因，发现女性之间的嫉妒似乎是造成这种认知差异的主要原因。对化妆女性进行评价的女性表示，她们会更嫉妒这些女性，并认为相比不化妆的女性，她们对男性更具吸引力。
化妆品的作用不只是让你拥有一张漂亮的脸。对于女性而言，了解化妆如何改变他人对自己的看法，尤其是在试图赢得他人的信任和钦佩时，可能非常有用。在求职面试中，了解招聘委员会由男性还是女性组成，可能会影响女性求职者是否化妆的决定。面试官是否会认为她具有吸引力、支配性和声望，可能会影响面试官的行为，甚至可能影响面试本身的结果。
你可能见过一些广告大肆宣扬无需任何意志力就能改变习惯的方法。但你真的能够在没有意志力的情况下改掉坏习惯或养成好习惯吗？要回答这个问题，我们首先必须问：“什么是意志力？”遗憾的是，大多数人只把它看作咬紧牙关、抵制诱人诱惑的能力。在这种看法中，意志力意味着自我克制和毫无乐趣。难怪人们希望不借助意志力就能做出改变。
我把意志力定义为“仅凭想到自己的动机来控制行为”。假设你的动机是“预防糖尿病”和“达到健康体重”。那么，当你在自助餐厅面对不限量供应的食物时，你会想到自己的动机——通过减重来避免糖尿病——于是少量取食，并避开甜点区。
所以，令人惊讶的是，意志力始于一个想法——一个改善生活或为他人做出贡献的好主意。这个好主意就是你的动机。
意志力技能专家沃尔特·米歇尔博士使用了“一个燃烧的目标”这一生动的说法。无论你把它称为动机、燃烧的目标，还是好主意，这个想法都是意志力背后的力量。
什么样的好主意——也就是动机——能够产生有效的意志力？事实上，任何一个你高度重视的目标都算在内。这个清单可能包括良好的健康状况、自尊、为家人创造更美好的未来、个人使命，以及成为孩子的榜样。所有这些都确实能够推动积极的改变。

transcript.text: Many people, myself included, have multiple areas of life they would like to improve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: For example, I would like to reach more people with my writing, to lift heavier weights at the gym, and to start practising mindfulness more consistently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Those are just a few of the goals I find desirable, and you probably have a long list yourself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The problem is, even if we are committed to working hard on our goals, our natural tendency is to return to our old habits at some point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Recently I've come across a few studies that will make these difficult lifestyle changes a bit easier.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: As you'll see, however, the approach to mastering many areas of life is somewhat counterintuitive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Research has shown that you are two to three times more likely to stick with your habits if you make a specific plan for when, where, and how you will perform the behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: For example, in one study, scientists asked people to fill out a sentence to specify during the next week they would do at least 20 minutes of vigorous exercise on which day, at what time of day, and at or in what place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were two to three times more likely to actually exercise compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Psychologists call these specific plans implementation intentions because they state when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: However, follow-up research has discovered implementation intentions only work when you focus on one thing at a time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In fact, researchers found that people who tried to accomplish multiple goals were less committed and less likely to succeed than those who focused on a single goal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Another science-based reason to focus on one thing at a time is that when you begin practising a new habit, it requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: After a while, however, the pattern of behavior becomes easier.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Eventually, your new habit becomes a normal routine, and the process is more or less mindless and automatic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The most important thing to note is that there is some tipping point at which new habits become more or less automatic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The time it takes to build a habit depends on many factors, including how difficult the habit is, your genetics, and more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It was a lazy, hazy, crazy day on the dwarf planet Pluto when New Horizons, a spacecraft from Earth, flew by at a speed of 31,000 mph (miles per hour) two years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The spacecraft took a bunch of photos, made some quick measurements of Pluto's atmosphere, and sent them all back here, giving planetary scientists their first up-close look of the distant dwarf planet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: One of the more bizarre things they found was that the haze in Pluto's atmosphere was much thicker than previously thought.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The planet also had an atmosphere much cooler than earlier estimates, topping out at −333.4°F.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Now, a study published in Nature links those two atmospheric observations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: A computer model developed by planetary scientist Xi Zhang and colleagues shows the haze of tiny droplets in the upper atmosphere is likely scattering light from the Sun, preventing heat from reaching the planet below.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: We see hazy skies on Earth too, from time to time, whenever solid particles get suspended in the air—from water-based fogs, to ash from fires, to the toxic droplets that make up a thick smog.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But on Earth, the overall temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: On Pluto, the authors suggest, haze might be more influential.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Particles can reflect light from the Sun here on Earth: It happens after volcanoes erupt, emitting clouds of particles that reflect the Sun's rays into the atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Some people even propose imitating this phenomenon to alleviate the effects of climate change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But our planet isn't dominated by that process, or at least it hasn't been for a few billion years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: If Pluto's atmosphere is very different from ours and from that of other nearby planets, it could help scientists expand their understanding of planetary atmospheres.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But right now, this is just a good guess based on data from New Horizons and a sophisticated computer model, not direct observations of the haze's composition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: There are other theories floating around to explain Pluto's cool temperatures, including blaming the cold air on gases in the atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Luckily, the authors will get a chance to test their notions when the James Webb Space Telescope launches later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: That observatory can detect different spectrums of light, which the hazy Plutonian atmosphere would be positively glowing with as it scattered sunlight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The researchers just have to wait and see if the light from the telescope validates their bright idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Parents have a small window where they can influence their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste, researchers have concluded.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The 24-month time frame comes at an age when youngsters are old enough to appreciate poetic lyrics and snappy tunes, but have not yet started to be embarrassed by their mother and father's preferences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Hauke Egermann, a lecturer in music at the University of York, carried out a literature review into more than a dozen studies looking at parental musical influence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: "Children have an openness to new music, and this means parents have an important role to play in developing the musical preferences of their kids," he said.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: However, time is of the essence as parental influence is most likely to be effective during the critical time period before age ten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: During adolescence, children tend to gravitate away from their parents' choices and are more influenced by their peers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: A separate survey of 2,000 British parents by music streaming service Deezer also found that nearly four-fifths of parents agreed that their children were far more receptive to their musical suggestions before the age of ten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In contrast, just 10 percent of parents reported positive reactions from their teenage children when they shared their favorite music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Some 79 percent of fathers said they had tried to influence their children's music, but just 69 percent of mothers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: However, mothers were more effective, with 38 percent reporting that their kids loved the tunes they shared, compared to 30 percent of dads who, in some cases, said their children cried or even fell asleep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Egermann claims introducing children to a variety of musical styles is the key to fostering good taste in later life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: "By playing children a variety of genres before this critical period, research on familiarization suggests they will enjoy lots of different types of music as adults," he added.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The benefits of having a wider taste in music include the ability to manage their emotions more effectively, socialize and bond with others more easily, and to have a better understanding of other cultures as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Egermann advises parents not to push their favorite music too hard on their children, but instead play it as background music while a child is playing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: They can also help create positive memories about artists and bands by going to concerts and live music events together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcriptTranslations: 包括我在内，许多人都希望改善生活中的多个方面。例如，我希望通过写作让更多人读到我的作品，希望在健身房举起更重的重量，也希望开始更加持续地练习正念。这些只是我认为值得追求的几个目标，而你自己可能也列有一长串目标。问题在于，即使我们决心为目标努力奋斗，我们的自然倾向仍然是在某个时候回到旧有习惯。要永久改变生活方式确实非常困难。

最近，我接触到了一些研究，这些研究将使这些艰难的生活方式改变变得稍微容易一些。不过，正如你将看到的，掌握生活中许多方面的方法有些违背直觉。研究表明，如果你针对自己将在何时、何地以及如何实施某种行为制订具体计划，那么坚持这些习惯的可能性会提高到原来的两到三倍。例如，在一项研究中，科学家要求人们填写一个句子，具体说明自己将在下一周的哪一天、一天中的什么时间，以及在什么地点进行至少20分钟的剧烈运动。研究人员发现，与没有为未来行为制订计划的对照组相比，填写了这个句子的人实际进行锻炼的可能性高出两到三倍。心理学家将这些具体计划称为“执行意图”，因为它们说明了你打算在何时、何地以及如何实施某种特定行为。
然而，后续研究发现，执行意图只有在你一次专注于一件事时才会奏效。事实上，研究人员发现，试图实现多个目标的人，比专注于单一目标的人投入程度更低，成功的可能性也更小。

一次专注于一件事还有一个基于科学的理由，那就是当你开始练习一种新习惯时，记得去做这件事需要付出大量有意识的努力。然而，过一段时间之后，这种行为模式会变得更加容易。最终，你的新习惯会成为一种日常惯例，而这一过程或多或少会变得无需意识参与，并且自动进行。需要注意的最重要一点是，存在这样一个临界点：在此之后，新习惯会或多或少地变得自动化。养成一个习惯所需的时间取决于许多因素，包括习惯的难度、你的遗传因素，以及其他因素。
两年前，在新视野号这艘来自地球的航天器以每小时31,000英里（英里/小时）的速度飞掠而过时，矮行星冥王星度过了慵懒、朦胧而疯狂的一天。这艘航天器拍摄了大量照片，对冥王星的大气层进行了一些快速测量，并将这些数据全部传回地球，使行星科学家们首次近距离观察到这颗遥远的矮行星。
他们发现的较为奇异的现象之一，是冥王星大气层中的霾比先前认为的厚得多。这颗行星的大气层也比早先估计的冷得多，最高温度仅为−333.4°F。
如今，《自然》杂志发表的一项研究将这两项大气观测结果联系了起来。行星科学家张希及其同事开发的一种计算机模型显示，高层大气中由微小液滴形成的霾很可能会散射来自太阳的光，阻止热量抵达下方的行星。地球上也会不时出现雾霾天气，每当固体颗粒悬浮在空气中时，就可能形成这种现象，从含水雾气到火灾产生的灰烬，再到构成浓重烟雾的有毒液滴，都是如此。但在地球上，行星的整体温度主要由大气层中气体的分布决定。
作者认为，在冥王星上，霾的影响可能更大。在地球上，颗粒物能够反射来自太阳的光：火山喷发后会释放出由颗粒物组成的云团，将太阳光线反射回大气层。有些人甚至提出模仿这一现象，以减轻气候变化的影响。但我们的行星并不是由这一过程主导的，至少在过去几十亿年里不是如此。
如果冥王星的大气层与地球以及其他邻近行星的大气层截然不同，这将有助于科学家拓展对行星大气层的认识。但目前，这只是基于新视野号获得的数据和一个复杂计算机模型提出的合理推测，而不是对霾的成分进行直接观测所得出的结论。
关于解释冥王星低温的理论还有其他一些，包括把寒冷的空气归因于大气层中的气体。
幸运的是，詹姆斯·韦布空间望远镜稍后发射后，作者们将有机会检验他们的观点。这座天文台能够探测不同光谱的光，而冥王星朦胧的大气层在散射阳光时很可能会发出大量这样的光。研究人员只需等待并观察望远镜接收到的光是否会验证他们的这个妙想。
研究人员得出结论，父母有一个短暂的窗口期，可以影响8至10岁孩子的音乐品味。这段24个月的时期处于这样一个年龄阶段：孩子已经足够大，能够欣赏富有诗意的歌词和朗朗上口的曲调，但还没有开始因父母的音乐偏好而感到尴尬。约克大学音乐讲师豪克·埃格尔曼博士对十多项有关父母音乐影响的研究进行了文献综述。他说：“孩子对新音乐持开放态度，这意味着父母在培养孩子的音乐偏好方面扮演着重要角色。”

然而，时间至关重要，因为父母的影响最有可能在十岁以前这一关键时期发挥作用。进入青春期后，孩子往往会逐渐远离父母的选择，并更多地受到同龄人的影响。音乐流媒体服务Deezer对2000名英国父母进行的另一项调查也发现，近五分之四的父母认为，孩子在十岁以前更容易接受他们的音乐建议。相比之下，只有10%的父母表示，孩子进入青少年时期后，在他们分享自己喜爱的音乐时会作出积极反应。约79%的父亲表示曾试图影响孩子的音乐选择，而母亲的这一比例仅为69%。不过，母亲的影响更有效：38%的母亲表示孩子喜欢她们分享的曲调，而父亲中只有30%的人得到这样的反馈；有些父亲甚至表示，孩子听着听着哭了起来，或者睡着了。
埃格尔曼博士认为，让孩子接触各种各样的音乐风格，是培养他们日后良好音乐品味的关键。他补充说：“有关熟悉化的研究表明，在这一关键时期之前让孩子聆听多种音乐类型，他们成年后将会喜欢许多不同种类的音乐。”拥有更广泛的音乐品味所带来的益处包括更有效地管理情绪、更容易与他人交往并建立联系，以及更好地理解其他文化。
埃格尔曼博士建议，父母不要过分强迫孩子接受自己喜爱的音乐，而应在孩子玩耍时将其作为背景音乐播放。他们还可以通过一起参加音乐会和现场音乐活动，帮助孩子对音乐家和乐队形成积极的记忆。

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say is really difficult?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） Making a permanent lifestyle change.
**题目译文**
说话者说什么是真正困难的？
A) 一下子改掉所有旧习惯。
B) 永久改变生活方式。
C) 实现自己设定的所有人生目标。
D) 改善生活的多个方面。
**定位** 问题是，即使我们致力于努力实现目标，我们的自然倾向还是在某个时刻回到旧习惯。永久改变生活方式真的很难。
**信号** 题眼词复现 + 总结句。题干中的 difficult 在 Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult 中直接复现；这是段落末尾的总结句，前面用 The problem is 铺垫，信息落点在 really difficult 上。
**替换** Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult↔Making a permanent lifestyle change同义复现
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱Eliminating all the old habits at once 盗用了 return to our old habits 里的 old habits，但原文说的是“回到旧习惯”，不是“一次性根除旧习惯”，且 at once 原文未提。借用原文： return to our old habits
C) 偷换概念Realizing all the life goals one has set 把 working hard on our goals 和 the goals I find desirable 改成“实现所有既定目标”，但原文只说“努力追求目标”，并未说实现所有目标，all 也过于绝对。借用原文： the goals I find desirable
D) 答非所问Improving multiple areas of one's life 在 multiple areas of life they would like to improve 中确实出现，但那是 speaker 列举的“人们想改善的方面”，不是题干问的“really difficult”的事。借用原文： multiple areas of life they would like to improve
questions.quote: The problem is, even if we are committed to working hard on our goals, our natural tendency is to return to our old habits at some point. Making a permanent lifestyle change is really difficult.

options.text: Eliminating all the old habits at once.
Making a permanent lifestyle change.
Realizing all the life goals one has set.
Improving multiple areas of one's life.

questions.prompt: What did researchers find about people with implementation intentions?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） They were more likely to implement a particular behavior.
**题目译文**
研究人员发现，具有执行意图的人有什么特点？
A) 他们更有可能实施某种特定行为。
B) 他们更有可能为自己的未来制订计划。
C) 他们往往致力于实现单一目标。
D) 他们往往一次专注于一件事。
**定位** 研究人员发现，填写了这句话的人真正去锻炼的可能性是对照组的两到三倍，而对照组没有为他们未来的行为制定计划。
**信号** 研究结论标志词。题干问 researchers find，原文 Researchers found that 正是结论信号；其后 two to three times more likely to actually exercise 给出量化结果。
**替换** two to three times more likely to actually exercise↔more likely to implement a particular behavior具体实例概括为行为实施how you intend to implement a particular behavior↔ implement a particular behavior词组复现
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱more likely to make plans for their future 盗用了 did not make plans for their future behavior 里的 make plans for their future，但原文说对照组“没有”做计划，而实验组是“已经做了计划”并被发现有计划后更可能去锻炼，不是“更可能去做计划”。借用原文： did not make plans for their future behavior
C) 张冠李戴tended to be committed to a single goal 把 focused on a single goal 从“专注单一目标的人更容易成功”移花接木到“有 implementation intentions 的人”，而题干问的是implementation intentions 组，不是单一目标组。借用原文： focused on a single goal
D) 偷换概念focus on one thing at a time 来自 focus on one thing at a time，但这是 follow-up research 关于“单一目标”的限制条件，不是 researchers 对 implementation intentions 组的发现。借用原文： focus on one thing at a time
questions.quote: Researchers found that people who filled out this sentence were two to three times more likely to actually exercise compared to a control group who did not make plans for their future behavior.

options.text: They were more likely to implement a particular behavior.
They were more likely to make plans for their future.
They tended to be committed to a single goal.
They tended to focus on one thing at a time.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, what is required of you when you begin practising a new habit?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） A lot of conscious effort to remember to do it.
**题目译文**
说话者认为，当你开始培养一种新习惯时，对你有什么要求？
A) 使这一过程自动化的能力。
B) 一份切实可行的实施时间表。
C) 需要付出大量有意识的努力来提醒自己去做这件事。
D) 专注于它将带来的好处。
**定位** 另一个一次只专注一件事的科学依据是，当你开始练习一个新习惯时，你需要付出大量有意识的努力去记住去做这件事。
**信号** 时间状语 + 需求动词。题干中的 when you begin practising a new habit 在 when you begin practising a new habit 中原样复现，紧随其后的 requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it 就是答案所在。
**替换** requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it ↔A lot of conscious effort to remember to do it名词短语截取
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 与原文相反The ability to make the process automatic 来自 the process is more or less mindless and automatic，但那是 after a while / eventually 之后的阶段，不是 begin 阶段；题干问的是刚开始，因此相反。借用原文： the process is more or less mindless and automatic
B) 张冠李戴A practical timetable for implementation 把 when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior 里的具体计划要素（when/where/how）包装成timetable，但这是关于 implementation intentions 的研究，不是开始养成新 habit 时的普遍要求。借用原文： when, where, and how you intend to implement a particular behavior
D) 未提及Concentration on the benefits it will provide 中 benefits 一词在录音中未被提及，属于用常识编造的干扰项。
questions.quote: Another science-based reason to focus on one thing at a time is that when you begin practising a new habit, it requires a lot of conscious effort to remember to do it.

options.text: The ability to make the process automatic.
A practical timetable for implementation.
A lot of conscious effort to remember to do it.
Concentration on the benefits it will provide.

questions.prompt: What was one of the more bizarre findings about Pluto's atmosphere?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） It has a haze much thicker than previously believed.
**题目译文**
关于冥王星大气层较为离奇的发现之一是什么？
A) 它以许多难以想象的方式与地球大气层相似。
B) 它的大气霾层比先前认为的厚得多。
C) 它比早先估计的温度低333.4华氏度。
D) 它远远超出了任何快速测量的范围。
**定位** 他们发现的一件更离奇的事情是，冥王星大气中的霾层比之前认为的要厚得多。
**信号** 题干关键词复现 + 比较级信息。录音中 One of the more bizarre things they found 与题干中的 finding 直接呼应，随后 was much thicker than previously thought 给出具体特征，正是答案所在。
**替换** the haze in Pluto's atmosphere was much thicker than previously thought↔It has a haze much thicker than previously believed.同义词 + 主谓压缩
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及录音通篇未说冥王星大气在‘不可思议的方面’与地球相似；A 项利用考生对地球类比的生活预设制造干扰，但原文没有依据。
C) 原词陷阱C 项盗用了 333.4°F 与 earlier estimates 两个原词，但把原文‘最高温度为 −333.4°F（比此前估算更冷）’偷换成‘低了 333.4°F’，既丢掉负号又混淆了绝对温度与温度差，是典型的数字原词陷阱。借用原文： 333.4°F
D) 未提及D 项说‘远超任何快速测量’，但原文 made some quick measurements of Pluto's atmosphere 只是提到做了快速测量，并未说它无法测量或超出测量范围。
questions.quote: One of the more bizarre things they found was that the haze in Pluto's atmosphere was much thicker than previously thought.

questions.prompt: What is said to determine the overall temperature on Earth?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） The distribution of gases in its atmosphere.
**题目译文**
据说是什么决定了地球的整体温度？
A) 空气中固体颗粒的积聚。
B) 其大气层中气体的分布。
C) 反射太阳光线的颗粒云。
D) 气候变化加剧的影响。
**定位** 但在地球上，行星的整体温度是由大气中气体的分布所主导的。
**信号** 转折后给出地球情况的结论。录音先用 Pluto 的 haze 机制做铺垫，随后用 But on Earth一转，指出 the overall temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere，直接回答题干中的 determine the overall temperature on Earth。
**替换** the overall temperature of the planet is dominated by the distribution of gases in our atmosphere↔The distribution of gases in its atmosphere.主被动转换 + 同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A 项的 solid particles in the air 直接来自 solid particles get suspended in the air，但原文说的是地球‘雾/霾天’的成因，并非决定地球整体温度的因素，属于盗用原词答非所问。借用原文： solid particles get suspended in the air
C) 原词陷阱C 项的 clouds of particles reflecting sun rays 来自 emitting clouds of particles that reflect the Sun's rays into the atmosphere，但那是火山喷发后的局部现象，不是决定地球整体温度的主因。借用原文： clouds of particles that reflect the Sun's rays into the atmosphere
D) 与原文相反D 项说 climate change 的加剧效应决定温度，而原文 alleviate the effects of climate change 讲的是‘缓解’气候变化，并非‘加剧’；选项把 alleviating 偷换成 aggravated，极性相反。借用原文： alleviate the effects of climate change

options.text: The accumulation of solid particles in the air.
The distribution of gases in its atmosphere.
The clouds of particles reflecting sun rays.
The aggravated effects of climate change.

**信号** 题干关键词 wait and see 原词复现。录音末句 The researchers just have to wait and see 与题干中的 wait and see 完全对应，随后的 if 从句就是答案所在。

questions.prompt: What do we learn from researchers' conclusion at the beginning of the talk?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） Parents can mould their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste.
**题目译文**
演讲开头研究人员的结论让我们了解到什么？
A) 父母可以在培养孩子的音乐天赋方面发挥决定性作用。
B) 孩子们因父母不欣赏自己的音乐而感到难堪。
C) 父母可以塑造8至10岁孩子的音乐品味。
D) 8至10岁的孩子已经足够大，能够创作富有诗意的歌词。
**定位** 研究人员得出结论：父母有一个短暂的窗口期，可以影响8到10岁孩子的音乐品味。
**信号** 研究结论标志词。答案句以researchers have concluded结尾，是典型的研究结论标志；同时句首直接给出结论内容，符合篇章开头'先给结论'的常见结构。
**替换** influence their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste↔mould their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste influence与mould同义替换Parents have a small window where they can ↔ Parents can small window限定为可能性
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱选项中的musical talent在原文中从未出现，原文讲的是music taste；同时decisive role把原文a small window夸大成'决定性作用'，与原文程度不符。借用原文： Parents have a small window where they can influence their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste
B) 原词陷阱原文have not yet started to be embarrassed by their mother and father's preferences说的是'还不会因父母的偏好感到尴尬'，而选项说成'Children are embarrassed by parents' failure to appreciate their music'，既把对象从'父母的偏好'偷换成'父母不欣赏孩子的音乐'，又把否定'not yet'变成了肯定。借用原文： have not yet started to be embarrassed by their mother and father's preferences
D) 原词陷阱原文old enough to appreciate poetic lyrics说的是'足够大去欣赏富有诗意的歌词'，选项却改成'produce poetic lyrics'，把appreciate偷换成produce，动作主体和方向都错了。借用原文： old enough to appreciate poetic lyrics
questions.quote: Parents have a small window where they can influence their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste, researchers have concluded.

options.text: Parents can play a decisive role in cultivating their children's musical talent.
Children are embarrassed by parents' failure to appreciate their music.
Parents can mould their 8- to 10-year-old children's music taste.

questions.prompt: What does Dr. Hauke Egermann say about adolescents?

Hauke Egermann博士对青少年有何看法？
A) 他们开始表现出自己的音乐偏好。
B) 他们往往更容易受到同龄人的影响。
C) 他们往往会逐渐离开家。

questions.tip:

questions.prompt: What is the key to fostering good taste in later life, according to Dr. Hauke Egermann?
questions.explanation:

**题目译文**
据Hauke Egermann博士说，培养日后良好品味的关键是什么？
A) 让孩子能够接受音乐专家的建议。
B) 帮助孩子培养管理情绪的能力。
C) 让孩子熟悉不同的音乐流派。
D) 让孩子接触各种音乐风格。
**定位** 埃格曼博士称，让孩子接触多种多样的音乐风格是培养其日后良好品味的关键。
**信号** 专家观点+the key to结构。原文Dr. Egermann claims是专家观点标志，紧接着出现is the key to fostering good taste in later life，与题干中的the key to fostering good taste in later life完全对应。
**替换** introducing children to a variety of musical styles↔Introducing children to a variety of musical styles核心名词短语保留claims ↔ according to Dr. Hauke Egermann claims与according to同义
questions.tip:
**排除**

questions.quote: Dr. Egermann claims introducing children to a variety of musical styles is the key to fostering good taste in later life.

options.text: Enabling children to be receptive to music experts' suggestions.
Helping children develop the ability to manage their emotions.
Familiarising children with different schools of music.
Introducing children to a variety of musical styles.

questions.prompt: How can parents help children create positive memories about artists and bands?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） By attending their concerts and live music events with children.
**题目译文**
父母如何帮助孩子对艺术家和乐队留下积极的记忆？
A) 通过提高孩子对其音乐的鉴赏力。
B) 通过强行让孩子接受他们的音乐。
C) 通过和孩子一起参加他们的音乐会和现场音乐活动。
D) 通过尽早向孩子介绍他们的音乐。
**定位** 他们还可以通过带孩子一起去听音乐会和现场音乐演出来帮助创造关于艺人和乐队的积极记忆。
**信号** 题干关键词复现+by doing方式状语。原文help create positive memories about artists and bands与题干完全复现，其后的by going to concerts and live music events together就是具体方式。
**替换** by going to concerts and live music events together↔By attending their concerts and live music events with children going to与attending同义，together与with children同义
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及选项中的enhancing children's appreciation of their music虽然与全文话题相关，但原文在P4中并未把它作为'create positive memories'的具体方法提出。
B) 与原文相反原文advises parents not to push their favorite music too hard on their children明确建议父母不要把喜欢的音乐强行推给孩子，而选项却说'By pushing their music hard enough upon children'，正好与专家建议相反。借用原文： advises parents not to push their favorite music too hard on their children

questions.quote: They can also help create positive memories about artists and bands by going to concerts and live music events together.

我知道。但纪念日就要到了，我还在手忙脚乱地找住宿。要么贵得离谱，要么已经全部订满。我开始有点慌了。
这样吧，如果你们要去整整一周，为什么不先在一个非常豪华的地方住几个晚上，然后把剩下的时间安排在海岸线再往北一点的地方，那里住宿更便宜，这样就能抵消住昂贵地方的费用了？
这或许是个不错的计划。租车也不算太贵，所以我们还是可以开车进城。对了，城外有很多地方带游泳池，而且提供全包服务，这样我们连吃饭和饮料的钱都不用另外付了。我现在就发个咨询，问问我们感兴趣的日期是否有空。
听起来太完美了。我相信简一定会高兴坏的。我真的很推荐去参观那座教堂。你们可以一直登到顶部，但要到那里必须爬一段非常陡的螺旋楼梯。
考虑到简恐高，我要是想让她去爬那个，我回来时可能就已经离婚了。不过还是谢谢你的帮助；这件事本来都快变成一场后勤噩梦了。
嗨，保罗。最近怎么样？
嗨，苏珊。就是忙着做平常的事，开处方药、和患者聊聊他们的用药情况之类的。你呢？
我也一样，不过今天早上来了一个挺有意思的病例。一位患者来咨询一种药，而这种药可能会和她已经在服用的另一种药产生相互作用。
哦，这种情况总是很棘手。你怎么处理的？
我尽可能向她解释了这个问题，并建议她再向医生确认一下。你猜怎么着？她真的听从了我的建议，最后医生给这位患者换了药。
啊，那太好了。你一定很有成就感。
完全是。这些时刻是我日常工作中最精彩的部分，运用我的药学专业知识来促进人们的健康和福祉。
我完全同意。遗憾的是，当患者太固执、不肯听我们的话时，情况就正好相反。
确实如此。另外，最近有很多人来接种流感疫苗，这总是件令人高兴的事。
很好，很好。我一直在为患有慢性疾病的患者制定一个新的药物治疗管理项目，帮助患者更有效地管理他们的用药。
听起来很有意思。
我们会检查他们所有的药物，确保他们按照处方服用。我们还会查找任何潜在的药物相互作用或副作用。到目前为止，患者的反响非常积极。有些人说自己的健康状况有所改善，看到这一点真的很令人欣慰。
听到这个真好。你们会使用短信提醒吗？
是的，当然会。
这是个很好的主意。用药依从性差是个大问题，尤其是对老年患者来说。
这个项目还处于早期阶段，但我希望它能真正改善我们患者的情况。

questions.prompt: What is the man planning to do?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） Celebrate his 10th wedding anniversary.
**题目译文**
这个男人计划做什么？
A) 庆祝他的结婚十周年纪念日。
B) 在巴塞罗那庆祝他的升职。
C) 给他的妻子一个惊喜。
D) 请假去巴塞罗那。
**定位** 下周是我结婚十周年纪念日，我答应 Jane 会给我们订一次城市短途旅行，因为我有年假要休，而且去个暖和的地方庆祝会很好。
**信号** 承诺句+原因铺陈。男士用 I promised Jane that I would book a city break for us 直接说明自己的计划，后面 as 引出原因；这是典型的'被问者应答'，直接承载答案。
**替换** It's my 10th wedding anniversary next week↔ Celebrate his 10th wedding anniversary.事件同义概括I promised Jane that I would book a city break for us↔Celebrate his 10th wedding anniversary.计划句→事件目的
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱Celebrate his promotion in Barcelona. 盗用了原文 in Barcelona，但录音说的是去Barcelona 庆祝周年纪念，而非庆祝升职，promotion 未提及。借用原文： in Barcelona
C) 过度推断Give his wife a pleasant surprise. 把原文 I promised Jane 的浪漫氛围曲解为 surprise，录音中男士是答应订旅行，并未说是惊喜。
D) 原词陷阱Ask for leave to visit Barcelona. 盗用原文 as I have annual leave to take，但录音说'有年假要休'，并非'申请请假'，动作被偷换。借用原文： as I have annual leave to take
questions.quote: It's my 10th wedding anniversary next week, and I promised Jane that I would book a city break for us, as I have annual leave to take, and it would be nice to celebrate somewhere warm.

options.text: Celebrate his 10th wedding anniversary.
Celebrate his promotion in Barcelona.
Give his wife a pleasant surprise.
Ask for leave to visit Barcelona.

questions.prompt: Why is the man starting to feel a bit frantic?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） He is unable to find some inexpensive accommodation.
**题目译文**
这个男人为什么开始感到有些慌乱？
A) 他找不到价格便宜的住宿。
B) 每年的这个时候，适合去的温暖地方很少。
C) 在度假之前，他有太多事情要做。
D) 他担心巴塞罗那可能没有预期的那么棒。
**定位** 但纪念日越来越近，我还在拼命找住宿。要么贵得离谱，要么已经订满。我开始有点慌了。
**信号** 问题铺陈+情绪词。I'm still scrambling to find accommodation 点明困难，Everything is either wildly expensive or already fully booked 具体说明，I'm starting to feel a bit frantic 直接回应题干情绪。
**替换** I'm still scrambling to find accommodation ↔He is unable to find some inexpensive accommodation.动作+结果同义改写Everything is either wildly expensive or already fully booked ↔He is unable to find some inexpensive accommodation.反向同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱There are few warm places to go at this time of the year. 盗用原文 somewhere warm，但原文说想找个暖和地方庆祝，没说暖和地方少，属原词陷阱。借用原文： somewhere warm
C) 过度推断There is so much for him to do before going on vacation. 把找住宿的困难扩大为'很多事要做'，录音未提及其他事务，属过度推断。
D) 与原文相反He is afraid Barcelona may not be so fabulous as expected. 与女士说的 fabulous cosmopolitan city 方向相反，且男士慌乱原因是住宿而非担心城市不好。借用原文： fabulous cosmopolitan city
questions.quote: But the anniversary is looming, and I'm still scrambling to find accommodation. Everything is either wildly expensive or already fully booked. I'm starting to feel a bit frantic.

options.text: He is unable to find some inexpensive accommodation.
There are few warm places to go at this time of the year.
There is so much for him to do before going on vacation.
He is afraid Barcelona may not be so fabulous as expected.

questions.prompt: What does the woman suggest the man do?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题）Spend a couple of nights in a glamorous hotel and the rest of the week in inexpensive places.
**题目译文**
这个女人建议这个男人做什么？
A) 租一辆车开进市区并前往景点，以节省交通费用。
B) 在豪华酒店住几个晚上，其余时间住在价格便宜的地方。
C) 寻找包含所有费用的住宿，这样就不必另外支付食物和饮料的费用。
D) 住在远离海岸的酒店，那里的住宿费用较低。
**定位** 嗯，如果你要去一整周，为什么不先找家很华丽的地方住两晚，然后剩下的时间住到海岸更北一点的地方，那里住宿更便宜，可以抵消贵地方的费用。
**信号** 建议句型 why don't you。why don't you do a couple of nights in somewhere really glamorous 是典型的建议句，且该句包含具体方案（住两晚贵的+其余住便宜的），直接对应题干。
**替换** do a couple of nights in somewhere really glamorous ↔Spend a couple of nights in a glamorous hotel and the rest of the week in inexpensive places.同义替换：地点下位化+动词替换do the rest of the week a bit further up the coast, where the accommodation is cheaper ↔Spend a couple of nights in a glamorous hotel and the rest of the week in inexpensive places.同义替换： cheaper accommodation = inexpensive places
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴Rent a car to drive into the city and scenic spots so as to save the expenses on transportation. 盗用原文 It's not too expensive to rent a car，但这是男士对建议的回应，不是女士原建议，属张冠李戴。借用原文： It's not too expensive to rent a car
C) 张冠李戴Find all-inclusive accommodation to eliminate the need to pay for food and drinks.盗用原文 all inclusive, so we wouldn't even need to pay for food or drinks，但这是男士想到的后续方案，并非女士最初建议。借用原文： all inclusive, so we wouldn't even need to pay for food or drinks
D) 偷换概念Stay in a hotel away from the coast where the accommodation is less expensive. 盗用原文 a bit further up the coast，但原文是'沿海岸更往北'，不是'远离海岸'，方向被改动。借用原文： a bit further up the coast
questions.quote: Well, if you are going for a whole week, why don't you do a couple of nights in somewhere really glamorous, and then do the rest of the week a bit further up the coast, where the accommodation is cheaper, and that will offset the cost of the expensive place?

options.text: Rent a car to drive into the city and scenic spots so as to save the expenses on transportation.
Spend a couple of nights in a glamorous hotel and the rest of the week in inexpensive places.
Find all-inclusive accommodation to eliminate the need to pay for food and drinks.
Stay in a hotel away from the coast where the accommodation is less expensive.

questions.prompt: What does the man say about his wife Jane?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） She is scared of heights.
**题目译文**
这个男人怎样评价他的妻子简？
A) 她肯定会喜欢那座大教堂。
B) 她内心是个浪漫的人。
C) 她不擅长安排事务。
D) 她恐高。
**定位** 考虑到 Jane 恐高，我觉得如果我硬让她上去，回来就得离婚了。
**信号** 人物评价形容词 terrified。Jane is terrified of heights 直接给出 Jane 的特征，是题干所问的答案句。
**替换** Jane is terrified of heights ↔ She is scared of heights.近义形容词替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴She is sure to like the cathedral. 盗用女士推荐 I really do recommend visiting that cathedral，但这是女士对景点的推荐，不是男士对妻子的评价，且男士暗示妻子不会爬上去。借用原文： I really do recommend visiting that cathedral
B) 张冠李戴She is a romantic at heart. 盗用原文 That sounds so romantic，但这是女士评价男士计划浪漫，不是说 Jane 浪漫。借用原文： That sounds so romantic
C) 偷换概念She is no good at logistics. 盗用原文 logistical nightmare，但 nightmare 说的是订行程麻烦，不是说 Jane 不擅长 logistics。借用原文： logistical nightmare
questions.quote: Considering Jane is terrified of heights, I think if I tried to make her do that, I would come back divorced.

options.text: She is sure to like the cathedral.
She is a romantic at heart.
She is no good at logistics.
She is scared of heights.

questions.prompt: What do we learn about the speakers?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） They are both pharmacists.
**题目译文**
我们了解到关于说话者的什么情况？
A) 他们经常分享彼此的经历。
B) 他们喜欢与患者互动。
C) 他们总是把事情做得很棘手。
D) 他们都是药剂师。
**定位** 嗨，苏珊娜。就是忙着平常的活儿，配药、跟病人聊他们的用药情况，诸如此类的事。
**信号** 工作内容即身份。男性说话者在开场问候后直接描述日常工作：filling prescriptions, talking to patients about their medications，这些正是药剂师的典型职责，从而泄露两人身份。
**替换** filling prescriptions, talking to patients about their medications↔They are both pharmacists下位职责→上位职业
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 过度推断对话中两人确实交流了工作情况，但 They often share each other's experiences 中的often 和 share each other's experiences 都是过度概括，录音并未支持。
B) 偷换概念录音提到 talking to patients about their medications，但那是工作内容，并未说 enjoy interacting with patients，选项把行为偷换成情感态度。
C) 原词陷阱They always do things tricky 盗用了录音中的 tricky 原词，但原文 that's always tricky指的是处理药物相互作用这件事棘手，不是说说话者做事狡猾或爱耍花招。借用原文： that's always tricky
questions.quote: Hi, Suzanne. Just keeping busy with the usual stuff, filling prescriptions, talking to patients about their medications, that kind of thing.

options.text: They often share each other's experiences.
They enjoy interacting with patients.
They always do things tricky.
They are both pharmacists.

questions.prompt: What does the woman say about an interesting case she had?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） The patient actually took her advice.
**题目译文**
关于她遇到的一起有趣的病例，女子说了些什么？
A) 医生最终承认了自己的错误。
B) 患者向另一位医生进行了咨询。
C) 患者实际上采纳了她的建议。
D) 医生向她进行了再次确认。
**定位** 我尽可能向她解释了这个问题，并建议她和医生再确认一下。你知道吗？她真的听从了我的建议，医生最终更换了病人的药物。
**信号** 强调词后出结果。女士先说建议内容，然后用 And you know what? 引出关键结果，再用actually 强调 She actually followed my advice，这是答案落点。
**替换** She actually followed my advice↔ The patient actually took her advice同义替换+代词还原
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱The doctor ended up admitting his mistake 盗用了录音中的 the doctor ended up switching the patient's medication，但把 switching the medication 偷换成了admitting his mistake，内容完全改变。借用原文： the doctor ended up switching the patient's medication
B) 偷换概念录音说 recommended she double-check with her doctor，是病人和自己的医生确认，不是咨询另一位医生，选项添加了 another。
D) 张冠李戴录音是女士建议病人 double-check with her doctor，即病人去和医生确认；选项 The doctor double-checked with her 把动作主体换成了 doctor，对象换成了女士，主谓宾关系完全颠倒。借用原文： recommended she double-check with her doctor
questions.quote: I explained the issue to her as best I could, and recommended she double-check with her doctor. And you know what? She actually followed my advice, and the doctor ended up switching the patient's medication.

options.text: The doctor ended up admitting his mistake.
The patient consulted another doctor.
The patient actually took her advice.
The doctor double-checked with her.

questions.prompt: What does the man say he has been working on?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） A new medication therapy management program.
**题目译文**
男子说他一直在进行什么工作？
A) 一份关于如何更有效地接种流感疫苗的提案。
B) 一个新的药物治疗管理项目。
C) 一种说服固执患者的新策略。
D) 一种针对病情相似患者的治疗方案。
**定位** 好，好。我一直在为我们的慢性病病人开发一个新的药物治疗管理项目。它帮助病人更有效地管理他们的药物。
**信号** 题干关键词复现。题干中的 has been working on 与录音中的 I've been working on 直接对应，这是典型的问答同构定位信号，紧跟其后的宾语就是答案。
**替换** I've been working on a new medication therapy management program ↔A new medication therapy management program直接对应，去掉主谓
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A proposal for applying flu shots more effectively 盗用了录音 get their flu shots 中的flu shots，但那是女士提到的人流疫苗接种话题，与男士 working on 的项目无关。借用原文： get their flu shots
C) 原词陷阱A novel strategy to persuade stubborn patients 盗用了录音 the patient is too stubborn and they refuse to listen to us 中的 stubborn，但那是两人感叹病人难劝，不是男士正在做的项目。借用原文： the patient is too stubborn and they refuse to listen to us
D) 偷换概念录音说 patients with chronic conditions（慢性病患者），选项 A therapy for patients with similar conditions 把 chronic 偷换成 similar，概念被替换。借用原文： patients with chronic conditions
questions.quote: Good, good. I've been working on a new medication therapy management program for our patients with chronic conditions. It helps patients manage their medications more effectively.

options.text: A proposal for applying flu shots more effectively.
A new medication therapy management program.
A novel strategy to persuade stubborn patients.
A therapy for patients with similar conditions.

questions.prompt: What is a big problem, especially for older patients according to the woman?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） Medication non-adherence.
**题目译文**
据女子所说，尤其是对老年患者而言，一个大问题是什么？
A) 无法发送短信。
B) 不信任药学专家。
C) 不按医嘱服药。
D) 需要不断提醒。
**定位** 用药不依从是一个大问题，尤其对老年患者来说。
**信号** 判断句与题干一一对应。女士直接说 Medication non-adherence is a big problem, especially for older patients，与题干 What is a big problem, especially for older patients according to the woman? 几乎逐词对应。
**替换** Medication non-adherence is a big problem, especially for older patients ↔Medication non-adherence原词复现
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱Inability to send text messages 盗用了录音 text message reminders 中的 text messages，但那是解决用药依从性的提醒手段，不是大问题本身。借用原文： Do you use text message reminders?
B) 未提及录音中没有提到患者或公众对 pharmaceutical experts 的不信任，选项属于无中生有。
D) 答非所问录音提到 text message reminders 是为了解决 medication non-adherence，Need for constant reminding 把提醒需求当作大问题，但女士明确说的大问题是 Medication non- adherence。借用原文： Do you use text message reminders?
questions.quote: Medication non-adherence is a big problem, especially for older patients.

options.text: Inability to send text messages.
Distrust in pharmaceutical experts.
Medication non-adherence.
Need for constant reminding.

transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: For many pregnant women, understanding what seafood is safe and healthy and what should be avoided because of mercury concerns comes with a lot of worrying.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In part, that's because the federal government's advice on the matter, first issued in 2004, has long been criticized as vague.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: That guidance has included advice on how much seafood to eat, and which species pregnant and breastfeeding women should avoid over concerns about mercury contamination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But critics say the government advisory has done more harm than good, scaring many pregnant and breastfeeding women away from eating seafood altogether.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The problem is real.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: According to a spokesman for the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA for short, the agency analyzed fish consumption data from more than 1,000 pregnant women in the US and found that 21 per cent of them ate no fish whatsoever in the previous month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: And those who did eat fish consumed far less than recommended by the dietary guidelines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Some 50 per cent ate less than two ounces a week and 75 per cent ate less than four ounces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: This week the FDA issued an update to the advice, listing more than sixty species in a chart that ranks fish as A Best Choice, Good Choice and Choices to Avoid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The goal is to make it easier for mothers-to-be to feel confident about the type of seafood they include in their diets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The new advice recommends consumers choose a variety of fish to eat, and it comes with an easy-to-understand illustration of what an appropriate portion size should be—four ounces for an adult and two ounces for children aged four to seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: And while expectant mothers have long been warned to stay away from shark and four other particular types of fish from the Gulf of Mexico, now there are three new species on the list of what to avoid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But not everyone is thrilled with the new advice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Critics say the new advice doesn't always agree with the agency's own scientific findings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: While mercury is of great concern when people are talking about pregnant women and seafood, it's not the only factor contributing to anxiety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The FDA maintains that its final consumption recommendations were based on thorough scientific analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Agency spokesman Cassell says the FDA believes their recommendations will increase confidence, not uncertainty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But critics disagree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: They think the FDA's advice is not based on the evidence in its own detailed report, and so it confuses everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Question 16. What does the speaker say about the federal government's advice on seafood safety?
