transcript.text: Now, believe it or not, people sometimes lie in order to maintain a good, honest reputation—even if it hurts them to do so.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: At least, this is what a team of scientists is suggesting, with evidence to prove it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Picture this scenario: You often drive for work and can be compensated for up to 400 miles per month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Most people at your company drive about 300 miles each month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But this month, you drove 400 miles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: How many miles do you think you'd claim in your expense report?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The scientists asked this exact question as part of the study we're discussing today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: With surprising results, they found that 12% of respondents reported the distance they drove as less than the actual figure, giving an average answer of 384 miles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In other words, they lied about the number of miles, even though they would forfeit money they were owed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The researchers believe this was to seem honest, with the assumption being that others would be suspicious of a high expense claim.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The researchers explain that many people care a great deal about their reputation and how they'll be judged by others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: If they care enough, their concern about appearing honest and not losing the respect of others may be greater than their desire to actually be honest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The researchers assert that the findings suggest that when people obtain very favorable outcomes, they anticipate other people's suspicious reactions and prefer lying and appearing honest to telling the truth and appearing as selfish liars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So why is this research important?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Well, experts generally agree there are two main types of lie-selfish lies and lies that are meant to benefit others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The first, as you may predict, is for selfish gain, such as submitting a fraudulent claim to an insurance company, while the second involves lying to help others or not offend others, for example, telling a friend whose outfit you don't like that they look great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But the researchers are suggesting a third type of lying—lying to maintain a good reputation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Now this hypothesis is new and some skeptics argue that this isn't a whole new category of lie.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But the findings seem intuitive to me.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: After all, one of the main motivations for lying is to increase our worth in the eyes of others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So it seems highly likely that people will lie to seem honest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Question 19. What did a team of scientists find in their study?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Question 20. Why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment according to the researchers?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Why do old people dislike new music?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: As I've grown older, I often hear people my age say things like "They just don't make good music like they used to".
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Why does this happen?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Luckily, psychology can give us some insights into this puzzle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Musical tastes begin to crystallize as early as age 13 or 14.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: By the time we're in our early 20s, these tastes get locked into place pretty firmly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In fact, studies have found that by the time we turn 33, most of us have stopped listening to new music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Meanwhile, popular songs released when you're in your early teens are likely to remain quite popular among your age group through the rest of your life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: There could be a biological explanation for this, as there's evidence that the brain's ability to make subtle distinctions between different chords, rhythms and melodies deteriorates with age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So to older people, newer, less familiar songs might all "sound the same".
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But there may be some simpler reasons for older people's aversion to newer music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: One of the most researched laws of social psychology is something called the "mere exposure effect", which, in essence, means that the more we're exposed to something, the more we tend to like it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: This happens with people we know, the advertisements we see and the songs we listen to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: When you're in your early teens, you probably spend a fair amount of time listening to music or watching music videos.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Your favorite songs and artists become familiar, comforting parts of your routine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: For many people over 30, job and family obligations increase, so there's less time to spend discovering new music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Instead, many will simply listen to old, familiar favorites from that period of their lives when they had more free time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Of course, those teen years weren't necessarily carefree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: They're famously confusing, which is why so many TV shows and movies revolve around high school turmoil.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Psychology research has shown that the emotions that we experience as teens seem more intense than those that come later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: And we also know that intense emotions are associated with stronger memories and preferences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Both of these might explain why the songs we listen to during this period become so memorable and beloved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So there's nothing wrong with your parents because they don't like your music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Rather it's all part of the natural order of things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcriptTranslations: 你知道吗,美国人现在拥有的空间大约是50年前的三倍?因此,你会认为我们应该有足够的空间来容纳所有物品。恰恰相反,个人仓储业现在是一个不断增长的行业。我们拥有三倍的空间,但我们已经成为如此热衷的消费者,以至于我们需要更多空间。这种现象导致了巨额信用卡债务、庞大的环境足迹,也许并非巧合的是,我们的幸福水平在同样的半个世纪里并没有提高。
我在这里建议一个替代方案:拥有更少实际上可能是一个更好的决定。我们许多人在某个阶段都体验过拥有更少的快乐。我认为更少的物品和更少的空间不仅可以帮助你节约,还可以简化你的生活。
我最近启动了一个创新项目,以发现一些创造性的解决方案,为我提供所需的一切。通过购买一套40平方米而不是60平方米的公寓,我立即节省了20万美元。更小的空间意味着更低的水电费,也意味着更小的碳足迹。因为它是围绕精选的物品设计的,仅限于我最喜欢的东西,我真的很期待住在那里。
我们如何能更简约地生活?首先,我们必须无情地剔除生活中不必要的物品。为了遏制消费,我们应该在购买前思考,并问自己:"它真的会让我更快乐吗?"显然,我们应该拥有一些好东西,但我们想要的是我们会喜爱多年的物品。
其次,我们需要空间效率。我们想要为经常使用而不是偶尔使用而设计的电器。当你连三个炉头都很少用时,为什么要拥有一个六炉头的炉灶呢?
最后,我们需要多功能空间和家居用品。我将可移动墙壁与变形家具相结合,以充分利用我有限的空间。看看我的咖啡桌,它可以扩大尺寸以容纳十个人。我的办公室被隐藏起来,很容易隐蔽。我的床可以从墙里轻松弹出。对于客人,我可以移动可移动墙壁并使用我安装的折叠客床。
我并不是说我们都应该住在小公寓里,但请考虑精简生活的好处。当你回家走进前门时,花点时间问问自己:"我能否进行一些生活精简?那会给我更多自由和更多时间吗?"
信不信由你,人们有时会为了维持良好、诚实的声誉而撒谎——即使这样做会损害他们自己的利益。至少,这是一组科学家提出的观点,并且有证据证明。
想象这样一个场景:你经常因工作而开车,每月最多可以报销400英里。你公司的大多数人每月大约开车300英里。但这个月,你开了400英里。你认为你会在报销单上申报多少英里?
科学家们在我们今天讨论的研究中提出了这个确切的问题。令人惊讶的是,他们发现12%的受访者报告的行驶距离少于实际数字,给出的平均答案是384英里。换句话说,他们在英里数上撒了谎,尽管这样做会放弃本应得到的钱。
研究人员认为这是为了显得诚实,假设是其他人会对高额报销申请产生怀疑。但为什么人们会编造对自己不利的数字呢?研究人员解释说,许多人非常在意自己的声誉以及别人如何评价他们。如果他们足够在意,他们对显得诚实和不失去他人尊重的担忧可能会大于他们真正诚实的愿望。
研究人员断言,这些发现表明,当人们获得非常有利的结果时,他们会预料到其他人的怀疑反应,并且更愿意撒谎显得诚实,而不是说真话显得像自私的骗子。
那么为什么这项研究很重要呢?专家们普遍认为主要有两种谎言——自私的谎言和旨在使他人受益的谎言。正如你可能预测的那样,第一种是为了自私的利益,比如向保险公司提交欺诈性索赔,而第二种涉及为了帮助他人或不冒犯他人而撒谎,例如,告诉一个你不喜欢其着装的朋友说他们看起来很棒。
但研究人员提出了第三种撒谎类型——为了维持良好声誉而撒谎。这个假设是新的,一些怀疑者认为这并不是一个全新的谎言类别。
但这些发现对我来说似乎很直观。毕竟,撒谎的主要动机之一是提高我们在他人眼中的价值。因此,人们很可能会为了显得诚实而撒谎。
为什么老年人不喜欢新音乐?随着年龄增长,我经常听到同龄人说"现在的音乐就是不如以前好"之类的话。为什么会这样?幸运的是,心理学可以为我们提供一些关于这个难题的见解。音乐品味早在13或14岁时就开始固化。到我们20岁出头时,这些品味就相当牢固地定型了。
事实上,研究发现,到我们33岁时,大多数人已经停止听新音乐了。与此同时,在你十几岁早期发行的流行歌曲很可能在你的余生中一直受到你这个年龄段人群的欢迎。
这可能有生物学上的解释,因为有证据表明,大脑区分不同和弦、节奏和旋律的能力会随着年龄增长而退化。所以对老年人来说,较新的、不太熟悉的歌曲可能都"听起来一样"。
但老年人厌恶新音乐可能有一些更简单的原因。社会心理学中研究最多的法则之一是所谓的"单纯曝光效应",其本质是指我们接触某事物越多,就越倾向于喜欢它。这适用于我们认识的人、我们看到的广告以及我们听的歌曲。
当你十几岁早期时,你可能会花相当多的时间听音乐或看音乐视频。你最喜欢的歌曲和艺人成为你日常生活中熟悉的、令人安心的组成部分。
对于许多30岁以上的人来说,工作和家庭义务增加了,因此用于发现新音乐的时间减少了。相反,许多人只会简单地听那些来自他们人生中有更多空闲时间的时期的旧的、熟悉的最爱歌曲。
当然,那些青少年时期并不一定是无忧无虑的。它们以令人困惑而著称,这就是为什么有那么多电视节目和电影围绕高中动荡展开。
心理学研究表明,我们在青少年时期体验到的情绪似乎比后来的情绪更强烈。而且我们也知道,强烈的情绪与更强的记忆和偏好相关联。这两点都可能解释为什么我们在这个时期听的歌曲会变得如此令人难忘和深受喜爱。
所以你的父母不喜欢你的音乐并没有什么问题。相反,这都是自然规律的一部分。

**答案** A （细节题） Their obsession with consumption.

B) 他们未能积累财富。
C) 不断上涨的住房成本。
D) 环境的恶化。
**定位** 我们的空间是过去的三倍，但我们变成了如此热衷的消费者，以至于需要的更多了。这一现象造成了大量信用卡债务、巨大的环境足迹，而且或许并非巧合的是，我们的幸福感在同样这半个世纪里始终没有上升。
**信号** 因果信号 has resulted in 串起原因与结果。答案句靠因果链定位：This phenomenon has resulted in 把前句的『现象』和后面包括『幸福感没上升』在内的一串后果连起来，而那个『现象』正是 we've become such enthusiastic consumers——听到 resulted in 就该把它前面的起因记牢。

The ever-increasing costs of housing.
The deterioration of the environment.

questions.prompt: What things should we possess according to the speaker?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） Things that we cherish most.
**题目译文**
根据说话者的观点,我们应该拥有什么东西?
A) 难以找到的东西。
B) 花费更少钱的东西。
C) 提高效率的东西。
D) 我们最珍视的东西。
**定位** 当然，我们应该拥有一些很棒的东西，但我们想要的是那种我们多年里都会一直喜爱的物品。
**信号** 转折 but 之后才是真意。答案句是个转折结构：we should possess some great stuff, but we want belongings that we're going to love for years，but 之前是垫场，but 之后『多年都会喜爱的东西』才是讲者真正主张的标准——转折后是落点。
**替换** belongings that we're going to love for years↔Things that we cherish most多年一直爱=最珍爱，同义改写
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及Things that are rare to find. 说要拥有『稀有难找』的东西，可录音里讲者强调的是『喜爱、要用很久』，从没把『稀有』当标准，属凭空添加。
B) 原词陷阱录音多次讲精简能省钱（如 less stuff and less space can not only help you economize），Things that cost less money. 就借这个『省钱』印象，把它歪成『要买便宜的东西』——可讲者说的是少买、买耐爱的，并非挑便宜的买。借用原文： less stuff and less space can not only help you economize
C) 张冠李戴原文谈 efficiency 是针对空间和电器（we require space efficiency），Things that boost efficiency. 把这个词挪来回答『该拥有哪类东西』，张冠李戴、答非所问。借用原文： we require space efficiency
questions.quote: Obviously, we should possess some great stuff, but we want belongings that we're going to love for years.

options.text: Things that are rare to find.
Things that cost less money.
Things that boost efficiency.
Things that we cherish most.

questions.prompt: What do we learn about the items in the speaker's home?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） They serve multiple purposes.
**题目译文**
关于说话者家中的物品我们了解到什么?
A) 它们有多种用途。
B) 它们有益于环境。
C) 它们大多经久耐用。
D) 它们容易丢弃。
**定位** 最后，我们需要多功能的空间和家居用品。我把一面可移动的墙和可变形的家具结合起来，从有限的空间里挖出更多用处。看看我的咖啡桌，它能变大、坐得下十个人；我的床直接从墙里翻出来。
**信号** 举例铺陈共同指向『多功能』。答案句先给总述 we need multifunctional spaces and housewares，再用咖啡桌能变大、床能翻出墙这些例子佐证——一连串例子都在证明同一个特征『一物多用』，总述句就是落点。
**替换** multifunctional spaces and housewares↔They serve multiple purposes multifunctional=serve multiple purposes，同义解释
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱录音前面提过小空间带来 a smaller carbon footprint（更小碳足迹），They benefit the environment. 就借这个环保印象，可它是讲『小房子』的好处，不是讲『家中物品』的特征，答非所问。借用原文： a smaller carbon footprint
C) 张冠李戴They are mostly durable.（大多耐用）听上去和精简很搭，但讲者说物品耐用/要用很久是在 17 题语境（love for years），描述家中物品时强调的是『多功能』而非耐用，张冠李戴。借用原文： belongings that we're going to love for years
D) 与原文相反They are easily disposable.（易于丢弃）和原文方向正相反——讲者主张留下能用很久、多功能的好东西，绝不是『随手可丢』；这是把极性听反的陷阱。借用原文： belongings that we're going to love for years
questions.quote: Finally, we need multifunctional spaces and housewares. I combined a movable wall with transforming furniture to get more out of my limited space. Consider my coffee table. It increases in size to accommodate ten. My bed simply pops out of the wall.

options.text: They serve multiple purposes.
They benefit the environment.
They are mostly durable.
They are easily disposable.

questions.prompt: What did a team of scientists find in their study?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） Over 10% of the respondents lied about the distance they drove.
**题目译文**
一组科学家在他们的研究中发现了什么?
A) 所有受访者都害怕提出高额费用报销。
B) 一些受访者给出的平均答案是400英里。
C) 超过10%的受访者谎报了他们驾驶的距离。
D) 大多数受访者因驾驶384英里而获得了补偿。
**定位** 结果出人意料：他们发现有 12% 的受访者把自己开的里程报得低于实际数字，给出的平均答案是 384 英里。换句话说，他们就里程数撒了谎，哪怕这样会让自己损失本应得到的钱。
**信号** 研究发现的标志句 they found that。they found that 12% of respondents reported the distance they drove as less than the actual figure 用 found that 直接领出"研究发现"，正是答案句；其后 they lied about the number of miles 又用 In other words 把发现点透，是双重信号。
**替换** 12% of respondents ↔ Over 10% of the respondents 12% 即"超过10%"，精确数→范围概括they lied about the number of miles↔ lied about the distance they drove number of miles = distance they drove，同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 过度推断选项借了录音的报销语境，但说成 All respondents were afraid of making a high expense claim：录音只说"有 12% 的人"少报，并非 All；"怕报高"也是录音没有的主观情绪，属把范围放大到全体的过度推断。借用原文： 12% of respondents reported the distance they drove as less than the actual figure
B) 原词陷阱选项 gave an average answer of 400 miles 盗用了录音原句式 giving an average answer of 384 miles，却把 384 换成 400。400 在录音里是"可报销上限"（compensated for up to 400 miles），不是"平均答案"，这是典型的"数字配错对象"的原词陷阱。借用原文： giving an average answer of 384 miles
D) 张冠李戴选项 Most of the respondents got compensated for driving 384 miles 拼凑了录音的compensated（见 can be compensated for up to 400 miles）与数字 384，但录音从没说"多数人"因开 384 英里而获补偿——384 是撒谎者报的均值，且撒谎者反而 forfeit money（丢钱），与"获补偿"相反。借用原文： they would forfeit money they were owed
questions.quote: With surprising results, they found that 12% of respondents reported the distance they drove as less than the actual figure, giving an average answer of 384 miles. In other words, they lied about the number of miles, even though they would forfeit money they were owed.

options.text: All respondents were afraid of making a high expense claim.
A number of respondents gave an average answer of 400 miles.
Over 10% of the respondents lied about the distance they drove.
Most of the respondents got compensated for driving 384 miles.

questions.prompt: Why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment according to the researchers?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） They wanted to protect their reputation.
**题目译文**
根据研究人员的说法,为什么人们会编造对自己不利的数字?
A) 他们回应了同事的怀疑。
B) 他们在意其他人的报销申请。
C) 他们想要保护自己的声誉。
D) 他们努力做到真正诚实。
**定位** 可人们为什么要不惜损害自己的利益去捏造数字呢？研究者解释说，许多人非常在意自己的声誉以及别人会怎样评价自己。如果在意到一定程度，他们"想显得诚实、不愿失去他人尊重"的顾虑，可能就盖过了"真心想做个诚实人"的愿望。
**信号** 自问自答 + The researchers explain 领出原因。录音先用 But why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment 自设问题，紧接 The researchers explain that many people care a great deal about their reputation 给出解答，explain 之后正是答案句。
**替换** many people care a great deal about their reputation↔wanted to protect their reputation care about reputation → protect reputation，动机同义not losing the respect of others↔protect their reputation不失他人尊重 = 维护声誉
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱选项 responded to colleagues' suspicion 借了录音的 others would be suspicious of a high expense claim 里的 suspicious。但"别人会起疑"只是研究者点出的表层诱因（assumption），题干问的是 according to the researchers 的根本原因，研究者真正归因于"在意声誉"，故 A 答非所问。借用原文： others would be suspicious of a high expense claim
B) 偷换概念选项 cared about other people's claims 借用了录音的报销语境（claim），并仿造 care about 句式，却把对象偷换了：录音说的是"在意自己的声誉与他人评价"（care a great deal about their reputation and how they'll be judged by others），不是"在意别人的报销单"。借用原文： care a great deal about their reputation and how they'll be judged by others
D) 与原文相反选项 endeavored to actually be honest 原样照搬了录音的 their desire to actually be honest，但录音说"维护声誉的顾虑"may be greater than（盖过）"真心想诚实的愿望"，也就是"真心诚实"恰恰是被压过、被否定的一方，与人们"谎报"的动机相反。借用原文： may be greater than their desire to actually be honest
questions.quote: But why would people fabricate numbers to their own detriment? The researchers explain that many people care a great deal about their reputation and how they'll be judged by others. If they care enough, their concern about appearing honest and not losing the respect of others may be greater than their desire to actually be honest.

options.text: They responded to colleagues' suspicion.
They cared about other people's claims.
They wanted to protect their reputation.
They endeavored to actually be honest.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker think of the researchers' findings?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （态度观点题） They seem intuitive.
**题目译文**
说话者如何看待研究人员的发现?
A) 它们似乎是积极的。
B) 它们似乎是直观的。
C) 它们具有说明性。
D) 它们是结论性的。
**定位** 不过在我看来，这些发现是符合直觉的。毕竟，撒谎的主要动机之一就是抬高自己在别人眼中的价值。所以人们为了显得诚实而撒谎，看上去是很有可能的。
**信号** 转折 But + 第一人称 to me 标出本人态度。前段刚说 some skeptics argue 有人质疑，本段以 But the findings seem intuitive to me 转折，并用 to me 明确这是说话人自己的判断，转折后 + 第一人称正是态度落点。
**替换** the findings seem intuitive to me↔ They seem intuitive原句 intuitive 与选项 intuitive 同词同义
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及选项 They seem positive 看似"说话人态度不错"，但录音里说话人只说发现 intuitive（符合直觉），从未用 positive 评价；这是把"觉得说得通"擅自升级为"持正面态度"的添加。
C) 偷换概念选项 They are illustrative（有示范性的）与正确词 intuitive 拼写、读音都接近，但录音明明说的是 seem intuitive to me（符合直觉），并非"有示范性"，C 是利用近形词制造的混淆。
D) 过度推断选项 They are conclusive（已成定论的）程度过重：录音里说话人前面刚承认这是 this hypothesis is new、还有 skeptics 质疑，自己也只说 it seems highly likely（看上去很可能），远未到"定论"，D 把说话人的口径拔高了。借用原文： it seems highly likely that people will lie to seem honest
questions.quote: But the findings seem intuitive to me. After all, one of the main motivations for lying is to increase our worth in the eyes of others. So it seems highly likely that people will lie to seem honest.

options.text: They seem positive.
They seem intuitive.
They are illustrative.
They are conclusive.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker mainly discuss in this talk?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （主旨题） Older people's aversion to new music.
**题目译文**
演讲者在这次讲话中主要讨论了什么?
A) 新音乐质量的下降。
B) 对好音乐特征的见解。
C) 老年人不断变化的音乐品味。
D) 老年人对新音乐的厌恶。
**定位** 老年人为什么不喜欢新音乐？随着我自己年纪渐长，我常听到同龄人说类似这样的话：“他们再也做不出过去那样的好音乐了。”
**信号** 开头设问即点题。篇章第一句就是一个问句 Why do old people dislike new music?，开门见山抛出全篇要回答的问题，这种开头设问句就是主旨信号，后面整段都在为它找答案。
**替换** Why do old people dislike new music? ↔ Older people's aversion to new music. dislike new music = aversion to new music
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A 项 Deterioration in the quality of new music. 借了原文里同龄人那句 They just don't make good music like they used to 的语气，但那只是老年人的主观抱怨、被原文当作要解释的现象，全篇并非在论证新音乐质量真的下降了。借用原文： They just don't make good music like they used to
B) 未提及B 项 Insights into the features of good music. 说要讲好音乐有哪些特征，但全篇从未分析什么是好音乐、好音乐的构成要素，只在解释老年人的口味为何固化，属未提及。
C) 偷换概念C 项 Older people's changing musical tastes. 看似贴近，但原文说口味是 these tastes get locked into place pretty firmly（锁定、固化），是不再变，而非在变化；且这只是众多成因之一，撑不起全文主旨。借用原文： these tastes get locked into place pretty firmly
questions.quote: Why do old people dislike new music? As I've grown older, I often hear people my age say things like "They just don't make good music like they used to".

options.text: Deterioration in the quality of new music.
Insights into the features of good music.
Older people's changing musical tastes.
Older people's aversion to new music.

questions.prompt: What have studies found about most people by the time they turn 33?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） They no longer listen to new music.
**题目译文**
研究发现大多数人到33岁时会怎样?
A) 他们不再听新音乐。
B) 他们觉得所有音乐听起来都一样。
C) 他们能够对音乐做出细微的区分。
D) 他们很少听青少年时期发行的歌曲。
**定位** 事实上，研究发现，到我们 33 岁的时候，大多数人已经不再听新音乐了。
**信号** 数字 33 顺听定位。原文 by the time we turn 33 与题干的 turn 33 完全对上，数字是听力里最醒目的定位锚；同时 studies have found 与题干 studies found 呼应，双重信号确认这就是答案句。
**替换** most of us have stopped listening to new music↔They no longer listen to new music. have stopped = no longer
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱B 项 They find all music sounds the same. 偷的是第 3 段 newer, less familiar songs might all "sound the same"，但那是在讲大脑辨别力下降的生理解释、且仅指新歌听起来像，并非 33 岁这项研究的发现，时间与归属都错位。借用原文： newer, less familiar songs might all "sound the same"
C) 与原文相反C 项 They can make subtle distinctions about music. 取自第 3 段 the brain's ability to make subtle distinctions between different chords, rhythms and melodies deteriorates with age，原文说这种细辨能力随年龄衰退，选项却说仍能细辨，极性恰好相反，且也不是 33 岁那项研究的内容。借用原文： the brain's ability to make subtle distinctions between different chords, rhythms and melodies deteriorates with age
D) 与原文相反D 项 They seldom listen to songs released in their teens. 与原文相反，第 2 段说少年时的热门歌 are likely to remain quite popular among your age group through the rest of your life，即一辈子仍爱听，并非 seldom listen。借用原文： are likely to remain quite popular among your age group through the rest of your life
questions.quote: In fact, studies have found that by the time we turn 33, most of us have stopped listening to new music.

options.text: They no longer listen to new music.
They find all music sounds the same.
They can make subtle distinctions about music.
They seldom listen to songs released in their teens.

questions.prompt: What do we learn from one of the most researched laws of social psychology?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） The more you experience something, the better you'll appreciate it.
**题目译文**
我们从社会心理学中研究最多的定律之一中了解到什么?
A) 你接触某事物越多,它对你就越熟悉。
B) 你接触某事物越多,你对它的理解就越深。
C) 你体验某事物越多,你记住它的时间就越长。
D) 你体验某事物越多,你就越会欣赏它。
**定位** 社会心理学中研究得最多的定律之一，叫作“纯粹接触效应”，它的本质是：我们越是接触某样东西，就越倾向于喜欢它。
**信号** 定义句 means that 引出本质。原文 the most researched laws of social psychology 与题干完全对上，紧跟的 in essence, means that（本质上是说）是一个明确的下定义信号，其后那句就是这条定律的核心内容、即答案所在。
**替换** the more we're exposed to something, the more we tend to like it↔The more you are exposed to something, the better you'll appreciate it. tend to like it = appreciate it
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A 项 The more you are exposed to something, the more familiar it'll be to you. 用familiar，原文说的是越接触越喜欢（like），不是越接触越熟悉；familiar 虽与第 5 段become familiar 沾边，但那是讲歌曲变熟、不是这条定律的内容，盗词跑题。借用原文： become familiar, comforting parts of your routine
B) 偷换概念B 项 The more you are exposed to something, the deeper you'll understand it. 把结果词换成 understand（理解），原文这条定律讲的是产生喜爱，与理解无关，understand是原文从未对这条定律说过的结果。
C) 张冠李戴C 项 The more you experience something, the longer you'll remember it. 把结果换成remember（记得更久），这是第 8 段 intense emotions are associated with stronger memories 的内容、属另一道题（25 题）的范畴，被挪到这里制造干扰。借用原文： intense emotions are associated with stronger memories and preferences
questions.quote: One of the most researched laws of social psychology is something called the "mere exposure effect", which, in essence, means that the more we're exposed to something, the more we tend to like it.

options.text: The more you are exposed to something, the more familiar it'll be to you.
The more you are exposed to something, the deeper you'll understand it.
The more you experience something, the longer you'll remember it.
The more you experience something, the better you'll appreciate it.

questions.prompt: What might explain the fact that songs people listen to in their teen years are memorable and beloved?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） Teenagers' emotions are more intense.
**题目译文**
什么可以解释人们在青少年时期听的歌曲令人难忘且深受喜爱这一事实?
A) 青少年的记忆更持久。
B) 青少年的情感更强烈。
C) 青少年要敏感得多。
D) 青少年要多愁善感得多。
**定位** 心理学研究表明，我们在青少年时期体验到的情绪，似乎比此后的情绪更强烈。而且我们也知道，强烈的情绪与更牢固的记忆和偏好相关。
**信号** intense emotions 起始的因果链。原文先说 the emotions that we experience as teens seem more intense（少年情绪更强烈），再以 intense emotions are associated with stronger memories 把强烈情绪与更牢的记忆和偏好连起来，associated with 是因果信号，这条因果链就是难忘的解释。
**替换** the emotions that we experience as teens seem more intense than those that come later↔Teenagers' emotions are more intense.几乎原句概括
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A 项 Teenagers' memories are more lasting. 盗用原文 stronger memories，但更牢的记忆是强烈情绪带来的结果、是因果链的中段，题目问的是更根本的因（情绪更强烈），且原文说的是 memories 更 stronger，并非笼统说 teenagers 的记忆更 lasting。借用原文： intense emotions are associated with stronger memories and preferences
C) 未提及C 项 Teenagers are much more sensitive. 的 sensitive（敏感）原文从未提及，原文只说少年情绪更 intense（强烈），强烈不等于敏感，属未提及。
D) 偷换概念D 项 Teenagers are much more sentimental. 的 sentimental（多愁善感）与正确项intense 都跟情绪沾边，但原文用的是 more intense（强烈），不是多愁善感；sentimental 与 C 的 sensitive 还互为近音干扰，专诱听不清的考生。
questions.quote: Psychology research has shown that the emotions that we experience as teens seem more intense than those that come later. And we also know that intense emotions are associated with stronger memories and preferences.

options.text: Teenagers' memories are more lasting.
Teenagers' emotions are more intense.
Teenagers are much more sensitive.
Teenagers are much more sentimental.

questions.prompt: What is the risk the man anticipates?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） Digital life could replace human civilization.
**题目译文**
男士预期的风险是什么?
A) 可能会有没人愿意做的工作。
B) 数字生活可能取代人类文明。
C) 人类会厌倦彼此交流。
D) 老年人将仅由没有感情的机器人照料。
**定位** 男：有一种风险是，人类文明可能被一种更高级的数字生命形式所取代。
**信号** risk预警词直接领出风险。男方原句以 There's a risk that 直接点出风险，预警信号词 risk一响，紧跟其后的 human civilization could be replaced by a superior type of digital life 就是答案所在——这种"信号词+正文"是细节题最干净的定位点。
**替换** human civilization could be replaced by a superior type of digital life↔Digital life could replace human civilization.被动改主动的同义句
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴There could be jobs nobody wants to do 盗用的是女方在 a lot of jobs which nobody will want to do 说的话，而且题干问的是"男方"预见的风险，这句既非男方所说、也不是他眼里的风险，张冠李戴。借用原文： a lot of jobs which nobody will want to do
C) 偷换概念Humans would be tired of communicating with one another 把原文说反了主语：男方说的是 AI will become tired of trying to communicate with humans（是 AI 厌倦与人交流），而非"人类彼此厌倦交流"，主体被偷换。借用原文： AI will become tired of trying to communicate with humans
D) 过度推断Old people would be taken care of solely by unfeeling robots 嫁接的是女方 robots to take care of the old guys 的说法，且女方把它当作正面用途、并无 solely、unfeeling 之意；这既非男方预见的风险，又添加了原文没有的"仅靠、无情"。借用原文： the robots to take care of the old guys
questions.quote: M: There's a risk that human civilization could be replaced by a superior type of digital life.

options.text: There could be jobs nobody wants to do.
Digital life could replace human civilization.
Humans would be tired of communicating with one another.
Old people would be taken care of solely by unfeeling robots.

questions.prompt: What is the man's concern about AI technology?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （态度观点题） It will be smarter than human beings.
**题目译文**
男士对人工智能技术的担忧是什么?
A) 生活将变得像科幻电影一样。
B) 它将完全取代人类的工作。
C) 芯片将被植入人类大脑。
D) 它将比人类更聪明。
**定位** 男：一旦 AI 完全发展起来，它会厌倦与人类交流，因为相比之下我们的思维要慢得多。
**信号** 对比中暗示AI更强。男方 we would be much slower thinkers in comparison 用人机对比，明说人比 AI 慢得多，再加 Computers can easily communicate incredibly fast，这条贯穿后半段的"AI 远超人类"主线，正是态度题要抓的核心判断。
**替换** we would be much slower thinkers in comparison ↔ It will be smarter than human beings.人更慢即AI更聪明Computers can easily communicate incredibly fast ↔ smarter than human beings快得多印证更强
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴Life will become like a science fiction film 盗用的是女方收尾的 you watch too many science fiction films，那是女方调侃男方想太多的话，并非男方对 AI 的忧虑，张冠李戴。借用原文： you watch too many science fiction films
B) 原词陷阱It will take away humans' jobs altogether 借用了男方 AI will make jobs kind of pointless 的工作话题，但题干问的是男方对 AI 的核心"忧虑"，他后半段反复强调的是 AI超越人类、而非"彻底抢光工作"；altogether 也属程度加码。借用原文： AI will make jobs kind of pointless
C) 原词陷阱Chips will be inserted in human brains 盗用了女方 Computers only have chips. People have brains 里的 chips、brains 两词，但女方原意是"电脑只有芯片、人有大脑"以反驳男方，根本没说"往人脑里插芯片"，既张冠李戴又是凭原词拼凑的无中生有。借用原文： Computers only have chips. People have brains
questions.quote: M: Once it's fully developed, AI will become tired of trying to communicate with humans, as we would be much slower thinkers in comparison.

options.text: Life will become like a science fiction film.
It will take away humans' jobs altogether.
Chips will be inserted in human brains.
It will be smarter than human beings.

transcript.text: While some scientists explore the surface of Antarctica, others are learning more about a giant body of water four kilometers beneath the ice pack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Scientists first discovered Lake Vostok in the 1970s by using radio waves that penetrate the ice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Since then, they have used sound waves and even satellites to map this massive body of water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: How does the water in Lake Vostok remain liquid beneath an ice sheet?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: "The thick glacier above acts like an insulating blanket and keeps the water from freezing," says Martin Siegert, a glaciologist from the University of Wales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In addition, geothermal heat from deep within the earth may warm the hidden lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The scientists suspect that micro-organisms may be living in Lake Vostok, closed off from the outside world for more than 2 million years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Anything found there will be totally alien to what's on the surface of the earth, says Siegert.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Scientists are trying to find a way to drill into the ice and draw water samples without causing contamination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Again, robots might be the solution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: If all goes as planned, a drill-shaped robot will melt through the surface ice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: When it reaches the lake, it will release another robot that can swim in the lake, take pictures, and look for signs of life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The scientists hope their discoveries will shed light on life in outer space, which might exist in similar dark and airless conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Recently, close-up pictures of Jupiter's moon, Europa, show signs of water beneath its icy surface.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Once tested in Antarctica, robots could be sent to Europa to search for life there too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The idea to study the American Indian tribe Tarahumaras came to James Copeland in 1984 when he discovered that very little research had been done on their language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: He contacted a tribe member through a social worker who worked with the tribesmen in Mexico.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: At first, the tribe member, named Gonzalez, was very reluctant to cooperate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: He told Copeland that no amount of money could buy his language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But after Copeland explained to him what he intended to do with his research and how it would benefit the Tarahumaras, Gonzalez agreed to help.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: He took Copeland to his village and served as an intermediary.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Copeland says, "Thanks to him, the Tarahumaras understood what our mission was and started trusting us."
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Entering the world of the Tarahumaras has been a laborious project for Copeland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: To reach their homeland he must drive two and a half days from Houston, Texas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: He loads up his vehicle with goods that the tribesmen can't easily get, and gives the goods to them as a gesture of friendship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The Tarahumaras, who don't believe in accumulating wealth, take the food and share it among themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: For Copeland, the experience has not only been academically satisfying, but also has enriched his life in several ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: "I see people rejecting technology and living a very hard, traditional life, which offers me another notion about the meaning of progress in the western tradition," he says.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: "I experience the simplicity of living in nature that I would otherwise only be able to read about.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: I see a lot of beauty in their sense of sharing and concern for each other."

transcriptTranslations: 当一些科学家探索南极洲表面时,其他科学家正在了解更多关于冰层下方四千米处一个巨大水体的信息。科学家在20世纪70年代首次通过使用能穿透冰层的无线电波发现了沃斯托克湖。此后,他们利用声波甚至卫星来绘制这个巨大水体的地图。
沃斯托克湖中的水如何在冰盖下保持液态?威尔士大学的冰川学家Martin Siegert说:"上方厚厚的冰川就像一条绝缘毯,防止水结冰。"此外,来自地球深处的地热可能使这个隐藏的湖泊保持温暖。科学家们怀疑微生物可能生活在沃斯托克湖中,与外界隔绝超过200万年。
Siegert说,在那里发现的任何东西都将与地球表面的东西完全不同。科学家们正在努力寻找一种方法来钻入冰层并抽取水样而不造成污染。机器人可能再次成为解决方案。如果一切按计划进行,一个钻头形状的机器人将融化表层冰。当它到达湖面时,它将释放另一个可以在湖中游泳、拍照并寻找生命迹象的机器人。
科学家们希望他们的发现将揭示外太空生命的奥秘,这些生命可能存在于类似的黑暗和无空气条件下。最近,木星卫星Europa的特写照片显示其冰冷表面下有水的迹象。一旦在南极洲测试成功,机器人也可以被送往Europa去那里寻找生命。

研究美国印第安部落Tarahumaras的想法始于1984年，当时James Copeland发现关于他们语言的研究非常少。他通过一位在墨西哥与部落成员打交道的社会工作者联系上了一名部落成员。起初，这位名叫Gonzalez的部落成员非常不愿意合作。他告诉Copeland，再多的钱也买不到他的语言。但在Copeland向他解释了研究意图以及这将如何使Tarahumaras受益之后，Gonzalez同意帮忙。他带Copeland去了他的村庄并担任中间人。Copeland说："多亏了他，Tarahumaras理解了我们的使命并开始信任我们。"
进入Tarahumaras的世界对Copeland来说是一个艰苦的项目。要到达他们的家园，他必须从德克萨斯州休斯顿驱车两天半。他在车上装满部落成员不容易获得的物品，并将这些物品送给他们作为友谊的表示。不相信积累财富的Tarahumaras接受了食物并在彼此之间分享。
对Copeland来说，这段经历不仅在学术上令人满意，而且在多方面丰富了他的生活。他说："我看到人们拒绝技术，过着非常艰苦的传统生活，这为我提供了关于西方传统中进步意义的另一种观念。我体验到生活在自然中的简单，否则我只能从书中读到。我在他们的分享意识和彼此关心中看到了很多美好。"

questions.prompt: What did scientists first use to discover Lake Vostok in the 1970s?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） Radio waves.
**题目译文**
科学家在20世纪70年代最初使用什么发现了沃斯托克湖?
A) 无线电波。
B) 声波。
C) 机器人。
D) 卫星。
**定位** 科学家在 1970 年代最早是用能穿透冰层的无线电波发现沃斯托克湖的。此后，他们又用声波甚至卫星来绘制这片巨大水体的地图。
**信号** first 与时间状语对准题干。答案句里的 Scientists first discovered Lake Vostok in the 1970s by using radio waves 同时含 first 和 in the 1970s，与题干的 first、in the 1970s严丝合缝。by using 后面跟的就是问题要的工具，这个 first+时间的呼应就是定位信号。
**替换** by using radio waves that penetrate the ice ↔ Radio waves.原句提炼为名词短语
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱录音确实念到了 they have used sound waves，但前面有 Since then（从那以后），说明声波是发现湖之后才用来绘图的，不是 first 时用的。听到 sound waves 就选，正中原词陷阱。借用原文： Since then, they have used sound waves
C) 原词陷阱录音后文提到 robots might be the solution，但那是后来用于钻冰取样的设想，跟 1970年代最初发现湖完全是两回事。听到 robots 这个全文反复出现的词就选，是被原词带偏。借用原文： robots might be the solution
D) 原词陷阱录音念到 even satellites to map this massive body of water，但同样在 Since then 之后，是用来绘图的，不是最初发现用的。和声波一样，落在 first 之外。借用原文： they have used sound waves and even satellites
questions.quote: Scientists first discovered Lake Vostok in the 1970s by using radio waves that penetrate the ice. Since then, they have used sound waves and even satellites to map this massive body of water.

options.text: Radio waves.
Sound waves.
Robots.
Satellites.

questions.prompt: What do scientists think about Lake Vostok?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） It may have micro-organisms living in it.
**题目译文**
科学家对沃斯托克湖有何看法?
A) 它可能正在冰川下快速冻结。
B) 它可能有微生物生活在其中。
C) 它可能含有某些稀有矿物质。
D) 它可能深达四公里。
**定位** 科学家推测，可能有微生物生活在沃斯托克湖中，这片湖与外界隔绝已超过两百万年。
**信号** suspect 引出推测。答案句以 The scientists suspect that 开头，suspect（推测）正是题干 think 所问的判断动词。这个带推测口气的引导词就是信号——它后面跟的 micro- organisms may be living 就是科学家的看法。
**替换** micro-organisms may be living in Lake Vostok↔ It may have micro-organisms living in it.主动改写为 have 结构
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 与原文相反录音念到 glacier 和 freezing 相关内容，但原文说的是 keeps the water from freezing（防止水结冰），意思是不结冰；选项 It may be freezing fast beneath the glacier. 反说成正在快速结冰，正好与原文相反。借用原文： keeps the water from freezing
C) 未提及选项 It may have certain rare minerals in it. 句式和正确项 B 几乎一样（It may have…），极易混；但 rare minerals（稀有矿物）在整段录音里根本没出现，是凭空添的。
D) 原词陷阱录音开头确实念到 four kilometers beneath the ice pack，选项 It may be as deep as four kilometers. 就盗用了这个数字。但 four kilometers 是讲湖的深度位置，不是科学家对湖的看法，与题干问的 think 不符。借用原文： four kilometers beneath the ice pack
questions.quote: The scientists suspect that micro-organisms may be living in Lake Vostok, closed off from the outside world for more than 2 million years.

options.text: It may be freezing fast beneath the glacier.
It may have micro-organisms living in it.
It may have certain rare minerals in it.
It may be as deep as four kilometers.

questions.prompt: What do the scientists hope their discoveries will do?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （目的题） Shed light on possible life in outer space.
**题目译文**
科学家希望他们的发现能做什么?
A) 帮助理解冰冻条件下的生命。
B) 帮助找到新的淡水来源。
C) 提供有关其他行星的信息。
D) 揭示外层空间可能存在生命的线索。
**定位** 科学家希望他们的发现能为外太空的生命提供启示，那里的生命可能存在于类似的黑暗、无空气的环境中。
**信号** hope 领出愿望句。答案句 The scientists hope their discoveries will shed light on life in outer space 以 hope 开头，与题干 hope 完全对应。篇章独白的目的/展望句常落在结尾段，这里正是末段第一句，hope 就是定位信号。
**替换** shed light on life in outer space↔Shed light on possible life in outer space.近乎原句仅加 possible
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱录音前文反复讲冰下、freezing 的环境，选项 Help understand life in freezing conditions. 盗用了 life、freezing 这些词。但科学家最终的 hope 是指向外太空生命，理解冰冻环境只是过程，不是题干问的最终目标。A 与 D 都谈 life，最易切不开。借用原文： shed light on life in outer space
B) 未提及选项 Help find new sources of fresh water. 谈寻找新淡水源，录音通篇讲的是探测湖、找生命，从未提把湖当淡水资源来开发，属凭空添加。
C) 偷换概念录音末段提到木星卫星 Jupiter's moon, Europa，选项 Provide information about other planets. 听起来像沾边，但科学家的 hope 是 shed light on life（启示生命），不是提供关于行星本身的信息，把对生命的启示偷换成了对行星的信息。借用原文： Jupiter's moon, Europa
questions.quote: The scientists hope their discoveries will shed light on life in outer space, which might exist in similar dark and airless conditions.

options.text: Help understand life in freezing conditions.
Help find new sources of fresh water.
Provide information about other planets.
Shed light on possible life in outer space.

questions.prompt: Why did James Copeland want to study the American Indian tribe Tarahumaras?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） He found there had been little research on their language.
**题目译文**
James Copeland 为什么想要研究美洲印第安部落 Tarahumaras?
A) 他发现对他们的语言几乎没有研究。
B) 他试图保护印第安部落的语言。
C) 他与一名社会工作者的接触极大地激发了他对该部落的兴趣。
D) 他与 Gonzalez 的会面使他渴望更多地了解该部落。
**定位** 研究塔拉乌马拉这个美洲印第安部落的念头，是 1984 年 James Copeland 发现几乎没有人研究过他们的语言时产生的。
**信号** 起因标志 when he discovered。答案句用 The idea to study… came to James Copeland in 1984 when he discovered that very little research had been done on their language，其中 when he discovered（当他发现……时）正是交代念头"如何产生"的起因信号，这一句即承载动机。
**替换** very little research had been done on their language↔there had been little research on their language被动句几乎原义保留、仅去掉 very he discovered ↔ He found discover 与 found 同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱He was trying to preserve the languages of the Indian tribes. 借用了原文反复出现的language 一词，但原文只说他要"研究 study"语言，从未说他要"保护 preserve"语言，把"研究"偷换成"保护"，过度拔高了动机。借用原文： very little research had been done on their language
C) 原词陷阱His contact with a social worker had greatly aroused his interest in the tribe. 盗用了原文的 social worker，但原文里社工只是 He contacted a tribe member through a social worker 的联络渠道，并非"激起他兴趣"的动机；兴趣的真正起因是发现研究空白。借用原文： He contacted a tribe member through a social worker
D) 张冠李戴His meeting with Gonzalez had made him eager to learn more about the tribe. 盗用了人名 Gonzalez，但原文里念头早在 1984 年发现研究空白时就产生了，之后才通过社工联系到 Gonzalez，是"先有动机、后遇此人"，选项把因果时序颠倒了。借用原文： He contacted a tribe member through a social worker
questions.quote: The idea to study the American Indian tribe Tarahumaras came to James Copeland in 1984 when he discovered that very little research had been done on their language.

options.text: He found there had been little research on their language.
He was trying to preserve the languages of the Indian tribes.
His contact with a social worker had greatly aroused his interest in the tribe.
His meeting with Gonzalez had made him eager to learn more about the tribe.

questions.prompt: How did Gonzalez help James Copeland?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） He acted as an intermediary between Copeland and the villagers.
**题目译文**
Gonzalez 如何帮助 James Copeland?
A) 他教 Copeland 说 Tarahumaras 语。
B) 他说服 Tarahumaras 人接受 Copeland 的礼物。
C) 他推荐了他最好的朋友之一担任口译员。
D) 他在 Copeland 和村民之间充当中间人。
**定位** 他把 Copeland 带到自己的村庄，并充当了中间人。
**信号** 人物动作句 served as an intermediary。答案句 He took Copeland to his village and served as an intermediary 直接描述 Gonzalez 做的事，其中 served as an intermediary（充当中间人）就是"怎么帮"的核心动作，是本题的落点。
**替换** served as an intermediary ↔ acted as an intermediary between Copeland and the villagers served as 与 acted as 同义、intermediary 原义保留
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及He taught Copeland to speak the Tarahumaras language. 借用了贯穿全文的 language话题，但原文从未说 Gonzalez 教 Copeland 说部落语言，"teach to speak"是原文没有的捏造动作。
B) 张冠李戴He persuaded the Tarahumaras to accept Copeland's gifts. 盗用了"村民接受东西"这一情节（take the food and share it among themselves），但那是第二段讲送礼，并非Gonzalez 劝说所致，把别处情节张冠李戴给了 Gonzalez。借用原文： take the food and share it among themselves
C) 偷换概念He recommended one of his best friends as an interpreter. 用 interpreter（翻译）来碰瓷原文的 intermediary（中间人），两词形近义近最易混；但原文是 Gonzalez 本人served as an intermediary，从未"推荐好友当翻译"，属偷换角色。借用原文： served as an intermediary
questions.quote: He took Copeland to his village and served as an intermediary.

He persuaded the Tarahumaras to accept Copeland's gifts.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about James Copeland's trip to the Tarahumaras village?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） Laborious.
**题目译文**
讲话者对 James Copeland 前往 Tarahumaras 村庄的旅行是怎么说的?
A) 不可预测的。
B) 不合理的。
C) 艰苦的。
D) 乏味的。
**定位** 对 Copeland 来说，走进塔拉乌马拉人的世界一直是一项艰辛费力的工程。
**信号** 直接定性词 laborious。答案句 Entering the world of the Tarahumaras has been a laborious project for Copeland 用 laborious 一词直接给这趟历程定性，紧接着用 he must drive two and a half days from Houston, Texas 举"开车两天半"为佐证，证实其"费力"，这就是答案信号。
**替换** a laborious project↔Laborious选项就是原文形容词，但靠语境判义而非靠原词偷懒
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及Unpredictable.（难以预料的）原文未提，行程被描述为路途遥远、艰辛，但没有任何"结果难料、变化无常"的意思，属凭空添义。
B) 未提及Unjustifiable.（无正当理由的、站不住脚的）与原文毫无关联，原文谈的是行程艰辛，没有任何"不合理、缺乏正当性"的评价。
D) 偷换概念Tedious.（枯燥乏味的）与正确项 laborious 中文都像"难熬"，但 tedious 侧重"单调无聊"，原文强调的是开车两天半的"耗费体力、艰辛"，侧重"累"而非"闷"，含义对不上。借用原文： he must drive two and a half days from Houston, Texas
questions.quote: Entering the world of the Tarahumaras has been a laborious project for Copeland.

options.text: Unpredictable.
Unjustifiable.
Laborious.
Tedious.

questions.prompt: What impresses James Copeland about the Tarahumaras tribe?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） Their sense of sharing and caring.
**题目译文**
Tarahumaras 部落的什么给 James Copeland 留下了深刻印象?
A) 他们对外来者帮助的感激。
B) 他们的分享与关怀意识。
C) 他们适应技术的准备。
D) 他们为自己创造财富的信念。
**定位** 我在他们彼此分享、互相关心的精神里看到了许多美好。
**信号** 直抒赞赏句 I see a lot of beauty in。答案句 I see a lot of beauty in their sense of sharing and concern for each other 用 see a lot of beauty in（看到许多美好）直接表达赞赏，是讲述者点名"被打动之处"的落点，正是 impress 题的答案信号。
**替换** their sense of sharing and concern for each other↔Their sense of sharing and caring. concern for each other 浓缩为 caring
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及Their appreciation of help from the outsiders. 原文从未提部落"感激外来者的帮助"；原文虽讲 Copeland 送礼示好，但被打动的是"分享精神"，而非部落对外人的感激，属无中生有。
C) 与原文相反Their readiness to adapt to technology. 盗用了原文的 technology 一词，但原文是 I see people rejecting technology（拒绝技术），选项却说他们"乐于接纳技术"，极性完全反了。借用原文： I see people rejecting technology and living a very hard, traditional life
D) 与原文相反Their belief in creating wealth for themselves. 与原文 The Tarahumaras, who don't believe in accumulating wealth 直接矛盾——原文说他们"不相信积累财富"，选项却说他们"信奉为自己创造财富"，意思反了。借用原文： The Tarahumaras, who don't believe in accumulating wealth
questions.quote: I see a lot of beauty in their sense of sharing and concern for each other.

Their sense of sharing and caring.
Their readiness to adapt to technology.
Their belief in creating wealth for themselves.

transcript.text: What is a radical?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It seems today that people are terrified of the term, particularly of having the label attached to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Accusing individuals or groups of being radical often serves to silence them into submission, thereby maintaining the existing state of affairs, and, more important, preserving the power of a select minority who are mostly wealthy white males in western society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Feminism is a perfect example of this phenomenon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The women's movement has been plagued by stereotypes, misrepresentations by the media, and accusations of man-hating and radicalism, when the basic foundation of feminism is simply that women deserve equal rights in all facets of life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: When faced with the threat of being labelled radical, women back down from their worthy calls and consequently participate in their own oppression.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It has gotten to the point that many women are afraid to call themselves feminists because of the stigma attached to the word.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: If people refuse to be controlled and intimidated by stigmas, the stigmas lose all their power.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Without fear on which they feed, such stigmas can only die.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: To me, a radical is simply someone who rebels against the norm or advocates a change in the existing state of affairs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: On close inspection, it becomes clear that the norm is constantly evolving and therefore is not a constant entity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: So why then is deviation from the present situation such a threat when the state of affairs itself is unstable and subject to relentless transformation?
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It all goes back to maintaining the power of those who have it and preventing the right of those who don't.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: In fact, when we look at the word "radical" in a historical context, nearly every figure we now hold up as a hero was considered a radical in his or her time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Radicals are people who effect change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: They are the people about whom history is written.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Abolitionists were radicals; civil rights activists were radicals; even the founders of our country in their fight to win independence from England were radicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Their presence in history has changed the way our society functions, mainly by shifting the balance of power that previously existed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Of course, there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity, but undeniably, there would simply be no progress without radicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: That being said, next time someone calls me a radical, I will accept that label with pride.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Virtually every American can recognize a dollar bill at a mere glance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Many can identify it by its sound or texture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: But few people indeed can accurately describe the world's most powerful, important currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The American dollar bill is colored with black ink on one side and green on the other; the exact composition of the paper and ink is a closely guarded government secret.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Despite its weighty importance, the dollar bill actually weighs little.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: It requires nearly 500 bills to tip the scales at a pound.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Not only is the dollar bill lightweight, but it also has a brief life span.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Few dollar bills survive longer than 18 months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The word "dollar" is taken from the German word "thaler," the name for the world's most important currency in the 16th century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The thaler was a silver coin first minted in 1518 under the reign of Charles V, Emperor of Germany.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The concept of paper money is a relatively recent innovation in the history of American currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: When the Constitution was signed, people had little regard for paper money because of its steadily decreasing value during the colonial era.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Because of this lack of faith, the new American government minted only coins for common currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Interest-bearing bank notes were issued at the same time, but their purpose was limited to providing money for urgent government crises, such as American involvement in the War of 1812.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The first noninterest-bearing paper currency was authorized by Congress in 1862, at the height of the Civil War.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: At this point, citizens' old fears of devalued paper currency had calmed, and the dollar bill was born.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The new green colored paper money quickly earned the nickname "greenback."
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Today, the American dollar bill is a product of the Federal Reserve, and is issued from the twelve Federal Reserve banks around the United States.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The government keeps a steady supply of approximately two billion bills in circulation at all times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: Controversy continues to surround the true value of the dollar bill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: American history has seen generations of politicians argue in favor of a gold standard for American currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: However, for the present, the American dollar bill holds the value that is printed on it, and little more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker

transcript.text: The only other guarantee on the bill is a Federal Reserve pledge as a confirmation in the form of government securities.

transcriptTranslations: 什么是激进分子?如今,人们似乎对这个词感到恐惧,尤其是害怕被贴上这样的标签。指责个人或团体是激进分子往往会让他们沉默并屈服,从而维持现有状态,更重要的是,保护在西方社会中主要由富有的白人男性组成的少数特权群体的权力。
女权主义就是这种现象的完美例证。女性运动一直饱受刻板印象、媒体歪曲报道以及仇恨男性和激进主义指控的困扰,而女权主义的基本理念不过是女性在生活的各个方面都应享有平等权利。当面临被贴上激进分子标签的威胁时,女性会从她们正当的诉求中退缩,从而参与到对自身的压迫之中。
事态已发展到许多女性因为这个词所附带的污名而害怕称自己为女权主义者。如果人们拒绝被污名控制和威胁,这些污名就会失去所有力量。没有了它们赖以生存的恐惧,这些污名只能消亡。
对我而言,激进分子不过是反抗常规或倡导改变现有状况的人。仔细审视就会发现,常规是不断演变的,因此并非一个恒定不变的实体。
那么,既然现有状况本身是不稳定的并且会经历持续不断的变化,为什么偏离当前情况会构成如此大的威胁?

这一切都归结于维护拥有权力者的权力,并阻止没有权力者获得权利。事实上,当我们从历史语境审视"激进分子"这个词时,几乎每一个我们现在奉为英雄的人物在其所处的时代都被视为激进分子。激进分子是促成变革的人。他们是历史书写的对象。废奴主义者是激进分子;民权活动家是激进分子;甚至我们国家的缔造者在为赢得独立于英格兰的斗争中也是激进分子。他们在历史中的存在改变了我们社会运作的方式,主要是通过改变此前存在的权力平衡。当然,也有一些激进分子对人类产生了负面影响,但不可否认的是,没有激进分子就不会有进步。话虽如此,下次有人称我为激进分子时,我会自豪地接受这个标签。
我们很容易受到周围人的影响。例如,你可能认识某个在海外待了一年左右后回来带着口音的人。我们成为所处环境的一部分。我们没有人能免受自己所处世界的影响,我们不要自欺欺人地以为自己不受生活中的事物和人的影响。
Fred去工厂开始新工作。Fred休10分钟的咖啡休息时间,但其他工人休半小时。Fred说:"你们这些人怎么回事?"两周后,Fred开始休20分钟。一个月后,Fred也休半小时了。Fred说:"如果你无法打败他们,就加入他们。我为什么要比别人更努力工作呢?"
作为人类,有趣的是我们通常意识不到自己的心态正在发生变化。这就像在新鲜空气中待了几周后回到城市雾霾中——只有那时我们才意识到自己已经习惯了难闻的气味。与爱批评的人相处,我们学会批评;与快乐的人相处,我们学会快乐。
这意味着我们需要决定自己想从生活中得到什么,然后相应地选择我们的同伴。你可能会说:"那需要付出一些努力。可能不会很舒服。我可能会冒犯现在的一些朋友。"没错,但这是你的人生。
Fred可能会说:"我总是身无分文,经常抑郁。我一事无成,从不做任何令人兴奋的事。"然后我们发现Fred最好的朋友们总是身无分文,经常抑郁,一事无成,希望生活更令人兴奋。这不是巧合。评判Fred也不是我们的事。然而,如果Fred想要改善生活质量,他首先需要做的就是认识到这些年来一直在发生的事情。
医生作为一个职业群体健康状况不佳并不奇怪,因为他们一生都与病人打交道。精神科医生的职业自杀率较高,原因也与此相关。传统上,父母吸烟的孩子中有十分之九自己也吸烟。肥胖在一定程度上是一个环境问题。成功的人有成功的朋友。故事就这样继续下去。
几乎每个美国人仅凭一瞥就能认出一美元纸币。许多人能通过声音或质地辨认出它。但确实很少有人能准确描述这种世界上最强大、最重要的货币。
美元纸币一面印有黑色油墨,另一面印有绿色油墨;纸张和油墨的确切成分是政府严格保守的秘密。尽管具有重大意义,美元纸币实际上重量很轻。需要将近500张纸币才能让天平倾斜一磅。美元纸币不仅重量轻,而且寿命也很短。很少有美元纸币能存在超过18个月。
dollar这个词源自德语单词thaler,这是16世纪世界上最重要货币的名称。thaler是一种银币,于1518年在德意志皇帝查理五世统治期间首次铸造。
纸币的概念在美国货币史上是一项相对近期的创新。当宪法签署时,人们对纸币不太重视,因为纸币在殖民时代价值持续贬值。由于这种缺乏信任,新成立的美国政府只铸造硬币作为通用货币。同时发行了计息银行券,但其目的仅限于为紧急政府危机提供资金,例如美国参与1812年战争。
第一种不计息纸币于1862年由国会授权发行,当时正值内战高潮。此时,公民对贬值纸币的旧有恐惧已经平息,美元纸币由此诞生。这种新的绿色纸币很快获得了greenback的绰号。
如今,美元纸币是联邦储备系统的产品,由分布在美国各地的十二家联邦储备银行发行。政府始终保持约二十亿张纸币的稳定流通供应量。
围绕美元纸币真实价值的争议仍在继续。美国历史上曾有几代政治家主张为美国货币建立金本位制。然而,就目前而言,美元纸币所持有的价值就是印在上面的价值,仅此而已。纸币上唯一的其他保证是联邦储备系统以政府证券形式提供的确认承诺。

**排除**
B) 未提及They find it hard to defend themselves. 听起来像『被压制』的合理延伸，但录音只说被压制到屈服，从未提及『难以为自己辩护』这层意思，属于自行脑补。
C) 与原文相反They will feel proud of being pioneers. 里的 proud(自豪)出现在录音结尾——但那是作者说『下次别人叫我 radical 我会自豪地接受』，与本题问的『被指控者通常的遭遇(被压制)』方向相反，C 把消极结果说成了积极。借用原文： next time someone calls me a radical, I will accept that label with pride
D) 与原文相反They will feel somewhat encouraged. 同样把结果说反：原文的 silence into submission 是被压制、退缩，绝非『受到鼓舞』，方向与答案句正相反。
questions.quote: Accusing individuals or groups of being radical often serves to silence them into submission, thereby maintaining the existing state of affairs.

options.text: They tend to be silenced into submission.
They find it hard to defend themselves.
They will feel proud of being pioneers.
They will feel somewhat encouraged.

questions.prompt: What is the speaker's definition of a radical?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） One who rebels against the existing social order.
**题目译文**
说话者对激进分子的定义是什么?
A) 主张用暴力实现变革的人。
B) 渴望不断变革的人。
C) 为受压迫者的利益行动的人。
D) 反抗现有社会秩序的人。
**定位** 在我看来，激进者无非就是反抗常规、或主张改变现有状态的人。
**信号** 下定义信号 To me… is simply someone who。To me, a radical is simply someone who rebels against the norm 里 To me… a radical is simply someone who 是典型的『作者亲口下定义』信号句，simply 还表明这就是他给的简明定义，定位到此即可。
**替换** rebels against the norm or advocates a change in the existing state of affairs↔rebels against the existing social order norm/state of affairs 同义于 social order
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱One who advocates violence in effecting change. 的 effecting change 确与录音Radicals are people who effect change 沾边，诱人去选，但作者的定义句里只说反抗常规、主张改变，从没把 violence(暴力)写进定义，A 凭空加了暴力限定。借用原文： Radicals are people who effect change
B) 原词陷阱One who craves for relentless transformations, 里的 relentless transformations 直接取自录音 subject to relentless transformation，但那句是在形容『社会状态本身不断剧变』，并非作者给 radical 下的定义，属张冠李戴。借用原文： the state of affairs itself is unstable and subject to relentless transformation
C) 未提及One who acts in the interests of the oppressed. 的 oppressed 让人联想全文为弱势翻案的基调，但作者的定义句只讲『反抗常规、主张变革』，从未说 radical 是『为被压迫者谋利的人』，这层限定原文没有。
questions.quote: To me, a radical is simply someone who rebels against the norm or advocates a change in the existing state of affairs.

options.text: One who advocates violence in effecting change.
One who craves for relentless transformations,
One who acts in the interests of the oppressed.
One who rebels against the existing social order.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker think of most radicals in the American history?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （态度观点题） They served as a driving force for progress.
**题目译文**
说话者如何看待美国历史上的大多数激进分子?
A) 他们试图用武力实现社会变革。
B) 他们破坏了国家的社会稳定。
C) 他们充当了进步的推动力量。
D) 他们对人类的害处大于益处。
**定位** 当然，有些激进者对人类造成了负面影响，但不可否认，没有激进者就根本不会有进步。
**信号** 让步转折 Of course… but undeniably… 后才是真态度。答案落在 Of course, there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity, but undeniably, there would simply be no progress without radicals：Of course… 先让一步承认有负面，but undeniably 一转才是作者真正的落脚——没有 radical 就没有进步，转折后才是态度真意。
**替换** there would simply be no progress without radicals ↔They served as a driving force for progress.否定+无则不能 转为肯定『推动力』
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱They tried to effect social change by force. 借了录音的 effect change，但加了原文没有的 by force(靠武力)；作者通篇讲 radical 推动变革，从没说他们靠武力，by force 是擅自添加。借用原文： Radicals are people who effect change
B) 与原文相反They disrupted the nation's social stability. 听着像『激进=破坏稳定』的常识，但作者立场恰恰相反——他在为 radical 翻案、强调其推动进步，绝不会说他们破坏国家稳定，与作者态度反向。
D) 与原文相反They did more harm than good to humanity. 正好踩在录音 there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity 这句让步话上，听到 negative impact、humanity 就想选；但那是 Of course 引出的退让，作者随即用 but 推翻它，D 把铺垫当成了结论。借用原文： there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity
questions.quote: Of course, there are some radicals who've made a negative impact on humanity, but undeniably, there would simply be no progress without radicals.

options.text: They tried to effect social change by force.
They disrupted the nation's social stability.
They served as a driving force for progress.
They did more harm than good to humanity.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about us as human beings?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） It is impossible for us to be immune from outside influence.
**题目译文**
说话者关于我们人类说了什么？
A) 我们中很少有人能够忽视我们周围环境中的变化。
B) 我们不可能不受外界影响。
C) 我们中很少有人能够对周围发生的事情毫无察觉。
D) 对我们来说，与自己的世界保持联系是重要的。
**定位** 我们没有谁能免疫于自身所处世界的影响，别自欺欺人地以为我们不被生活中的事和人所触动。
**信号** 总括性强调句。None of us are immune to the influences of our own world 用 None of us（我们没有一个人）这种全称否定做总括强调，紧接着又用 let us not kid ourselves（别自欺欺人）加重语气，这种把范围拉到所有人的强调句，正是说话人对人类下总论断的答案句。
**替换** None of us are immune to the influences of our own world↔It is impossible for us to be immune from outside influence全称否定改写成 impossible
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱A 里 changes in our immediate environment 借用了原文 We become part of our immediate environment 的原词 immediate environment，听到这个词容易顺手就选；但 A 说的是很少有人能忽视环境变化，原文那句讲的是我们成为环境的一部分，并未说人能否忽视变化，属于借原词答非所问。借用原文： We become part of our immediate environment
C) 偷换概念C 的 unaware of what happens around us 让人联想到第三段 we are unaware that there are changes taking place in our mentality 里的 unaware；但原文说的是我们意识不到自己心态在变，并非意识不到周围发生了什么，而且原文恰恰强调人受影响，C 反说很少有人察觉不到周围，与本篇主线不符。借用原文： we are unaware that there are changes taking place in our mentality
D) 未提及D 说 It is important for us to keep in touch with our own world（与自己的世界保持联系很重要），听上去积极正面；但全篇主旨是我们无可避免地被外界影响、要慎选所处环境，并没有把保持联系当作一种应当去做的要求，属于把基调说反、且原文未提的劝导。
questions.quote: None of us are immune to the influences of our own world, and let us not kid ourselves that we are untouched by the things and the people in our life.

options.text: Few of us can ignore changes in our immediate environment.
It is impossible for us to be immune from outside influence.
Few of us can remain unaware of what happens around us.
It is important for us to keep in touch with our own world.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say Fred should do first to improve his quality of life?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） Recognise the negative impact of his coworkers.
**题目译文**
说话者说Fred应该首先做什么来改善他的生活质量？
A) 下定决心重新开始。
B) 停止对他人做出不公正的评判。
C) 尝试在别处找一份更令人兴奋的工作。
D) 认识到他同事的负面影响。
**定位** 不过，假如 Fred 真想改善自己的生活质量，他要做的第一件事，就是认清这些年来一直在发生的事。
**信号** 转折 However 加顺序词 the first thing。这句以 However 转折开头，把前面别去评判Fred 的话拨回正题，再用 the first thing he'll need to do 明示第一步，转折后加顺序词的位置正是答案句所在。
**替换** recognize what has been going on all these years↔Recognise the negative impact of his coworkers笼统 what has been going on 具体化为同伴影响
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 过度推断A 说 Make up his mind to start all over again（下决心从头再来），动作幅度远大于原文。原文第一步只是 recognize what has been going on（先认清现状），并没有让 Fred推倒一切重来，属于把建议拔高、过度发挥。
B) 张冠李戴B 的 Stop making unfair judgements of others 借用了原文 Nor is it our business to stand in judgment of Fred 里的 judgement；但原文是说我们（旁人）不该评判 Fred，主语是我们，而 B 却要 Fred 自己别评判他人，把这句话安到了错的人头上。借用原文： Nor is it our business to stand in judgment of Fred
C) 原词陷阱C 说 Try to find a more exciting job somewhere else（去别处找更刺激的工作），盗用了 Fred 自述里的 never do anything exciting 的 exciting；但那是 Fred 抱怨现状的话，不是说话人给的第一步建议，原文要他先认清现状，而非换工作。借用原文： I never do anything exciting
questions.quote: However, if Fred ever wants to improve his quality of life, the first thing he'll need to do is recognize what has been going on all these years.

options.text: Make up his mind to start all over again.
Stop making unfair judgements of others.
Try to find a more exciting job somewhere else.
Recognise the negative impact of his coworkers.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about psychiatrists?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） They are quite susceptible to suicide.
**题目译文**
说话者关于精神科医生说了什么？
A) 他们相当容易自杀。
B) 他们改善人们的生活质量。
C) 他们深受健康不良之苦。
D) 他们帮助人们解决心理问题。
**定位** 精神科医生这一行业的自杀发生率较高，原因与此相关。
**信号** 职业名直接领出的陈述句。Psychiatrists have a higher incidence of suicide in their profession 由职业名 Psychiatrists 直接开头，是专门描述该群体的唯一一句，定位无需犹豫。
**替换** Psychiatrists have a higher incidence of suicide in their profession ↔They are quite susceptible to suicide higher incidence 改写为 susceptible to
questions.tip:
**排除**
C) 张冠李戴C 的 suffer a great deal from ill health 盗用了同段 doctors as a profession suffer a lot of ill health 的原句；但 suffer ill health 说的是医生（doctors），而本题问的是精神科医生（psychiatrists），把前一句对医生的描述安到了精神科医生头上。借用原文： doctors as a profession suffer a lot of ill health
B) 偷换概念B 说 They improve people's quality of life，其中 quality of life 来自第五段谈 Fred 的improve his quality of life；但那是说 Fred 改善自己的生活，与精神科医生提升他人生活无关，原文从未说精神科医生提升人们的生活质量。借用原文： improve his quality of life
D) 未提及D 说 They help people solve mental problems（帮人解决心理问题），听上去正是精神科医生的本职，很有迷惑性；但原文谈精神科医生只说他们自杀率较高这一负面事实，从未提及他们帮人解决心理问题这一功能，属凭常识脑补。
questions.quote: Psychiatrists have a higher incidence of suicide in their profession for related reasons.

options.text: They are quite susceptible to suicide.
They improve people's quality of life.
They suffer a great deal from ill health.
They help people solve mental problems.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about the American dollar bill?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） Few people can describe it precisely.
**题目译文**
说话者关于美元纸币说了什么？
A) 很少有人能识别它的质地。
B) 很少有人能准确描述它。
C) 它的真实价值可以有不同的解读。
D) 它的重要性常常被高估。
**定位** 许多人能凭声音或质感认出它。但极少有人能准确描述这种世界上最强大、最重要的货币。
**信号** 转折 But 后才是真意。前半 Many can identify it by its sound or texture 是铺垫，真正的落点在转折词后 But few people indeed can accurately describe，But 之后才是说话人要强调的重点，正是答案句。
**替换** few people indeed can accurately describe↔Few people can describe it precisely accurately=precisely 的同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱Few people can identify its texture. 借了录音里真出现过的 texture 一词，但录音说的是‘许多人能凭质感 identify 认出它’，是‘多数人能’而非‘少数人能’，且谈的是认出不是描述，属听到原词就想选的原词陷阱。借用原文： Many can identify it by its sound or texture
C) 张冠李戴Its real value is open to interpretation. 说的是价值有争议，这是录音末段 Controversy continues to surround the true value of the dollar bill 的内容，与本题开头所问的‘能否描述’无关，是张冠李戴到本题。借用原文： Controversy continues to surround the true value of the dollar bill
D) 未提及Its importance is often over-estimated. 称重要性被高估，但录音只说它是 the world's most powerful, important currency，从未说这种重要性被‘高估’，over-estimated 是录音没有的评价，属无中生有。
questions.quote: Many can identify it by its sound or texture. But few people indeed can accurately describe the world's most powerful, important currency.

options.text: Few people can identify its texture.
Few people can describe it precisely.
Its real value is open to interpretation.
Its importance is often over-estimated.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about the exact composition of the American dollar bill?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） It is a well-protected government secret.
**题目译文**
说话者关于美元纸币的确切成分说了什么？
A) 它从未发生过任何变化。
B) 它与颜色有很大关系。
C) 它是政府严密保护的秘密。
D) 它是许多伪造者研究的对象。
**定位** 纸张和油墨的确切成分是受到严密保护的政府机密。
**信号** 对所问对象直接下定性的判断句。录音用 is 把 the exact composition of the paper and ink 直接定性为 a closely guarded government secret，这句对所问对象给出明确判断，就是答案句。
**替换** a closely guarded government secret↔ a well-protected government secret closely guarded=well-protected 同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及It has never seen any change. 称从未有变化，但录音对 exact composition 只说它是机密，从未提它变没变过，属无中生有。
B) 原词陷阱It has much to do with color. 借了录音真念过的 colored with black ink on one side and green on the other 里的颜色信息，但那句讲的是纸币‘外观颜色’，而本题问的是‘确切构成（成分）’，颜色和成分是两个对象，属偷换概念的原词陷阱。借用原文： colored with black ink on one side and green on the other
D) 未提及It is a subject of study by many forgers. 称构成是众多伪造者的研究对象，录音通篇没有出现 forgers 或伪造者研究这一说法，属未提及。
questions.quote: the exact composition of the paper and ink is a closely guarded government secret.

options.text: It has never seen any change.
It has much to do with color.
It is a well-protected government secret.
It is a subject of study by many forgers.

questions.prompt: Why did the new American government mint only coins for common currency?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） People had little faith in paper money.
**题目译文**
为什么新成立的美国政府只铸造硬币作为流通货币？
A) 人们对纸币缺乏信心。
B) 它们在流通中能保存更久。
C) 它预测它们的价值会增长。
D) 它们更难被伪造。
**定位** 由于这种缺乏信任，新生的美国政府只铸造硬币作为通用货币。
**信号** 因果信号 Because of。录音用 Because of this lack of faith 直接点出‘只铸硬币’的原因，Because of 是明确的因果信号，紧随其前的 this lack of faith 即原因所在，本句为答案句。
**替换** people had little regard for paper money↔People had little faith in paper money little regard for=little faith in 同义替换
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 张冠李戴They could last longer in circulation. 谈‘流通中更耐久’，录音里确有寿命话题 Few dollar bills survive longer than 18 months，但那是讲纸币短命、不是讲硬币因更耐用才被选，属张冠李戴。借用原文： Few dollar bills survive longer than 18 months
C) 与原文相反It predicted their value would increase. 说预测价值会上涨，但录音说的是纸币 its steadily decreasing value（价值持续下跌）才导致不信任，方向正相反，属与原文相反。借用原文： its steadily decreasing value during the colonial era
D) 未提及They were more difficult to counterfeit. 称硬币更难伪造，听来像个合理理由，但录音从未把‘只铸硬币’归因于防伪，counterfeit 一词原文也没出现，属未提及。
questions.quote: Because of this lack of faith, the new American government minted only coins for common currency.

options.text: People had little faith in paper money.
They could last longer in circulation.
It predicted their value would increase.
They were more difficult to counterfeit.

questions.prompt: What have generations of American politicians argued for?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） A gold standard for American currency.
**题目译文**
几代美国政治家主张什么？
A) 稳定美元价值。
B) 发行政府证券。
C) 美国货币采用金本位制。
D) 美元稳步升值。
**定位** 美国历史上一代又一代的政治家都主张为美国货币确立金本位。
**信号** 表态短语 argue in favor of。录音用 argue in favor of a gold standard 这一表态短语直接说出政治家支持的对象，argue in favor of 是判定‘主张什么’的信号，其后的 a gold standard 即答案核心。
**替换** argue in favor of a gold standard for American currency↔A gold standard for American currency.近乎原词对应的主张对象
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及The stabilization of the dollar value. 谈稳定币值，录音末段虽讲到币值 the American dollar bill holds the value that is printed on it，但从未说政治家‘争取稳定币值’，属未作为主张提及。借用原文： the American dollar bill holds the value that is printed on it
B) 原词陷阱The issuing of government securities. 借了录音真念过的 government securities，但原文说那是美联储担保的形式，不是几代政治家所争取的目标，属听到原词就想选的原词陷阱。借用原文： a Federal Reserve pledge as a confirmation in the form of government securities
D) 与原文相反A steady appreciation of the U.S. dollar. 称‘美元持续升值’，录音并无政治家主张升值之说，反而说现状是 holds the value that is printed on it, and little more（仅值面额、别无更多），与升值方向相左，属未提及兼与原文相反。借用原文： holds the value that is printed on it, and little more
questions.quote: American history has seen generations of politicians argue in favor of a gold standard for American currency.

options.text: The stabilization of the dollar value.
The issuing of government securities.
A gold standard for American currency.
A steady appreciation of the U.S. dollar.

transcriptTranslations: 你是牛津大学的物理学教授。你是欧洲核子研究组织的高级顾问。你似乎还不知疲倦地在全球巡回演讲。此外，你还有自己的每周科学电视节目。你哪来这么多精力？
哦，我就是热爱我做的事情。能过上这样的生活，做我热爱的事，我感到非常幸运。
教授，你的目标到底是什么？你为什么做这些？
嗯，就像你说的，我确实在做很多不同的事情。但我认为这些可以分为两类：科学教育和对科学的进一步理解。
这两件事不会互相妨碍吗？我的意思是，做演讲不会占用实验室的时间吗？
其实不会。我热爱教学，我不介意现在比过去花更多时间在这上面。而且，我要说的是，教授一门学科能帮助我自己更好地理解它。我发现当我必须清楚地解释某件事时，当我必须帮助别人理解它时，当我必须回答有关它的问题时，这会增进我自己的知识。对任何人来说，高水平的教学都是非常有启发性的，无论他们在所教授的领域已经有多少专业知识。
你有没有看到即将出现的科学突破，我们能期待很快会有重大发现或发明吗？
世界一直在进行科学研究，不断有新事物被发现。事实上，现在我们的电脑里有太多数据。比如，我们有成千上万张望远镜拍摄的火星照片，但从来没人看过。我们有这些照片，但没人有时间亲眼看它们，更别说分析它们了。
你觉得梦有特殊含义吗？
不，我觉得没有。
我也不这么认为。但有些人相信。我会说那些相信梦有特殊含义的人是迷信的，尤其是在现在。在过去，在古埃及、希腊或中国时期，人们曾经相信梦能预见未来。但今天，有了我们掌握的所有科学知识，我认为要相信这类事情就难多了。
我奶奶很迷信，她认为梦能预测未来。有一次她梦到自己第二天要坐的航班坠毁了。你猜她怎么做的？她没坐那个航班。第二天她甚至都没去机场。相反，她坐了同一个航班，但是一周之后的。结果当然一切都好好的，没有飞机坠毁。
真有意思！你知道吗，坐飞机实际上比任何其他交通方式都安全？这在统计学上已经得到证实。人们有时候真是太不理性了。
是的，完全同意。但即使我们觉得它们很荒谬，情感有时可以和理性思考一样强大。
没错。人们会因为非理性的感受做各种疯狂的事。但实际上，一些心理学家认为我们的梦是当天情感和记忆的结果。我记得好像是Sigmund Freud说过，儿童的梦通常是他们愿望的简单呈现，是他们希望发生的事情。但在成年人身上，梦是他们更复杂情感的更为复杂的反映。
心理学家试图用科学方法去理解像梦这样奇异的东西，这不是很有趣吗？心理学就像是对非理性感受的理性研究。

questions.prompt: Why does the woman say she can be so energetic?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） She can devote all her life to pursuing her passion.
**题目译文**
女士为什么说她能如此精力充沛?
A) 她可以倾其一生追求自己的热爱。
B) 她积累的专业知识帮助她实现目标。
C) 她可以在每周的电视节目上传播自己的学术思想。
D) 她的研究成果在世界范围内广受赞誉。
**定位** 哦，这个嘛，我就是热爱我所做的事。我极其幸运能拥有这样的生活，做着自己热爱的事。
**信号** 被问者的直接应答。男方上一句问她"哪来这么多精力"，女方紧接的应答 I just love what I do 就是答案句——对话题里，问句之后被问者的第一句正面回应往往就是落点。
**替换** I just love what I do↔pursuing her passion love what I do = pursuing her passion doing what I love doing↔ devote all her life to pursuing her passion一生热爱 ↔ devote all her life
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 原词陷阱Her accumulated expertise helps her to achieve her goals. 里的 expertise 来自后文第6 段 no matter how much expertise they may already have，但那是在谈教学的好处，与"为何有精力"无关，是把别处原词搬来骗选。借用原文： no matter how much expertise they may already have
C) 张冠李戴She can spread her academic ideas on a weekly TV show. 的 weekly TV show 出自男方提问 you have your own weekly TV show on science，那只是介绍她的身份背景，并非她解释精力来源，张冠李戴。借用原文： you have your own weekly TV show on science
D) 未提及Her research findings are widely acclaimed in the world. 借了 research、world 这类访谈高频词，但全文从没说她的研究成果"广受赞誉"，属未提及，更答非"为何有精力"。
questions.quote: Oh, well, I just love what I do. I'm extremely fortunate to have this life, doing what I love doing.

options.text: She can devote all her life to pursuing her passion.
Her accumulated expertise helps her to achieve her goals.
She can spread her academic ideas on a weekly TV show.
Her research findings are widely acclaimed in the world.

questions.prompt: What has the woman been engaged in?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） Science education and scientific research.
**题目译文**
女士一直从事什么工作?
A) 为欧洲的核实验室提供指导。
B) 环游世界参加科学电视节目。
C) 在牛津大学监管两个研究小组。
D) 科学教育和科学研究。
**定位** 嗯，正如你所说，我手头确实有不少不同的事。但这些，我认为，可以分成两大类：科学教育，以及对科学的进一步理解。
**信号** 归并信号 divided into two groups。她用 can be divided into two groups 把零散事务收成两类，这种"归类"句正是回答"主要从事什么"的落点；冒号后两项就是答案核心。
**替换** the education of science and the further understanding of science↔Science education and scientific research education+understanding ↔ education+research
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 原词陷阱Provision of guidance for nuclear labs in Europe. 借男方介绍里的 a senior advisor at the European Organization for Nuclear Research，但那只是她诸多身份之一，不是她对"从事什么"的总括，以偏概全。借用原文： a senior advisor at the European Organization for Nuclear Research
B) 原词陷阱Touring the globe to attend science TV shows. 把男方提到的 tour the globe tirelessly, giving talks 和 weekly TV show on science 两件事拼一起，既非她的归类、内容也被改装（去做讲座变成去上电视秀），原词陷阱。借用原文： tour the globe tirelessly, giving talks
C) 原词陷阱Overseeing two research groups at Oxford. 里的数字 two 与地名 Oxford 极具迷惑性，但原文只说她是 a professor of physics at the University of Oxford，从未提"管两个研究组"，数字属无中生有。借用原文： a professor of physics at the University of Oxford
questions.quote: Well, as you said, I do have different things going on. But these, I think, can be divided into two groups: the education of science and the further understanding of science.

options.text: Provision of guidance for nuclear labs in Europe.
Touring the globe to attend science TV shows.
Overseeing two research groups at Oxford.
Science education and scientific research.

questions.prompt: What does the woman say about the benefit teaching brings to her?
questions.explanation:
**答案** A （细节题） A better understanding of a subject.
**题目译文**
女士如何评价教学给她带来的益处?
A) 对某一学科有更深入的理解。
B) 迎接挑战的意志更加坚强。
C) 对相关领域有更广泛的了解。
D) 与年轻人建立更紧密的关系。
**定位** 另外，我想说的是，教一门学科能帮助我自己更好地理解它。我发现，当我必须把某件事讲清楚时，这会增进我自己的知识。
**信号** 受益句 helps me comprehend it better。她用 teaching a subject helps me comprehend it better myself 直说教学的好处，helps me 是受益标志句，答案就锁在这里。
**替换** helps me comprehend it better↔ A better understanding of a subject comprehend better = better understanding
questions.tip:
**排除**
B) 过度推断A stronger will to meet challenges. 看似呼应第 6 段 Teaching at a high level can be very stimulating，但 stimulating 指"令人有激情/受激励"，并非"更强的迎难意志"，属过度推断。借用原文： Teaching at a high level can be very stimulating
C) 偷换概念A broader knowledge of related fields. 借了她说的 furthers my own knowledge 里的knowledge，但她讲的是同一学科理解"更深"，C 却改成相关领域"更广"，深被偷换成广。借用原文： it furthers my own knowledge
D) 未提及A closer relationship with young people. 像是从 aid others in understanding it 联想"帮助别人→拉近关系"，但原文谈的是教学增进她自己的理解，从未说"与年轻人关系更近"，未提及。
questions.quote: Also, what I will say is that teaching a subject helps me comprehend it better myself. I find that it furthers my own knowledge when I have to explain something clearly.

options.text: A better understanding of a subject.
A stronger will to meet challenges.
A broader knowledge of related fields.
A closer relationship with young people.

questions.prompt: How does the woman say new scientific breakthroughs can be made possible?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （细节题） By making full use of the existing data.
**题目译文**
女士认为如何才能实现新的科学突破?
A) 通过应用最新的研究方法。
B) 通过充分利用现有数据。
C) 通过在先前发现的基础上进行研究。
D) 通过使用更强大的计算机。
**定位** 事实上，眼下我们有太多数据躺在电脑里。我们手握这些数据，却没人有时间亲眼看过它们，更别说分析了。
**信号** 现状落差暗示出路。她强调 right now we have too much data sitting in computers 却nobody has had time to look at them——点出"数据已有、只是没人去用"的落差，言下之意突破靠把现有数据用起来。
**替换** we have too much data sitting in computers↔ making full use of the existing data已有大量数据 ↔ existing data nobody has had time to look at them with their own eyes, let alone analyze them↔making full use of the existing data没人去看分析 ↔ 该 full use
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及By applying the latest research methods. 听起来合理，但原文谈的是"数据已有、没人去看"，从未提"用最新研究方法"，无中生有。
C) 偷换概念By building upon previous discoveries. 像是呼应 there are constantly new things being discovered 里的 discovered，但她的重点是"用好已有数据"，不是"在前人发现上加盖"，借 discover 一词擦边偷换。借用原文： there are constantly new things being discovered
D) 原词陷阱By utilizing more powerful computers. 直接抄了录音里的 computers（data sitting in computers），但电脑在原文只是"数据存放处"，她从没说要"用更强的电脑"，听到computers 就选正中圈套。借用原文： we have too much data sitting in computers
questions.quote: In fact, right now we have too much data sitting in computers. We have them, yet nobody has had time to look at them with their own eyes, let alone analyze them.

options.text: By applying the latest research methods.
By making full use of the existing data.
By building upon previous discoveries.
By utilizing more powerful computers.

questions.prompt: What do both speakers think of dreams?
questions.explanation:
**答案** B （态度观点题） They have no special meanings.
**题目译文**
两位说话者对梦的看法是什么?
A) 梦能够预测未来事件。
B) 梦没有特殊含义。
C) 梦具有文化内涵。
D) 梦无法轻易解释。
**定位** 男：你觉得梦有特殊含义吗？女：不，我觉得没有。男：我也不觉得有。
**信号** 被问者的直接应答。男方一开口就问"梦有无特殊含义"，女方 No, I don't think they do.是直接应答，男方紧接 I don't either. 表示"我也不"，一问两答把双方立场都钉死，这正是答案句信号。
**替换** No, I don't think they do. ↔ They have no special meanings.否定提问=否定其内容
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 与原文相反They can predict future events. 抓的是录音 dreams could foresee the future，但那是男方转述"古人曾经相信"的旧观念，并被他用 much harder to believe in these sorts of things 否定，不是两人现在的看法。借用原文： people used to believe that dreams could foresee the future
C) 未提及They have cultural connotations. 听上去高级，但录音通篇没说梦有"文化内涵"，cultural connotations 是凭空添加，无任何对应句。
D) 答非所问They cannot be easily explained. 录音从未说梦"难以解释"；两人讨论的是梦有没有特殊含义，而非解释难度，与他们表达的看法不符。
questions.quote: M: Do you think dreams have special meanings? W: No, I don't think they do. M: I don't either.

questions.prompt: Why didn't the woman's grandmother take her scheduled flight?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） She dreamed of a plane crash.
**题目译文**
为什么这位女士的祖母没有乘坐预定的航班?
A) 航班因恶劣天气被取消了。
B) 她睡过头了,错过了航班。
C) 她梦到了飞机失事。
D) 航班被推迟到第二天。
**定位** 有一次她梦见自己第二天要坐的那班飞机坠毁了。你猜她怎么做？她没坐那班飞机。
**信号** 因果叙事链。女方先说 she dreamed that the flight… crashed（梦见坠机），紧接 She didn't take that flight.（于是没坐），前因后果一气呵成，"梦见坠机"就是没坐航班的原因，是本题答案信号。
**替换** she dreamed that the flight she was due to take the following day crashed↔She dreamed of a plane crash.长句概括为短句
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 未提及It was canceled due to bad weather. 录音从没提天气或航班被取消，是凭空编出的常见原因，无对应句。
B) 答非所问She overslept and missed the flight. 录音明说 She didn't take that flight.（主动选择不坐），而非睡过头错过；"主动不坐"和"被动错过"性质相反。
D) 原词陷阱It was postponed to the following day. 偷了录音里的原词 the following day，但原文the following day 是说"她原本第二天要坐"，且她是改坐一周后的航班，根本不是航班被推迟到第二天。借用原文： the flight she was due to take the following day
questions.quote: Once she dreamed that the flight she was due to take the following day crashed. Can you guess what she did? She didn't take that flight.

options.text: It was canceled due to bad weather.
She overslept and missed the flight.
She dreamed of a plane crash.
It was postponed to the following day.

questions.prompt: What does the woman say about people's emotions?
questions.explanation:
**答案** D （细节题） They can have an impact as great as rational thinking.
**题目译文**
这位女士关于人的情绪说了什么?
A) 情绪可能会受到人童年经历的影响。
B) 情绪有时在理性思维看来可能显得荒谬。
C) 情绪通常源于人的不愉快记忆。
D) 情绪可以产生与理性思维同样大的影响。
**定位** 但即便我们觉得它们荒唐，情绪也可以和理性思考一样强大。
**信号** 让步转折后的主句。女方这句用 even if we think they are ridiculous（让步）退一步，真正要强调的是转折之后的主句 emotions can be just as powerful as rational thinking，让步从句是幌子、主句才是观点，正是答案信号。
**替换** emotions can be just as powerful as rational thinking↔They can have an impact as great as rational thinking. powerful换成great impact
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴They can be affected by people's childhood experiences. 蹭的是后文 children's dreams 里的"孩子"印象，但那处讲的是"梦"不是"情绪"，且女方没说情绪受童年经历影响。借用原文： children's dreams were usually simple representations of their wishes
B) 原词陷阱They may sometimes seem ridiculous to a rational mind. 抓住了原词 we think they are ridiculous，但那只是女方让步退一步说的半句，她真正强调的是转折后的"情绪同样强大"，只取让步句等于漏掉了观点。借用原文： even if we think they are ridiculous
C) 偷换概念They usually result from people's unpleasant memories. 录音虽提过 memories，但没说情绪"源于不愉快的记忆"，unpleasant 是凭空加的限定，与女方所说不符。借用原文： our dreams are the result of our emotions and memories from that day
questions.quote: But even if we think they are ridiculous, emotions can be just as powerful as rational thinking.

options.text: They can be affected by people's childhood experiences.
They may sometimes seem ridiculous to a rational mind.
They usually result from people's unpleasant memories.
They can have an impact as great as rational thinking.

questions.prompt: What did psychologist Sigmund Freud say about adults' dreams?
questions.explanation:
**答案** C （细节题） They reflect their complicated emotions.
**题目译文**
心理学家Sigmund Freud关于成年人的梦说了什么?
A) 梦需要科学方法来解释。
B) 梦反映了人们长久以来珍视的愿望。
C) 梦反映了人们复杂的情绪。
D) 梦常常与非理性情感有关。
**定位** 但在成人身上，梦是他们更为复杂精微的情感的、远更复杂的反映。
**信号** But转折切到成人。前句讲 children's dreams… simple representations of their wishes（孩子的梦=愿望），随后 But in adults 用 But 转向成人，这句才是题干问的成人梦，是答案信号——转折后才是本题落点。
**替换** dreams are much more complicated reflections of their more sophisticated sentiments↔They reflect their complicated emotions. sentiments=emotions改写
questions.tip:
**排除**
A) 张冠李戴They call for scientific methods to interpret. 抓的是结尾女方 psychologists try to understand using the scientific method，但那是女方的感叹、谈的是"心理学家研究梦"，并非弗洛伊德对成人梦的说法。借用原文： psychologists try to understand using the scientific method
B) 原词陷阱They mirror their long-cherished wishes. 盗用原词 their wishes，但弗洛伊德说"愿望"指的是 children's dreams（孩子的梦），题问的是成人，对象被偷换。借用原文： children's dreams were usually simple representations of their wishes
D) 张冠李戴They are often related to irrational feelings. 蹭的是前文 irrational feelings，那是男方说"人因非理性情绪做疯狂事"，并非弗洛伊德对成人梦下的定性。借用原文： People do all sorts of crazy things because of their irrational feelings.
questions.quote: But in adults, dreams are much more complicated reflections of their more sophisticated sentiments.

options.text: They call for scientific methods to interpret.
They mirror their long-cherished wishes.
They reflect their complicated emotions.
They are often related to irrational feelings.
