title: When People Stepped Back: What Lockdowns Revealed About Wildlife

sentences.text: For decades, ecologists have known that human activity changes the way wild animals behave, but separating the different parts of that influence has proved surprisingly difficult.
Roads, farms and buildings permanently reshape the land, while people themselves come and go, and the two pressures usually rise and fall together.
As a result, it has rarely been possible to say whether an animal avoids an area because of the concrete or because of the crowds.
The COVID-19 pandemic offered an unexpected solution.
In the spring of 2020, lockdowns abruptly reduced the number of people moving through many landscapes, even though the roads and towns themselves remained exactly where they had been.
A team led by Ruth Oliver of the University of California, Santa Barbara, and Scott Yanco of the Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute saw this as a rare natural experiment.
The work formed part of the COVID-19 Bio-Logging Initiative, an international collaboration involving roughly 600 partners.
The researchers compared weekly GPS records from 4,581 individual birds and mammals, belonging to 37 species, across the continental United States in matching periods of 2019 and 2020.
To measure human presence, they turned to anonymised mobile-phone location data, recorded at the level of neighbourhoods rather than individuals.
According to the team, this was the first time such data had been used to examine how people affect animal movement.
The information is normally held by private companies, and the researchers were able to obtain it only because of the circumstances of the pandemic.
The results, published in the journal Science, showed that both kinds of pressure mattered.
Human presence on its own was linked to changes in the size of territories or ecological niches for around two-thirds of the mammal and bird species studied.

More than half of all species responded to both human presence and landscape modification, and the two effects were intertwined: the impact of people depended partly on how developed an area was, and vice versa.
Perhaps surprisingly, animals were most sensitive to people in relatively undeveloped places such as national parks, rather than in cities.
Individual species reacted in very different ways.
Wolves used more space as human presence increased, possibly in an effort to keep their distance from people.
White-tailed deer widened their niches in modified landscapes but narrowed them when more people were around, while sandhill cranes showed the reverse pattern.

For this reason, the authors argue that conservation measures may need to be tailored to particular species, taking into account not only infrastructure but also where and when people are physically present.
The study does have limits.
It covers only birds and mammals in the United States, and the lockdown period was, by any standard, highly unusual.
More importantly, it shows that animals changed their behaviour but not whether those changes helped them or were a sign of stress.

sentences.text: Cooperation is often thought of as something that happens within a single species, such as a pack of wolves hunting together or worker bees sharing food.
Yet many animals also work with partners from entirely different species, trading food, protection or cleaning services.
A recent review in the journal Animal Behaviour, written by 58 researchers from fields as varied as biology, anthropology and linguistics, set out to understand how such partnerships are coordinated.
The project grew out of a workshop on interspecies cooperation held in Cambridge in July 2023.
One of the best-known examples involves a small African bird, the greater honeyguide.
Using special calls, the bird leads human honey-hunters to wild bees' nests, and once the hunters have opened a nest, it feeds on the wax left behind.
The relationship works in both directions, since the honeyguide also responds to calls made by the humans.
Similar exchanges take place elsewhere.
Warthogs adopt particular body postures to invite banded mongooses to remove ticks from their skin, giving the mongooses an easy meal in return.
On coral reefs, cleaner fish and cleaner shrimp use bright colours and distinctive movements to advertise their role, which allows them to approach large predatory fish safely.
Their customers, in turn, often signal that they want to be cleaned by holding their bodies in predictable positions, such as standing on their heads or tails.
Some butterfly larvae even produce chemical and vibrational signals that persuade ants to guard them instead of eating them.

According to the authors, communication is central to these relationships because partners frequently need to time their actions precisely, something that is harder when two species perceive the world in very different ways.
Signals also help animals judge whether a partner can be trusted and so avoid being exploited.
Because many species communicate through several senses at once, the researchers warn that studies focusing only on what animals see may overlook important signals.
The review also found that these signals vary considerably.
Some systems are highly consistent, while others differ depending on location, the species involved and whether the signals are inherited or learned.
For example, fishers who work alongside dolphins in some regions interpret particular dolphin behaviours as a cue to cast their nets, and these cues are not the same everywhere.
Many signals appear to have begun with a completely different purpose, such as caring for young or settling disputes, before being adapted for cooperation with other species.
The authors stress that much remains unknown about how these systems develop and change over time.
They call for research on a wider range of animal groups, together with experiments that test how signals arise and persist.
Such work, they suggest, could reveal how interactions between species help to shape entire ecosystems.

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture given by a university researcher about the benefits of woodland, which aims to explain how forests contribute to human wellbeing, to children's education, and also to the economy.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'd like to discuss the wide-ranging benefits that woodlands bring to people and societies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These advantages can be considered in terms of wellbeing, education, and even the economy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To begin with, within forest environments, plants release valuable oils with proven therapeutic properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are now incorporated into a range of medicines and beauty treatments worldwide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This demonstrates how natural resources from woodlands are not only important for traditional remedies but also for modern industries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, the refreshing smell of trees and leaves is one of the forest's most powerful features.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many people say it brings an instant sense of tranquility.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That sensory experience is one of the reasons why forest walks are becoming so popular among people living stressful urban lives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, research shows that walking in forests can enhance sleep patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It allows the body to reset its rhythms and promotes overall wellbeing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These findings are supported by health studies showing that time spent in green spaces lowers stress hormones, which in turn improves the quality of rest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Equally significant is the cultural role of woodlands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In many regions, woodland areas preserve ancient stories that shaped local identity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Passing them on allows each generation to connect with its history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Forests, therefore, act as living museums where traditions and narratives are kept alive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What is more, there is a quiet magic that lingers among trees and streams.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It reminds people of myths, legends, and hidden possibilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For many, forests are not just physical spaces, but symbolic places of wonder that continue to inspire creativity and imagination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turning now to the younger generation, young learners gain valuable experience by handling basic tools under supervision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This exposure helps them appreciate both safety and craftsmanship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Such hands-on practice is difficult to achieve in classrooms, but becomes natural in outdoor programs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the same way, children also develop respect for the natural world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead of capturing them, children are guided to notice the movements of various insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This method fosters respect for living things and builds awareness of ecosystems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Through these activities, children not only learn science, but also build empathy for the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, it is worth highlighting the economic perspective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rural forests may generate more reliable wealth than metropolitan property.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This stability results from renewable resources rather than fluctuating housing markets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, long-term investments in woodlands can provide steady returns through timber, ecotourism, and even carbon credits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to financial profit, forests also support farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rows of trees around farmland create natural shade that lowers ground temperature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This cooling effect can reduce the demand for extra watering.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By moderating the microclimate, woodlands help farmers save water and reduce costs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, pollination is another critical service.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the wind is reduced by planted trees, pollinators like bees can work more effectively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their activity directly benefits farmers by raising the quality and quantity of harvests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This shows how woodland management has positive ripple effects across the agricultural sector.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite regulations, vegetable farming comes with several challenges.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's consider the environmental factors that influence vegetable growth.

transcript.text: Vegetables with high moisture content, such as lettuce, cucumbers, and zucchinis, depend on a reliable source of water for healthy growth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Insufficient hydration can lead to poor growth, reduced yield, and a lack of flavor in the final product.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some vegetables, like onions and garlic, require a longer growing season and are typically planted in the autumn to be harvested the following year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Understanding the best planting time for each type of vegetable is essential for ensuring successful harvests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's explore some scientific aspects related to vegetable cultivation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The history of cultivating vegetables has its roots in ancient civilizations from thousands of years ago, such as Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Early agricultural societies selectively bred plants for desirable traits, leading to the domestication of many vegetables we consume today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over time, improvements in farming techniques, such as crop rotation and soil enrichment, have contributed to higher yields and better quality produce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another fundamental factor in plant growth is sunlight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This natural resource is essential for photosynthesis, allowing plants to convert light energy into food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without adequate exposure to sunlight, vegetables may grow weak, producing smaller or misshapen crops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers often adjust planting arrangements to maximize sun exposure, ensuring that taller plants do not overshadow smaller ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Greenhouse technology has also been developed to regulate light conditions, allowing for year-round vegetable production even in colder climates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some vegetables have unique growth characteristics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, carrots, potatoes, and beets develop underground and depend on an extensive root system to absorb nutrients from the soil.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Root vegetables are often rich in vitamins and minerals, making them an essential part of a balanced diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, their growth can be affected by soil conditions, requiring farmers to rotate crops regularly to maintain soil health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, one of the most distinctive qualities of vegetables is their taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The flavor of vegetables like tomatoes, peppers, and cucumbers can vary significantly depending on ripeness, soil composition, and climate conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, a tomato grown in nutrient-rich soil under full sunlight will likely have a sweeter taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture for teacher trainees on using drama activities in the classroom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So now we're going to look at some of the reasons why it's beneficial to include drama activities such as role play in your teaching practice in a range of subject areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: There's a lot of evidence to show that drama helps a child's personal development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Firstly, creating the space for children to express themselves freely in a group situation helps to give them confidence in their own opinions and ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And of course, drama activities can work especially well for shy or introverted children who usually don't participate in other types of classroom situations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Secondly, unscripted improvisation activities where children work from their imagination, if done in a supportive way, give children the opportunity to gain experience in taking risks and encourage them to say things that they might normally be afraid to say.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Drama can also support the child's educational development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For example, the emphasis placed on cooperative activities in drama means that group members must learn the value of listening to one another.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Being involved in any sort of performance, which relies on everyone working together and playing their part, also helps children to be responsible not only for their learning but for their general behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These are just a couple of ways in which drama can benefit a child's learning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now I'd like to look at how role play can be such a valuable learning tool in the classroom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The value of role play for children who are having difficulties as a means of therapy is now widely accepted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The experience of doing a role play where children act out aspects of their own life without explicitly stating that it is a direct representation of their own experiences can help children to judge their own behavior in an objective way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One obvious example would be doing a role reversal with a bully role-playing a victim.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Because this approach doesn't involve direct confrontation, it may help the bully to see his or her behavior in a different light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: More generally, role play also allows the teacher to explore potentially controversial or taboo subjects in a safe setting in which children feel at ease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's obviously essential for children to feel they won't be criticized or judged for voicing certain views.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Getting children to examine their thoughts and opinions carefully can lead to a deeper self-knowledge and a stronger awareness of morality.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This is an important factor in developing social skills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Let's look at a specific subject area now and think about how drama can enrich the learning process for the study of history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Bringing characters from the past to life in the classroom by doing classroom drama activities is an easy way to improve the level of the children's participation in the lesson.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So drama in the history classroom makes for a livelier atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But getting children to reenact scenes from history can also be extremely useful as it helps them to remember what happened and why it was important, as well as helping to bring the past alive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another way of doing this is to ask children to find solutions to historical problems using role play.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This can help to focus attention on why certain decisions were taken.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For example, children can be asked to decide how best to defend their town from attack or where to build a new settlement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, what I'd like to do now is to think about your next teaching practice session and in groups discuss how you would incorporate an element of drama into your lesson plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 录音提到在小组环境（group situation对应题目中的group participation）中自由表达能赋予孩子们信心（confidence），即对应题目中的发展信心。

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the subject of why living in the city may be better for the environment than living in rural areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today we're looking at urban migration, the movement of people migrating from outside cities into cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think it's easy to jump to the conclusion that a rural lifestyle is greener.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, recent studies have suggested otherwise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, if we take the land area of the Earth, the proportion that cities take up is a mere three percent, and these same cities actually produce thirty to forty percent of the carbon that is released into the atmosphere, a lower amount than the sixty to seventy percent from non-urban areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, let's imagine that most people decide to migrate to the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What kind of impact would that have?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For a start, this movement of people from the countryside should lift the pressure of intensive agriculture from the land, allowing forests to regenerate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another point in favor of urban migration is that it can be far more energy efficient if services are concentrated in the city, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is true for electricity and, as you can imagine, water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, once you remember that rural communities are often very spread out, you can see yet another green reason to live in the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rural citizens rely on the car to make their journeys far more than city dwellers who have other, more environmentally friendly forms of transport that they can use, such as buses and trains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The journeys tend to be shorter, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet another point in favor of urban migration is the kind of recycling schemes that can only take place where the population is concentrated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take, for instance, Seattle in the USA, where methane gas is being put to good use and is generating energy for the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's produced from the city's rubbish, which could not be collected so efficiently from rural areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, another factor that threatens the environment is the growing world population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's estimated that seventy-five million babies are now born every year, and in some countries the birth rate shows no signs of slowing down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Urban migration may provide an answer here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now in cities, one of the reasons that women tend to have fewer children is that they get married later and start their families later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the reason for this is that it's far easier to find a job and, once you have one, to get a promotion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So yes, the focus isn't on bearing children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it would be foolish to pretend that there are no downsides to urban living when clearly there are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The thing that critics often mention is the idea that migrants may end up losing their culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although some studies have found the opposite is true.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rather than give up their traditions, people actually work hard to maintain them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More evident is the fact that compared to the lower rate that is observed in rural areas, we can see that there is more crime occurring in cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There won't be many of us here today who can say we haven't been directly or indirectly affected by it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's another issue that we have to deal with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So many cities, including our own, now suffer from high levels of pollution, so that the air we breathe is far from pure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And another factor against the urban is greener idea is that urbanization often drives a country's economy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Put simply, when there is greater wealth in society, more energy is consumed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the direct effects of a stronger economy, something that many citizens will now experience every day and may well find stressful, is the amount of traffic on the road, despite the other options we mentioned earlier.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is a problem that is not about to go away, although there are some solutions that could be considered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's have a look at some of those-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 演讲者指出城市产生的碳（carbon）占30%到40%，这个数量低于非城市区域的60%到70%。
questions.tip: 听到 "produce... less... than" 的比较结构时，抓住原文中的 "lower amount than" 对应的名词 carbon。
questions.quote: Speaker: ...these same cities actually produce 30 to 40% of the carbon that is released into the atmosphere, a lower amount than the 60 to 70% from non-urban areas.

questions.explanation: 人口向城市迁移可以减轻对土地的农业压力，从而允许森林（forests）再生。

questions.quote: Speaker: For a start, this movement of people from the countryside should lift the pressure of intensive agriculture from the land allowing forests to regenerate.

questions.explanation: 城市居民拥有比农村居民更环保的交通（transport）形式，如公共汽车和火车。
questions.tip: 原文列举了 buses and trains，但题目需要一个概括性名词，对应原文 "forms of transport"。
questions.quote: Speaker: Rural citizens rely on the car to make their journeys far more than city dwellers, who have other more environmentally friendly forms of transport that they can use such as buses and trains.

transcript.text: You will hear a professor of environmental biology talking about urban biodiversity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today I want to talk about urban biodiversity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the amazing variety of plant and animal life that we find in cities throughout the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cities are providing new opportunities for wildlife through habitats provided in spaces such as parks and empty, undeveloped lots.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With some help from humans, species can be preserved despite living close to people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sometimes species survive more successfully than in rural areas where they may be threatened by hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though this is increasingly regulated by governments, another threat they face in rural areas is the ever-encroaching spread of farms and suburban housing, which reduces natural habitat significantly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once you start to look, you will be amazed by the variety of life which exists side by side with people in cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look at the wildlife which share our buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are moss and lichens on older buildings, and particularly numerous are the insects which find breeding places and shelter there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And urban environmentalists have for a long time been aware of the particular attraction of garden walls made of wood, stone, brick, and even concrete, which provide ideal spots for smaller plant and animal species to thrive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over time, many species that were initially crowded out from their habitats return to the sites of their original inhabitation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in the heart of cities, this is particularly true in the case of birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: London is today home to the peregrine falcon, a bird once thought close to extinction there, but now doing very well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This magnificent falcon has actually learned how to search for food by night when its urban prey is more likely to be active instead of its traditional forays for food by day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the seagull now living in cities provides safety for its offspring from urban predators by building its nest using trash from the streets below.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This adaptation of urban animals can be compared with the adaptation of humans themselves about ten thousand years ago, when they developed as a society from being hunter-gatherers to a much more geographically stable system dependent upon agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This process led initially to lower life expectancies, in part because the diet of these early humans became less varied and thus, ironically, less healthy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, as humans began to live in ever more dense population centers, disease increased significantly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But over several thousand years, new human gene variants slowly allowed them to cope with these threats to their very existence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Special urban biodiversity projects are being set up in a number of big cities across the world, including Toronto and Singapore, where inhabitants are being encouraged to create a record of the biodiversity in their environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Glasgow has recently launched a plan for volunteers from interested community groups to record information using surveys to determine residents' ideas about how to increase local biodiversity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gathering such data has led to a variety of schemes promoting wildlife.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the UK, a group called Biodiversity Strategy is conducting a special program to encourage the introduction of thousands more trees in urban areas because of their particular suitability as shelter for large numbers of wildlife species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Certain animals, including most famously rats and pigeons, have adapted incredibly successfully to cities, and in fact have done so well in some instances that they have become nuisances and a hazard to health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Likewise, among plants, some weeds often adjust well to urban life, much to the annoyance of landscape specialists and gardeners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many urban dwellers will tolerate nature only if they can control it and if it is relatively clean, not messy or random.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In other words, if wildlife is not truly wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to Part 4.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about underwater archeology and what it reveals about ancient civilizations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In today's lecture, we'll be examining the role of underwater archeological sites in uncovering details about ancient civilizations that might otherwise have been lost to time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These sites are particularly significant for studying cultures that left little to no formal records.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A good example is the Maoris of New Zealand, whose history was passed down orally rather than through written documents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, they are frequently recognized as a society that lacked any form of written script.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This made physical discoveries all the more important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's fascinating is how much we can learn about people's daily routines and social behavior from these remains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The arrangement of objects on board, for instance, can offer clues about the lifestyle of those who sailed centuries ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The process of studying these shipwrecks has changed dramatically thanks to advancements in equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers now rely heavily on underwater drones, sonar scanners, and imaging software.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Collectively, this modern technology has made excavation more precise and far less invasive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, when we talk about causes of shipwrecks, it's easy to imagine warfare or piracy, but more often than not, the wrecks occurred due to natural forces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most commonly cited causes is exposure to a violent storm, which ships at the time were not well equipped to withstand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, the material recovered is sometimes used for more than just academic research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Museums and film producers often collaborate to create immersive exhibitions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In one recent case, artifacts were used in the making of a historical film gallery that visually narrated life on board a seventeenth century trading vessel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That said, researchers frequently face barriers in these investigations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In many locations, fragile ecosystems, unpredictable tides, and limited access have severely restricted the amount of research that can be conducted on site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One particularly compelling case involved a ship that appeared to be equipped for combat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The wreckage included what was believed to be a gun used to defend against pirate raids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A rare find that adds a dramatic dimension to our understanding of maritime risks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Equally intriguing was the discovery of a navigational map, still partially intact, which outlined the ship's intended course through trade routes active at the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These maps not only reveal destinations, but also show the maritime knowledge of the era.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So why were these voyages made in the first place?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, much of it came down to profit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of these vessels were transporting precious materials, particularly gold, which was in high demand across expanding empires.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, it's not unusual for wrecks to yield personal and luxury items.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In several cases, archeologists have uncovered treasure collections featuring fine jewelry and antique coins, shedding light on both wealth and craftsmanship of the period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a Japanese museum comprised mainly of underground space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For the last few sessions, we've been looking at the different architecture for both their utilitarian purposes and aesthetic features as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's lecture, I want to continue this series by first introducing to you a unique underground museum in Japan, and then we'll discuss the pros and cons of underground architecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, this museum was built in nineteen ninety-six, and around eighty percent of the museum is buried underground to preserve the lush natural beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It houses an impressive collection of artworks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The exhibits consist of works from ancient civilizations, including the Egyptians, Romans, and various Asian cultures, with the pieces mainly coming from the founder's private collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But perhaps the most intriguing aspect of the museum is the design of its structures and how they are integrated into their natural surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The museum is humbly embedded in mountains close to a subway station connecting the nearest metropolis in about an hour.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The design was inspired by an ancient Chinese story titled Peach Blossom Valley.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The architect read it when he was a schoolboy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is about a fisherman who loses his way and his boat carries him upstream.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He is drawn into a cave by the fragrant scent of a forest of blossoming peach trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After traveling through a narrow road behind the cave, the man finds an idyllic village amid the splendid view.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The museum has been conceived as a real-world version of this village.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Visitors must pass through a tunnel first and then a cable bridge suspended over a gorge before arriving at the museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The museum's details reflect the designer's innovative endeavor to break new ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The architect changed the design numerous times to ensure the building was in harmony with the natural landscape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It becomes evident as tourists walk around the building as the detail is very fastidious and makes for a unique experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once visitors enter the museum, a sloping roof made of wide expanses of glass draws their attention right away.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The web-like structure filtered the light through and scattered it across the surface, making visitors feel like being outside with a vibrant backdrop of seasonal colors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is now clear that underground buildings have many advantages over traditional above ground houses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And many architects are looking into the possibilities of this type of subsurface structure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most important advantage of these houses, especially in the current scenario of environmental degradation, is that they can better preserve indigenous flora and fauna.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the advantages of underground architecture go beyond that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For one thing, the earth surrounding the homes absorbs noise and thus provides natural soundproofing, creating a quiet living space with privacy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Choosing an underground house will be peaceful and calming even in a noisy region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, there is less part of underground houses that can catch fire.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the most part, wood is no longer needed for building a home underground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The concrete foundations and metal structures of these homes all ensure good fireproofing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now underground houses also have the potential to save energy in the long run as they can tap the earth's heating or cooling power.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The earth's temperature doesn't vary as much as the temperature of the air outside.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It ensures that even though the climate outside fluctuates between extremes, the conditions inside the subterranean homes remain more or less stable

transcript.text: However, there are also concerns over earth-sheltered homes.

transcript.text: Good afternoon.

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about an innovative water management solution that has revolutionized small-scale farming in India, the treadle pump.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This simple yet effective device has not only enhanced the livelihoods of countless farmers, but also promoted sustainability in agricultural practices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The treadle pump was designed with the specific needs of Indian smallholders in mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Traditionally, these farmers relied heavily on seasonal rainfall to irrigate their crops, limiting them to cultivating just one crop per year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the dry season, many families were forced to migrate to urban areas in search of temporary employment to sustain their income.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The introduction of the treadle pump provided a much-needed alternative, enabling farmers to efficiently irrigate their fields and reduce the necessity for seasonal migration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The concept of the treadle pump is akin to that of an exercise bicycle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, instead of wheels, it features two treadles, usually made of bamboo, on which the user stands and pedals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This action powers two metal pump cylinders, which are connected to a water source, such as a pond or well, by a plastic tube.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the user pedals, water is drawn up and directed into the fields or irrigation canals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This system is particularly advantageous during cooler parts of the day, making the task less strenuous for the user.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Initially designed for use in the rural areas of Eastern India, the treadle pump has undergone several adaptations since its inception in two thousand and six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: New versions have been developed to cater to different environmental conditions, including coastal regions where the presence of saline water and sand can cause blockages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To address this issue, the design was improved by adding a filter made of bamboo, effectively preventing solid materials from clogging the system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The benefits of the treadle pump extend across various domains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Economically, the treadle pump has been a game-changer for many farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has been estimated that the income of the average household using a treadle pump more than doubles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This significant increase in earnings is a testament to the pump's effectiveness in enhancing agricultural productivity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From a health perspective, the availability of a reliable irrigation system has enabled farmers to diversify their crops, leading to a more varied and nutritious diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This improvement in dietary intake has far-reaching implications for the overall well-being of farming communities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Environmentally, the treadle pump offers several advantages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By substituting traditional diesel-powered pumps, it reduces reliance on fossil fuels and consequently, the emission of greenhouse gases.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This eco-friendly approach to irrigation aligns with global efforts to combat climate change and promote sustainable agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of sustainability, the treadle pump stands out for its simplicity and ease of use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can be manufactured from locally available materials, making it accessible to farmers in even the most remote regions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The installation process is straightforward, and the pump requires minimal maintenance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Local mechanics can be trained in just two days to provide the necessary support for the upkeep of the pumps, ensuring that every farming community has access to technical assistance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The treadle pump's success has also been evident in the commercial market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the best-selling products in the company's portfolio is toys that incorporate the pump's technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These toys, designed to resemble animals, have become incredibly popular among children, providing a fun and interactive way for them to engage with technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To foster innovation and attract talent, the company organizes annual robotics design competitions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These events provide a platform for participants to showcase their skills in robotics design and contribute to the field of technological invention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The initiative not only promotes creativity, but also offers opportunities for individuals to make a meaningful impact in the realm of technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In conclusion, the treadle pump represents a remarkable example of how appropriate technology can address the specific needs of small-scale farmers, enhancing their resilience and sustainability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As we continue to explore innovative solutions in agriculture, the treadle pump stands as a testament to the power of simple, effective design in transforming lives and landscapes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for your attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I look forward to our next session, where we will delve further into sustainable agricultural practices and explore other technological innovations that are shaping the future of farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the end of today's lecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please remember that attendance is mandatory, and I look forward to seeing you in our next session.

transcript.text: Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer in development studies talking about transhumance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the way groups of people move from place to place with their animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about what may be a new concept to you, the movement of people with their herds of animals from place to place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is known as transhumance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These peoples are pastoralists, and their animals include cows, sheep, goats, horses, camels, and reindeer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, researchers sometimes make a distinction between 2 types of transhumance, fixed and nomadic, and talk about various factors which differentiate between them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The 1st and most important distinction they make is to do with the climate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fixed transhumance occurs in countries such as Switzerland, where seasons are predictable in terms of weather and timing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nomadic transhumance, on the other hand, is generally practiced in areas where climatic conditions are difficult to predict.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: An example of such a location is Somalia, as the anticipated rains often just don't appear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Secondly, researchers sometimes look at the type of journey that pastoralists make, their movement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For fixed transhumance, the pattern is sometimes known as vertical because it typically consists of a journey from lower ground in the winter season to higher ground in the summer, and vice versa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the wild, of course, animals frequently follow these kinds of migration patterns themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nomadic transhumance generally takes place over a longer distance, and it's far more complex.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The actual pattern varies from year to year, and it's determined primarily by the animals' needs for grass and also for water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another distinction is sometimes made in terms of homes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the case of fixed transhumance, the group will typically have permanent homes in the valley and a shelter which is semi-permanent in the mountains, such as a cabin, to offer some protection from the weather.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In nomadic transhumance, however, the pastoralists always live in temporary shelters which are transported by their livestock from place to place and are usually light and portable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In northern Kenya, for example, the Gabra pastoralist carries the frame of his home on his camel and then covers it with branches when he stops for the night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A 4th factor often mentioned is the number of people taking part.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the case of fixed transhumance, only the people who actually look after the herds travel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These are normally the young ones because they can withstand adverse physical conditions more easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By contrast, in nomadic transhumance, the whole group moves with their livestock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The last points of comparison often made by researchers are diet and goods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fixed transhumance, those who do not move from the valleys often start working as farmers, cultivating the land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They build up contacts with other communities, and in some cases, they may also trade animals for grain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In nomadic transhumance, there are fewer contacts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The group are generally regarded as providers of all their own needs, and they obtain food such as cheese and meat and also their clothing from their herds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another example is found in Algeria in North Africa to see how far this model applies to transhumance there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fixed transhumance from valley to mountain pastures is common in the area, but some recent pastoralists also take their herds on longer journeys at the end of spring, from the Sahara in the south to the plains in the north, where there is more abundant rainfall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They have traditionally assisted local farmers with the harvest, which takes place while they are temporarily a resident there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have to decide whether their move would fall within the category of fixed or nomadic transhumance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is true they live in tents, and these are movable and temporary right through the year, whether they are in the Sahara or in the north of Algeria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, in considering their homes, they appear nomadic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, in relation to their patterns of movement, they do not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They drive their livestock through the same passes and mountains each year, which suggests fixed transhumance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, in fact, we have a case showing some features of both types of transhumance, which we might more precisely refer to as intermediate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This all goes to show that you should treat every theory with great care and not force your case history into a model if it doesn't fit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.quote: Another distinction is sometimes made in terms of homes. In the case of fixed transhumance, the group will typically have permanent homes in the valley and a shelter which is semi-permanent in the mountains, such as a cabin, to offer some protection from the weather.

questions.quote: In nomadic transhumance, however, the pastoralists always live in temporary shelters which are transported by their livestock from place to place and are usually light and portable. In northern Kenya, for example, the Gabra pastoralist carries the frame of his home on his camel and then covers it with branches when he stops for the night.

questions.quote: A 4th factor often mentioned is the number of people taking part. In the case of fixed transhumance, only the people who actually look after the herds travel. These are normally the young ones because they can withstand adverse physical conditions more easily.

questions.quote: The last points of comparison often made by researchers are diet and goods. In fixed transhumance, those who do not move from the valleys often start working as farmers, cultivating the land.

questions.quote: In nomadic transhumance, there are fewer contacts. The group are generally regarded as providers of all their own needs, and they obtain food such as cheese and meat and also their clothing from their herds.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about time measurement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about the research project I've been involved in on time measurement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Do you know how time is measured?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Consider how we measure length and how, with time, we encounter a difficulty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Before we could grasp it, it would slip through our fingers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In fact, as we can see, we are forced to have the resource to measure something else, the movement of something in space or a set of movements in space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: All the methods that have been employed so far really measure time by a motion in space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The measurement of time is no easy matter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A scientific unit only arrived at after much thought and reflection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As the most primitive form of measurement, the sun seems to be natural.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Ever since man first noticed the regular movements of the sun and stars, we have wondered about the passage of time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Prehistoric people first recorded time according to the sun's position.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: To start off, let us take noon, which is when the sun is on the meridian at the highest point of its course across the heavens and when it casts the shortest shadow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But this measurement, which was regarded as a major one in ancient times, was less important than the natural events that occurred.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The earliest natural events that had been recognized were in the heavens.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But during the course of the year, there were many other events that indicated significant changes in the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Seasonal winds and rains, the flooding of rivers, the flowering of trees and plants, and the breeding cycles or migration of animals all led to natural divisions of the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And the further observation and local customs led to the recognition of the season.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Years later, precise measurements were invented because the passage of time was extremely important for astronomers and priests who were responsible for determining the exact hour for daily rituals and for important religious festivals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Apart from the connection with religion, accurate time measurement was also related to the government, since they divided the day or the night into different periods in order to regulate work and various events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For thousands of years, devices had been used to measure and keep track of time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The current sexagesimal system of time measurement dates back to approximately two thousand BCE from the Sumerians.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It was found that the earliest ancient timekeepers were mainly invented and used in Mesopotamia, where the water clock was introduced from.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As well as in North Africa, especially in the area of ancient Egypt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So now, I'd like to introduce you to some of the most well-known ancient timekeepers, as well as the disadvantages of them, for which they were replaced by various new forms of clocks that were used afterwards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A sundial is a device that tells the time of day by the apparent positioning of the sun in the sky.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In the narrowest sense of the word, it consists of a flat plate and a gnomon which casts a shadow onto the dial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As the sun appears to move across the sky, the shadow aligns with different hour lines, which are marked on the dial to indicate the time of day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, it was quickly noted that the length of the day varied at different times of the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Therefore, there could have been a difference between clock time and sundial time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In addition, the sundial was of no use at night, so a water clock was invented.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The water clock, or clepsydra, appeared to have been invented around one thousand five hundred BCE and was a device which relied on the steady flow of water from or into a container.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Measurements could be marked on the container or on a receptacle for the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It was reliable, but the water flow still depended on the variation of pressure and temperature from the top of water in the container.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As the technology of glassblowing developed from sometime in the fourteenth century, it became possible to make sandglasses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Originally, they were used as a measurement for periods of time, like lamps or candles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But as clocks became more accurate, they were calibrated to measure specific periods of time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The drawback, however, as you can imagine, was the limited length of time they could measure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The last timekeeper to be introduced is the fire candle clock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Candle clocks took advantage of a simple concept, the slow and consistent nature of a burning wax candle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: By utilizing this process, our ancestors were able to keep steady track of the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The clocks were created by engraving the length of the candle with evenly spaced markings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Each marking represented a single unit of time, and as the wax burned down, each hour would disappear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, the drafts and the variable quality of the wax mainly influenced the time of burning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Like oil lamps, candles were used to mark the passage of time from one event to another, rather than tell the time of day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a student presentation about work on an archaeological site in Southern Europe.

transcript.text: For my presentation, I'm going to talk to you about the archaeological dig I went on in the summer at the site of Trimara in Southern Europe, near the Mediterranean Sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The site is backed by a range of mountains to the north, overlooking a green, fertile plain to the south.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me first give you an idea of the history of the area and the growth of the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first evidence we have of human settlement in the Trimara area is of hunter-gatherers around twelve thousand years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, about five thousand years ago, farmers settled along the many rivers which cut across the plain, and later still, from about two thousand five hundred years ago, the city of Trimara was established, and it soon became a regional center for trade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The city was first invaded by the Greeks around three hundred BC, then the Romans in one hundred BC.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Under the Romans, it became very prosperous and traded in grain, olives, and pottery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then in five eighteen AD, an earthquake destroyed Trimara, and the city was abandoned.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, much of the city was covered with soil and rock by the earthquake, and so luckily for us archaeologists, many of the ruins survived intact.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first report on the ruins dates back to around seventeen oh six when a French explorer passed through the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He thought that what he was seeing were the ruins of a castle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the nineteenth century, a British archaeologist began to explore the site, and later, a Polish count made the first map of the area and recorded some of the inscriptions which were visible on the surface.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it was not until nineteen eighty-two that a Swedish archaeologist made a full survey of the ruins of Trimara.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first remains to be excavated were identified as those of the market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Archaeologists were trying to establish how trade was organized here and the type of goods which were commonly bought and sold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In and around this area, various examples of silver coins have come to light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the Roman period, it appears that the city was completely reorganized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The public squares were paved, as were the main streets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is also some proof to suggest that textile production was an important industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The huge prosperity during this period was helped by the fact that the city was responsible for provisioning the Roman army in the eastern region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, what I'd like to do is talk about some of the more important buildings in some detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, the Doric House.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This Greek building is located to the east of the city, near the copper mines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This building is where the local population would come to get their water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The fact that the ruins were so well preserved has meant that the team of archaeologists excavating the site has been able to partially reconstruct the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The remains of a theater are to be found in the northwest of the city, adjacent to the river, where a magnificent bridge made of stone has recently been unearthed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Roman times, the theater appears to have been extended and may have been able to take up to five thousand spectators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the southwestern corner of the city are the remains of an elegant stairway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It dates back to about thirty-seven AD.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The stairway is decorated with sculptures of lions as opposed to bears found in other parts of the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is possibly because of trading links with Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, the most recent discovery has been at the site of the Roman baths in the central area of Trimara.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, a huge statue of an emperor from the Roman period was excavated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It appears to have been carved in pieces and then taken to the site and put together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The statue is very finely detailed and the recent discovery of marble toes and the hem of a dress suggests that a companion statue may also be buried in the bath site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the dig, I was responsible for many...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear an ecologist giving a presentation on research on a type of snail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The topic I've chosen for my presentation is a snail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Snails belong to a group of animals called mollusks, soft-bodied creatures normally protected by a hard shell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about a particular example, the white-lipped grove snail, and the research which is being done into it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll start by giving some background information about this variety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The white-lipped snail lives on land and is air-breathing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its shell is easy to recognize because of its clear stripe, but it varies considerably in color from pale pink to yellow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The snail gets its rather strange name from the fact that it has a white edge, or lip, to its shell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its principal source of nutrition is plants which are either already dead or in the process of rotting, a characteristic it shares with a number of other species of snail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of this, its normal habitat is similar to other land snails, and it can be seen in urban settings such as gardens, as well as uncultivated areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A final point about its ecology is that it also needs calcium and other minerals to keep it healthy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To get these, it frequently consumes soil, which contains these minerals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So far, nothing I've said would seem to set this variety apart from other land-dwelling, air-breathing snails.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, as long ago as the early 19th century, naturalists observed that these white-lipped snails appeared to live in 2 strikingly separate areas, many hundreds of miles apart, namely Ireland and the Pyrenees, the large mountain range on the border of France and Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what is most surprising is that there was no record of the variety being found anywhere in between these places, so the distribution seemed very strange.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This age-old puzzle has intrigued a group of present-day researchers at the University of Nottingham, and they've decided to undertake a detailed study to investigate the strange distribution pattern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: 1st of all, they wanted to make sure that the distribution 1st noticed 200 years ago is in fact correct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Via the internet, they set up what is known as a mega lab, recruiting numerous volunteers across Europe to be responsible for the collection of snail specimens, which were then sent to the university lab.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Like many of these mega lab initiatives, it was generally very successful, with high rates of participation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The research team then did a genetic analysis of the material they received.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They confirmed that there were characteristics shared by the 2 sets of white-lipped snails from Ireland and from the Pyrenees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most importantly, this variety does not seem to occur anywhere else.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How could this split have happened, and when?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, fossils indicate that the white-lipped snail has been living in the Pyrenees for tens of thousands of years, but that in Ireland, its arrival was relatively recent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This fact was very telling for the researchers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It generated a number of different theories to explain the strange distribution phenomenon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The 1st theory the researchers looked at is one called convergent evolution, which basically means that the 2 sets of snails would have developed entirely separately by complete coincidence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the underlying similarities between the 2 sets are too close to be purely a matter of chance, so this seems an unlikely explanation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The 2nd theory proposed is called natural migration, which would necessitate the snails swimming the sea to Ireland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was ruled out because they hate salt and simply wouldn't have embarked on the journey across the sea, or had they tried, wouldn't have survived.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The team then started looking at different kinds of evidence, reviewing findings from various locations in the Pyrenees which showed that mounds of white-lipped snail shells had been thrown away in caves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Clearly, these had been inhabited by Stone Age communities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This led to the conclusion that the snails must have been used over a long period by these Stone Age humans as food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And interestingly, this was before the advent of agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The team then looked at other types of archaeological evidence from prehistoric times in Ireland and the Pyrenees, and they found evidence that very early on there had been trade between the people living in these widely separated areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For all these reasons, the research team have tentatively concluded that the most likely way in which the snails traveled from east to west was in boats, and that they were transported live to keep them fresh for consumption on the journey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The research team acknowledge that their study is in the early stages and needs further work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They recognize, for example, that they need to look at a broader sample of the snails.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also feel that other animals and plants might shed light on their research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They have found that there is probably at least one other type of organism which shows the same distribution pattern, the clear split between the Pyrenees and Ireland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is a species of tree which they want to look at in more detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Perhaps its story will corroborate that of the humble migrating white-lipped snail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about Viking life and culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0
