transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The Vikings, known for their seafaring skills, were not only warriors but also traders and explorers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Their voyages extended far beyond Scandinavia, reaching as far as North America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One significant piece of evidence confirming this is the discovery of a small silver coin found in a site associated with indigenous settlements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This finding suggests that Viking traders may have engaged in exchanges with indigenous people, possibly bartering metal goods or textiles for local resources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Warfare played an important role in Viking society, and they were skilled in producing and using a variety of weapons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Archaeological digs have unearthed a range of armaments, including spears, axes, and an especially well-crafted weapon likely used both in combat and for ceremonial purposes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These weapons were often passed down through generations, signifying status and craftsmanship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One of the Vikings' most impressive achievements was their advanced shipbuilding techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They designed sleek, sturdy vessels capable of enduring long sea voyages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A key feature of their longships was a large sail, allowing them to harness wind power and travel efficiently across vast distances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This innovation enabled them to raid, trade, and establish settlements across Europe and beyond.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Given the harsh conditions at sea, preserving food for long voyages was crucial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Vikings employed various methods to prevent spoilage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One commonly used technique involved drying or curing meat, but they also relied heavily on a natural preservative, mainly salt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This ensured that their supplies remained edible for extended periods, particularly during their voyages to distant lands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Everyday life among the Vikings was quite different from modern times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For instance, their drinking vessels were often made from natural materials rather than glass or ceramics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A common choice was a horn, which was both lightweight and durable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Eating utensils, on the other hand, were simpler than those we use today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Rather than using spoons and knives exclusively, Vikings commonly carried a fork, which served multiple purposes, including assisting in eating and even as a small tool.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Viking sailors frequently encountered storms and rough waters, which often led to ship damage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, they were highly skilled in maintaining and restoring their vessels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Rather than abandoning damaged ships, they made on-the-spot repairs, reinforcing wooden planks, sealing leaks, and replacing worn-out parts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Their ability to repair ships ensured their survival during long and dangerous sea journeys.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Vikings also had a remarkable ability to craft objects from raw materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They were particularly adept at working with oars, transforming them into tools and weapons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One of the most essential materials they relied on was metal, which they shaped into swords, armor, and farming implements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Like many ancient societies, Vikings passed down their history through oral traditions rather than written records.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They often gathered around fires or in great halls to listen to recitations of heroic tales and myths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These narratives were preserved and transmitted through poems, which kept their cultural heritage alive for generations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Unlike in some contemporary societies of the time, Viking women had certain legal rights.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They were able to inherit property and manage businesses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: More notably, they had the right to approach a court if they wished to end their marriage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In such cases, a woman could formally request a divorce, a practice that was relatively uncommon in many other medieval cultures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a marine creature called the red sea urchin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last week, I talked about various research methods in the natural sciences, and you did some background reading on that topic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I want to take up that theme again and look at a specific example of how data gained using newer techniques has really pushed our knowledge forward, more or less overturning existing theories.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I'm going to look at the case of the red sea urchin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, some background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the name suggests, this is a marine animal, and it's found in shallow coastal waters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It grazes on plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's an herbivore, in other words.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here in North America, we can find it all along our West Coast, from Alaska down to California.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So many of you will be familiar with it, and it survives very well because it's covered in spines, which are very sharp, and these deter most predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in the nineteen sixties in this country, the sea urchin was thought to be partly responsible for the sudden decline in kelp, a plant which supports an extensive ecosystem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So in fact, it was considered to be a pest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Incidentally, since the nineteen sixties, the thinking on that has changed, and humans are now thought to be to blame.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But anyway, red sea urchins weren't popular, and people even tried to poison them to get rid of them in any way possible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But then in the nineteen seventies, attitudes changed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, this had nothing to do with science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There were no new insights into the biology of the sea urchin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was, in fact, a purely economic development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It became apparent that there was a demand for the red sea urchin in Asia, where certain parts of the animal were considered to be a great delicacy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And so a commercial fishery was established based on sea urchins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They brought high prices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, at one point during the nineteen nineties, they were one of the most valuable marine resources in the state of California.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So people began to look at the sea urchin in a different light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And just at this time, people noticed an apparent decline in the numbers of sea urchins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This prompted a wave of scientific studies with the purpose of getting more information about the species, its life cycle, its biology, survival rate, growth patterns, and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what did research uncover?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the most significant findings came from research based on biochemical techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Basically, individual sea urchins were tagged and injected with tetracycline, which allowed researchers to track their growth rates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it quickly became apparent that the sea urchins grew a lot more slowly and lived a lot longer than had previously been thought.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Astonishingly, they can have a vast lifespan greater than that of almost any other terrestrial or marine species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They can live to be one hundred years old, and some may even reach two hundred.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just imagine, an individual red sea urchin that hatched early in the nineteenth century may still be thriving and even breeding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was found that this animal does grow fairly quickly when it's young.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the age of two, it can grow from two to four centimeters in just one year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even then, according to scientists who conducted the research, it still takes six or seven years before it's big enough to be harvested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the time the red sea urchin is a teenager, its growth slows quite dramatically.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And from the age of twenty-two, when it's about twelve centimeters long, it grows at just point one of a centimeter a year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But somehow, the animal never really stops growing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It just grows incredibly slowly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of the largest and probably the oldest sea urchins were found off the coast of British Columbia between Vancouver Island and the mainland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And now another very recent study, one using an entirely different technique, has produced independent evidence for these findings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study measured levels of radiocarbon, and it has shown that even very old sea urchins show almost no sign of aging when something finally kills them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike when someone looks at you or me, you can't look at a sea urchin and say whether it's young or middle-aged.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in addition to that, even when they're incredibly ancient, they are still able to breed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So by now, you may be wondering how with this phenomenal lifespan, there aren't a lot more sea urchins around than there actually are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there is a suggestion that reproduction rates for the species are low because not many red sea urchins are able to survive the first year of life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study also confirmed the finding that in older sea urchins, there is a very steady, very consistent rate of growth, and this growth is independent of ocean conditions and other variables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what are the implications of these findings?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
The Red Sea Urchin
Background
The red sea urchin:
• feeds on {{31}}
• is covered in {{32}} that protect it
• used to be regarded as a {{33}}
From 1970s onwards:
• it became clear that {{34}} was an important market for red sea urchins
• scientific interest increased because of a {{35}} in red sea urchin population
Research findings
Study based on biochemical techniques
Red sea urchins:
• grow very slowly
• live a very long time (maximum life span: up to {{36}} )
• can be harvested only after 6–7 years
• after 22 years, only grow {{37}} per year
Study measuring radio carbon
• no evidence of {{38}} when sea urchins die
• they can still {{39}} when very old
• growth not connected to {{40}} or other external factors

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到海胆“grazes on plants”（以植物为食），这里的 graze on 完美对应题干的 feeds on。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到紧随其后的 herbivore（食草动物），但题目需要填的是它具体“吃什么”而不是“它是什么动物”，且填 herbivore 也不如 plants 直接。
questions.quote: It grazes on plants. It's an herbivore, in other words.

questions.explanation: 录音提到它能很好地存活是因为“covered in spines”（长满尖刺），这直接点出了起保护作用的覆盖物。
questions.tip: 千万不要因为听到了后面的 predators（捕食者）就填进去，录音说的是尖刺能“震慑”（deter）捕食者，捕食者是防御对象而非它身上的东西。
questions.quote: And it survives very well because it's covered in spines, which are very sharp, and these deter most predators.

questions.explanation: 录音里原话总结说“it was considered to be a pest”（它被认为是一种害虫），这里的 considered to be 直接同义替换了题干的 regarded as。
questions.tip: 前面出现的 kelp（海带）是一个强干扰，但那是海胆导致数量减少的植物，并不是海胆本身被赋予的称呼。
questions.quote: Now, in the nineteen sixties, in this country, the sea urchin was thought to be partly responsible for the sudden decline in kelp, a plant which supports an extensive ecosystem. So in fact, it was considered to be a pest.

questions.explanation: 听到“became apparent”和表示需求的“demand”后，紧接着定位到的地点就是“in Asia”（在亚洲），对应题目的重要市场（important market）。
questions.tip: 你可能会被前面提及的 economic development 干扰，但这只是交代大背景，真正的市场区域词只有 Asia。
questions.quote: It was, in fact, a purely economic development. It became apparent that there was a demand for the red sea urchin in Asia, where certain parts of the animal were considered to be a great delicacy.

questions.explanation: 录音指出人们注意到海胆数量出现了明显的“decline”（下降），这促发了一波科学研究（prompted a wave of scientific studies），对应题干的科学兴趣增加。
questions.tip: 不要单填 numbers，题目问的是种群数量发生了“什么”变化导致了研究，填“下降”才符合完整逻辑。
questions.quote: And just at this time, people noticed an apparent decline in the numbers of sea urchins. This prompted a wave of scientific studies with the purpose of getting more information about the species, its life cycle, its biology, survival rate, growth patterns, and so on.

questions.explanation: 录音提到它们能活到100岁，随后补充说有些甚至能达到（reach）两百岁（two hundred），这才是题目要求的最大寿命（maximum life span）。
questions.tip: 注意，不能填“200 years old”。题干里的“寿命长达……”后面问的是“多长时间”（200 年），而“200 years old”意思是“200 岁”，英语里不能说“寿命长达 200 岁”，只能说“寿命长达 200 年（200 years）”。另外，极容易听到 one hundred years old 就赶紧写上，忽略了题干中 maximum（最大）这个限定词，一定要听完句子的后半部分转折或递进。
questions.quote: They can live to be one hundred years old, and some may even reach two hundred. Just imagine, an individual red sea urchin that hatched early in the nineteenth century may still be thriving and even breeding.

questions.explanation: 录音里明确指出，从22岁开始，它每年仅仅生长“point one of a centimeter”（0.1厘米）。英文的单位是：只要前面的数字不是 1，单位就必须加 s，除非你写成0.1cm.
questions.tip: 前面抛出的 twelve centimeters（12厘米）是个巨大的陷阱，那是它22岁时的“总身长”，而不是题干所问的“每年生长量”。
questions.quote: And from the age of twenty-two, when it's about twelve centimeters long, it grows at just point one of a centimeter a year.

questions.explanation: 录音明确指出，即使是很老的海胆在死时也几乎没有“aging”（衰老）的迹象（no sign of），这里的 no sign of 直接替换了题干的 no evidence of。
questions.tip: 有些同学可能会试图拼写 radiocarbon，但那是研究测量的手段，而不是海胆死亡时缺乏的“证据”。
questions.quote: The study measured levels of radiocarbon, and it has shown that even very old sea urchins show almost no sign of aging when something finally kills them.

questions.explanation: 录音提到，哪怕它们已经极其古老（incredibly ancient = very old），它们仍然能够“breed”（繁殖）。
questions.tip: 跟丢的同学可能会觉得 ancient 不是 old，但其实就是 very old 的同义替换，死死盯住“still able to”就能抓出动作 breed。
questions.quote: And in addition to that, even when they're incredibly ancient, they are still able to breed.

questions.explanation: 录音结尾总结这种生长独立于（independent of）“ocean conditions”（海洋条件）和其他变量，independent of 就是 not connected to 的直接替换。
questions.tip: 很容易只填 ocean 或者只填 conditions，要注意听完整这个名词短语，少字会导致意思不精确而被扣分。
questions.quote: The study also confirmed the finding that in older sea urchins, there is a very steady, very consistent rate of growth, and this growth is independent of ocean conditions and other variables.

33.q: used to be regarded as a

34.q: was an important market for red sea urchins
34.s: there was a demand for the red sea urchin in Asia

35.s: prompted a wave of scientific studies
in the numbers of sea urchins

36.s: can live to be one hundred years old
some may even reach two hundred

title: The Preservation Of Organisms And Fossils

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk about fossils and their preservation at a fossil park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome everyone to today's talk on fossils and their preservation here at Green Mountain Fossil Park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our goal is to give you an overview of how fossils are formed and classified, as well as how you can acquire them as souvenirs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's start with the three main types of fossils found here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first type is transitional fossils, which are quite rare.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These fossils display characteristics that bridge the evolutionary gap between ancestral species and their modern descendants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A well-known example would be fossils that show traits of both dinosaurs and birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, the second type is actual fossilized remains of ancient organisms, which is categorized under preserved ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike the first type, preserved fossils maintain much of the original structure, making it possible to see distinct features of plants or animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The third category is ichnofossils, which can help to trace fossil size and forms through the actual remains of an organism, but instead provide evidence of their activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These include footprints, burrows, or tunnels left behind by prehistoric creatures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's explore how fossils are formed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One way is when an organism gets trapped in volcanic ash, which preserves it in great detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, a more common process is petrifaction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first step is that after an animal dies, it gets buried in the mud or silt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over time, the mud surrounding the remains dries and hardens, creating a protective layer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Eventually, the bones decay and are replaced by minerals in the surrounding soil, which leaves behind a stone-like fossilized structure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This process allows us to uncover fossils millions of years later, providing valuable insights into prehistoric life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if you'd like to take home a fossil as a souvenir, there are two places you can purchase them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can visit the shop outside the park or explore the fossils available at the park's exhibitions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As for the prices, don't worry, most fossils can be afforded by customers, although larger ones can be quite expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During your visit, you will come across various tools that will help you learn more about fossils.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, a tape measure is provided next to each fossil, so you can record the dimensions of the specimen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another one is a notebook and pen, which will allow you to document different types of rocks as geology plays an essential role in fossil studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you have a camera, feel free to take photos of the fossils.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This can help you review details later and compare different formations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lastly, a compass can help explore soft sediments, which are often key indicators of fossil locations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you have any questions, feel free to ask our staff members.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Enjoy your visit, and we hope this experience sparks a deeper interest in the fascinating world of fossils.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk about research into learner persistence given by a university lecturer to her colleagues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40 on pages 7 and 8.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: My talk is about a research study I did over a period of 5 years on learner persistence, why some people stick at academic study better than others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As teachers, you will know that there is a tremendous variation in the learner's response to certain things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, a short period of illness might completely destabilize some students and cause them to give up their degree studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other learners might overcome tremendous difficulties to stay the course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am particularly interested in this 2nd group who are the ones with learner persistence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What I decided to do was design a research study using a sample of my university's 3rd year undergraduate students, 295 in all, who obviously had already stayed the course pretty well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The sample was drawn from a range of ages, but there was deliberately a significant number of mature students, and all respondents were living at home in the local region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I wanted to have this element of consistency, not having some coming from outside the area and living in university accommodation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It should be noted, though, that there was significant variation in home background to reflect the variation in our student population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I designed questionnaires which were devised to elicit what their concerns had been as they started the course and what had sustained them throughout the 3 years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Findings from the 1st section indicated that their worries when they started varied from financial concerns, though this had not been as strong as I expected, to career prospects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But mature students with children tended to emphasize uncertainties about their relationship with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The 2nd section of my questionnaire looked at learner persistence under 3 main headings, social and environmental factors, other factors, and intrinsic or personal characteristics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I identified 3 levels of importance for each of these.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the 1st level, those points identified by participants as most important in learner persistence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For social factors, many respondents said how crucial it had been to have good support, though there was no one specific source.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It could be family or friends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As regards other factors, students are heartened not so much by high grades, but by what they regard as success in study.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And for personal characteristics, many respondents reported that they took pleasure in challenge and that this was regarded as very significant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the 2nd level of importance, in the 1st category, a sizable percentage talked about the fact that they had enjoyed themselves in school as an important social factor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the 2nd column, other factors, a number of people said that what was of most importance was decent health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This had a fairly strong influence on their persistence in their studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then under the heading of personal characteristics, there were quite a large percentage of respondents who mentioned they felt it was important to have lots of interests in their everyday lives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This gave them a depth and sense of perspective which less persistent learners might lack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then onto the 3rd level.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Under social factors, several respondents talked about good relationships with their tutors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For other factors, they mentioned lack or absence of any problems in their families.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, under column 3, they identified an ability to juggle several roles, what we might call their capacity for multitasking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, these findings obviously helped inform the design of activities, as I mentioned.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in addition, a number of further recommendations emerged.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, I propose that the department distributes questionnaires to first-year students to help get an idea of their maturity when starting the course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is really our overriding concern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Secondly, I recommend we look into ways of offering induction courses for some selected students to allow them to take on the role of advisors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We think they are the best people to act in that role.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This policy will make support much more accessible to our students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thirdly, this help is often most needed in the evening and night when offices are closed, and so we should set up online services instead of the more traditional telephone services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research has shown that these services are actually more accessible to the majority of students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, it is often important to be proactive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If students are not meeting deadlines, then someone should contact them rather than wait for them to come to us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, are there any questions about the points...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

title: The New Zealand Artist Will Burton

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the contemporary New Zealand artist, Will Burton.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome back to this series of lectures on contemporary New Zealand artists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, Will Burton.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Will Burton stands out from the other artists we've considered in these lectures because of his choice of materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From a young age, Burton has enjoyed making art from rubbish and waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, today, this might not be thought particularly unusual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, lots of artists are doing this sort of thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But at the time when Burton started using this approach, the nineteen fifties, the art world in this country was traditional, to put it politely, and his ideas were highly original.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's for this reason that I want to focus today's lecture on Will Burton's early years when he formed his pioneering approach to art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Burton grew up in the Wellington seaside suburb of Moa Point in the years after the Second World War, and both the place and the time were important influences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He initially spent a lot of time painting, but eventually gave this up because it placed too many limits on his imagination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was then that he started to explore new materials, and in particular, the idea of using rubbish for creative purposes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of his first pieces were made from waste he found in the domestic environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, for example, he did a series of sculptures using glass bottles, but he was also attracted to anything made from plastic, which was then relatively new and exotic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another feature of Moa Point was the beach, and this became an important influence on his work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here he found examples of what he considered to be natural waste, things which nature had discarded, if you like, things like shells, for example, which he often used in his art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, those of you who are familiar with Moa Point will know that the suburb has one other prominent feature, the large rubbish dump, and it was here, perhaps more than anywhere else, that Burton liked to hunt for materials to use in his art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He collected all sorts of things from the dump, as you might imagine, but in particular, he was inspired by any sort of electrical equipment, which in the nineteen fifties was just beginning to be introduced to many homes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, it's perhaps not surprising that most of the artwork he produced during this period has not survived, but the Wellington Museum has managed to hold on to a number of pieces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the things he often found at the dump were old light bulbs, and on display in the museum today is a wonderful series of photographs Burton took of these bulbs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When he left his parents' home, Will Burton studied at the Canterbury School of Fine Arts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here he developed those more formal skills normally associated with students of fine art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the ability to draw in pencil, and in fact, produced many wonderful portraits of his friends, often on a very large scale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But of course, he also pursued his own ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, we can see in his student years the beginnings of Burton's interest in movement and motion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Indeed, I believe that had he wanted to, Burton might easily have found success creating movies, such is his skill in working with movement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another of his great interests in life also began when Burton was at art school.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Like many students in those days, he spent the summer holidays going around the country and then ventured further afield to Australia and Southeast Asia, and this passion for travel has stayed with him throughout his life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Returning to his art, what other themes are of importance?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So much of Burton's output explores the way in which ordinary objects can seem to change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One thing in particular that drives his work is the way appearances change depending on how much light is available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another point is that throughout his career, Burton has been an astute observer of modern society and often a highly critical one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And there is often a wonderfully light and playful character to Burton's work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, he often uses sections of text in his photographs or sculptures to express his sense of humor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this alone would not be enough to secure his importance among our contemporary artists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ultimately, what gives his work its depth is the way the artist so often expresses his sense of loss for those people and places which he will not see again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well now, if there are any questions, please don't hesitate...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about the life and music of the Italian composer Salvatore Sciarrino.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We're really pleased that our university is going to hold a concert featuring the music of the Italian composer Salvatore Sciarrino.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: He's considered one of the leading composers of modern classical music in Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: His music is highly unusual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So in order to prepare you for this concert, I'm going to talk about his life and music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, some biographical details.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Salvatore Sciarrino was born in the Italian city of Palermo in nineteen forty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Though he did receive some music lessons, he is mainly self-taught as a composer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: After a few years of university in his home city, he moved to Rome in nineteen sixty-nine, where he studied electronic music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This experience served as a turning point in the development of Sciarrino as a composer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Turning to his work, he composed a great deal in the nineteen seventies and was a music teacher until nineteen eighty-two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Apart from composing music and teaching, he has also produced a large number of essays on a range of topics, such as the philosophy behind his work and musical form.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Throughout his career, he has won numerous prestigious awards, most notably a major prize in twenty eleven, which recognized his musical originality.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So you could say that he is one of the most important composers of our times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now I'll talk about the characteristics of his music, which some people are a bit surprised by.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The first thing that many listeners will notice about Sciarrino's music is the frequent use of silence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What is also striking about his music is his preference for extremely soft sounds that are sometimes at such a low volume that they can hardly be heard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The other unusual aspect of his music is that he frequently requires musicians to play their instruments in unconventional ways so that, for example, a violin may end up sounding very strange and creating sounds we generally associate with nature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Actually, his novel instrumental techniques have often been imitated by other composers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As a result, he's widely regarded as a pioneer in terms of creating new sounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It may sound strange, but Sciarrino himself has likened his music to a volcano viewed from afar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As you'll see, it builds up slowly to an exciting climax.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Let's move on to talk about the particular piece that we'll hear at the concert.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Many people consider it to be his finest work to date.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's an immense piece of music for piano, chorus, and orchestra that was completed in nineteen seventy-nine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The work is dedicated to a friend who died unexpectedly, so it was written as a kind of memorial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In many ways, it is representative of his work as a whole in terms of the sound that it creates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's technically formidable, and it's a very challenging piece for musicians to play.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The piece opens with a low sound of great complexity that is similar to thunder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This low-pitched noise is sustained almost uninterrupted for forty-five minutes, which may sound quite boring, but I found it to be very haunting and atmospheric.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The sound, by the way, is created by large vibrating sheets of metal, which are slowly manipulated by two percussionists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: There are very quiet and strange chords produced by string instruments and very complex piano melodies that quietly appear and then disappear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Even though the piece will be, for many people, very unusual in terms of the sounds it creates, it actually has a very conventional structure, which is just another surprising aspect of Sciarrino's work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now let's move on to another work...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about a tall palm tree called the Lontar and its role in sustaining human life on the island of Roti.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As part of this semester's geography project, I'm going to talk about a tall palm tree called the Lontar, which mainly grows on the island of Roti in the south of the Indonesian archipelago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the Lontar is a truly amazing example of how one tree can sustain human life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The locals call it the Tree of Life, and with good reason, because the tree provides them with virtually everything they need in the way of food, drink, utensils, and shelter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Lontar juice is the most amazingly refreshing juice you'll ever taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The juice is collected from high in the tree in a process known as tapping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Basically, a slice is cut into part of the tree and the sap flows slowly from it into a container.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's then collected twice daily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Male and female Lontar trees are different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Male Lontars can be tapped all their lives, so they are preferred.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If the female tree is left untapped, a large fruit develops, like a coconut in appearance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The watery interior of the fruit can be drunk, but these fruits are often left to fall to the ground as animal feed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Men and older boys climb to the tops of the trees to do the tapping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They don't use safety equipment, but make things easier for themselves by tying stones to the trunk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What is amazing is that so much of the equipment they use in the tapping process is actually made from the tree itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The men attach all the tools they need to a belt that they wear when climbing the tree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In most cases, climbers own particular trees within their family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ownership involves not only care of the trees themselves, but also a share in the maintenance of the fence, which belongs to the local community.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, more about this incredible juice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tapping reaches a peak at the end of the dry season, which runs from September to October, as villagers work frantically to get their harvest in before the rains come and it gets too wet and windy to climb.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Whatever juice isn't drunk immediately has to be processed as quickly as possible, as it turns sour very rapidly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the rainy season, when no fresh juice is available, the locals drink a concentrated form with water added.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The locals also use this rainy season version of the drink in other ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, it can be used to make biscuits of brown sugar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the Lontar palm supplies much more than sustenance for the Rotinese.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The broad Lontar leaves are woven into a huge number of things: containers for watering the garden and bags for transporting chickens to market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People also use them to cover the roofs of their homes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the leaves are replaced every five years or so, the old ones are burned on the garden as a fertilizer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you see, the leaves are never wasted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Rotinese also make a distinctive hat out of the leaf.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Design-wise, they were inspired by sixteenth-century Portuguese helmets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are many for different occasions, ranging from simple ones for everyday use to larger and more elaborate hats used for a celebration, which are painted in bright colors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Lontar leaf even provides the Rotinese people with a unique musical instrument known as the sasando.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The leaf is made into a sounding board and has strings attached, which are plucked in the manner of a harp, and the sound produced is also similar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even that isn't all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The stalks of the Lontar leaves can also be used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are really strong and grow up to one point five meters long, and local people produce ropes from them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even when a Lontar tree becomes old and unproductive and no longer can be used for tapping, the whole tree is cut down and the thick trunk is utilized for building houses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their immense strength means that they are highly valued for this purpose.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, one thing I haven't spoken about is...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about the symbiotic relationship between humans and a bird called the greater honeyguide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The greater honeyguide bird is a fascinating creature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've spent the last eight years studying the species in southern Africa with the Yao community in the Niassa Reserve in Mozambique.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The birds do help local hunters find wild beehives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The male bird is recognizable by its pink beak, black throat, and yellow shoulder patch.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The female has a black beak and a duller color, while the young birds have a distinctive yellow throat and a noticeable ring around the eye.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The collaborative arrangement between hunters and greater honeyguides was first documented as early as 1588.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But only in our most recent study have we realized the extent to which birds and humans communicate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The reason this relationship has developed is because the trees in the Niassa Reserve, therefore, the hives are especially high, sometimes up to 30 meters, which makes them very hard to find.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The birds locate the beehives stashed away in holes in trees, which the hunters then access in order to make off with the pure, sticky honey inside.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they also leave something behind for the greater honeyguides.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are among the few bird species that can eat and digest wax in this way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The interaction between humans and birds benefits both parties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The relationship between the greater honeyguide and the hunters in Mozambique remains very strong.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Yao community considers their communication with the greater honeyguide to be part of their identity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in some countries outside Mozambique, villagers are now turning more to farming and keeping their own hives, which has led to the role of the bird in honey collection growing smaller.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The phenomenon of the greater honeyguides and the honey hunters is really quite remarkable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This level of complex communication is otherwise unheard of in nature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, what we found with these greater honeyguides is the only known example of targeted two-way communication between people and a free-living species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most remarkable thing about this relationship is the signals people use to communicate with the greater honeyguides.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But how do the birds learn to work with people?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we believe the behavior is innate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The birds inherit the knowledge and then refine it to match their region as they grow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In different parts of the world, they learn to respond to different sounds made by humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the Yao people are ready to hunt, they make a specific noise by unrolling their tongues in a particular way to let the greater honeyguides know.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Tanzania, on the other hand, greater honeyguides listen for a whistle as a sign to begin hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While in Zambia, the sound of chopping wood is the cue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The methods used for gathering honey in the Niassa Reserve are actually no different from those used by most beekeepers around the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to relax the bees and make the process less chaotic, smoke is blown into the hive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although the basic procedure is the same, the conditions that the hunters work in are a lot more difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Besides the obvious risk of being stung by angry bees, the hunters must also be wary of being trampled to death by elephants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is also the risk of injury involved in climbing up to get to the hives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A less serious problem with this style of honey hunting is that the hunters are often required to travel large distances and carry buckets weighed down with honey back to the village, which is not an easy task.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The honey eaten in the Yao community is wildly different from the honey you buy at the grocery store, which has usually been collected from several different colonies mixed together and boiled down to become sweeter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The raw honey from the hives in Mozambique has a strong flavor that almost stings your throat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Raw honey draws its flavor from both the type of bees and the plants from which it is made to form a distinct taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And there are hundreds of quite unique varieties of honey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have 45 seconds to check your answers to Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on rural development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, you'll remember that last week we looked at the migration of people from the interior of West Africa to various coastal towns, with special reference to Ghana.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, today we're going to focus on the people known as the Berbers who live in North Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Berbers inhabited this part of Africa as long ago as the seventh century, and their society was based on tribes which were scattered throughout a number of countries: Algeria, Morocco, Libya, and Mali.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, at some point in the twelfth century, the area was invaded by Bedouin Arabs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These people destroyed the Berber's peasant economy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, many Berbers left their settlements to lead a nomadic life, uh, by wandering with their animals through the deserts and across the different mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the centuries, many Berbers migrated to other countries like Spain and France, uh, to work as laborers, taking with them their culture and traditions, and their descendants remain there until this day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Not all the Berbers led a fully nomadic life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There were three different groups.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, some became farmers, cultivating the lowlands in the winter and grazing their flocks of animals in the mountains during the summer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are called seasonal nomads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some Berbers, who led a completely nomadic life, tended to move from one oasis to another.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A third group settled by the oases and grew fruit and vegetables like dates and eggplants, as well as making olive oil, which they used for cooking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Traditionally, Berbers kept cattle, sheep, and goats, together with oxen, mules, and horses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in the Sahel region of North Africa, th-that's the area south of the Sahara Desert, the region became, and still is becoming, increasingly dry and arid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the Berbers relied more and more on camels for transporting their families and their goods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How did these different groups of people survive in such harsh conditions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where did they live?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, Berbers who stayed put in one place built single-story stone houses for protection by quarrying the local rock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Whereas nomadic Berbers carried their homes with them and erected temporary tents, settled Berbers developed various small-scale industries such as pottery making and weaving, but these tasks were generally left to the Berber women.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you might expect, though, the life of a settled community was governed by the men, who met regularly in the village square to discuss affairs and make decisions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's turn to the Tuaregs, who belong to a nomadic Berber group and move mainly in the central and western Sahara Desert, north of the River Niger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The word Tuareg comes from the Arabic Tawarek and means God-forsaken.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Desert Tuareg carried tents made of strips of goat skins sewn together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As many as, uh, forty skins were needed to make a complete tent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If the skins weren't available, they wove mats made of grass or palm leaves and hung them over a frame so that the tent looked like a humped dome.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tuareg society was traditionally very feudal and organized as a strict hierarchy, ranging from nobles or aristocrats downwards to laborers whose ancestors had once been slaves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tuaregs were famous for their warlike qualities and fierce independence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, one of the greatest insults was to suggest to a Tuareg that his father had died in his bed and not while fighting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tuareg men were sometimes called Blue Men, as all adult males wore a dark blue veil in the presence of women, strangers, and in-laws.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Legend had it that a Tuareg man couldn't be recognized unless he was wearing this veil.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this custom of the veil began to disappear as more and more Tuaregs became urbanized and moved to the towns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I mentioned earlier how dry the Sahel region has become, and there have been very severe droughts over the past thirty years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This has meant that the number of Tuaregs living in the area has declined.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Those whose animals were fortunate enough to survive have moved away from the southern Sahara into Burkina Faso in order to find new grazing lands for their herds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If there's one city which people associate with the Sahara Desert, it's probably Timbuktu.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what most people don't know is that Timbuktu was founded by Tuareg nomads almost a thousand years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The city became the focal point of the trans-Saharan caravan routes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: North African merchants flocked there to do business, and trading in gold and salt flourished.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For many years, Timbuktu was considered inaccessible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But today, what is left of the city attracts a small number of tourists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The tourism department of the Mali government employs some Tuaregs who act as guides.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Essential, really, when you realize that it's only the Tuaregs who can find their way around the desert using the sand dunes as landmarks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll take questions now before I go on to discuss Tamasheq, the language spoken by the Tuaregs, which also has an alphabet called...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk at a university open day to students interested in following a course in textiles and business studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on pages seven and eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Thank you first of all for coming along to the university's open day, and in particular for coming to this talk to find out about our course in Textiles with Business Studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The cooperation between the Faculty of Arts and Architecture and the Business Faculty enables us to offer this undergraduate and integrated master's course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the five years this course has been running, we've learned a lot, and it's become very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, thanks to the Faculty of Engineering, we're also able to offer a really exciting opportunity to those who would like to further diversify and would like to carry their learning through into new disciplines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the aims of this course are firstly to create innovative and highly motivated textile practitioners within the disciplines of knitted textiles, an increasingly popular area as you will have seen on the catwalks, printed, and of course, woven textiles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Secondly, we also ensure that our students gain an in-depth knowledge and understanding of related business operations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We make sure that our students have sufficient hands-on experience by arranging interesting and relevant work placements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The focus of the integrated component of the work placement is the global market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our aim is to locate studio work in this increasingly important context.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on to what we do in each year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the first year, students explore the three subject areas of textiles in rotation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The emphasis for the first year is experimentation, and we ask for evidence of visual research, which must be supported by documentation and proposals for its application.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In year two, design and technical skills are related to the real world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike many other university textile courses these days, we give our students the opportunity to choose an extra module on the traditional processes of design, which gives a historical perspective on their work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This can be done before introducing students to computer-aided design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Students at this point, year two, decide if they intend to complete the course at year three with a BA ons or progress to year four and conclude with a master's in design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Students can also have tutorials if they feel they need help making this important decision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This reflects our commitment to student support at all times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Year three consolidates the knowledge gained using a particular learning style.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's called reflective practice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That means you look back on what you've done and analyze and evaluate your subject in both academic and professional contexts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This helps and encourages deeper understanding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Students produce a dissertation on a topic of their own choosing and a portfolio of their textile collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, to help underpin the commercial aspect of the course, we ask for a business plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the subject of career opportunities, many graduates work directly within the textile business, with careers commonly found as stylists and retail managers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it shouldn't be forgotten that there are many other exciting opportunities out there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, careers in journalism for those with a flair for words or trend forecasting for those with their eye on the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We are certain that we shall see broader and more varied opportunities for our graduates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you like what you've heard today and are thinking of applying for the program and you'd like to talk to us further, please come back tomorrow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll have the opportunity to do a brief interview where we'll be able to assess your aptitude for this subject area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many students who haven't studied related subjects may be surprised to find that they're quite well suited to our program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After that, of course, you'll need to go through the usual application procedures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture related to how technology contributes to education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, and welcome to today's seminar about education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Education is a lifelong process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is no limit on when to start and stop, and we have been using technology so much these days in each and every sector of our lives, including education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have we ever taken out a second to wonder if it's leaving a positive impact on our work, or it's just that we have been relying on it so much that we've become used to it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Earlier, there was a lot of debate about technology in education amongst the faculty at our school.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Everyone had their own views.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, some believed that the use of email between students and teachers made them interact with each other less, and this was not a good thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But gradually, as technology was embraced by more educational institutes, they realized the importance of technology in education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Technology and education are a great combination if used together with a right reason and vision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, there is a strong relationship with the local economy when it comes to the effectiveness of the use of IT in education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the more developed areas, the schools and institutions have better access to more advanced technology, and the teachers are better trained to use the technology to improve the quality of their classes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In contrast, in some less developed regions and remote areas where technology is not so common, the effectiveness can't be guaranteed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, wherever they are, the most common example for teachers using technology in education is the usage of computers in their teaching methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In most classrooms, you can see teachers using computers to present teaching notes and other materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This year, the IT school of Westbrook University has implemented a brand new education mode.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since its implementation, both teachers and students have been praising this new mode.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It involves a kind of software which allows students as well as teachers to talk and discuss with each other more easily, and they said they enjoy this way of communication.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's more, the mode offers students a channel to post any work that they are proud of, whether it's a nice photograph that they take, a case study they do, a song they record, or even just a great idea they have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it gives them a chance to showcase their strength and build up their confidence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many students use this feature to show the best of themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It also provides students an opportunity to choose what they learn on the Internet, so they no longer have to sit in the classroom listening to something they are bored with, and they don't have to wait all night trying to register for their favorite elective courses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Compared with the traditional platform, it is more flexible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The open source which the new mode provides is free for students to use when they are trying to look up for online materials for their papers or researches, and the data will not easily be found on the Internet because only registered users have access to the database.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the way, all the materials are original works of teachers or scholars, so there is no need to worry about the quality of the content.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And with the overwhelming amount of unwanted information on the Internet, this mode gives students a new search engine they can use on campus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So information like advertisements and skeptical sources will be filtered easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is a perfect example of new solutions to new problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Apart from that, students can arrange their daily activities and improve their time management skills by simply ticking the boxes in the timetable online.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They can set up their own starting time and their deadline for each assignment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Based on statistics, the use of this function has a positive effect on the students who constantly procrastinate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the end of the first term, the number of students who asked for extension for their papers had decreased by ten percent, which was quite an achievement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another feature that seems very creative to me is that students can help people who have questions or problems relating to their field of studies on a special platform.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They can even have some income by providing people with good solutions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this new mode is making the most of the IT...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
