transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk about filing and paying taxes given by a man from a central government tax agency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for attending tonight's presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am Mr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dawkins from the Central Government Tax Agency, and I am here to provide you with information regarding filing and paying your taxes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First off, let me tell you that in preparing to file your taxes, evidence that can confirm your actual income has to be adequate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then it should be submitted to the local authority.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can't just guess what your income was, or you may be charged a large sum of penalty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Income can come in different forms, including wage statements, independent freelancer statements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Currently, apart from invoices, we also take bank statements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our tax period usually lasts for one year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Different states have different policies, but here it runs from April to the end of March next year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All of your current supervisors within the tax period are required to provide you with a wage statement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you have not received an annual wage statement within one month of the end of the fiscal year, you should contact us, and we will request them to send this statement immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you need to ask your employers to provide the employment statement because that's something we can't help.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A failure to pay, along with the evasion of or resistance to taxation, is punishable by law.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you do not file an annual tax return, you may find that you will have to pay a penalty up to three thousand dollars in some instances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you'd better file your taxes promptly, since the government does not tolerate this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Everyone should make sure they file a tax return in a timely manner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions thirty-six to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions thirty-six to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, I suppose you have known something about tax.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are very important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I hope you can always keep them in mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And here are some random tips which are also helpful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When you purchase a new car during the tax period, please note that you will need to work out the latest tax rate and pay a line item tax for this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For those who just started getting to know tax filing, I do not recommend that you take multiple types of taxes into consideration at your first attempt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The calculation will be more straightforward with just one type of tax.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please know that most people use their computers to deal with their taxes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When using your computer to do your taxes or subscribe to an online tax service, you will find many advantages that don't exist when you do it at an office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the advantages of preparing your taxes online is that you can save whatever information you have gathered and then resume your preparations at another time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In doing this, since the tax information won't take much of the storage space, you don't have to worry about whether your computer will be able to accommodate the information you have gathered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, in doing your taxes online or in using an online tax service, you will find that mistakes are less likely to happen as the online tax preparation programs have safeguards to prevent you from omitting required information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Generally, to begin working on your taxes, you will go to the tax office and inquire the office workers and finally fill in some forms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But for now, you can go to our website and download some.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If necessary, you can take some time to complete a questionnaire, which will give you advice on which type of form you should fill in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If there are any questions you cannot answer, you can call to speak to someone in person.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for attending tonight's presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please know that my Central Government Tax Agency associates and I are always willing to help you with your tax preparation by answering any questions you might have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on sustainability given by a scientist as a scientific topic of current general interest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This week's lecture on a scientific topic of current general interest is on sustainability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The term sustainability is not new.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was first coined in nineteen eighty-seven in a report for the United Nations World Commission on Environment and Development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since then, however, the term has been applied to everything from cars to agriculture and even economics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My specific focus, in fact, derives from this problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I want to analyze what seems to me to be the confusion that surrounds sustainability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That UN document defined sustainable development as development that allows both the present and all future generations to meet their needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here is the first myth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sustainability is not simply about the environment, which may come as a surprise to you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the original definition says nothing about it at all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sustainability is not about protecting the world around us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The original focus was on finding ways to help poor nations catch up with richer nations, which primarily meant giving them similar rights to natural resources, water, food, energy, the things that many of us take for granted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The consequence and ultimate goal was improving living standards for all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another myth is that sustainability is a synonym for green, as in green movement, green products, et cetera.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although there is some overlap between the terms, green suggests a preference for natural living, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When you go shopping, products marketed as green imply the absence of high technology and mass manufacturing processes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Those groups who campaign for sustainability, we can call them the lobby for sustainability, acknowledge that the situation is desperate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The main problem they state correctly is time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With six billion people on the planet now and a billion more expected in the next thirty years, only technology will be able to provide everyone with an acceptable and safe lifestyle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Electric cars, wind turbines, and solar cells are key examples of this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They make great use of renewable resources while emitting fewer noxious chemicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nuclear power, too, is something the sustainability lobby has come to accept, unlike most greens.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And here's the third myth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It concerns the role of technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Technology is not rejected as evil, but we should not overemphasize the role of technology either.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take electric cars, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers are currently working on plans to electrify the world's car fleet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: New technology is currently being developed to make better batteries, giving longer performance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But a better way of thinking is perhaps to have battery stations for drivers to use on roads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the battery is getting low, they simply swap the old one for a fully charged one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In other words, new business thinking, not new technology for a sustainable future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are similarities in agriculture where knowledge can be more productive than new technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Agriculture uses up about three quarters of the world's water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some crops are very thirsty and require a lot of water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So many farmers who believe in sustainability are now planting crops like sunflowers and wheat instead of corn, which are happy with much less water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of water consumption, one of the biggest problems is that our diet is changing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As countries develop and people become richer, they aspire to a diet with more meat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, admittedly, most of the new births that will take our population to over six billion are going to be born in countries with largely vegetarian diets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, most of them will be born in the city, and this is where water consumption is highest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That introduces the topic for next week's lecture, and we will be discussing...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the ways that supermarkets use layout to increase sales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We've been looking at marketing techniques which influence buying decisions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of these techniques are related to the way the products are presented in the store.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For supermarkets, the store layout is not as random as it seems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Decisions have to be made about the arrangement of the aisles where the customers walk, and the shelves and so on, where the products are displayed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most common layout pattern is the grid layout, where parallel aisles are arranged in a rectangular pattern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Supermarkets like this layout as it allows them to utilize floor space efficiently by providing the greatest amount of display space proportionate to aisle space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, this layout helps to manage traffic flow, as it encourages people to all walk in one direction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The main weaknesses of the grid layout are the monotony of rows of aisles and the fact that it is easier for customers to rush through the supermarket without lingering.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another layout pattern used by supermarkets is known as the free form.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, displays and aisles are arranged in a random pattern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The good thing about this layout is that customers tend to spend more time in the store as they wander about looking for different products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its main weakness is the inefficient use of space, which means it is less cost-effective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then we have the boutique layout, where everything is organized around a food specialty, such as the bakery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The advantage of this layout is that it divides parts of the store into smaller areas, which may be distinguished by changes in flooring or displays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A further advantage is that this style of layout is attractive to shoppers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Space, however, is not used economically, and it is therefore expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The choice of location of particular types of items in the store is also important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A supermarket's design aims to direct customers to the store's side and rear walls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Items typically displayed along the rear length of the store include meat and dairy products, since these appear on the grocery list of the majority of shoppers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This means shoppers must pass by a large number of other items to get to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Items which consumers tend to spend more time considering before buying, such as cosmetics, are usually placed away from the busy areas so that people can look at them in comfort without feeling rushed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Products placed at the end of aisles are clearly visible, and therefore these locations provide a greater opportunity for shoppers to view the products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Consumers tend to assume that items on display at the end of an aisle are on sale, but this is often not the case.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, supermarket managers often place products which are not selling quickly enough in these positions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The placement of products on shelves is very carefully planned.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Supermarket executives use computer-generated plans to help them place products on shelves in a way that ensures consumers spend more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The eye level of the average woman is one meter sixty centimeters off the floor, which is the height of the middle shelves, so the things which cost more are placed here, while cheaper products are placed on higher or lower shelves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Only items targeted at children break this rule.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are placed on the lowest shelves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Supermarkets also use a range of other marketing techniques to encourage consumers to spend more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's no accident that in nearly every supermarket, the fruit and vegetable department is the first shoppers come to as they enter the store.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These, together with flowers, produce a greater profit than any other department.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After complaints from parents, many supermarkets no longer place popular products aimed at children on the shelves next to the checkout.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, you are most likely to find products aimed at impulse buyers, such as chocolate, magazines, and other treats here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many supermarkets have also expanded into non-food areas such as clothing, entertainment, and stationery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about the importance of nutritious fatty acids in cognitive and behavioral health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we're going to talk into the profound impact that long-chain fatty acids, particularly omega-3 fatty acids, have on cognitive function and behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our discussion will weave through a narrative involving a wise grandfather, dive into robust scientific research, and conclude with actionable dietary recommendations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Imagine a scenario where a knowledgeable grandfather pretends to go fishing not just as a bonding experience but also as a teachable moment for his grandchildren.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He uses this opportunity to emphasize that the fish they are catching are not just food but are packed with omega-3 fatty acids essential for brain health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This tale not only entertains but also embeds a powerful lesson about the importance of diet passed down through generations, emphasizing traditional wisdom in our modern health understanding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's explore the scientific evidence supporting the benefits of omega-3 fatty acids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Extensive research has demonstrated that long-chain fatty acids, like those prevalent in fish oil, are fundamental to optimal brain function.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These fats are crucial for the structure of cell membranes and are essential for healthy neurotransmission and neuroprotection, impacting everything from learning to memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, studies indicate a worrying trend.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Children with learning difficulties frequently display lower levels of essential fatty acids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This connection suggests that insufficient intake of these crucial nutrients can significantly impact cognitive development, underscoring the necessity for maintaining adequate levels from a young age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may be curious about the timeline for observing the benefits of omega-3 supplementation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although individual responses can vary, there are documented instances where children have shown improved cognitive functions after taking fish oil supplements consistently for three months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This evidence highlights the importance of regular consumption to achieve noticeable cognitive benefits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it's important to consider that some people may find it challenging to digest fatty acid supplements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This difficulty underscores the potential advantages of obtaining these nutrients directly through dietary sources, which may be more effective and less problematic for some individuals, emphasizing the importance of tailored dietary plans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the clear benefits, only one-third of the population regularly includes omega-3-rich foods in their diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This significant nutritional shortfall presents a public health issue that requires immediate attention to improve both cognitive and overall health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the USA, research has demonstrated a link between regular fish consumption and higher academic performance, particularly in mathematics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Similarly, in Japan, studies have found that consistent fish intake is associated with reduced reading difficulties among students, highlighting the profound impact of diet on academic success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In response to these findings, governments around the world are urging people to increase their fish consumption as part of a public health strategy to enhance cognitive functions and academic performance on a broad scale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: An interesting study from Ireland has also shed light on the behavioral implications of dietary deficiencies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It found that prisoners often exhibit increased aggression due to low levels of omega-3 fatty acids and other minerals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This connection between diet and behavior further illustrates the critical role of a balanced diet in mental and emotional health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This completes our overview of the importance of omega-3 fatty acids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for your attention as we discussed these vital dietary components.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the end of part four.

transcript.text: You will hear a presentation introducing the geographical features, history, and archeological findings on St.

transcript.text: Ninian's Isle in Northern Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to introduce a small island called St.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ninian's Isle, which lies off the coast of the Shetland Islands in Northern Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it is quite small, it has become extremely important for historians and archeologists because of several fascinating discoveries made there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin with the physical landscape of the island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Along this part of Scotland's coastline, there are a number of narrow sea inlets cutting into the land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the local Scottish dialect, people use a special word to describe this kind of coastal feature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The term voe is used locally, and it refers to what most English speakers would simply call a bay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another interesting point about the island today is that it does not have a permanent population anymore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No one lives there throughout the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the island is far from empty because it supports a wide variety of wildlife, particularly seabirds that nest along the cliffs and rocky shores.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These animals are now the island's most common inhabitants, meaning the place is largely populated by birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on to the archeological findings, researchers have carried out several excavations in the ruins of early religious buildings on the island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During these investigations, they uncovered many remains that were clearly human.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among the discoveries were numerous bones, which provided valuable evidence about the people who once lived and worshiped there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Perhaps the most famous discovery, however, was made not by a professional archeologist, but by a local schoolboy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While exploring the island, he came across a small wooden container buried in the ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it was opened, researchers found that every object inside had been made from the same precious metal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All of the items were crafted from silver, which immediately suggested that the collection was extremely valuable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's look more closely at the objects discovered inside the wooden box because these items tell us a great deal about the people who owned them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, the fact that the objects were made of precious metal immediately suggested that the owner was not an ordinary individual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Items like these would have required considerable wealth, and therefore, archeologists believe that the person who possessed them must have held a relatively high status within the local community.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When researchers examined the contents of the box more carefully, they discovered a group of eating vessels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers counted eight pieces of tableware in total, most of which were small bowls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most were probably used for everyday meals, although one was noticeably larger and may have been intended for ceremonial purposes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another particularly interesting item was a spoon with a decorated handle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the end of the handle, craftsmen had carved the image of an animal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The design clearly represented a dog, and the carving showed the animal's head, a decorative style that can still be seen in later metalwork traditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to the bowls and spoons, archeologists identified another unusual object among the collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was a small metal implement whose exact purpose is still debated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, based on its shape and design, experts believe it functioned as a small tool designed to remove shellfish from their shells while eating.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For many years, researchers assumed that the collection of objects must have belonged to a church since the items were discovered close to the ruins of religious buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, more recent interpretations suggest a different explanation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The style and variety of the objects indicate that they were probably part of a private collection owned by a family rather than property belonging to the church itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The final mystery concerns why the items were hidden in the first place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Archeologists believe that the owners deliberately buried the box in order to protect their valuables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At that time, communities in the region sometimes faced raids or attacks, so it is likely that the people who hid the treasure believed they were in danger and hoped to return later to retrieve it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, it seems that they never came back, leaving the treasure to remain hidden for centuries until it was eventually rediscovered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on soundscape ecology as an environmental and scientific topic of general interest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, we'll delve into the interdisciplinary field of soundscape ecology, a discipline that deciphers the complex relationships between sound and ecosystem health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The concept of a soundscape, defined as the acoustic environment of a given area, was first introduced by Murray Schafer, a famous Canadian composer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Schafer's work in the nineteen seventies revolutionized how we perceive urban and natural environments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He argued that soundscapes are not random noise but layered compositions with inherent meaning, reflecting cultural values and ecological interactions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To systematically study soundscapes, ecologists divide them into three fundamental categories based on their sources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first category, biophony, encompasses sounds produced by living organisms or creatures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Australian ecosystems, for example, this includes the croaking of frogs in wetlands during monsoon season.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These amphibians use distinct frequency bands to avoid vocal overlap, ensuring their mating calls are heard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second category, geophony, refers to non-living natural sounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A striking example is the resonance of rain on the broad leaves of Daintree Rainforest flora, a phenomenon so rhythmic that indigenous communities historically used it to predict seasonal changes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, anthrophony captures human-generated sounds, from Sydney’s tram networks to agricultural machinery in the Murray-Darling Basin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike biophony and geophony, anthrophony often disrupts natural acoustic patterns, masking critical animal communication.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bernie Krause, whose background in music profoundly influenced his ecological research, uncovered several groundbreaking principles in soundscape analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Through decades of fieldwork, Krause demonstrated that every organism contributes a distinctive signature to the acoustic landscape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the harmonics of a lyrebird’s mimicry in Tasmania differ measurably from those in New South Wales, allowing researchers to track population health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, Krause’s recordings revealed that healthy ecosystems maintain balance in both loudness and frequency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the Kimberley region, intact ecosystems exhibit acoustic niches: species avoid overlapping frequencies, much like instruments in an orchestra.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Conversely, degraded habitats show chaotic frequency collisions, akin to static interference.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beyond their compositional complexity, soundscapes serve as sensitive indicators of environmental health, offering early warnings of ecological changes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Acoustic monitoring in the Australian Alps detected altered bird migration timings, signaling shifts in climate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Similarly, sudden drops in insect biophony, such as the silence of bees in Western Australian orchards, can warn of invisible pollution like pesticides.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Studies linked these acoustic voids to neonicotinoid pesticides, which impair insect navigation long before chemical traces appear in soil tests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, modern research relies heavily on advanced tools like acoustic recorders, which capture vast datasets across diverse habitats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These devices enable scientists to create detailed maps in three dimensions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, those of the Great Barrier Reef revealed that fish choruses peak during full moons, synchronizing with spawning cycles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A question often posed in public forums is: which organism dominates nature’s soundscape?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While sperm whales and howler monkeys are contenders, the champion is a marine invertebrate: the snapping shrimp.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Colonies inhabiting Australia’s Ningaloo Reef snap their claws at two hundred and eighteen decibels, louder than a gunshot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This cavitation bubble implosion stuns prey and creates microhabitats for other species, proving that even the tiniest organisms can shape entire ecosystems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer giving a talk to design and technology students about a new device which uses the sun to purify water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For many parts of the world today, a lack of clean drinking water is a major problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In some developing areas, bore water, which is water that comes out of the ground, is the only water available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, bore water may be dangerous to drink because it contains excessive amounts of salts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In recent months, I've been working with a research team to develop a device that will help solve this problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we came up with is a solar water purifier, which we have called the SW-Forty,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: and this device not only makes bore water drinkable, it can even process seawater.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it even passed the rigorous testing standards applied by hospitals to determine whether water is sterile enough for use there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only problem we do face at the moment is with its manufacturing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The present method involves a process called vacuum forming, which tends to be rather slow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'd like to change to an injection mold of process, which is much faster but would cost quite a lot to switch to, around one million Australian dollars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are a number of private companies that are very keen to go into partnership with us over this, but my preferred option would be a global aid agency known as Health International that sponsors projects like ours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has a long history of working in these areas, and although it may take a little longer to get an agreement, it should mean a better deal all around.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So just how useful is this device of ours?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the amount of pure water it is capable of producing each day varies as the amount of sunlight available varies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, on a hot day when the temperature is around about twenty-five to thirty degrees Celsius with the sun shining clearly through a blue sky, it produces anywhere from seven liters per day to as much as nine liters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, most people can survive on one to two liters per day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So even under difficult conditions, one family could live off one of these devices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So a normal sized village would require several of these to supply all its needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's look at the device in more detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It weighs eight kilograms and is the size of a medium-sized suitcase.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The SW-Forty has no filters, no electronics, no moving parts, and uses no chemicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how does it work?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there's a rectangular box with a glass lid on it, and on the edge of the box is a steel frame to hold everything together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And inside the box is a piece of black plastic, which is divided up into pockets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You need an incline, so the water flows through the device.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The optimum is twelve point five degrees to the horizontal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it can be one or two degrees above or below that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Impure water is piped in at the top of the box and flows down through the little pockets until they're all full.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You then let Mother Nature in the form of the sun do its work as it shines through the glass window.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It produces infrared light which heats the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time, ultraviolet light from the sun, or UV as we more commonly call it, is also radiated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If there are germs present in the water, prolonged exposure to this type of light will kill them.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a presentation to biology students on new research into sea lions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everybody.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm here today to tell you about a new research study that my team here at the university is doing on the sea lions that live along the coast of Western Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may be wondering why we've been studying this animal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, Australian sea lions have been identified as an endangered species, so there's a real need to count them and find out just how many there are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Up until eighteen ninety-two, the population of these animals was severely depleted because of hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's no longer allowed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But today, there is a new danger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sea lions often forage for food in the same areas along the coastlines where there are nets used to catch sharks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, they tend to get caught up in the nets by accident and drown.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we wanted to monitor the population of sea lions in this area, but we weren't sure of the best way to do it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are several different animal tracking methods which vary in their effectiveness, and there are different factors to consider.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most important of these is the cost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you also have to consider how easy your chosen method is to use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may choose a traditional method like a plastic tag.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're relatively straightforward to attach, but they're really only suitable to use with animals that you can catch quite easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You might also go with a more modern method like GPS tracking, which uses satellite technology to transmit data on the animal around the clock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One drawback for marine animals, though, is that they don't transmit a signal in the ocean.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You only get data when they're on land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are certain large animals in remote areas that have to be tracked using a helicopter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The polar bear is a good example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, an important part of tracking is being able to clearly identify the animal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some, like zebras, are identified by markings such as their stripes, while the dolphin usually has distinguishing scars on its body that can help tell them apart.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sea lions don't have any markings like this, which is just one of the challenges of tracking them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When researchers in Perth tried to use electronic tags in a sea lion study, they found that the sea lions had removed their tracking devices by deliberately rubbing up against rocks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was something the researchers hadn't anticipated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers in California studying American sea lions tried a different method.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They applied paint to the animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They thought this would be a better, less invasive means of identification.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, this didn't work so well either because sea lions molt every year and shed their fur along with the identifying mark.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's look at our current study.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have several aims that we'd like to achieve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first of these is to try to establish whether sea lions can be identified from the whiskers on their face.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These are much coarser than a cat's whiskers, so easier to see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our theory is that the pattern of these whiskers may be as individual as a fingerprint on a human.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this is in fact true, then we think this could be an effective way to identify them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our second aim is to come up with a diagram of sea lion whisker patterns, so this can be used as a guide for us and other studies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're using a few different methods to help us do all this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that we need to build up a wide range of visual data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So firstly, we've been in touch with zoos around Australia to gather photographs from them of the faces of any sea lions they have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This won't be enough to achieve our purpose, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we're also broadening our search by inviting the public to take part in our research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're hoping this will result in hundreds of useful images we can use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

• Until 1892, numbers were affected by hunting.

Animal tracking systems
• Considerations when choosing a tracking method include {{32}} and ease of use.
• Plastic tags: the animal must be easy to {{33}} .
• GPS tracking will not work in the {{34}} .
• In isolated regions, some animals are tracked by {{35}} (e.g. the polar bear).
• Some animals are identified by markings (e.g. the dolphin is identified by its scars).
Challenges of tracking sea lions
• Perth study: the sea lions lost their tags. (They rubbed against {{36}} to remove them.)
• Californian researchers used {{37}} to identify sea lions. (This was unreliable due to regular loss of fur.)
Our study
Aims:
i) to find out if sea lions' whiskers can be used to identify them
ii) to create a {{38}} to use as a guide
Methods:
i) contacting {{39}} in Australia for photographs
ii) asking the {{40}} to get involved

questions.explanation: 录音提到海狮觅食的区域有很多用来捕捉鲨鱼（sharks）的网，导致海狮被误捕。

questions.explanation: 录音明确指出选择追踪方法时，最重要的考虑因素之一就是成本（cost）。
questions.tip: 你可能会想填 effectiveness（有效性），但题目要求填入和“易用性”并列的因素，且录音中用了 One of the most important 来强调 cost。

questions.tip: 你可能会听到 patterns（图案），但题目问的是要“create（创造）”一个什么东西，patterns 是图表里的内容。

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about predictions for future scientific developments given to students on a history of science course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In this final lecture of our course on the history of science, I would like to look to the future and tell you about some predictions that have been made about scientific developments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The content for my talk is based on some research in which 30 scientific leaders were invited to comment on the developments that they envisage as likely to come about in their own discipline within 50 years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After summarizing some of their most interesting contributions for you, I'll ask you to give me your opinions as to the likelihood of these changes occurring within this timescale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may also like to suggest some other likely changes yourselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So 1st, let's start with computer science, as this is clearly an area where there are bound to be dramatic developments and, even more significantly perhaps, these developments are likely to impact on every other field of learning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The invention of computers represents an enormous leap forward in the field of human endeavor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It could indeed be considered as being as momentous a development as when our predecessors in caves 1st learnt to make fire and use it for all sorts of purposes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the future, the computational revolution is certain to be generally recognized as a transformation as significant as, say, the Industrial Revolution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The computer scientists in the study I referred to felt that in the coming decades, lives will be significantly enhanced by automated reasoning systems of different types.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was considerable agreement that people will increasingly perceive these computer systems as intelligent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although many of these will be deployed behind the scenes, others will be in the foreground, serving in an elegant, often collaborative manner to help people do their jobs, to learn and teach, to reflect and remember, to plan and decide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without going into further detail about this at this point, let's turn to what predictions psychologists had to make.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their key point was that psychological research would inevitably become increasingly varied.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It would move into such areas as behavioral economics and social neuroscience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is likely to be further expansion into domains with more practical relevance as increasing numbers of women become research scientists, so areas such as health, environment, family, and social identity will receive more attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time as they broaden their horizons, psychologists will also intensify their search to discover what exactly determines how we act.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They will be assisted in this by imaging devices that will be inserted into the brain and provide a great deal of information about how it behaves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There should be some fascinating discoveries coming to light very soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another field that is currently undergoing enormous changes is that of genetics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not new to suggest that average life expectancy is likely to continue rising in most countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, today, geneticists emphasize that it is vital that the increasing number of the elderly in society must take quality of life into account.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how will genetics help this to happen?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To start with, they hope to develop technologies that can sequence each person's genome extremely cheaply.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This information about our DNA enables healthcare providers to predict our likelihood of suffering from any particular disease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From there on, it is a matter of weighing up various factors with a view to determining what can be done to minimize each individual's level of risk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With such information in hand, new treatments will be developed, and the current one-size-fits-all approach to healthcare will give way to a more personal approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The final subject area that I wish to bring to your attention is that of zoology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once again, computers and technology have a key role to play here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Experts comment specifically on the importance of satellites for future developments in this field.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These enable people to explore the world from their homes, offices, and schools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is now possible, for instance, to go online and see for yourself the abundant wildlife in one part of East Africa and, in the surrounding region, the harm people have done by destroying the forests, all supposedly in the name of development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zoologists believe the breakthrough that lies ahead is how people act on such information as this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They hope that we will learn to connect our minds to our hearts and apply this knowledge to help protect our planet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They express a clear hope that a greater understanding of the consequences of human shortsightedness will make people anxious to rectify what we can before it is too late.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You now have 45 seconds to check your answers to Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

Scientists were asked to predict changes in their own field in the next 50 years.
Computer science

• Computers will be seen as being {{32}} .
Psychology
• Research will become much more {{33}} , and also more practical since more {{34}} will be working in the field.
• Imaging devices will give information about the behaviour of the {{35}} .
Genetics
• With increased life expectancy, it is important to consider the {{36}} of elderly people's lives.
• Knowledge of a person's genome will indicate whether they are likely to be affected by a {{37}} .
• The approach to treatment will be on an increasingly {{38}} basis.
Zoology
• People can explore the world via satellite.
• For example, it is possible to see the effects of the destruction of {{39}} in East Africa.
• Such increased awareness should enable us to do more to look after the {{40}} .

questions.explanation: 录音用“make... and use it”替换了题干的“create and use”，听到这里可直接锁定其后的核心词 fire。
questions.tip: 你可能会被前一句的“leap forward”干扰，但要注意填空处需要的是能够被“创造和使用（create and use）”的具体事物。
questions.quote: The invention of computers represents an enormous leap forward in the field of human endeavor. It could indeed be considered as being as momentous a development as when our predecessors in caves 1st learnt to make fire and use it for all sorts of purposes.

questions.explanation: 录音里的“perceive...as”完美同义替换了题干的“be seen as being”，紧跟其后的 intelligent 即为答案。
questions.tip: 你可能会被前一句出现的“enhanced”或“automated”带偏，但它们描述的是系统本身的功能，而不是人们“看待（perceive）”它的方式。
questions.quote: There was considerable agreement that people will increasingly perceive these computer systems as intelligent.

questions.explanation: 题干的“become much more”对应录音中的信号词“become increasingly”，其后修饰的 varied 就是你要填的答案。
questions.tip: 你可能容易漏听或者把 varied 拼错，做题时一定要紧抓“increasingly”这种明显的程度副词。
questions.quote: Their key point was that psychological research would inevitably become increasingly varied.

questions.explanation: 录音中的“increasing numbers of”替换了题干的“more”，“working in the field”对应“become research scientists”，核心名词 women 就是答案。
questions.tip: 此句前面的信息较长，你可能会把注意力放在“practical relevance”上而错过后半句的真正主语。
questions.quote: There is likely to be further expansion into domains with more practical relevance as increasing numbers of women become research scientists, so areas such as health, environment, family, and social identity will receive more attention.

questions.explanation: 题干的“give information about the behaviour”被录音替换为“provide a great deal of information about how it behaves”，而这里的 it 明确指代前半句的 brain。
questions.tip: 你可能会误把复数名词 devices 当成答案，但题目问的是设备给出“谁”的行为信息，千万别填错对象。
questions.quote: At the same time as they broaden their horizons, psychologists will also intensify their search to discover what exactly determines how we act. transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the evolution of school building design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's lecture, we're going to explore the fascinating evolution of school building design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For a long time, the physical environment where children learned was largely ignored by educational theorists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But recently, architects have started adopting entirely new philosophies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin by looking at a fascinating project in Asia, the Indian Mountain School.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The architects here fundamentally challenged the nineteenth century industrial model of education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You see, historically, schools were designed to operate much like a factory where students were processed on an assembly line in uniform, identical boxes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the new approach here was to build the school as a true student-centered learning environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When considering construction materials, the designers wanted to blend local heritage with contemporary needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They could have easily used brick or concrete, which are standard worldwide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But instead, the main structure is built from natural stone found in the nearby region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This gives the building a very traditional exterior appearance, while the interior layout remains entirely modern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another priority for this school was integrating the building with its natural surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We all know that students need adequate ventilation, but the architects went a step further.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A special feature of this design is ensuring every classroom provides a clear view of the scenery outside.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research actually shows that being able to look out at nature can improve students' concentration levels significantly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on, let's look at another innovative example, Northland School.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, the educational philosophy recognizes that teaching methods are constantly evolving, so the building itself must be able to adapt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Therefore, the core belief of the builders was that the environment needed to be extremely flexible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They achieved this by using movable partitions and modular furniture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The architects at Northland School also realized that education isn't exclusively about academic achievement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They spent months watching how children behave when they are not in class.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, the overall design places a huge priority on the social requirements of the students, creating comfortable breakout areas and collaborative spaces where informal interaction can take place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's travel to Europe and examine a school in Denmark, specifically in Hellerup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This school completely abandoned the traditional concept of long corridors with rows of closed classrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, they organized the open-plan space into smaller units called home bases.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's particularly interesting is that every one of these units is equipped with a small kitchen alongside dedicated places for studying.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of this unique layout, the atmosphere of the Denmark school is quite different from what you might expect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, rather than an institution, the feeling you get there is often likened to a small village.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Students belong to their small home base community, but they can also access shared central facilities, much like residents interacting in a small town square.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, I'd like to discuss a recently completed eco-school in England.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This project had a strong focus on sustainability and utilizing natural resources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of the interior environment, the design aims to let in the greatest possible amount of light to the classrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They achieved this by carefully positioning the building and using reflective surfaces to bounce the sun's rays deep into the rooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To further reduce the school's carbon footprint, the building generates its own power.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You might expect to see traditional solar panels bolted onto the top of the building, but here, the top structure actually features specialized glass to help collect solar energy more efficiently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This innovative material allows them to heat the building during the winter months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But energy isn't the only resource they are conserving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The designers also wanted to address water usage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So an integral part of the sustainable system is that the facility gathers water when it rains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is then filtered and used for non-potable purposes like flushing toilets and watering the school gardens.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as we can see from these diverse examples, modern school design is...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.text: For my investigation into the history and uses of plant products, I have focused on the cultivation and production of saffron, an expensive, bright yellow spice made from crocus flowers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike most other species of crocus, the saffron crocus doesn't flower in February or March, but in October, when it produces fragrant lilac-colored flowers which are harvested at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the harvest, the flower petals are discarded and only the stigmas, the three dark orange or red-colored reproductive parts of the flower, are commercially used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One person must pick for almost four hundred hours to produce just one kilo of saffron and amazingly, to produce just fifty grams, it takes about fourteen thousand individual stigmas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No wonder the spice is so expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After this painstaking harvesting, and to preserve the intensive taste, smell, and color of the product, the stigmas are subject to a process of drying by which some ninety-eight percent of their moisture content is removed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This makes it possible to keep saffron on the shelf to be used for many years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The highly prized spice is famous for the flavor and aroma it imparts, which are often compared to that of honey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Saffron is also prized for its rich golden color, which makes food look so tempting and indulgent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you want to buy some of this fabled spice, you will find that saffron is either sold as whole stigmas or ground up as a powder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, saffron is used in both Eastern and Western cuisines to add both color and flavor to an enormous range of recipes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though cooks would agree that it is most commonly added to recipes for the cooking of rice, because somehow it seems to complement such dishes perfectly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is found to varying degrees in Italian, Spanish, Indian, and Iranian food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although food preparation is its most common present-day use, medical research indicates that saffron may have important applications as a drug in the clinical treatment of a number of eye disorders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Patients given saffron in their regular diet seem to show remarkable signs of recovery from serious conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And although scientists are still unsure of exactly why, recent experiments with laboratory rats have shown saffron to be effective in protecting the animals from damage caused when they are exposed to potentially harmful lights.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'd like to give a few examples of how saffron has been used since ancient times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of the earliest evidence of saffron cultivation comes from archaeological excavations dating back four thousand years on the island of Crete, where paintings and other artifacts have been found indicating that women wore beautiful saffron-colored clothes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is the earliest evidence of saffron being used as a dye.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the Roman Empire, saffron oil was produced, which, because of both its color and aroma, was used to create cosmetics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But only the wealthiest citizens could afford these.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another use of saffron was to be found in the public baths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There, saffron was used as a perfume to keep the places smelling fresh and aromatic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is even said that the streets of Rome were strewn with saffron threads to greet Emperor Nero as an extravagant and sweet-smelling gesture when he made a triumphal entrance into the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other parts of the ancient world used saffron extensively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most well-known examples was in Persia, which is modern-day Iran, where saffron was a vital part of the process of manufacturing carpets, being used as a traditional dye along with other natural products like berries and minerals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To end my presentation, I'd like to read out a recipe written by a...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the role of sleep in humans and animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today’s lecture, I’m going to talk about the role of sleep in humans and animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of all the biological processes in the animal kingdom, sleep is perhaps the most important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A human can survive for almost two weeks without eating, but did you know that one week without sleep can be fatal?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It’s even worse for animals, especially for those who must avoid predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without sleep, an animal is much less capable of avoiding an attack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is the case for all animals, whether they are reptiles, mammals, or fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let us look now at how different animals sleep, reasons for their ways of rest, and the potential problems they might encounter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In marine life, sleep must be balanced with breathing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the dolphin must float to the surface as it sleeps in order to breathe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Like other large sea mammals, they keep one eye open and one half of the brain awake at all times to maintain some amount of consciousness required to breathe and to watch out for possible threats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They sleep with only one brain hemisphere in slow-wave sleep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds also have unusual sleeping patterns, mostly due to being constantly on edge in the presence of numerous predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They usually sleep quite lightly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, Swainson’s thrush, also called olive-backed thrush, is a medium-sized thrush that takes hundreds of naps during the day, each of which lasts just a few seconds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While migrating, migratory birds tend to function well on micro naps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Horses, on the other hand, do most of their sleeping standing up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists think that horses developed their habit of sleeping upright as a defense mechanism, a way of protecting themselves against predators, and a standing position keeps a horse in a constant state of readiness to race away if danger should approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, horses do occasionally take short naps lying down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Horses are heavy animals with big muscles, but their bones are surprisingly delicate, so lying in one position for a long time could well injure a horse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just like humans, animals can also have sleeping problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: John Hendricks and Adrian Morrison from the School of Veterinary Medicine, University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, determined that certain diseases were primarily associated with the sleep states in animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In their research, they emphasized that because so much in this area still remains unclear, animal models were very important for studies of sleep disorders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The physiology of sleep in animals is similar to that of humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But why do we humans sleep?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers and scientists believe it helps us organize our memories of the day, that sleep acts as a kind of filing system for the brain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Without it, our thoughts become disorderly and confused, which leads to increased likelihood of accidents and a tendency to say and do bizarre things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers also believe that sleep plays a key role in learning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We sleep so that the brain can integrate new knowledge and form new associations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of the similar sleeping pattern to that of humans, rats are often studied in order to increase our knowledge of human physiology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In one study, rats were kept awake for almost two weeks and their behavior was observed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers found the sleep-deprived rats could hardly remember anything of what they had been taught that day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, one rat had been taught to recognize pictures of various Parisian landmarks in order to receive food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pressing a button below a picture of the Louvre would result in food being released, and so forth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, when deprived of sleep, they would press buttons seemingly at random.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to rats, the fruit fly, a small insect that feeds and breeds on spoiled fruit, also has been used as a model organism and thousands of scientists around the world work on it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But why was the fruit fly chosen to be studied?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was for practical reasons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most important one is that the relationship between fly and human genes is so close that the sequences of newly discovered human genes, including genes that show a susceptibility, can often be matched against their fly counterparts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This provides an indication of the function of the human gene and could help in the development of effective drugs to help people with sleeping disorders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Therefore, many scientists today choose to study the genetic structure of the fruit fly, which could make a particularly important contribution to the understanding of developmental processes in humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In conclusion, sleep is a necessary part of life, not just for humans, but for the entire animal kingdom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I’d be happy to answer any questions you may have.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 录音提到如果没有睡眠，动物在躲避攻击（avoiding an attack）方面的能力会大大降低，对应题目中更容易遭受（suffer from）攻击。

questions.quote: It’s even worse for animals, especially for those who must avoid predators. Without sleep, an animal is much less capable of avoiding an attack.

questions.explanation: 录音原句直接列举了 reptiles（爬行动物）、mammals（哺乳动物）和 fish（鱼类），按顺序填空即可。
questions.tip: 这道题是明显的并列结构，你只要紧跟 reptiles 这个定位词，准确拼写出紧接着读出的 mammals 即可，一定不要漏掉复数 s。
questions.quote: This is the case for all animals, whether they are reptiles, mammals, or fish.

questions.explanation: 录音提到海豚睡觉时必须浮出水面，目的是为了呼吸（in order to breathe），精准对应题目中的 because they need to breathe。
questions.tip: 你可能听到前面的 breathing 就想填，但题目给的结构是 need to，后面必须跟动词原形 breathe。
questions.quote: In marine life, sleep must be balanced with breathing. For example, the dolphin must float to the surface as it sleeps in order to breathe.

questions.explanation: 录音在提到鸟类时，原句直接说出了 constantly on edge in the presence of numerous predators，填入空缺的词组即可。
questions.tip: 你可能对 on edge（紧张不安）这个词组不熟悉，导致听到了却没反应过来是什么词，平时要注意积累此类常见短语。
questions.quote: Birds also have unusual sleeping patterns, mostly due to being constantly on edge in the presence of numerous predators.

questions.explanation: 录音提到长时间躺着会弄伤马，原因在前面已经交代了，是因为它们的骨头（bones）非常脆弱（delicate）。
questions.tip: 录音中先说了答案 bones，后说了题干里的定位信息 injure a horse，这种答案前置的情况要求你听懂整个句子的因果关系，不能只等定位词出现，同时不要错抓成前面的 muscles。
questions.quote: Horses are heavy animals with big muscles, but their bones are surprisingly delicate, so lying in one position for a long time could well injure a horse.

questions.explanation: 录音开门见山地说，就像人类一样（Just like humans 对应 the same as humans），动物也会有睡眠问题（sleeping problems）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 sleep 或者 problems 觉得意思差不多就只填了一个词，但根据整体语义，这里填 sleeping problems 才是完整且最准确的信息。
questions.quote: Just like humans, animals can also have sleeping problems.

questions.explanation: 录音原句直接读出了 helps us organise our memories of the day，句子结构和题干一模一样。
questions.tip: 这个空非常直接，你唯一的失误可能就是听写时漏掉了复数 s，一定要注意听到什么写什么。
questions.quote: But why do we humans sleep? Researchers and scientists believe it helps us organise our memories of the day, that sleep acts as a kind of filing system for the brain.

questions.explanation: 题干直接把录音里的原句搬了过来，听到 plays a key role in，后面紧跟的 learning 就是答案。
questions.tip: 录音在这句话之前说了很长一段关于缺乏睡眠的后果，你可能在前面乱入的信息中迷失了方向，必须抓牢 plays a key role 这个核心信号词把节奏找回来。
questions.quote: Researchers also believe that sleep plays a key role in learning.

questions.explanation: 录音完全照读了前半句作为铺垫，然后主语直接给出老鼠（rats）被研究，逻辑顺畅，直接填入即可。
questions.tip: 这是一个极其还原原文的白给题，但你可能因为粗心大意漏写复数 s，导致单复数不匹配而失分。
questions.quote: Because of the similar sleeping pattern to that of humans, rats are often studied in order to increase our knowledge of human physiology.

questions.tip: 题干的逻辑在录音中是倒置的（录音先说目的，再用 Therefore 引出做法），你如果死板地等 know the function 之后再找答案，很可能会错过，或者错抓成前面重复出现的 genes。
