transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about an unusual crab species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today's lecture is about the arrival and growing influence of an unusual crab species in northern waters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll begin with some general observations before moving into behavior, impacts, and long-term management.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To start, local fishermen say the creature has started showing up in spots where it was never recorded before.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tracking devices placed on several individuals revealed they originally traveled from an area located further south, although the reasons for leaving that region are still debated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some oceanographers believe changes in water layers may have encouraged this new movement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Along with the shift in location, one worrying trend is the noticeable drop in octopuses, which disappear quickly whenever the crab population increases.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dive groups have reported fewer sightings on their usual routes, even in places that used to be reliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Guides say visitors often ask why these clever animals are becoming harder to spot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on, people who work at the harbor sometimes find discarded pieces of its shell, usually washed up after storms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These fragments feel surprisingly dense when handled, much heavier than most expect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The texture is so rugged that some compare it to building material rather than something from a living creature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to this, younger crabs tend to remain in shallow inlets because these places offer hiding spots from larger predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Seaweed clusters and rock edges create small pockets where they can rest safely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Only after they grow stronger do they begin moving toward deeper channels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When we look at their movement patterns, in some northern villages, people have noticed long tracks along the water's edge after large groups have passed through.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These patterns often appear on exposed coastlines, especially in places where tides are strong.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Photographers sometimes wait for these rare gatherings to capture unusual images.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the year progresses, during the colder months, local crews often change their work routines because the animals become harder to find.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As winter approaches, the crabs usually shift into darker, deeper waters where conditions are more stable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This movement makes it challenging for researchers to continue monitoring them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in terms of human activity, a number of crews mentioned that certain items on board have been causing unexpected delays during routine work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One recurring issue involves the nets, which often return in a condition that requires extra time to sort out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of this, some teams have begun experimenting with new equipment to avoid interruptions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time, several groups in the area have been debating how recent changes in the sea might influence different activities on shore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some believe these shifts could eventually reach the wider economy, though no one agrees on what that outcome might look like.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A few remain optimistic, suggesting that unexpected benefits could appear over time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, documents from decades ago describe a carefully organized operation that introduced the species into unfamiliar waters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to those notes, a group of engineers handled the practical side of the initiative during its early stages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The long-term effects of their involvement were not considered at the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In recent years, several research groups have reviewed new data about how the species is spreading.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A number of scientists argue that some surrounding habitats may struggle if certain trends continue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Others think the situation can be stabilized with consistent monitoring and periodic adjustments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That concludes today's talk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
The Red King Crab
Introduction
- The Red King Crab is migrating into European waters from the far {{31}} .
- Its rapid spread threatens local marine species such as {{32}} , which it preys on.
Physical characteristics
- The Red King Crab has a deep red {{33}} that develops after several molts.
- Juvenile crabs often remain in {{34}} waters where predators are fewer.
Migration behaviour
- When travelling in large groups, the crabs damage long stretches of {{35}} .
- During {{36}} , they tend to move into deeper water.
Impact on people
- Fishermen complain that their {{37}} are frequently damaged.
- Some communities are concerned about the effect on their local {{38}} .
Management and control
- In the 1960s, Soviet {{39}} intentionally introduced the Red King Crab to boost fishery production.
- Today, environmental {{40}} warn that its ecological impact may be greater than expected.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到追踪设备显示这些螃蟹最初是从一个位于更南边（further south）的区域迁移过来的。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "from the far" 对应录音里的 "from an area located further"，紧接着的方向词就是答案，不要填成 specific location。
questions.quote: Speaker: Tracking devices placed on several individuals revealed they originally travelled from an area located further south, although the reasons for leaving that region are still debated.

questions.explanation: 演讲者提到一个令人担忧的趋势是章鱼（octopuses）数量的显著下降，它们被螃蟹捕食。
questions.tip: 听到 "drop in..."（下降）时要警觉，这通常意味着该物种受到威胁；另外注意 octopus 的复数形式拼写。
questions.quote: Speaker: Along with the shift in location, one worrying trend is the noticeable drop in octopuses, which disappear quickly whenever the crab population increases.

questions.explanation: 在港口工作的人有时会发现被丢弃的螃蟹壳（shell）的碎片，摸起来密度很大。
questions.tip: 录音中把 shell 的质地比作建筑材料，不要因为听到 "building material" 就走神，核心名词是 shell。
questions.quote: Speaker: Moving on, people who work at the harbour sometimes find discarded pieces of its shell, usually washed up after storms.

questions.explanation: 年幼的螃蟹（younger crabs）倾向于留在浅水（shallow）的入海口，以躲避捕食者。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "Juvenile"（青少年的）对应录音里的 "younger"，"waters" 对应 "inlets"，中间的形容词 shallow 是答案。
questions.quote: Speaker: In addition to this, younger crabs tend to remain in shallow inlets because these places offer hiding spots from larger predators.

questions.explanation: 当大群螃蟹经过时，人们在裸露的海岸线（coastlines）上注意到了长长的痕迹。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "damage" 在录音中体现为留下的 "tracks"（痕迹），发生地点是 exposed coastlines。
questions.quote: Speaker: When we look at their movement patterns... These patterns often appear on exposed coastlines, especially in places where tides are strong.

questions.explanation: 随着冬天（winter）的临近，螃蟹通常会转移到更深的水域中去。
questions.tip: 虽然前面提到了 "colder months"（更冷的月份），但题目要求填一个词，后面的 "As winter approaches" 才是精准的对应点。
questions.quote: Speaker: As the year progresses during the colder months... As winter approaches, the crabs usually shift into darker, deeper waters where conditions are more stable.

questions.explanation: 渔民们遇到的一个反复出现的问题是他们的渔网（nets）经常受损，需要额外时间清理。
questions.tip: 录音中说 nets "return in a condition that requires extra time to sort out"（需要额外时间清理的状态），这就是 damaged 的同义替换。
questions.quote: Speaker: One recurring issue involves the nets, which often return in a condition that requires extra time to sort out.

questions.explanation: 社区正在争论海洋的变化如何影响岸上（shore）的不同活动（activities）。
questions.tip: 这道题有些争议。
questions.quote: Speaker: ...several groups in the area have been debating how recent changes in the sea might influence different activities on shore.

questions.explanation: 几十年前的文件显示，一群工程师（engineers）负责处理引入该物种的实际操作。
questions.tip: 一定要区分开 engineers（负责引入的）和后面出现的 scientists（负责研究现状的），不要张冠李戴。
questions.quote: Speaker: According to those notes, a group of engineers handled the practical side of the initiative during its early stages.

questions.explanation: 许多科学家（scientists）争论说，如果某种趋势继续下去，周围的栖息地可能会陷入困境。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "warn"（警告）对应录音里的 "argue that ... may struggle"（争论...可能会挣扎/受困），主语是 scientists。
questions.quote: Speaker: A number of scientists argue that some surrounding habitats may struggle if certain trends continue.

31.s: from an area located further south

32.s: disappear quickly whenever the crab population increases

37.s: often return in a condition that requires extra time to sort out

39.s: handled the practical side of the initiative

40.s: may struggle if certain trends continue

transcript.text: Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear the beginning of a lecture about the Pleasanton Town Market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the last few lectures, we've been covering the social and political pressures that influenced the rise of the rebellion of 1679.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I would like to focus on the Pleasanton Town Market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, why are we talking all about some market?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not like it was the 1st market ever, or even a particularly large market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Pleasanton Town Market is important because it is often mentioned in the literature found in the library.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you have ever been there, you have probably seen all of the handcrafted items sold there now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what was originally bought and sold in the town market?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the beginning, the market sold products such as meats, furs, and simple tools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over time, though, it became known as the place to find quality livestock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People came from all over the world to find the biggest and best cows, pigs, and chickens.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the profits from the town market became the savior of a plummeting economy during a time of much turmoil.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Not to be confused with the Reconstruction Era, a period of rapid development came about in the 1660s as a result of the market's vendors contributing their profits to building up much needed public facilities and defense, which would later make a huge impact on the outcome of the war.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For many years, the market flourished and began to draw in large tourism crowds in addition to the throngs of livestock customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, as revolutions in farming came about, more people moved to farms far from the city center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Customers grew more and more reluctant to travel all the way to the town center for their meats when they could easily choose to buy from local farmers near them for a fraction of the price.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With such a fall in the profits of the town's major profit generator, some quality town planning was needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the mayoral election of 1668, a young man of little fame just barely claimed the popular vote, none other than the now legendary John C.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Wylie.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Wylie's 1st decision as mayor of Pleasanton was to deal with the quickly failing town market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The building with the large clock was a landmark that had symbolized growth in Pleasanton for a generation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Wylie decided to use the notoriety of the town market to set an example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the historical Rotterdam Rebellion, Wylie gave all those involved lifetime prison sentences in the very same building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It stayed a prison for about 50 more years until they transported all remaining prisoners to other facilities and turned it into the historical monument today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now that you know the basics of the history of the Pleasanton Town Market, I will introduce your next group project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I want you to make a short film based on the real historical events that occurred in Pleasanton before and during the uprising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I will give you some class time to look through the library's reference section, but you will be responsible for conducting further research outside of class.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I suggest starting by looking for information on the market itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll find plenty of information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, some students complain that there is actually too much information on it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture given to material science undergraduates on the use of plastics in the home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the second in my series of lectures, The Appliance of Science, I'm going to outline developments in plastics since the 1930s, focusing on the unique properties of the different discoveries and how they impact on so many aspects of our daily lives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's hard to imagine what we'd do without plastics in their domestic application and also increasingly for leisure pursuits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's start with one of the earliest forms of plastics, polythene, which was invented in 1933.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It essentially evolved into two forms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first, low-density polyethylene, better known as LDPE, is very flexible, and indeed this is probably its most significant feature and one which its developers recognized as important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This means that it's suitable for making things like film and also carrier bags and other packaging materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: High-density HDPE is more robust, and it can be made more so by exposing it to a type of gas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's particularly used for making rigid containers, for example, for milk or for household cleaners such as bleach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But going back to the 1930s, another key development in plastics was polyurethane.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's still widely used in two forms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first form is known as blown, and this type is used in the manufacture of furniture for the padded parts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Blown polyurethane is also still widely used in the infrastructure of houses as a means of providing insulation in loft and roof spaces in particular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Polyurethane is also useful in its non-blown form.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can be made into extremely comfortable and stretchy fiber, and nowadays it's widely used for sportswear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving to the 1940s, there was another significant departure when polyethylene terephthalate, or PET, was developed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its first application was in fabric under the brand names of Dacron and Terylene.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to being able to be made into fabric, PET has the valuable property of being particularly impermeable and is unaffected by carbonation, which tends to attack other plastics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it's used in the manufacture of bottles for fizzy drinks and is therefore probably present in most of our fridges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: PET is also very resistant to abrasion, and for this reason, it is used in the home for trays and other items that are often heavily scratched.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turning now to the 1950s, which for many people was when plastic really impacted on their lives for the first time with a large number of new inventions and applications.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most visible parts of this plastics invasion was Earl Tupper's Tupperware, a line of sealable polyethylene food containers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The products were well-designed and highly effective, greatly reducing spoilage of foods in storage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, what Tupperware is probably best known for is the revolutionary techniques its inventor developed for sales.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He set up through a network of housewives who sold Tupperware as a means of bringing in extra money.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For many people, this method was the first encounter they had with the product.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, the 1960s.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'd like to finish by talking about a type of plastic, which to my mind is one of the most versatile materials ever invented, polytetrafluoroethylene, PTFE, better known as Teflon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is a non-stick material with hardly any friction, which can be deposited on metal surfaces as a protective coating.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was initially discovered by accident as long ago as 1938, but it took until the 1960s for Teflon non-stick frying pans to become an indispensable consumer item.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teflon was later used to synthesize the so-called miracle fabric, Gore-Tex.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The best-known use of this is for making rainwear and outdoor gear that in principle breathes to keep the wearer's moisture from building up and so is particularly comfortable to wear for walking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, Gore-Tex has other uses which are less well known.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is increasingly being used for making materials used for a variety of medical applications.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if anyone has any questions, I'd be happy to answer them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about a museum exhibition on the history and development of plastics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name's Susan Mossman, and as well as being a part-time lecturer on the university's museum science degree, I'm also curator of a new exhibition opening at the Bidmouth Museum called Plasticity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This traces the history of plastics and ways they are being developed and used today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first type of plastic was originally developed in response to a call from the makers of sports equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Animal-derived materials were becoming extremely expensive, so manufacturers launched a competition to find an alternative to ivory for making pool and billiard balls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although various forms of plastic were developed, none of them were good enough to win the competition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the inventors knew they were onto a good thing and started researching a variety of different substances, partly based on organic material, what we call semi-synthetics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the early semi-synthetic materials produced was the first commercially produced celluloid or plastic film, which was made by dissolving cotton in a strong acid, such as nitric acid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, this had a tendency to explode, so technicians had to be very careful with it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also experimented with making plastics out of products derived from milk, but this didn't really work and efforts were therefore concentrated on other organic material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the first uses of plastic was in the production of artificial fabric, and the earliest successful one was a substitute for silk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was obviously a very expensive fiber, so artificial alternatives were thought to be worth investing in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The next significant breakthrough came in nineteen oh seven with the invention of Bakelite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was the first entirely synthetic plastic made in a laboratory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was invented by Hendrik Bakeland, a chemist who had made a fortune from producing paper used in photographic processes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bakelite is a pretty unusual type of plastic because it actually gets hard when it's heated, whereas most other plastic becomes more malleable when hot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is, they become more plastic, which is, of course, where the name for the category of materials comes from.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So strictly speaking, Bakelite isn't a plastic at all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But now let's look at the exhibition itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In it, we show a variety of semi-synthetic and totally synthetic plastics, some of them dating back a hundred years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of the older plastics on display are unstable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This means that when they are in the process of degrading, they may produce gases which are acidic and which can cause neighboring objects in the display to disintegrate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We had to be very careful with these displays because there is one thing which causes plastic objects to degrade or break down, and that is light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we've had to think of ways to get around this problem when setting up the objects on display.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have about eight hundred and fifty objects in the exhibition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our most interesting is a magnificent chandelier, a lamp designed to hang in the center of the ceiling of a big hall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's only when you look carefully that you can see this is a wonderful example of recycling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's made entirely of pens, ones which we use and throw away every day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A second exhibit which is drawing a lot of attention is a car made entirely from plastic, which is now in small-scale production in Japan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture on the phenomenon of photic sneezing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome to this lecture in the health sciences intended to inspire you and get you thinking about your research project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I want to show you how even ordinary human behavior like sneezing, which normally happens when you get a cold, may be worth studying.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Have you ever been walking outside when a bright shaft of sunlight hits you between the eyes?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The reaction of some people is immediate, an unpleasant prickling in the nose, an increase in their breathing rate, and an uncontrollable watering of the eyes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, almost as quickly, they sneeze and gain relief.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This may happen every time they go into the sun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This so-called photic or light sneeze is a reflex, which means it can't be controlled, and it's very common.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anything between one in ten and one in three people might be affected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, a sneeze is triggered by an irritation of some sort in the linings of the nostrils.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The result is a cascade of reactions, beginning with the stimulation of the nerve endings all over the face and generating an explosive expulsion of air at up to ninety-five miles an hour, like an extremely localized personal hurricane.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The body's coordination of such reactions is complicated and belongs to the subconscious control hardware that regulates other things, for example, tears in the eyes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People have been interested in the phenomenon of photic sneezing for thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Greek philosopher Aristotle asked, "Why does the sun prompt us to sneeze, whereas the heat of a fire does not?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A partial answer came two thousand years later when the English philosopher Francis Bacon showed that his photic sneeze had nothing to do with heat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If he closed his eyes when going into the sun, he didn't sneeze even though the heat was still there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Henry Everett, a consultant psychiatrist at John Hopkins University Hospital in Baltimore, was the first to make a systematic attempt to understand the condition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Noting in nineteen sixty-four that thirty percent of the staff employed in the medical department were photic sneezers, Everett did some further investigation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He found that while eighty percent of sneezers reported other sneezers among their relatives, only twenty percent of non-sneezers did.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, there are factors that are certain indicators of a photic sneeze.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, those with the condition almost always sneeze a set number of times on exposure to light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to this, the sneeze depends on a contrast in visible brightness, such as when the sun moves out from behind a cloud,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: and the sneezing fit won't be repeated immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The body needs time before it can be recharged.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if you go back into a darkened space and then immediately reenter bright light, you will not sneeze again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now on to possible applications of research in this area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The photic sneeze had long been overlooked because its effects are generally less than serious.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although the government did once study it as a risk factor for pilots.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet work on such a simple disorder might lead to important discoveries on more acute conditions such as migraine or epilepsy, which are also caused by cross wires in the nervous system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is why I encourage you to select something similar for your first investigative medical project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It could be the beginning of something even more useful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
Background
• Some people react to sunlight by:
◦ a prickle in the nose
◦ faster {{31}} , relieved by a sneeze
◦ watery eyes
• The "photics" sneeze cannot be controlled and is a {{32}} reflex.
• Sneezing in general
◦ A sneeze is caused by some kind of irritation in the nose.
◦ Nerve endings in the {{33}} are stimulated, leading to an explosion of air.
◦ It is co-ordinated by the same mechanism that controls the production of {{34}} .
Research into photic sneezing
• The condition has been known for thousands of years.
• Aristotle: Why does the sun cause sneezing while a {{35}} does not?
• Bacon showed the cause was light.
• Everett found 80% of photic sneezers shared the habit with {{36}} .
• Photic sneezers usually produce the same {{37}} of sneezes.
• The reaction is caused by a {{38}} in brightness.
• The sneeze takes {{39}} to recharge.
Application
The condition was often ignored apart from some research on photic sneezing among {{40}} .

questions.explanation: 原文提到这种反应的一个症状是呼吸频率增加（increase in their breathing rate），频率增加对应的就是题目中的“更快（faster）”。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了 "rate"，但题目结构是 "faster ... "，这里填 "breathing"（呼吸）才能构成完整的“呼吸变快”的语义，只填 rate 语意不明。
questions.quote: The reaction of some people is immediate, an unpleasant prickling in the nose, an increase in their breathing rate, and an uncontrollable watering of the eyes.

questions.explanation: 录音中紧接着说这种反射“非常普遍”（it's very common），并给出了每三到十人中就有一人受影响的数据来支持。
questions.tip: 题目问的是这是一种什么样的反射（形容词），不要被后面的数字（one in ten）干扰，直接抓形容词 "common"。
questions.quote: This so-called photic or light sneeze is a reflex, which means it can't be controlled, and it's very common, anything between one in ten and one in three people might be affected.

questions.explanation: 录音详细描述了喷嚏的连锁反应，始于遍布脸部（all over the face）的神经末梢受到刺激。
questions.tip: 虽然前面提到了 "nostrils"（鼻孔），但题目特定问的是 "Nerve endings in the..."（哪里的神经末梢），录音明确对应的是 Face。
questions.quote: The result is a cascade of reactions, beginning with the stimulation of the nerve endings all over the face, and generating an explosive expulsion of air at up to 95 miles an hour...

questions.explanation: 录音提到这种身体协调机制属于潜意识控制硬件，它也调节其他事物，例如眼泪（tears）的产生。
questions.tip: 不要填 "eyes"，题目问的是 "production of..."（产生什么），显然是产生眼泪，而不是产生眼睛。
questions.quote: The body's coordination of such reactions is complicated and belongs to the subconscious control hardware that regulates other things, for example tears in the eyes.

questions.explanation: 亚里士多德提出疑问：为什么太阳会引发喷嚏，而火的热量（heat of a fire）却不会？
questions.tip: 题目是拿 "sun" 和另一个具体事物做对比，不要填 "heat"，因为 heat 是这两个事物的共同属性（或者说差异点），对比的主体是 fire。
questions.quote: The Greek philosopher Aristotle asked, why does the sun prompt us to sneeze, whereas the heat of a fire does not?

questions.explanation: Everett 发现 80% 的光喷嚏者报告说他们的亲戚（among their relatives）也有这个习惯。
questions.tip: 不要主观臆断填 "family" 或 "parents"，雅思填空要求“所听即所得”，录音原词是 relatives。
questions.quote: He found that while 80% of sneezers reported other sneezes among their relatives, only 20% of non-sneezers did.

questions.explanation: 录音说患有此症的人在接触光线时，几乎总是打固定次数（set number of times）的喷嚏。
questions.tip: 不要只听到 "times"，题目结构是 "the same ... of sneezes"，这里需要填核心名词 number。
questions.quote: Now there are factors that are certain indicators of a photic sneeze, first of all, those with the condition almost always sneeze a set number of times on exposure to light.

questions.explanation: 录音明确指出，打喷嚏取决于可见亮度的对比（contrast in visible brightness），比如太阳从云后出来。
questions.tip: 题目问的是 "caused by a ... in brightness"，即亮度的某种变化状态，答案是 contrast 而不是 light 或 sun。
questions.quote: In addition to this, the sneeze depends on a contrast in visible brightness, such as when the sun moves out from behind a cloud.

questions.explanation: 录音说身体需要时间（needs time）才能重新充电，所以喷嚏不会立刻重复。
questions.tip: 题目中 "take" 对应录音中的 "need"，这是一个非常经典的时间表达同义替换。
questions.quote: And the sneezing fit won’t be repeated immediately. The body needs time before it can be recharged, so if you go back into a darkened space and then immediately re-enter bright light, you will not sneeze again.

questions.explanation: 录音提到政府曾经研究过它，将其作为飞行员（pilots）的一个风险因素。
questions.tip: 注意听前面的 "government did once study it"，不要误填为 government，题目问的是 "among..."（在哪些人群中），即研究对象是 pilots。
questions.quote: The photic sneeze had long been overlooked because its effects are generally less than serious, although the government did once study it as a risk factor for pilots.

31.s: an increase in their breathing rate

35.s: the heat of a fire does not

36.s: reported other sneezers among their relatives

37.s: sneeze a set number of times

39.s: The body needs time before it can be recharged

40.q: was often ignored apart from some research
40.s: Although the government did once study it

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a museum curator giving a presentation about her museum's collection of perfume containers, also known as perfume ornaments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on pages six and seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning and welcome to the Walden Gallery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's open lecture, I'm going to be talking about our collection of perfume ornaments or containers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These beautiful objects now form a significant part of the museum's collection and are very popular with the public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this has not always been the case.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Up until relatively recently, the large collection of perfume ornaments held in store, donated by Lady Walden at the beginning of the last century, was not considered to be of much interest and was not on show to the general public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, as late as nineteen eighty-nine, a visiting professor from the Victoria and Albert Museum commented that some of the objects were worth a great deal, and so the display was created much as you see it here today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, before I say anything more about the perfume containers, I thought I'd briefly touch on the background to the development of perfumes themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the West, perfumery really began as late as the eleventh century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bathing and laundering were considered hazardous undertakings because even though there were ample supplies of water, it was often dirty or even infected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a consequence, as you can imagine, the air was heavy with unpleasant smells, which had to be countered or covered up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In those early days, perfumes were in solid form and mainly made from spices, leaves, and animal fixatives in paste form.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, musk and ambergris.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Wealthy people, the only people who could afford them, carried small globular vessels known as pomanders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've brought out one ornament from the collection, the oldest one, in fact, from the fourteenth century, which I'll pass round for you to sample.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These pomanders are solid paste balls made of ambergris impregnated with fragrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The name was derived from the French for apple of ambergris.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They must have had a powerful aroma in those days because even now you can smell the fragrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, during the medieval period, basically up until the sixteenth century, perfumes not only made your surroundings smell sweeter, they were believed to have other special properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers in the nineteenth century revealed that in medieval times, people thought perfumes could help overcome all kinds of bodily ills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But only recently, researchers at our museum have found that they were also believed to significantly raise the spirits of the wearer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turning now to some more technical details.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With the advent of liquid perfume from the mid-eighteenth century, craftsmen had to use precision techniques to ensure there was an airtight seal on the container.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is clear that however beautiful these seemingly fragile objects were, they were essentially utilitarian, designed to stop the extremely valuable substances inside them from evaporating.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's turn now to have a look at some of the key developments in perfume containers in the last two hundred years or so.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From the late eighteenth century onwards, the vinaigrette came into vogue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The vinaigrette was a miniature box which opened on a hinge containing a tiny sponge soaked with perfume.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was placed under a grill through which you could smell the fragrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was widely used to carry the highly corrosive scent known as vinegar water, hence the name.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The outer box could be made of any material, but the lining was gold because the perfume tended to corrode other substances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From the mid-nineteenth century, vinaigrettes were replaced by more conventional bottles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were often made of glass, of course, but metal was another common material used, and very occasionally, they were made of more unusual materials like horn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By now, these beautiful objects were more affordable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was the age of the Industrial Revolution in Western Europe, and the bottles were mass-produced and thus available not just to the very wealthy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the last quarter of the nineteenth century, one company above all became associated with the design and production of perfume bottles, the Tiffany Company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They developed a wide range of designs, most notably based on those of the furniture of the period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their particular achievement was their stylish and clever working of crystal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although these perfume ornaments were very expensive, Tiffany & Co were able to use catalogs to reach a wider clientele.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many innovative designs were used in perfume ornaments produced in the nineteen twenties and thirties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most notable was probably the vanity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was an ingeniously designed case used not only for holding perfume, but also makeup in a whole maze of tiny additional compartments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was made in the first instance of ivory, but later Bakelite was used, the resinous plastic which was so popular with all kinds of designers of the period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I've brought along a selection of the items in the collection, which I've set out here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you'd like to come and get...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about an archaeological investigation into medieval Nubian life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.

transcript.text: The investigation of the medieval town of Debra on the western bank of the Nile between the modern villages was deliberately planned to gather a maximum amount of information on the domestic aspects of medieval Nubian life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The objects found and the nature of some of the buildings were more elaborate than had been anticipated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first tribe in this area dates back ten thousand years, although some experts argue it was fifteen thousand years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though further empirical evidence is needed to support these two periods, the site was abandoned and covered with wind-blown sand just north of the student frontier, revealing a cemetery far larger than any previously found in Nubia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research conducted by members of the expedition from 1972 to 1973 showed that although the tombs had been plundered and burned, the fragments of pottery and optics found were numerous, varied, and of high quality.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Paintings dating from the same period were discovered as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were found on many temple walls in Nubia, signifying the unification of Upper Egypt, represented by the lotus, with Lower Egypt, represented by the papyrus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Modern physical anthropology goes beyond measuring indicators such as skull size or body weight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It attempts to reconstruct the entire biological structure of a population or a segment of a population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The expedition examined a total of one hundred and seven skeletons from children and women.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Questions arose.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where were the women buried, and why did some of the children receive the same distinctions as grown men?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Several female corpses were found to have unusually large teeth among this period's skeletons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Surprisingly, a large number were found to have lost their teeth at a comparatively early age, twenty-five to thirty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, archaeologists investigated the fingers and bones of women to find answers to these questions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A large collection of remains, representing fifteen forty-six individuals, dating from the beginning to the end of the Christian period, around 1500 AD, was submitted for computer analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The age distribution shows that the Nubian population, as a rule, died at an early age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The expedition examined the tomb of an official in the Egyptian administration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We even have a clear enlargement of a photograph of his big toe, with detailed shape and fragments held in the museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we discovered was that culturally, there was no single Nubian people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, the people of Nubia had met diverse environmental circumstances with a wide range of adaptive social responses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers are in pursuit of the Nubian people's homeland, lost to floods, which are most likely the reason that pushed them to the edge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dental problems were a major concern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Evidently, small stones in the grain were not separated, and therefore the teeth were damaged from making bread from grain without separating them first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A diet of such bread eventually ground the teeth away, exposing their roots to decay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the harvest, the heavier grain fell back to the threshing floor while the lighter chaff blew away.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After collection, the grain was placed on the ground, ready for milling, using a stone shaped like a rolling pin with a curve to match.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The grinding surface was rowed back and forth, grinding the grain into flour.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, normal cavities were rare because of the absence of sugar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Egyptians had no sugar, nor could the average person afford it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Examination of mummies, both young and old, found severely worn teeth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although Egyptians had specialists for many medical problems, dentistry was not one of these.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about oxytocin and trust.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The development of trust is an essential social tool, allowing people to form productive and meaningful relationships, both at a professional and personal level.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Trust is indispensable in friendship, love, families, and organizations, and plays a key role in economic exchange and politics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Much recent evidence indicates that trust contributes to economic, political, and social success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: When we make contacts with strangers, such as doing business with the clients who we meet for the first time, our trust in them can only rely on their kindness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So from our own judgment or the comments from other people, we can have a rough idea if the stranger is trustworthy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Trust is important because it is the basis around which all human relationships evolve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Without trust, there can be no relationship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Trust can come naturally, or it can be manifested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you find trust of this magnitude in life, then you are lucky.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Also, you can always count on them to protect through all, if not most, of life's perils.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Trust is important because if you don't trust someone, then they are not available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Believe it or not, reducing the chance of suffering from poverty is to understand trust, because when you trust other people, you can have more support and resources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, our ability to trust others varies from individual to individual, just like different people's ability of recognizing a person's face is not the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Bonds of trust are also extremely fragile.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A single act of betrayal, such as a marital affair, can instantly erase years of trustworthy behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The consequences of such breaches in confidence can be disastrous, and not only for a relationship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The study demonstrates how oxytocin can facilitate social interactions after trust has been violated by potentially lowering defense mechanisms associated with social risks and by overcoming negative feedback that is important for adapting behavior in the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Luckily, oxytocin in our body has the ability to inspire trust in and among people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This chemical is released whenever interaction happens between people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: To study social interactions, economists and more recently neuroscientists take advantage of a simple experiment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Two participants play the so-called trust game.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The first participant is faced with the decision to keep a sum of money or share it with the second participant, who has no obligation to give the money back.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: He would get more money if the second person returns it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In this game, the first person is left with an important social dilemma: to trust or not to trust.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Although it is more profitable to trust, doing so leaves the investor at risk of betrayal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Trust is not something that naturally occurs when two people meet for the first time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It involves a process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One person has to show the quality of being trustworthy to the other person.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This can be achieved by certain behaviors and communication.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Therefore, trust is conditional.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: People should not take it for granted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Oxytocin does not only exist in human beings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Animals also have this gift, and it can be seen when they have cooperation with each other.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Oxytocin in monkeys, for example, allow them to work together to find food and to fight against enemies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The Nash equilibrium's game theory, the first participant will make the best decision he can, with no expectations that the second participant would change his decision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The second participant will do the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So the outcome depends on the decision of the other person.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This game is similar to the one we just talked about.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The oxytocin level doesn't stay the same in a person's body.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Studies have found that people who are under a lot of stress would have higher levels of oxytocin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Oxytocin causes a substantial increase in trust among humans, thereby greatly increasing the benefits from social interactions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's also noted that the effect of oxytocin on trust is not due to a general increase in the readiness to bear risks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: On the contrary, oxytocin specifically affects an individual's willingness to accept social risks arising through interpersonal interactions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: To sum up, oxytocin is like a kind of social glue that is helpful in social bonding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Further research is needed to explore oxytocin and trust, and how this hormone can be used to strengthen our trust in others and even treat mental disorders that specifically relate to deficiencies in social behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Next, we're going to talk about...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on organic farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What I'm going to talk about today is organic farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's 1st look at what organic farming is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can be defined as one or more systems of production which don't use synthetic fertilizers, man-made pesticides, herbicides, antibiotics, or livestock feed additives to grow crops and raise animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Virtually all organic farmers prefer to use renewable resources and recycling to give what conventional farmers might consider waste back to the soil of Mother Nature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From this, we can see organic farming is a sustainable production system, which is one of its advantages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Organic farmers use numerous techniques to promote the quality of life of plants and animals within existing ecosystems and minimize pollution that occurs with all conventional farming practices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another benefit is that with the increasing consumer demand for a healthier, more nutritionally balanced product, the sales of organically produced food are promoted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to the research, it has become the fastest-growing sector of agriculture and has shown an annual increase of at least 20 percent during the last 6 years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's more, both chemical fertilizers and synthetic pesticides consume non-renewable resources such as oil and coal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the development of organic farming can lower the demand for these fertilizers and pesticides, so it is conducive to the conservation of essential energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time, it also can reduce industrial pollution caused by the production of these chemical substances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Organic farming differs greatly from the traditional one in a number of ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's discuss it from the perspective of agricultural biodiversity, firstly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, earthworms are an important indicator of soil fertility.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Studies have shown that the density and species number of earthworms in organically managed soils are 3 times as high as those in conventional fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, the biodiversity in organic farming can also be reflected in the number of insects, which is twice as many as those in traditional farms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This might be highly related to the fact that organic vegetables are grown without any human-made pesticides, making these vegetables more likely to be damaged.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other main difference between organic and traditional farming lies in crop yields, one of the biggest concerns of organic farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Organic farms, though possibly well-adapted for certain local environments, produce less food per unit of land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, organic vegetables like tomatoes and potatoes yielded are 40 percent less than conventional ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, research has also found the number of weeds produced in winter is about 90 percent at present, which has decreased by 10 percent than before.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, lower crop yields in organic farming are still inevitable at the moment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, organic farming is a new direction for agricultural development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These days, a variety of organic products are cultivated not only for humans, but also for animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, organic grass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is commonly used in organic farms to feed cows.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of the non-use of synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, it can protect cows from diseases brought by large-scale breeding, thus ensuring the quality of raw milk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But an interesting phenomenon is that its production has remained constant these years, which is quite unique compared with other types of crops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research on organic farming has covered various aspects and involved many countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to one study, organic farming was proposed in India in the early 1960s when it was faced with acute shortages of food grains due to the ever-increasing population and natural disasters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it could not be applied successfully at 1st, as farmers had been familiar with conventional instructions, proponents of organic farming claimed that organic agriculture emphasized biodiversity and effective soil management could enhance the capacity to mitigate and even reverse the effects of climate change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So India needed organic farming along with modern scientific agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study shows that in 2016, India became the country with the largest number of organic products, and the production of crops kept growing year on year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another international review about organic farming presents in the 1st part that people today have become increasingly interested in organic food, and this opinion is quite the same as that of other articles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what impressed me most was the volume of the investigation the author did in different countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He conducted a survey in 99 countries, of which 66 are convinced that organic farming is beneficial to animals, while 8 hold the opposite opinion, and the remaining 25 say it is inconclusive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Therefore, the last part of the review is mainly talking about whether organic farming brings positive effects to animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can see there are different views about the advantages of organic farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some may think it can provide more nutritious and healthier food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Others may say it can protect the natural environment and benefit wildlife.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, as far as I'm concerned, it's you, the ones who buy organic products, that will decide what they can bring to you because market demand determines everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, that's all I want to say.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's open it up for discussion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a university lecturer talking to students about the world's oldest mechanical computer, which is called the Antikythera mechanism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about what is sometimes described as the world's oldest mechanical computer, the Antikythera mechanism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This device was able to calculate where the sun, moon, and planets would be in the sky on any date in the past or future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has transformed our understanding both of the world of ancient Greece and of the history of science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mechanism was discovered in nineteen hundred at the bottom of the sea off the Greek island of Antikythera, hence the name by which it's now known.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was in the cargo of a ship that sank about two thousand one hundred years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Divers brought various items to the surface, and they were taken to a museum for examination.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One item was assumed to be a lump of rock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, a few months later, the object started splitting, and a museum curator realized that it was actually something man-made, covered with shells and other objects from the sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Further investigation revealed that it was in fact some sort of mechanism, and they decided to call it the Antikythera mechanism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it was badly damaged, it had survived in three main parts and around eighty smaller fragments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Antikythera mechanism has been studied a great deal since its discovery, and particularly in recent years, when highly sophisticated equipment has been available to analyze it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One machine called a dome can surround a sample and take photographs with the light coming from slightly different angles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This has made far more of the inscriptions on the mechanism legible, even though they're faded and worn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another state-of-the-art machine, the Blade Runner, has been used to take X-rays which show parts of the mechanism that would otherwise be invisible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite weighing nearly eight tons, it was transported from its place of manufacture to Greece, as the Antikythera mechanism is too fragile to be moved from there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Blade Runner was originally designed to examine engines for cracks, and it can work at an accuracy of less than a tenth of a millimeter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It seems the device was originally about thirty-three centimeters high, seventeen centimeters wide, and nine centimeters thick.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It consisted of at least thirty metal gear wheels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is, wheels which interlocked with each other.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The surfaces of the gear wheels were inscribed with the names of the months, explanations of how the different parts of the device were to be operated, and other information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These gear wheels in turn operated small movable models of the sun, moon, and the five planets that were known to the ancient Greeks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mechanism is thought to have been mounted in a frame for which wood was used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what was the Antikythera mechanism used for?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It clearly had an astronomical function.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The person using the device simply rotated a handle to operate the gear wheels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These engaged with each other to move the sun, moon, and planets around the Earth to show how they would appear on whatever particular date the operator was interested in, which could be years into the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bearing in mind that the ancient Greeks believed the sun and planets all revolved around the Earth, their movements are shown with remarkable accuracy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Perhaps most astonishing of all, the mechanism also showed when an eclipse was going to take place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was very important in the ancient world, and being able to predict this accurately would have given the user great power.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mechanism probably also helped in planning the timing of festivals, both agricultural and religious, by acting as a kind of calendar of events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Surprisingly, to the best of our knowledge, no device equaled the complexity of the Antikythera mechanism for at least a thousand years afterwards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The ideas seem to have survived in some form, however, particularly in the Byzantine Empire of the Eastern Mediterranean.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Around the thirteenth or fourteenth century, knowledge of the technology seems to have reached Western Europe, and a large number of clocks were made, providing astronomical information as well as showing the time of day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's hard to believe that nothing reached the sophistication of the Antikythera mechanism for a thousand years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet that might well be the case, and that has implications for our understanding of how scientific knowledge progresses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk about recent research into the design of workplaces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I recently completed some important research into the way office space is designed and its impact on employees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The open plan office had been the norm for offices around the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you can picture one, a big room with maybe fifty or a hundred workers sitting at their workstations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You might think open plan designs are a recent phenomenon, but they actually came about in the early twentieth century when businesses needed large numbers of people to do typing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These employees, usually women, used to have to sit in rows, working away at their typewriters under the watchful eye of their supervisor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the years, designers have come up with several variations on the open theme.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, this has been achieved through furnishings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The early designs featured separate desks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A subsequent design introduced the concept of the cubicle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These can have either high screens that workers can't see over or a screen just low enough to keep a lookout for the manager.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And nowadays, with the increase in large call centers, a phenomenon known as hot desking is common.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this system, employees working on different shifts are asked to share the same workstation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you can imagine, this is not very popular with staff as there is little opportunity to personalize your workspace.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, my research shows that employees in general dislike the open plan design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a part of my research, I conducted a survey of the staff in several large companies with open plan offices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The employees all voiced similar concerns about the design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, they felt that the open plan took away their privacy, but many also felt the need to carry their valuables with them at all times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So to some extent, they also felt there was less security with these designs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another common complaint may be something for employers to consider when choosing this type of design, and this was that these types of office space are bad for the health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I was intrigued by this possibility, but looking at staff records, it does seem to be borne out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if this design is so unpopular, why is it so commonplace?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the answer to that is in the benefits that the employers feel this type of design has.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there is the obvious benefit that this design significantly reduces costs, both in terms of rent and even in terms of energy use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Employers also argue that an open plan design leads to better teamwork and communication.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also feel that new staff can learn from observing other workers, so this design can actually help in training staff.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the complaints voiced by employees seem to suggest that the disadvantages far outweigh the advantages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The reality is that unhappy workers are unlikely to work well together, and there is plenty of evidence to suggest workers are frequently distracted from their work by the noise that is all around them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What is clear is that as designers, we need to think carefully about the impact that our design has both on the staff involved and the work that they do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
