transcript.text: Today, I'm going to be talking about the first year of a regeneration project in a mangrove forest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mangrove forests are found along river estuaries and coastlines and are important because they prevent flooding by acting as a barrier between the land and sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mangrove trees have special roots which can breathe and allow them to survive in thick, airless mud.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are also a very important habitat for wading birds, fish, and other animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the area where the project is taking place, there have been a number of problems since the area was first settled over one hundred years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of the mangrove trees were initially burnt as firewood by local farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The mangrove forests were also poisoned by settlers' farming methods because the farmers used fertilizer to increase crop yields, and this started to seep into the water, eventually killing part of the mangrove forest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farming in the area wasn't successful, and what was left of the mangrove forest area wasn't valued by local people as crops couldn't be grown there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And so what happened was that the area started to be used as somewhere to dump trash.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Action was urgently needed to protect the mangrove forest and prevent flooding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And so the Mangrove Regeneration Project was set up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The conservationists involved decided to construct a sand barrier around the forests, but unfortunately, this proved to be ineffective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only way forward appeared to be to grow new mangroves from seed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Several species of mangrove inhabit the forests in this area of the United States, but it is the gray mangroves that we are concerned with here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The seed of this plant is about the size of an almond, and most seeds fall only when they are fully ripe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Mangrove Regeneration Project first began three years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first set of seedlings was planted in small pots and left to germinate in a hothouse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The plants thrived and large roots appeared at the bottom of the pots.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ideally, these seedlings should have been conditioned with increasingly salty water before being planted in the sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They had, in fact, only been watered with rainwater.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the plants weren't used to a saline environment, it was decided to plant them out on the south side of a small island nearby.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was hoped that this would allow them to get used to salt water gradually since this part of the island was flooded every day at high tide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There were over one hundred plants planted in this particular spot, and it was necessary to protect them, not from the large number of wading birds which visit the area looking for food, but from the large rabbit colony living in the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The process for the second set of seedlings was completely different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Young seedlings were collected from the forests and then taken to a new site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The seedlings were then planted in the seabed behind old mangrove roots for protection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this method did not prove very successful and the vast majority of these seedlings were washed away in a storm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Luckily, the first set of seedlings survived, and this method is the one which the project will continue to use in the future.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'd like to describe in more detail the process...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about airport design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, last week we looked at some of the architectural features of modern house design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And today we're going to move on to look at airport design and how this has changed over the years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if we start by going back to, um, the nineteen sixties and seventies, when there were a lot fewer airports than there are today, well, check-in desks, customs and waiting areas were all very basic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were rather like a bus station, uh, designed to allow air traffic in and out of the terminal, but not very welcoming for passengers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even though passengers spent a lot of time there, the important features were related to the flights rather than the people who took them or indeed the places where the airports were built.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But that all changed in the next few decades.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you look at any big airport now, it's more like a mini city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It combines a transport center with a mall full of shops and facilities designed to make passengers feel more comfortable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So airports have been transformed and as with any city building, their design now takes into account features outside the airport terminal as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So why did this change happen?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there are two main reasons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first was the huge increase in passenger numbers, in the number of people traveling by plane.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And this was a direct result of mass tourism with things like, um, cheap holiday packages and low-cost airlines, with the construction of high-rise hotels and hotel complexes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then people started traveling more regularly from one country to another for things like meetings, and so the growth in international business also pushed numbers up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, passenger growth has been so significant over the past thirty years that it's estimated that some twenty-first century airports will need to handle up to fifty million passengers a year by twenty twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second reason for the change is, and this is a key aspect of airport design, people have realized that the airport is the first place you see when you visit another country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This means it forms your first impression of that country, and that impression has to be good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Airports are now called gateways to the cities they serve, and that raises visitor expectations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, what are the changes that have taken place in airport design?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the interior design, the inside of most airports is now completely different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, the dark enclosed airports of the past have been replaced by large open areas that look out onto the surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look at this picture of Beijing Airport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a huge amount of space and light, and this is typical of many airports today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Second, well, in the past, you had to go outside the airport to get trains to terminals, but now these are integrated into the design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, airport walkways are wide and can cope with the large volume of people, people who want to feel calm and relaxed, who want to get around the airport easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this way, the stress of modern travel has been minimized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Outside, the buildings have changed, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Airports were once ugly buildings with large towers and concrete boxes around them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now they're designed to fit into their surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look at this picture of the Arctic Circle Airport in Norway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The airport itself is surrounded by mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as you can see, the roof of the airport has been designed so that it's shaped like a range of mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are peaks at the top and then steep sides that touch the ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the same way, these airports in Thailand and India have beautiful shaded gardens all around them that reflect the landscape of the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also provide a connection with local tradition and art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another feature that is important inside airports, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And there's one final but very important issue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been said that airports are a new building type.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're often light steel structures with what looks to the passenger like a lot of glass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this is special glass that can maximize daylight and comfort and cut down on energy use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bangkok's main airport is flooded with controlled daylight in a tropical climate, and this is achieved through the use of new materials and modern technology, which have also allowed engineers to come up with methods of reducing costs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's take a closer look at some of these prin-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a psychology lecture on the topic of laughter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today I'm going to talk about something I hope you will find amusing because the topic is laughter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite its prominence in daily life, there has been little research on laughter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So after I became interested in this subject, I started off by having three of my psychology students conduct an observational survey as a component of the course which was designed to focus on the methodology used in this field.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The students and I observed twelve hundred people laughing spontaneously in their day-to-day worlds, from the university library to the city streets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Whenever we heard laughter, we noted down information about the exchange.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As to our findings, well, we usually think of laughter coming from an audience after something funny has been said by a single speaker.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But contrary to our expectations, the speakers we observed laughed about fifty percent more often than their audiences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our observations also showed that simple everyday comments like, "Where have you been?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: are far more likely to precede laughter than a joke is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, only ten to twenty percent of the laughter episodes we witnessed followed anything actually funny.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The gender difference in laughter is also striking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In our twelve hundred case studies, we found that while everyone laughed a lot, females laugh one hundred and twenty-six percent more often than their male counterparts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But men seem to be the main instigators of humor across cultures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I also had students in my classes note down in a diary instances when they themselves laughed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When they analyzed the results, they found that laughter for them was thirty times more frequent in social situations than when they are alone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This suggests that laughter is a signal we send to others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, moving on from this research to some more general observations, what do we know about the phenomenon of laughter and its psychological features?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oftentimes, if one person laughs, those around that person will also laugh even if they didn't hear or see what caused the laughter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Consider the extraordinary outbreak of laughter at one boarding school some years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The symptoms appeared when three students started laughing and couldn't stop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The symptoms rapidly spread, eventually affecting ninety-five students and forcing the school to close until the laughing stopped.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Quite an amazing tale, I think you'll agree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What part of the brain controls laughter?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, when a speaker laughs, the laugh usually occurs at the end of sentences or phrases rather than being randomly scattered through the sentence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This suggests that different regions of the brain are involved in speech, which is largely based on cognition and laughter, which is based on emotion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The physiological effects of laughter are incompletely documented, and their medical benefits are even less certain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it is known that in many people laughter does, at least temporarily, raise blood pressure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Results of other studies have proved less definite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At least one study reported that comedy and laughter increased the levels of certain chemicals in the urine that were known to be associated with stress.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, other research in the US reported that laughter reduced these same chemical levels, which indicated the exact opposite effect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it is far from certain what the effects of laughter are on these particular chemicals, and thus the ultimate effects of laughter in this regard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, one of laughter's most promising applications, which has been rather extensively noted experimentally, is the reduction of the extent to which we feel pain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One American university study found that this was tolerated better by subjects who laughed at the films of certain comedians than by other subjects who did not watch the films.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In another American study, patients who had undergone surgery and then watched comedy films requested fewer aspirin and tranquilizers than others who had viewed serious dramatic films.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And science has long understood that laughter causes the prefrontal cortex of the brain to release a certain hormone which makes the person feel happy, although the exact mechanism is not completely understood, nor is its effect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Is laughter universal among humans?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You'll hear a lecturer giving a presentation about the Klondike Gold Rush.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'm gonna talk about an incredible event in the history of Canada, the Klondike Gold Rush.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Between eighteen ninety-six and eighteen ninety-nine, over one hundred thousand people set out to seek gold in the Klondike region, a remote area in northwestern Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Only four thousand people were actually successful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's start by considering the journey people had to take in order to reach the Klondike River and start looking for gold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For most gold seekers, their journey began in Alaska in a town on the coast called Skagway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From Skagway, one option was to take the White Pass Trail through the mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It probably looked easy enough at the beginning of the trail, but rocks made it difficult to make progress.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On top of this, the men and their horses got stuck in the thick mud that covered long sections of the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other option was the Chilkoot Trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, although this trail was only about thirty-five miles long, it took about three months for the gold seekers to cover this distance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is because the trail was incredibly steep, and people had to make the same trip multiple times in order to transport their equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most people really had very little idea about how difficult the journey was gonna be.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So although one hundred thousand may have set out on those two trails, only about thirty thousand got to the end.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So yes, the majority gave up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Often, they were suffering from starvation or disease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also came to the terrible realization that their journey was likely to end in failure, and so they turned around.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, for those gold seekers who did continue, they eventually reached Lake Bennett.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They might have expected that their journey was gonna become easier at this point, but no.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because the lake was frozen over, many people had to wait until spring before they could continue their journey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the meantime, a tent was the only protection they had from the cold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While they were waiting, people cut down trees and made boats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the ice melted, they could sail across the lake and start down the Yukon River.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, this wasn't the end of their troubles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once they reached a point of the river called Miles Canyon, things became very dangerous indeed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many boats were destroyed in the rapids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to proceed down the Yukon River, the gold seekers needed to employ a real sailor, someone who could steer their boats and get through the canyon safely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From here on, the worst was over, and the gold seekers could sail to a place called Dawson at the mouth of the Klondike River.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So earlier on, I mentioned that gold seekers needed to make multiple trips up and down the two trails.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is because they had to transport an enormous amount of equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This equipment was set out on a very long list.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was actually the police who gave gold seekers the list since they knew how unprepared many people were for the journey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People were obliged to take enough supplies to last them a year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the list included clothing like boots and warm winter coats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was also the food the gold seekers required.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Perhaps items like tea weren't too hard to carry, but four hundred pounds of flour would have been very heavy indeed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The gold seekers had to take a lot of tools as well, everything they needed for digging, for building, and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Things like rope were essential and could be packed away without too much difficulty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But imagine having to carry two or three buckets with you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All these things were compulsory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So some people became very successful because of the Gold Rush and not because they'd actually found gold themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Those who were business-minded saw many opportunities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They sold the supplies that the gold seekers needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They established hotels and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then there were people like Jack London.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: London was one of the gold seekers that actually survived the terrible journey, but he didn't find much gold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Still, he was inspired to write.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Through his vivid description, his readers could share the feeling of adventure even from the comfort of their armchair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, it wasn't just men that tried to seek their fame and fortune.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many women also headed up the trails.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among them were Annie Hall Strong and Emma Kelly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the US and in other parts of Canada, ordinary citizens were keen to read about life in the Klondike.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Working for different newspapers, Hall and Kelly often described their firsthand experience of danger and hardship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another thing that needs to be discussed-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear an environmental science lecture about a plant called Jatropha and its uses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you know, the world is running out of fossil fuels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is crude oil, coal, and natural gas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As an alternative, certain plants are now being considered as biofuels, which are fuels made from organic plant material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These are possible sources of energy once the fossil fuels have gone forever.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, one such plant goes by the name of Jatropha.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was first a native of Central America, and it's now found across the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A few things that make this plant especially attractive is that it can survive in very poor quality, infertile soil, as it does, for example, alongside train tracks in India on the line between Mumbai and Delhi.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And for up to three years, it's resistant to drought.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can do without rain for that long.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And even if it's not actually a plant that people can eat, it's still worth having it on your land as it prevents erosion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And we looked at the dangerous consequences of that in a previous lecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, Jatropha seeds can be slowly distilled to produce diesel oil, and it's this kind of fuel, of course, that's of interest to scientists and power companies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After processing, the seeds can yield up to four times the oil that soybean can and ten times the amount compared to corn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you can see why it's causing such interest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And not much is wasted in the processing procedure either.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After the oil has been extracted from the seeds, the residue is processed into biomass, which can run power stations, which in turn can provide electricity for thousands of local homes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, whereas our fossil fuels cannot be replaced, the energy produced by biofuels such as Jatropha is renewable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not gonna run out because the plants just go on growing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's no doubt that it is a remarkable plant and one that has been very beneficial to man.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In various African communities, it's been used to operate water pumps and refrigerate medicines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can be used to produce candles or as a fencing plant to keep some animals enclosed and some animals out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can also treat a number of health problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the boiled leaves can do much to relieve the suffering of people with malaria, and some Jatropha species have seeds which are used to treat digestion problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, that's not what the European corporations who are buying vast amounts of land for Jatropha plantations are focusing on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They claim that people who are dependent on rural economies will benefit from growing Jatropha, and that it will help them bring an end to poverty by providing a long-term local industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also point out that few or no modifications would be necessary in modern diesel engines since they were originally designed to run on biofuels such as peanut oil and ethanol anyway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, when the plants are burnt, they release carbon dioxide, but they absorb great amounts when they're growing, making them a considerably greener alternative to fossil fuels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But not everyone shares the excitement over Jatropha nor other biofuels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Western Australia, Jatropha has in fact been banned since the seeds of some species are toxic, and it only takes three or four to kill a person, and animals are also very vulnerable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, skeptics also point out that as there are many species of Jatropha, its oil productivity is unreliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from this, critics of Jatropha and other biofuels claim that farmers now have a strong economic incentive to grow them rather than food crops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Poor countries would be particularly affected because they would have to rely on imported foods to survive, and people would end up having to pay greatly inflated prices for basic foods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also the concern over environmental damage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to provide land for palm oil or sugarcane plantations, for instance, companies are cutting down vast areas of rainforest, which can never be replaced, and this in turn results in the disappearance of wildlife which depended on that habitat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can also imagine that such deforestation makes a considerable contribution to global warming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, opponents also reject the idea that biofuels are a carbon neutral source of energy and say...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answer for part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 虽然燃烧时会释放二氧化碳，但植物在生长过程中会吸收（use up）大量的 carbon dioxide（二氧化碳）。
questions.tip: 题目中的 use up（用光/消耗）对应录音中的 absorb（吸收）。

questions.explanation: 这种森林砍伐对 global warming（全球变暖）这一问题做出了相当大的“贡献”（负面影响）。

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a linguistics lecture about attempts to invent a universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome back to the series of linguistics lectures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll be talking about the idea of inventing a universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What does that mean?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, most human languages were never invented.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, they evolved over time, and the result is, you know, they're irregular and difficult to learn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for centuries, people have dreamed of inventing a perfect universal language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The early invented languages that did exist were either created by priests to be used for religious purposes or developed to help establish trade between different nations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scholars have found evidence that around nine hundred languages have been invented over the centuries in various parts of the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the linguist Arika Okrent believes that the exact figure is unclear because she suspects many of these languages are now lost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No record of them survives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first really serious attempt to invent a language was made by William Spencer in the seventeenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Like so many others, he was frustrated by the irregularities in all existing languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Accuracy was particularly important for Spencer because he wrote books.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His subject was science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, he wanted to create a language where words had only one meaning, so everyone would understand precisely what they meant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, he thought the only way to do this was instead of using the usual letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, and so on, he tried to substitute numbers for them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this attempt failed, mostly because he couldn't describe complex ideas in this way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So Spencer went back to using the alphabet, but he grouped words together in a different way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When his dictionary was published in sixteen sixty-eight, the words weren't classified in alphabetical order.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What he'd done was he'd used the same system with which plants were divided up into groups based on their type.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another important attempt to invent a universal language was made by Ludwig Zamenhof, who was born in eighteen fifty-nine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof's language reflects his own background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He grew up speaking Polish, English, French, German, and Russian.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So rather than create a completely new language, he mixed together five or six existing European languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then Zamenhof used an interesting technique to help him develop his new language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He used it to write quite a few different songs, and this made his work more enjoyable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He also thought that most European languages were too complicated, which meant that it was very difficult for people to learn them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof wanted to create a more simple language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for example, he had a single prefix that was used before adjectives or verbs to make them negative, which is obviously much easier than English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then finally, he published a book introducing his language to the world in eighteen eighty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, like other invented languages, no one was very interested at first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So again, Zamenhof used an interesting approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to publicize the completed language, he made a list of everyone he knew and posted a letter to all of them using the new language.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many people were surprised how easily they could understand it, and the language began to attract attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Zamenhof's language was never used all around the world as he had hoped, but still, it's probably the most successful of all the invented languages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the twentieth century, an Australian named Bruce Goldie tried something completely different.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Goldie thought that a universal language would be easier to use if the starting point for each word was a picture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Goldie spent more than twenty years designing his new language and eventually published a book giving all the details in nineteen forty-nine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He also went on a lecture tour to promote it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But although the general public were often quite interested, much to Goldie's disappointment, his language was ignored by all of the major universities despite frequent attempts to make them interested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It wasn't until the nineteen seventies that his language had some success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was in Canada, in fact, where it was used to teach a group of disabled children in a hospital to read.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And as a result, Goldie got some recognition for his work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what can we say in conclusion?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the truth is all attempts to create a universal language have failed, and there are a number of reasons for this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, most universal languages have been seen as rather technical and plain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're not good at conveying emotion, so they've never been very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another reason is the spread of English as a global language in the twentieth century, particularly resulting from the film industry in Hollywood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then lastly, the type of people who invented the languages began to change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the past, it had been academics, but more recently, the languages have often been created by writers, usually for entertainment, so they haven't been taken seriously.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, there's one other issue I'd like to consider, and that's the use of-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

Introduction

William Spencer
• He wrote books about {{32}} , so he needed an accurate language.

Ludwig Zamenhof
• He mixed together existing European languages.
• He wrote {{34}} to help develop his new language.
• He wanted simplicity, e.g. one prefix to make words {{35}} .
• He sent a {{36}} to his friends to publicise his language.
• He created the most successful invented language.
Bruce Goldie
• Each word of his language was based on a {{37}} .
• His language did not get academic recognition at first.
• Children in a Canadian {{38}} learned to read using his language.
Conclusion: why have invented languages failed?
• They cannot express {{39}} .
• English became the global language.
• They are now invented by {{40}} , just for entertainment.

questions.quote: At first, he thought the only way to do this was instead of using the usual letters of the alphabet, A, B, C, and so on, he tried to substitute numbers for them.

questions.quote: Then Zamenhof used an interesting technique to help him develop his new language. He used it to write quite a few different songs, and this made his work more enjoyable.

questions.quote: Zamenhof wanted to create a more simple language. So for example, he had a single prefix that was used before adjectives or verbs to make them negative, which is obviously much easier than English.

questions.quote: In order to publicize the completed language, he made a list of everyone he knew and posted a letter to all of them using the new language.

questions.explanation: 录音提到每个词的“起点”是一幅画（picture），这里的“起点”和题目中的“基于”是一个意思。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没听懂 starting point 和 based on 是一回事，导致没反应过来后面的答案词。

questions.explanation: 录音提到在加拿大，这门语言被用来教医院（hospital）里的残疾儿童阅读。
questions.tip: 你可能会错填成 Canada，但加拿大在题目里已经给出，你需要听的是在这门语言被使用的具体场所。

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the research on the invasion of a plant called buckthorn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome to today's biology lecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We are going to talk about a couple of invasive plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What is an invasive species?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, an invasive plant has the ability to spread aggressively outside its native range in a new habitat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Invasive plants can even cause economic or environmental harm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At the same time, they threaten local plants by competing for nutrients, light, and water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Invasive species have contributed to the decline of many endangered and threatened species in the US.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As many of you have noticed in your own life, some of these species outcompetes other plants and take over a whole garden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So, they have become a serious problem that both the government and the public must deal with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These species are often brought out of their native range by humans or birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They unknowingly carry the seeds with them to a new environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now let's take a look at some invasive species and see how they are affecting native environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Common broom, or Scotch broom, is a plant native to Western and Central Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It typically grows to one to three meters tall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is found in sunny sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In America, this species has become an ecologically destructive plant, especially in grassland, shrubs, and woodlands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has a competitive advantage over native trees and shrubs in North America, and since its introduction, it has caused not only ecological, but also economic problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It even affected the performance of the commodity industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is estimated that it is responsible for the lost timber production, which was worth fifteen million US dollars last year in Oregon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As common broom can cause such a big problem, how can we control it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One way to start is by targeting the common broom plants that are producing fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then we need to remove these fruit-bearing trees, and that will reduce the amount of seeds added to the soil each year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another way is biological control, like introducing some insects from its place of origin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They will disturb the growth of this invasive plant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Next, there's Japanese barberry, which is native to Japan and Eastern Asia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It tolerates a wide range of soil and moisture conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is found along woodland edges, roadsides, stream banks, old fields, and forests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This species was brought to America from Russia in nineteen seventy-five, and it is now widely seen throughout the US.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has yellow flowers and bears bright red fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's used widely as landscape and hedge material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has been replacing native species in America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Furthermore, the plant can change soil condition and cause diseases to plants like wheat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In recent years, Japanese barberry has been recognized as an invasive species in many parts of the Eastern United States.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A variety of techniques, including both mechanical and chemical controls, may be effective in dealing with this species, but the exact method should be tailored to the specific conditions on the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Buckthorn, or common buckthorn, is a species of tree-like plant which usually grows two to three meters tall, but it occasionally reaches up to ten meters tall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It has smooth, dark green leaves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Common buckthorn produces berry-like black fruits in late summer and autumn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is invasive in many parts of the western part of the United States.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is native to Europe, and it was introduced to North America in the early nineteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It causes damage to local soil and plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Buckthorn can spread widely with the help of birds that eat its fruits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They then carry the seeds long distances along their path of migration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What can we do to control it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, we need to learn how to identify common buckthorn.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is different from sea buckthorn, which is a plant that can be used to treat serious digestive problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then we should avoid using it in gardens and landscape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You can contact the Invading Species Hotline if you find common buckthorn in the wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So let's look at some pictures of these.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

questions.quote: It even affected the performance of the commodity industry. It is estimated that it is responsible for the lost timber production, which was worth fifteen million US dollars last year in Oregon.

questions.explanation: 录音明示“biological control, like introducing some insects”，“like”对应题目的“such as”，直接得出 insects。
questions.tip: 听写时要注意名词的复数尾音“s”，这种细节没听清极容易导致拼写错误从而丢分。

questions.explanation: 录音提到“brought to America from Russia in nineteen seventy-five”，“brought to”替换了“introduced to”，直接得出源头国家 Russia。
questions.tip: 同一句话里同时出现了 America 和 Russia，你需要根据题干的“from”准确分辨出表示来源的地点是 Russia。
questions.quote: This species was brought to America from Russia in nineteen seventy-five, and it is now widely seen throughout the US.

questions.explanation: 听到录音描述“yellow flowers and bears bright red fruits”，根据题目给出的颜色线索 yellow，锁定对应的名词 flowers。
questions.tip: 紧接着出现了干扰信息“red fruits”，你不要因为注意力滞后或没看清题目要求的颜色而误填为 fruits。
questions.quote: It has yellow flowers and bears bright red fruits.

questions.explanation: 录音描述叶子特征为“smooth, dark green leaves”，直接对应题目中与 dark green 并列的形容词 smooth。
questions.tip: 在两个形容词连续修饰一个名词时，第一个词发音往往比较快，你需要紧跟主语“leaves”抓取前面的所有修饰语。
questions.quote: It has smooth, dark green leaves.

questions.explanation: 录音指出鸟类将种子带去很远的地方“along their path of migration”，填入表示鸟类行为活动的 migration 契合题意。
questions.tip: 听到“path”时你可能就急着下笔了，但题干“birds' ___”要求填入的是鸟类的一种特定行为，且后半句的“migration”才是这一语义块的真正落脚点。
questions.quote: Buckthorn can spread widely with the help of birds that eat its fruits. They then carry the seeds long distances along their path of migration.

questions.tip: 这是一个较长的学术词汇，发音可能会让你短暂卡壳，你需要根据读音规律迅速拼写，并注意别把前后的修饰词跟核心名词搞混。
questions.quote: It is different from sea buckthorn, which is a plant that can be used to treat serious digestive problems.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear an engineering student giving a presentation about a research project on design features of the International Space Station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For my presentation, I'm going to summarize the findings of a research project on life aboard the International Space Station in the early days of its operation, its teething problems as it were.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll start by giving a little background information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The space station crew were essentially a constantly changing team of scientists from different countries who lived on the space station for several months at a time, and they conducted a number of experiments, including some studies of living conditions in space, which is what I'm going to be looking at now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So what was life like on board in the very confined conditions of the space station?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the early impressions recorded by the astronauts were very different from what people had expected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They'd expected that the air would smell stale or artificial, but the astronauts found that it was fresh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So that was one very positive finding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And although they were in such a confined space and people worried that it would get very hot, in fact, they found that it was very easy to turn the temperature up or down in order to keep it within a comfortable range.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The feedback on the food was also positive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Astronauts on previous space stations had described the meals as boring, but the International Space Station meals were praised for their variety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So that was another good piece of feedback.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And something which is taken for granted today, but was a key morale booster in those days, was communication between the space station and Earth, which the astronauts said was clear and reliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So in the early days, it seems that the mood was overall very positive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: However, after a few days, the difficulties and frustrations became clearer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Above all, the crew complained about the constant noise caused by the air filters, which used to rattle and buzz twenty-four hours a day, interrupting their sleep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As well as that, the astronauts complained that the Velcro fasteners, which were positioned all over the station, didn't work well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And so a lot of the time, objects weren't secure in the cabin, but floated about.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A particularly serious problem was that the systems used on the space station had been developed in a number of different countries, and they didn't always work well together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For example, it was impossible to mix the water produced from different systems because it contained different sorts of preservatives, and these reacted together and blocked the pipes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another problem was connected to repairs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: At the best of times, these took up an inordinate amount of time on the station, and the crew complained that many of the tools that they'd been provided with weren't suitable for the jobs they had to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So they had to improvise, which meant that jobs took a lot longer than they needed to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another related problem was to do with access to equipment that needed maintaining.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because the instructions on the equipment were often located in places where they were difficult to read, like on the back of equipment, it was often difficult or impossible to read them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So having identified these problems, the researchers came up with a number of suggestions about how conditions could be improved on subsequent missions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: First, it became clear that although there had been a great deal of consultation with the crews, the systems and equipment on the space station needed much more wide-ranging testing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then the whole issue of language training came under review.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Astronauts from different countries had to be able to talk to the controllers on Earth and to understand them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, although they'd had extensive language training, the astronauts sometimes had problems comprehending what was said because they weren't familiar with the accent of the speaker, and this sometimes led to quite dangerous misunderstandings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Finally, and this is the point I found most surprising, the researchers felt that the designers of the space station were paying too much attention to safety rather than considering operating issues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is, how the station could be run comfortably and smoothly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the recommendation was to make changes here at quite a fundamental level.

transcript.text: So those were the main points I covered in the...

groups.content:
Life on the International Space Station
Background
• Station was occupied by international teams of scientists over several months.
• Research was done on living conditions.
Early impressions
• The air smelt {{31}} .
• The temperature was easy to adjust.
• The food had enough {{32}} .
• {{33}} was efficient.
Problems
• Difficulties with air filters caused lack of {{34}} .
• It was difficult to keep cabin objects secure.
• Systems were incompatible, e.g. there were problems when mixing {{35}} because of the preservatives
• The {{36}} available were not always suitable for their purpose
• It was difficult to access the {{37}} for equipment maintenance
Suggested improvements
• Systems and equipment should undergo more extensive {{38}} .
• In language training, astronauts needed practice in understanding the controller’s {{39}} .
• There should be less emphasis on {{40}} and more on other issues

questions.explanation: 录音提到人们本来预期空气味道会不好，但宇航员发现空气其实很“fresh”（清新），直接填入即可。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了stale（污浊的）或者artificial（人造的），但那是人们“预期的（expected）”错误情况，要注意听后面的转折词but，它引出的才是真实的答案。
questions.quote: Well, the early impressions recorded by the astronauts were very different from what people had expected. They'd expected that the air would smell stale or artificial, but the astronauts found that it was fresh. So that was one very positive finding.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到国际空间站的餐食因为其“variety”（多样性）而受到赞扬，这和题目里“有足够的……”完美对应。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了boring，但录音明确说那是“之前的空间站（previous space stations）”的食物，做题时千万不要张冠李戴。
questions.quote: The feedback on the food was also positive. Astronauts on previous space stations had described the meals as boring, but the International Space Station meals were praised for their variety. So that was another good piece of feedback.

questions.explanation: 录音提到空间站和地球之间的“communication”（通讯）非常清晰可靠（clear and reliable），也就是题目所说的efficient（高效）。
questions.tip: 你可能会在录音里死等efficient这个词，但雅思最喜欢用同义替换（比如用clear and reliable来替换），做填空题一定要理解整体语义。
questions.quote: And something which is taken for granted today, but was a key morale booster in those days, was communication between the space station and Earth, which the astronauts said was clear and reliable. So in the early days, it seems that the mood was overall very positive.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说到空气过滤器会24小时发出噪音，“interrupting their sleep”（打断他们的睡眠），也就是题目里问的导致了lack of sleep（缺乏睡眠）。
questions.tip: 你可能会想填noise，但题干前面已经有caused（导致）了，空气过滤器的问题导致的结果是“缺乏睡眠”，一定要看清题目的因果关系。
questions.quote: However, after a few days, the difficulties and frustrations became clearer. Above all, the crew complained about the constant noise caused by the air filters, which used to rattle and buzz twenty-four hours a day, interrupting their sleep.

questions.explanation: 录音举例说没法混合不同系统产生的“water”（水），因为里面含有不同的防腐剂（preservatives），对应题目“混合……时遇到问题”。
questions.tip: 这个答案其实给得很直接，容易错是因为你可能会被后面紧跟着出现的一大串复杂生词（如preservatives）分散注意力，导致大脑空白忘了写答案。
questions.quote: A particularly serious problem was that the systems used on the space station had been developed in a number of different countries, and they didn't always work well together. For example, it was impossible to mix the water produced from different systems because it contained different sorts of preservatives, and these reacted together and blocked the pipes.

questions.explanation: 录音提到宇航员抱怨提供给他们的很多“tools”（工具）不适合他们要干的活（weren't suitable），完美对应题目“提供的……不总是适合其目的”。
questions.tip: 你可能会填repairs或jobs，但题目缺的是一个能够“被提供、被使用（available）且不适合”的具体物品名词，要精准捕捉“tools... weren't suitable”这个搭配。
questions.quote: Another problem was connected to repairs. At the best of times, these took up an inordinate amount of time on the station, and the crew complained that many of the tools that they'd been provided with weren't suitable for the jobs they had to do. So they had to improvise, which meant that jobs took a lot longer than they needed to.

questions.explanation: 录音里说设备上的“instructions”（说明书）经常贴在设备背面等难读的地方，对应题目“难以获取设备的……”。
questions.tip: 你可能光顾着听equipment（设备）去了，但题目问的是“难以获取设备的什么”，录音明确说难读到的是instructions，一定要抓准句子的核心主语。
questions.quote: Another related problem was to do with access to equipment that needed maintaining. Because the instructions on the equipment were often located in places where they were difficult to read, like on the back of equipment, it was often difficult or impossible to read them.

questions.explanation: 录音提到系统和设备需要更多广泛的（wide-ranging）“testing”（测试），这里的wide-ranging直接同义替换了题目中的extensive（广泛的）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了consultation（咨询），但这出现在although（尽管）引导的让步状语从句里，是已经做过的事，真正的建议和重点永远在主句里。
questions.quote: So having identified these problems, the researchers came up with a number of suggestions about how conditions could be improved on subsequent missions. First, it became clear that although there had been a great deal of consultation with the crews, the systems and equipment on the space station needed much more wide-ranging testing.

questions.explanation: 录音指出宇航员有时候理解困难，是因为对说话人的“accent”（口音）不熟悉，对应题目“需要练习听懂控制员的……”。
questions.tip: 你可能一听到language training就想填language，但这只是引入的大话题，往下听具体导致“听不懂（comprehending）”的原因其实是对accent不熟。
questions.quote: Then the whole issue of language training came under review. Astronauts from different countries had to be able to talk to the controllers on Earth and to understand them. Now, although they'd had extensive language training, the astronauts sometimes had problems comprehending what was said because they weren't familiar with the accent of the speaker, and this sometimes led to quite dangerous misunderstandings.

questions.explanation: 录音里提到设计师在“safety”（安全）上放了太多注意力（paying too much attention to），这也就是建议中应该减少强调（less emphasis on）的部分。
questions.tip: 你可能听到operating issues就想当答案填进去，但录音里说的是应该多考虑（rather than considering）操作问题，而对安全关注太多，理清这层对比关系才不会填反。
questions.quote: Finally, and this is the point I found most surprising, the researchers felt that the designers of the space station were paying too much attention to safety rather than considering operating issues. That is, how the station could be run comfortably and smoothly. And the recommendation was to make changes here at quite a fundamental level.

34.s: the constant noise caused by the air filters

35.s: they didn't always work well together
because it contained different sorts of preservatives

36.s: the tools that they'd been provided with
for the jobs they had to do

37.q: It was difficult to access the
37.s: it was often difficult or impossible to read them

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture's introduction to Insect Biology one oh one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, and welcome to Insect Biology one oh one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: I'd like to begin this course with a few remarks about good insects and bad ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Bugs are all around us, and that's both a benefit and an annoyance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Sometimes maybe even serious harm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, let's talk about the good things that insects do for us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Probably the most important insect for humans, and maybe for all other life, is the bee.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Bees help plants in the process of pollination, and thus are necessary to most flowering plants and fruit trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is, they carry pollen from male flowers to female.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If it weren't for bees, we'd have very few food plants and no fruit either.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In fact, there would be no we.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: No lesser thinker than Albert Einstein pointed out that without bees, humanity would be dead within a year or less.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We'd starve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's that simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That should maybe make us just a little humble.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A little less dramatic is the fact that bees also make the honey we eat, and they produce beeswax, which is useful in candles and is also used as a first-rate polish for furniture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Sure, these may not be vital to our lives, but they can serve as reminders of how important bees are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That's a point I keep coming back to in this course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Though in all fairness, I should point out that butterflies aid in pollination as well as bees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, here in Michigan, what's the worst part of summer?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Yep, that's right, mosquitoes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But I'm talking about helpful insects, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So let's look at the dragonfly first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If there were no dragonflies, there would be even more mosquitoes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Dragonflies mainly eat mosquitoes and also a few other insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Yes, that's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They don't just fly around, and they also help to eliminate harmful insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So the next time you see a dragonfly, don't you dare kill it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, let's talk a little about those harmful insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Take the mosquitoes I just mentioned as an example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Not so many years ago, mosquitoes here in America weren't just annoying.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Some were even deadly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They carried malaria and yellow fever.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: My own ancestor, the Confederate General John Bell Hood, lived through the worst battles of Civil War, only to die at age thirty-eight from yellow fever.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A pest, not a bullet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, besides the mosquitoes, in summer, there is also a kind of insect that never seems tired.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Right, that is the fly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Before I go on talking, I must mention an African fly called the tsetse fly, which feeds on blood and can cause serious diseases in the people and animals that it bites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Besides, it is still a bearer of sleeping sickness, which affects around three hundred thousand people every year in Africa and can be treated only with toxic drugs that are hard to administer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Worse still, the drugs sometimes don't work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Other insects, of course, destroy food crops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In China, for instance, locusts continue to be a danger to the harvest in some areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Less important, but still annoying, moths eat people's clothes and dust mites slowly destroy carpets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Worse, but still in the home, termites or white ants eat wood, the wood of your house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If they are not stopped, they can eventually destroy the whole building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Usually, they seriously damage a building before anyone even notices them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So, as we all know, insects can be a real trouble.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So what to do?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You can go ahead and start killing harmful insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In the early decades after the Communist revolution in China, Chairman Mao encouraged the people to swat every fly they could see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Slogans on the walls of buildings has called them little capitalists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But flies reproduce too quickly for this to be a long-term solution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For some decades in the West, to kill insects with chemicals seemed a good remedy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Unfortunately, chemicals can only be used in a limited area for a limited time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's a small-scale solution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The insects come back.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Worse still, some of the poisons used, like DDT, were found harmful to the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Many kinds of wildlife, like hawks, were harmed, and people in chemical-using rural areas have one of the highest rates of liver cancer in the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's no secret that chemicals remain harmful to humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Like all species, insects adapt to their changing environments at an amazing rate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: When a new chemical is introduced to their habitat, the insects survive are generally the ones with some way of resisting the harmful effects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They then breed with the other survivors, and just like that, insects become resistant to most poison in a few generations An insect generation, remember, is a couple of months at most.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So again, we have to ask what to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, there are biological solutions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Some of these are pretty simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One is destroying the insect's habitat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You take away their home or food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Cleaning your kitchen is the best way to prevent roaches.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: No garbage, no food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Getting rid of marshes and swamps eliminates mosquitoes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Other solutions might include bringing in dragonflies or bats in areas where mosquitoes are many.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This is a cheaper alternative to chemicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Biological methods like this also bring no extra pollution to the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But you have to be careful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you change the environment too much, you might be hurting other forms of life accidentally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One recent method of controlling insect populations involves interrupting their breeding cycle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What does that mean?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It means birth control for bugs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Insects are provided with food that makes them unable to reproduce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Since they can't have babies, the population disappears or nearly so.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And since no young are born, resistance is not a problem, with no young insects developing increased resistance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Interrupt the life cycle, eliminate the bug.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's clear that we must have an understanding of the life cycle of the insect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At least that's the plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We'll go into more detail as the course goes along.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, I will stop here to see whether you have any questions or not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of an environmental studies lecture about the possibility of using insects as a source of food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the last few weeks, we've been talking about the challenges of producing food for the global population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And, uh, there's been a lot of interest recently in new sources of food, and one of the most interesting is insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, why should insects be considered as a food source?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, for a start, a number of them are full of protein, and many also have certain vitamins, which may surprise you, more so than a typical farm animal, in fact.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And compared to farm animals, whose waste products contain a great deal of ammonia, the waste products of insects are far less acidic and would therefore do very little damage to the soil or to any of the rivers that run through farmland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, when it comes to the production of insects, the expense would be very low.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No trees need be chopped down or forest turned to pasture, so the space that they would occupy would be radically smaller than for, say, cows or sheep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even if some consumers decided that they'd rather not put insects in their shopping basket, we could also consider how insects might be added to animal feed, the food given to farm animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's already known that some insects, if they were part of the animal feed, would act as a sort of natural antibiotic within a cow or sheep's digestive system, thus removing the need for human intervention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This would be a cost-effective and environmentally friendly alternative for farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, if consumers do decide that insects are a potential superfood, a way of feeding the world,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: then the next question is where do we source them from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The wild, perhaps?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Or should they be bred on insect farms?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, if we take from the wild, one potential consequence of this is that too many will be taken, and in turn, a species could become endangered or extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, for insects which are harvested from the wild, we have no way of knowing where they have been or what they have come in contact with, and this could have harmful consequences for human health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Imagine the scenario if food producers or retailers were supplied with insects that were carrying bacteria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is not something we want to add to the food chain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If insects are bred on farms, the problems I've just outlined could be avoided.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in many countries, it's already the case that demand for insects is growing, really growing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it's not in rural areas where you'd expect, but, in fact, in the cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Thailand, for example, where the demand has really shot up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, people in countries where insects are traditionally what people eat, they'll tell you that when insects are intensively farmed, their taste is simply not the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ironically, this is the same accusation that people have when it comes to the way that cows and sheep are raised.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Insect farmers also face a series of challenges, and researchers are keen to assist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, when it comes to breeding, different insects have different requirements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For a start, it's essential to maintain a suitable temperature for many species to reproduce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this isn't right, nothing's going to happen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another problem is something that often happens when any species is bred in a confined space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And so far, researchers and farmers have not come up with any clear or long-term effective solution to it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're talking about the problem of disease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You don't want a whole colony wiped out in one go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also the question of where insects need to be kept.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If insects are to be bred as a superfood, then the tanks used to house them have to be better designed, and this has to happen so that cleaning takes up less time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If we're talking about mass production, we don't want this to be a time-consuming activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, like I said before, insects have long been part of the diet in some countries, but not so in others.
