transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the Swedish film director Ingmar Bergman given to media studies students by a film critic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You can read a great novel, listen to a great symphony, or go to see a painting by a great artist, and you'll want to experience it again and again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And every time you do, you'll learn something new from it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Very few films achieve this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of them are mere entertainment, and very few of them could be said to be works of art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They simply don't have the depth that a work of art has, and this means that you may see them once, but you won't want to watch them again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why is it that so many commercial films today have such a limited shelf life?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One problem is that for many films, once you've seen them once and you know what happens, that's it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They rely on the element of surprise to keep you interested, and once that's lost, that feeling of what's going to happen next, there's nothing left.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, the commercial nature of filmmaking means that rather than focusing on the development of characters in the film, many films are just becoming vehicles for actors, box office successes who essentially play the same part each time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, as well as this, many critics would argue that the greatest black and white films had their own special world with its own special atmosphere and that nowadays it's harder to create this because the director is unable to play with light in the same way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another problem is that many directors lack the ability to focus the camera on the important points.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There may be impressive visual images, but they don't contribute to the meaning of the film.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Which brings me on to Ingmar Bergman, the great Swedish film director who died in two thousand and seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No other director has equaled Bergman in his ability to convey emotion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His films have the dramatic force of a work by the world's greatest playwrights, such as Ibsen or Shakespeare.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Watching Bergman's films is an enriching experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nothing is immediately obvious or predictable, but gradually it becomes clear where he is taking you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you study a film such as Wild Strawberries, you'll see that every little detail is significant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Each image on the screen is there for a purpose and gradually builds up an understanding of the central meaning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With Bergman, too, you know that a small gesture made by a character or the expression on a character's face can tell you just as much as the words uttered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In his film Persona, the central character says nothing, but meaning is conveyed by what we see on the screen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But Bergman wasn't just a great cinematographer, he was also a great storyteller.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Each of his films follows a similar pattern in that the story is organized on two levels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, on the level of a straightforward dramatic narrative, but secondly, on the level of myth, and the story works throughout the film on both these levels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Bergman's film Wild Strawberries, an old man travels back to the places he knew as a child and a young man.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the film, we can identify themes that occur again and again in Bergman's work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, we have the idea of the journey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Part of the journey is a real one, but linked with that is the theme of dreams, where they can take us and what we can learn from them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another theme which was to be central to Bergman's work throughout his life is that of relationships, and in particular, the ties that join the members of a family together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, as the old man in Wild Strawberries struggles to make sense of his life, we have another theme which underlies all his work, no matter how anxious or unhappy his characters may appear to be, and that is that we have to accept everything that life can give.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not a fashionable philosophy, and it may be why Bergman's films have fallen out of fashion, but in the end-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear an anthropology lecturer talking about early migration to the Americas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Scientists from several different disciplines, anthropology, archaeology, and geology all agree that at some stage there was human migration from Asia to the Americas, but they disagree over when, how, or why these humans first came to the Americas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll run through some of the evidence briefly and try to explain the timeframe, method, and reason for these migrations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For a long time, most scientists had accepted that the original route into the Americas was from Northern Asia to Alaska.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the far North America, evidence suggests that humans arrived via a land bridge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This consisted of a dry grassland plain about two thousand kilometers wide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They think this environment would have been similar to present-day tundra with long, cool winters and perpetual winds, but crucially, no ice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Geologists estimate that the land bridge existed between seventy-five thousand and fourteen thousand years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The theory is that these first humans were hunting animals, which they followed into what is now Alaska.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Biological evidence as well as archaeological remains have been found which support this theory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, anthropologists have found a high incidence of similarly shaped teeth in people in Northern Asia and in North America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The archaeological evidence also indicates that from Alaska in North America, people began to travel far south.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The problem is no one's sure yet what route people took or how humans would have been able to survive because much of the land would have still been covered in glaciers and it would have been very hard to find resources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other problem with this theory was that the evidence from Alaska only dated back thirteen thousand years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was in the form of weapons used for hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But evidence found at human settlements in other parts of the Americas dated further back than this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most significant of these settlements is on Monte Verde site in Chile in South America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Evidence from the site includes biological remains which date back over fourteen thousand years, making Monte Verde the earliest known human settlement in the Americas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This meant the date of the arrival of humans in Alaska had to be revised backwards by about two thousand years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some scientists also think that the first settlers moved down in haste from North to South America on the Pacific side, and findings at Monte Verde would seem to support this view.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although no boats have been discovered yet to support this theory, we all know that earlier people in other parts of the world had made use of this technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The site at Monte Verde was discovered in nineteen seventy-six, and excavations revealed a small settlement of twenty to thirty people living in a dozen huts along a small stream.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists were surprised to discover nine species of marine plants, including seaweed material that the Monte Verdeans must have brought from the sea, which is over sixty kilometers away.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A variety of other items, including flat pebbles, were also found, which suggests the group had a tradition of exploring the sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, there are still a number of prominent archaeologists who don't accept that the first humans arrived via Alaska and have put forward a theory of transoceanic migration instead.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They say that at this time, the climate in Alaska would have been too inhospitable for humans to survive in, and so the first people must have arrived across the Pacific Ocean.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, there's a lot of controversy surrounding this theory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many scientists doubt that people at this time had the navigational expertise for such a long voyage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this idea does offer an alternative explanation as to how people were able to settle as far south as Monte Verde.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People who support this theory believe that crossing the Pacific would have been possible because of a powerful current in the Pacific Ocean, which would have carried boats from Japan to America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, there's no real evidence to support this theory, but some archaeologists believe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of human memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's psychology lecture, I'll be talking about human memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what I want to do first is establish the historical context.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I'll outline various ideas about human memory and how they've changed over time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So first, early cultures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in the earliest times, let's say before three thousand years BC, people were dependent on being able to remember things, perhaps even more than we are today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's because humans could not write.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The skill hadn't been developed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So a good memory was important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For one thing, it helped people navigate in the area around their homes, and it was the only way to access family history and ancestry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's more, a good memory might be the difference between life and death.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most people were hunters and gatherers, so it was essential to understand which foods were poisonous and which were not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was particularly true of plants because they sometimes looked very similar, and the only way to store this information and pass it on to the next generation was to remember it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, because it was so long ago, there's limited information about what techniques were used to assist memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so moving on now to the ancient Greeks, and the Greek poet named Simonides, who lived around five hundred BC, was the man sometimes described as the father of memory training.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Simonides' most important idea was that it's much easier to remember information if we connect it with one particular place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, over hundreds of years, other Greek scholars developed his ideas about memory, and a lot of this information has survived.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we know that by the first century, the Greeks believed that people could use their human senses to improve their memory, and this was particularly true when it came to sight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was a strong connection there, they believed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, next I should talk about the ancient Romans, who, like the Greeks, believed memory training was extremely important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They used memory in many different ways, obviously, but most of all, in ancient Rome, people thought that one of the greatest skills was the ability to give an impressive speech in public, and memory was one of the keys to doing that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this was why, from about one hundred BC, the Romans wanted to develop techniques to improve memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And an important figure here was Cicero, a Roman political leader.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of Cicero's ideas was that humans actually have two types of memory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a memory that can be developed, which he called the artificial memory, and there's another type of memory which he called natural.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the point is that you can learn techniques to help improve your artificial memory, an idea that's interested some academics ever since.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So moving next to later European history, and the first thing to note is that during the Middle Ages, a group of academics called the Scholastics were also interested in memory techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Scholastics used these techniques when they were instructing pupils about religion, and this raised the profile of memory techniques.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But later, attitudes towards memory began to change, and this started in the seventeenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People began to see memory training as an art form, and that didn't interest them so much anymore because they thought that science had the answers to most human questions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This attitude really continued into the nineteenth century as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Children weren't taught memory techniques, but were expected to learn lots of facts, and to do this by constantly repeating things like dates and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so then we come to modern times, and in the nineteen forties, a remarkable series of studies was conducted with a man known simply as S.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Psychologists found that S never made notes about anything, although he was a journalist and never forgot facts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The researchers concluded that S had an unusual medical condition, which meant he developed incredible memory skills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was important as it seemed to support the ideas of the ancient Greeks and other much earlier scholars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in the later part of the twentieth century, the focus switched to computers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, well, that's the historical context.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's now turn to-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk given by a lecturer discussing the significance of honeybees from ancient times to modern science and agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we'll take a closer look at the crucial role honeybees have played in human history and their relevance in modern times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These remarkable insects are not only essential for our ecosystem but have also left their mark on various aspects of human culture and science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin by tracing their historical significance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The earliest indications of human interaction with bees date back thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Archaeological evidence shows that ancient humans harvested honey from natural hives found within a hollow structure deep underground, such as a cave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These findings suggest that early societies valued honey as a prized resource.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, in ancient civilizations, honey gained spiritual importance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, it was common to offer honey in sacred spaces, such as a place of worship, including a temple, as a gesture of devotion and reverence for the gods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on, early societies recognized the versatile uses of honey and beeswax in daily life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beeswax, for example, was often applied to preserve or weatherproof materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Objects crafted from wood were frequently coated with this substance to enhance their durability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Meanwhile, honey itself became an essential part of traditional healing practices, valued for its ability to treat infections and accelerate recovery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was regarded as a natural form of medicine and held in high regard for its antibacterial properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, let's consider the agricultural and environmental roles of honeybees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers and observers have long noticed that bee behavior is intricately linked to shifts in atmospheric conditions, making them reliable indicators of changing weather patterns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, in some parts of the world, bees adapt their hive-building techniques to suit their surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In regions with harsher climates, they may incorporate clay-like substances, such as mud, into their hive structures to provide extra insulation and protection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This adaptive behavior is a testament to their resilience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, the physical structure of bees has fascinated scientists for centuries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their ability to collect and transport pollen is made possible by the specialized hairs on their appendages, commonly referred to as legs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This unique feature allows them to play an indispensable role in pollinating crops and supporting ecosystems worldwide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lastly, let's discuss the modern applications of honeybee products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In agriculture, bees directly contribute to the cultivation of crops, including various fruits and leafy plants, as well as staple foods like greens and other vegetables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, byproducts like propolis, a resinous material produced by bees, are now used in treating issues affecting human skin, thanks to their antimicrobial properties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Beeswax, on the other hand, has gained popularity in the culinary world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is often employed in food preparation, especially in cooking, where its heat-resistant qualities make it ideal for creating natural coatings for certain dishes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.text: They’re more durable than wood, and they don’t warp in the rain.

transcript.text: The biggest improvement, however, was the development of the chain and sprocket system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are connected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This meant you did not push the bike.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You used pedals just like today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You had to try harder to balance, so it took some practice to figure out how to use the pedals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it made the ride so much easier.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, the good thing was that you could ride a lot more smoothly and with very little effort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the 1880s, another big change was the use of rubber wheels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These became pretty common at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though the first ones were solid rubber, the ride was a good deal more comfortable than the old iron and wood system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is a big consideration because the faster you go, the more you feel every bump.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Air-filled tyres, pneumatic tyres, didn’t really come into use till around the year 1900, as you can see from this exhibition over here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That made the ride even more comfortable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So by 1890 or so, people were going a lot faster and a lot more smoothly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was one problem when you were going quickly and comfortably: Oh no!
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: How do I stop?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, we all laugh now, but for a long time, the only way to stop was to drag your feet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That didn’t work very well, and it would be dangerous if you were going fast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the crowded cities of those years, New York, Chicago, and so on, you’d get killed if you couldn’t stop for, say, a streetcar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Plus, look at this bike.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The front wheel is nearly a meter and two-thirds tall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They made them that way so you could see over people in wagons, but you couldn’t drag your feet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This model is called the velocipede, a speed pedal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another characteristic of the bike in this period is that it has two equal-sized wheels, which signaled a big change in bikes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For with the velocipede, brakes appeared.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you wanted to stop, you just pushed the pedal backwards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Doing that stopped the back wheel of the bike.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This technique worked a lot better than dragging your feet or jumping off the high seat there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This meant that bikes became a great deal safer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It would have been safer if people wore helmets, but the first bicycle helmet wasn’t invented until years later, and even then, it was little more than a leather ball cap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It really wasn’t until the 1970s that the bike helmet was modified to provide some real protection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before continuing on to look at developments since the 1890s, let’s say a word more about safety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Everyone knows if you’re going downhill, you can get going dangerously fast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To go more than a hundred kilometers an hour isn’t all that difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even on level ground, it’s easy to go too quickly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On a city street, today’s bicycles can be ridden at a speed of over forty miles an hour over a short distance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That’s about sixty-four kilometers an hour.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, you’re on a bike, not in a car.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There’s nothing to protect you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People are killed in single bicycle accidents every day just from hitting the road.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A good rule to remember is if you’re going faster than the cars, slow down, and please wear a helmet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nearly one-quarter of the epilepsy cases come from head injuries in accidents on bikes and motorcycles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I don’t mean to scare you, but safety is everyone’s business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now that’s a good question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why are today’s bikes so much faster?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it’s not just that today’s athletes are faster.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The answer is partly mechanical.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you look closely here at the back wheel, you’ll see a number of gears.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Changing gears is what makes those fast speeds possible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can shift gears depending on the terrain and how hard you wish to pedal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you can put it on a higher gear for downhill and a lower gear for uphill travel to make it easier to climb that slope.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You’ll notice this gear-shifting mechanism is attached to the back wheel, and when the rider shifts on the handlebar gear shifter, the chain moves to the appropriate sprocket.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And speaking of changing gears, let’s look over here at our Tour de France exhibit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about ancient techniques for producing paint.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: [chime] Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we're looking at the history of paint.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you're about to see, there's a lot to be said about it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So today, I'm just going to focus on ancient techniques for producing paint.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll deal with prehistoric times to about the end of the Roman Empire.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's start with the prehistoric era.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I'm sure you're all aware, it's impossible to determine exactly when colors were first used by humans in art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what we do know is what those first colors were made of and how they were applied.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have determined that the first colors came from clay, which was most likely used to create marks on the face.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, the art from this paint, as we'll call it, wasn't permanent, so it's difficult for us to know much more about what it was used for or who used it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, some evidence of ancient paint has been found in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There, scientists have discovered early forms of paint in drawings inside caves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, as you'd expect, the colors used in these drawings are simple, earthy colors, and people would have had to make them from naturally occurring materials around them, such as charcoal from their fires.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the problems with the ancient paint was that it didn't last long.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was only temporary because it faded easily or got blown away by the wind or washed off in rain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It wasn't until people introduced other elements, such as animal fats, to the paint that this problem was solved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In studying this ancient paint, scientists have determined that another popular additive, something that you wouldn't have expected at all, was honey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Surprising perhaps, but there you go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It worked well enough for us to be able to enjoy their artwork today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With the advent of more permanent colors, paints could be transported long distances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is important because there is evidence to suggest that colors were valuable and may have been used at one time or another as a type of money in some of these early societies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The next important stage in paint history was in the time of the ancient Egyptian Empire.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With wealth and power, monuments were constructed and decorated, and also a large number of temples.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This led to the development of a wider range of paint.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, we now know that one of the problems with much of the paint used at that time, and actually for centuries after, was that it was toxic, though it is unlikely that the artists of the time were aware of that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Egyptian era saw the introduction of many new colors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Egyptian blue is one of the best-known colors of that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is thought to be the first paint color made by man.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not a color that exists in nature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Craftsmen of the time had perfected the art of making this unusual dark blue color, and it's a color that historians strongly identify with Egyptian culture at this time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The color Egyptian blue was produced by crushing up blue glass very finely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This color was very popular in Egypt, and it was common for the wealthy to use it as decoration on their tombs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Red earth, another paint color that emerged at that time, was also created by a crushing process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This color was produced when minerals that were red in color were ground into a very fine powder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Roman Empire also contributed a lot to the expanding range of paint colors available to artists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They extracted all sorts of colors from a wide variety of plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But perhaps the most interesting color of Roman times was a paint pigment called dragon's blood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As its name suggests, it was a red-colored pigment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was incredibly popular at the time, most likely due to the belief that the paint was a mixture of the blood from fights between dragons, which people really believed in then, and elephants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the time, the idea of dragons was very exotic and exciting, and the color was much sought after.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, of course, the paint color was not actually from any animal at all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It came from the tree trunks of a species of tree from Southeast Asia, or more specifically, the gum from the trunks of those trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Not nearly as exciting as dragons, sadly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now we'll st-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is difficult to determine exactly when the term extremely sports came to refer to certain modern sports.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This nickname was given to a well-preserved natural mummy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The man reportedly lived between 3400
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: and 3100 BC.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, bags were called purses, exclusively carried coins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These purses were essential as pockets in clothing were not developed just yet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the fourteenth century, and without pockets in clothing, a purse was attached to the strings from the waist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From the sixteenth century onward, priests often wore their purses, a hook with chains to which small things could be attached, such as keys, knife cases, scissors, and sewing tools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since purses were often crafted from precious metals, they were also considered as a symbol of status.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The design and accessories evolved in the course of centuries, but it wasn't until the beginning of the twentieth century that the handbag finally replaced it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bags and purses came in a variety of designs for a number of purposes, such as bags with clasps, leather pouches.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These were all worn attached to the belt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The introduction of pockets towards the end of the sixteenth century meant that men's bags slowly disappeared in the course of seventeenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From then on, bags belonged to almost exclusively to the women's domain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the seventeenth and eighteenth century, women's clothing was so large that one or two bags or pockets could easily be hidden underneath the skirt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Such pockets were usually worn in pairs, one hanging from each hip.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hence the name thigh pockets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thigh pockets remained fashionable for most of the nineteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The dark times of the medieval age gave way to manufacturing a curious portraits on purses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Medieval purses were not only used as coin purse, they also were closely connected with marriage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, they commonly showed love stories.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly enough, this connection is deduced from connection between the handbag and fertility.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bags altered to serve their uses to optimize their wearer's way of life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At least such was the case with sweetie bags, which are the bags that filled with sweet-smelling material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In a time when personal hygiene was poor, sweet bags were stuffed with sweet-smelling spices to get rid of bad smelling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, lavenders or perfumed balls of cotton.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the long run, sweet bags were also stored with clothes and linens used for aromatherapy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The bag continued to be highly functional and had many different nicknames and uses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Purses were often used as decorative package for gifts such as money, perfume, or jewels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Notably, towards the end of the century, purses became more sophisticated, evolving from simple drawstring design to more innovative shapes with dynamic materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Seemingly, texture and manufacturing attributes were the only details left to be stylized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, the 1930s saw the Art Deco style arrival.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This particular style specifically highlighted abstraction, just like any time period which experiences new industrial materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The bag integrates them as well as within its design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this particular case, plastic and zippers were introduced to the bag.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the 1960s began, the bag experienced a self-expression as if being dynamic and versatile wasn't already be part of bag's characteristics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The bag experienced a brave awakening, specifically colorful patterns, and flower power introduced energy into the fabric of the bag.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The end of the 1960s saw the shoulder bag return, and with it came lots of buckles, all of which indicated that women and their bags were ultimately fit and ready for the beginning age of feminism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All in all, the 1980s saw an expansion in active consumption.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The bag quickly changed to accommodate purchasing power, providing logos to indicate the priorities of the owner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, sports bags such as Nike bags matched athletic shoes were most popular at this time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, book bags and even the briefcase specifically featured a pocket which were exclusively created to hold this new invention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear a student who's studying energy technology reporting on a field trial of heat pumps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: I'm going to talk about a field trial that was carried out on heat pumps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But first, some background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The UK has adopted a very ambitious target for reducing carbon emissions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Twenty-seven percent of British carbon dioxide emissions come from the energy used in homes, so around a quarter of all reductions must also come from that sector rather than industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it's not surprising that the government, private companies, and independent agencies have been looking into green energy alternatives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At present, the most popular green energy from a range which includes wind, biomass heating, and ground heat is solar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This has been the most readily accepted by the public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the field trial I've looked at researched heat pump technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Heat pump technology is relatively new to the UK market, and because there is such limited experience of this technology, people have been reluctant to invest in it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So a field trial was needed to monitor this in a sample of heat pumps in real situations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The heat pumps in this trial are used for the same reason you'd use a boiler, but rather than burning a fuel to produce heat, they move heat from a low temperature heat source and pump it to a higher temperature, where it can be used to provide central heating or domestic hot water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most heat pumps take heat from either the ground or the air, but water from ponds or rivers may occasionally be used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The general advice in the UK is that the temperature of the hot water stored in a cylinder should be periodically put up to sixty degrees centigrade to kill off bacteria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is sometimes necessary to use an electric immersion heater to achieve this temperature, as most heat pump installations will be designed to produce domestic hot water at temperatures between fifty and fifty-five degrees centigrade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For this field trial, eighty-three UK sites were monitored, and they provided a wide spectrum of performance results, even in installations that seemed similar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some installations performed as well as heat pumps studied in European field trials, but many failed to meet these levels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This field trial monitored two central heating systems, radiators, and the increasingly popular underfloor systems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The observations of the field trial led to some key conclusions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One was that heat pumps are sensitive pieces of equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In some of the early installations, there were problems because the engineers hadn't fitted the heat pump correctly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This observation emphasizes the need for better training for everyone involved in the installation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many different systems were monitored in the field trial, and it was found that in most cases, designs which were simple were more efficient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this is something which both pump manufacturers and installers should bear in mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many customers mistakenly came to the conclusion that their system wasn't working as well as they'd expected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, when this was further investigated, it was found that they had not realized how to regulate the controls properly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There had been a failure to explain this in sufficient detail to the householders,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: and it was often the case that for the installation, all sorts of workmen might be involved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, a groundworks contractor, a plumber, a heat pump installer, and an electrician.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was obvious that a supervisor should be appointed to oversee and be responsible for the whole installation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what are the implications of this technology on a wider...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.tip: 题目中的 "earth" 对应录音中的 "ground"，你需要填剩下的那个来源；不要填 water/ponds，录音说那只是 "occasionally"（偶尔）使用。
questions.quote: Most heat pumps take heat from either the ground or the air, but water from ponds or rivers may occasionally be used.

questions.explanation: 录音指出将水温升至60摄氏度的目的是为了杀灭“细菌”。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "destroy" 对应录音中的 "kill off"；注意不要被后面的 50 或 55 degrees 干扰，那是普通热水的温度。
questions.quote: The general advice in the UK is that the temperature of the hot water stored in a cylinder should be periodically put up to 60 degrees centigrade to kill off bacteria.

questions.explanation: 试验监测了两种中央供暖系统：越来越流行的地暖系统以及“散热器”。
questions.tip: 听到 "two central heating systems" 后紧跟的就是答案，注意要填复数形式 radiators，因为录音中是复数且与 systems 对应。
questions.quote: This field trial monitored two central heating systems, radiators and the increasingly popular under-floor systems.

questions.explanation: 录音提到早期安装出现问题，这强调了为所有参与安装的人员提供更好“培训”的必要性。

questions.quote: For example, a ground works contractor, a plumber, a heat pump installer and an electrician. It was obvious that a supervisor should be appointed to oversee and be responsible for the whole installation.

transcript.text: Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk on the research of the graphical symbol.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today I'm going to talk about the graphical symbol.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A graphic symbol is a written symbol that is used to represent speech, such as those used in the Greek alphabet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The term graphic symbol encompasses anything from the logographs used in Egyptian hieroglyphic writing to ancient Chinese pictograms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Early symbols were based on pictographs and ideograms before they were developed into logographic writing systems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These systems are still in use in some non-literate cultures in Africa, the Americas, and Oceania.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Indeed, elements of pictography are still found in modern Chinese characters, and it is often an interesting exercise to trace the origins of some Chinese characters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pictographs remain in common commercial use today as signs, instructions, or statistical diagrams.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Road signs and public toilet signs, and even flat-pack assembly instructions utilizing pictures are considered pictographic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ancient graphic writing systems provide researchers with a wealth of knowledge about past civilizations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In 1799, one of the most important historical discoveries was made by accident when members of Napoleon's expedition to Egypt found a stone in Rosetta that exhibited 3 different scripts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The stone, now known as the Rosetta Stone, was studied in significant depth by scholars and was 1st deciphered by Frenchman Jean-François Champollion in 1822.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He was able to correctly determine the phonetic values of the symbols, and later research has confirmed his findings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In many of these symbols, lines are used to portray a multitude of meanings, and knowledge and understanding of these lines holds the key to comprehension of graphic writing systems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A key moment in the history of communication was the invention of the camera obscura, or camera.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although the concept can be traced back to the 5th century BC Chinese philosopher Mo Ti, the 1st photographic image was ultimately created in 1826 by Joseph Nicephore Niepce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Photography, as it was later known, enables researchers to piece together and better understand history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, photography forms a huge part of everyday life, and most publications contain a vast number of photographs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Photography is used in advertising and is now becoming a way to increase awareness of existing world issues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, animal welfare charities are increasingly using photography to advertise animals that are at high risk of endangerment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Charity workers are sometimes flown to far-flung locations to document the suffering endured by high-risk animals in an attempt to raise human awareness of their consumption activities and how they impact others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One recent high-profile campaign was undertaken by attaching a camera to the foot of a bird in order to obtain photographs of the animals in their natural habitats and understand how often they come into contact with human waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A soon-to-be-released documentary about the suffering of animals on Midway Island shows the full extent to which human consumption is harming animals thousands of miles away from us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As photography continues to progress, with the use of drones now becoming somewhat commonplace, we should expect more and more objects to be included in the future, expanding the horizon of photography ever further.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Indeed, the downward pressure on traditional media prices means that media companies are being forced to get creative on how to make a profit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many have found that the answer to this lies in advertising, and companies are now willing to devote a large portion of their budgets to advertising in newspapers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the same token, marketing has become an essential part of a company's business model, often meaning the success or failure of a company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, much time and money has been pumped into the development of effective branding, with attractive packaging playing a large role in this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, many governments are now seen to be cracking down on marketing and packaging in an attempt to protect consumers from being misled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, tobacco companies are now subject to ever-increasing regulation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, in the United Kingdom, legislation is soon to pass preventing any form of branding or differentiation on cigarette packaging in efforts to curb the harmful effects of smoking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, one must not forget the fundamental role that graphic writing systems have had to play in mathematics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Graphs, icons, and diagrams often form the very basis of these branches of academia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Indeed, one needs to look no further than chemistry's periodic table to see a perfect example of graphic writing systems in use today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a geography professor telling his class about an upcoming field trip to the far north of Quebec in Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Listen
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next week is the Geography three thirty-one field trip to the far north of Quebec.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll discuss your trip and your tasks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you know, you will be close to the Arctic Circle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You're going to travel up the James Bay Road through a region that is very remote and uninhabited, yet very beautiful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The highway is six hundred and twenty kilometers long, but it's fully paved for the entire length.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where the highway begins, there is a roadside office where you must stop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The road is remote, so your registration is very important in case of an emergency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The office is staffed twenty-four hours per day, seven days per week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You have to sign in to go up the road and sign out upon your return.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For additional safety, at different places along the highway, telephones have been installed which connect with staff in the office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, there is no mobile service in this remote area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first work of your field trip is at the end of the James Bay Road in Radisson, a small town of only three hundred inhabitants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will stay at Radisson Research Center, which works with various universities and Hydro-Quebec to carry out studies into the ecology of the region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because the research center and the road exist as a result of the development of hydroelectricity complexes in northern Quebec, Hydro-Quebec is responsible for all emergency assistance and security of all visitors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your first few days at the center will be spent attending lectures about their past research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear that they have paid particular attention to any disturbance to the land caused by insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After that, you will visit the various outpost stations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are three of them, and when you visit them, you'll be able to observe how data on the varying patterns of the climate is collected and published for scientific research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second part of your field trip is back down the James Bay Road to the Trans-Taiga Road, which is the northernmost continuous unpaved road in eastern North America.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's very uneven gravel, so drivers have to be very careful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hydro-Quebec cautions that driving over rocks on the rough road may cause severe damage to the car.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Any breakdown is serious as repairs are costly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Along the way, you will be stopping at two hydroelectric generating stations, each on a different river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There you will meet with engineers who will explain and demonstrate how rainfall has an impact on producing electric energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your last two days of the trip will be spent camping out in the taiga on the Canadian Shield.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Taiga is the Russian term for a type of forest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will find the region is relatively poor in the number of plant species, yet there is a great variety of wildlife that can be seen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll go to an area that once had forest fires, and you'll see how the landscape has naturally small rocky hills which confine the lower wetlands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These low-lying areas are called muskeg, which is made up of slowly decomposing plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not safe to walk on it as it has pools that are not easily seen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So keep to the rocks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The muskeg is home to many small birds and waterfowl.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, there are at least sixty varieties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So keep your waterproof digital cameras handy so you can take plenty of pictures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then we will have documentation of the existing waterfowl as some are becoming extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Water is a problem in this area, so you'll also be collecting test tubes of water to bring back to our research lab for analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It needs to be monitored for pollution that may be caused by rainfall coming from the south.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a zoology lecturer talking about a group of primitive animals called gastropods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this module, we've been looking at various field survey methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And now I'm going to give you a brief introduction to the specific organism that we'll be focusing on during our first field trip.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And that's the gastropod.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gastropods are invertebrates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're organisms without a backbone, and they're more commonly known as snails, or if they haven't got a shell, slugs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, in terms of their evolution, gastropods go back a long way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As with other primitive animals, the minerals in their body fluids are very similar to the mineral composition of the sea, indicating that they began life there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And their fossilized remains have been found in rocks dating back at least five hundred million years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Looking at the physical features of the gastropods, well, they all have one muscular foot for swimming or walking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This foot is lubricated with mucus, and it's this that leaves the sticky trail that you see behind snails and slugs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also have an organ called a radula, which they use for feeding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, of course, the snails, though not the slugs, have a shell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of their dimensions, snail shells in Britain range from the dwarf snail, which is one point five millimeters long, to the Roman snail, whose shell can be as big as fifty millimeters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as size variations, you get a lot of differences in the form of snail shells.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the majority coil to the right, but there are a few that coil to the left.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then some shells, for instance, the plated snail, have regularly spaced ribs, while the prickly snail has prominent spines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are even a number of species with hair on their shells.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Colors on the shells also vary, as do patterns, so appearances are really varied.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, let's turn now to feeding habits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of you who are gardeners will know to your cost that some gastropods eat healthy plants, but you may not realize that these are the minority.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most species feed on rotting plants, or they eat fungi and algae.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some species eat dead animals, and there are some that are actually carnivorous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They prey on live animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, the shield slug feeds on worms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And apart from their own feeding habits, I should point out that gastropods themselves have plenty of predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds and frogs are the main ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there's even an entire family of flies that have specialized in preying on gastropods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And of course, last but not least, I should mention human predators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was the Romans who probably first introduced edible snails into Britain during the first century, and they are still eaten today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the collection of wild snails for cooking has caused local extinctions of one species, which is also under threat internationally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So there are lots of predators, but to protect themselves, gastropods have often developed special defenses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll just give you one example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The glutinous snail avoids predators by folding its mantle over its shell and turning itself into a very slippery blob of jelly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, turning now to gastropod habitats, most species like dampness and shade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In general, both very hot and very cold weather is bad for gastropods, but dry conditions are the least favorable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Snails cope with this by withdrawing into their shells, and often they form a thick film of mucus over the mouth of their shell to minimize loss of water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Habitats with a long, stable history tend to support the biggest range of gastropod species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for instance, long established forests usually support more species than newer plantations of trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And old natural meadowland is much better than land which has recently been farmed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And there is a small number of highly specialized species that live in unusual habitats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, the blind snail spends its whole life buried under the ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been reported living at depths of two meters and particularly likes the cavities in old buried bones, apparently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But species like these are exceptional.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But wherever they live, gastropods are often sensitive to pollution, and they don't thrive in areas contaminated by agrochemicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This means that they are a reliable indication of how healthy our environment is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, at this point, I'd like to consider habitat management in relation...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer talking about the use of games techniques in business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, we are going to look at how the phenomenon known as gamification has really exploded in recent years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what exactly is gamification?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has been defined as the use of games thinking and mechanics in non-game situations, such as for business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Up to now, its most common function has been marketing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is extremely popular with big companies, but as we'll see, it also has many other uses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gamification techniques work on our natural desire for competition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One way they do this is by providing a reward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, badges or points, or providing a type of virtual currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But don't be fooled into thinking the concept is a novel one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just think of the frequent flyer incentive schemes that were initiated by airlines to try and retain customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's been around for years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it has become more prolific with advances in technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how is gamification being used?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it is seen as an excellent way of obtaining almost instantaneous feedback through common social media sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, there are other areas where it is increasingly being used, in particular as a means of trying to convince people through fun activities to alter their behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another use is in education or training in the workplace, especially when it is just not feasible to train people on the real thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good examples of this are the aircraft simulators used by pilots or the urban simulators used by town planners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's look at a few examples of the successful implementation of gamification.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One perhaps surprising use of gamification has been in official campaigns by governments and authorities who have quickly seen its potential.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Australia, the government developed a smartphone app called My FitBuddy, whose aim was to help people get off the sofa and exercise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The app provided plenty of motivational content to ensure people got the encouragement they needed to increase their levels of activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Overseas in one city, instead of just punishing the drivers caught driving too fast, a local authority conducted a trial where they rewarded good drivers with free entries into a draw.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The trial was so successful that it resulted in a twenty-two percent reduction in speeding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gamification is also playing its part in helping people make healthy choices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In an attempt to get commuters to walk instead of using the escalators in an underground station, the staircase next to it was transformed into a piano.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It had a touch pad underneath which played notes as people stepped on it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it was in use, almost everyone opted to use the stairs instead of the escalator.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another example is a medical research company in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They realized the potential of gamification to help the elderly recover much more quickly from accidents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the elderly fall, the most common injury is not to the arm or the leg, but to the hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So they took an already popular computer game which involved people smashing fruit and adapted it so patients could practice their fine motor skills in a fun way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, there are a number of things to consider when using gamification.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, there is no way it can work unless it is fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, without that element, it could have the complete opposite effect on the consumer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, as companies are often obtaining a lot more personal information and data on their customers this way, they should always be mindful of their legal obligations in terms of legislation relating to privacy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So now it's over to you to think of other examples of gamification that you might have come across.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0
