transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture given to students in a food science department about safety standards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's lecture, I'm going to talk about food safety and the factors involved in setting standards for the food industry with particular reference to the situation here in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, before anyone can decide what kind of standards need to be set for ensuring that any specific food product is safe, scientists have to carry out a risk assessment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in doing this, they have to consider several potential problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, they have to consider the ingredients of the product.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They have to decide whether any of these might make the finished product more susceptible to harmful bacteria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then they have to consider the process used in the preparation of the food and whether or not it includes a step designed to eliminate unwanted microorganisms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After that, they've got to consider the way products are stored, for instance, in warehouses or cold stores and distributed to retailers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it doesn't end there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The analysts even have to be aware of problems that might occur after the food has reached the supermarket.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Things like frozen foods being defrosted and then refrozen because the temperature fluctuated or foods being kept past their expiry date.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, any assessment of the overall risk has to take into account the way the end users, consumers normally handle food at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as you see, the risk assessment is quite complicated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, there are several factors affecting what kind of food we eat, only one of which is legislation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another is the attitudes of consumers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A good example of this is the dislike that many Australians have for additives in their food, even when these additives are considered safe and without them, products have a shorter shelf life or a substandard appearance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This has led to the phenomenal expansion of the market for organic food in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another important influence on what we eat is the food industry itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In some large supermarkets, low prices are the main strategy for attracting customers, while for more upscale marketers, image is more important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But we should bear in mind for all of them, the key consideration is profitability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, there's the influence of the mass media, which is the most important source of information for most people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, this has a rather negative effect because in general, they are not very objective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For one thing, the prime motivation of the media, as with the food industry, is sales, and this has a major influence on the way in which the topic is dealt with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A further problem is that news is regarded as a type of entertainment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Often the issues that get a top billing are those that are sensational or controversial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it's not at all surprising if the public ends up with a rather distorted understanding of food and food safety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On top of that, up till now, food safety and nutrition have never been considered a really interesting topic for the public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Very few TV or radio shows address the issues, and even those shows that are devoted to cooking or eating generally ignore them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At this point, I'll just offer a personal opinion on this subject of food safety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I firmly believe in food safety education starting at primary schools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that many children who have been taught about the benefits of exercise come home and lecture their parents about it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the same could be done for food and food preparation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And at the same time, the countless educational television shows-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.

questions.explanation: 录音直接提到需要考虑产品的“ingredients（成分）”，并紧跟着解释这可能会让产品更容易滋生有害细菌，完美对应题目考点。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“finished product”想填product，但题目里已经有“product's”了，填空题一定要注意识别前后修饰关系，避免词义重复。
questions.quote: Firstly, they have to consider the ingredients of the product. They have to decide whether any of these might make the finished product more susceptible to harmful bacteria.

questions.explanation: 录音中明确提到要考虑产品是如何被“stored（储存）”以及“distributed（分发）”的，与题干中的“are ____ and distributed”构成完全平行的被动语态并列。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为听到“warehouses（仓库）”或“cold stores”就急着填这些名词，但题目问的是动作“how products are...”，需要结合语法填入动词的过去分词形式。
questions.quote: After that, they've got to consider the way products are stored, for instance, in warehouses or cold stores and distributed to retailers.

questions.explanation: 录音提到冷冻食品解冻又重冻是因为“temperature fluctuated（温度波动）”，这里的fluctuated就是题目中“changes in（变化）”的同义替换。
questions.tip: 你可能会觉得“fluctuated”是个生僻词而瞬间卡住，但只要抓住它前面的核心名词“temperature”就能直接得分，不要被修饰词吓退。
questions.quote: The analysts even have to be aware of problems that might occur after the food has reached the supermarket. Things like frozen foods being defrosted and then refrozen because the temperature fluctuated or foods being kept past their expiry date.

questions.explanation: 录音指出人们不喜欢食品添加剂，接着用“led to the phenomenal expansion”表示这就导致了澳洲“organic（有机的）”食品市场的扩张，“expansion”直接对应题目的“growth”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“additives”就停留在上一句的内容里，注意原声中“This has led to...”引导了因果关系，真正的答案在下一句的结果里。
questions.quote: A good example of this is the dislike that many Australians have for additives in their food, even when these additives are considered safe and without them, products have a shorter shelf life or a substandard appearance. This has led to the phenomenal expansion of the market for organic food in Australia.

questions.explanation: 录音提到一些大超市用“low prices（低价）”吸引顾客，而用“while（然而）”转折后引出高端市场更看重“image（形象）”，直接对应题目的“price or ____”。
questions.tip: 你可能会被“more upscale marketers”这一长串词吸引注意力而漏掉后面紧跟的“image”，做并列题时要特别注意听“while/but”这类连接词前后的对比结构。
questions.quote: In some large supermarkets, low prices are the main strategy for attracting customers, while for more upscale marketers, image is more important. But we should bear in mind for all of them, the key consideration is profitability.

questions.explanation: 录音非常直接地提到大众媒体是大多数人最重要的“source of information（信息来源）”，词组完全照搬了题干结构。
questions.tip: 这道题因为太直白，你可能会过度思考反而不敢写，记住录音里的“most important”就是题目的“main”，“most people”对应题目的“many”。
questions.quote: Finally, there's the influence of the mass media, which is the most important source of information for most people.

questions.explanation: 录音解释了媒体不够客观的原因，指出他们的主要动机（prime motivation，即题目的concern）和食品工业一样，都是“sales（销量）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“food industry”就想填这个词，但题目的大主语是在分析“mass media（大众媒体）”不客观的原因，需要抓准动机相关的词汇。
questions.quote: Unfortunately, this has a rather negative effect because in general, they are not very objective. For one thing, the prime motivation of the media, as with the food industry, is sales, and this has a major influence on the way in which the topic is dealt with.

questions.explanation: 录音明确指出另一个问题是新闻被看作是一种（a type of）“entertainment（娱乐）”，这导致了公众对食品安全的理解出现偏差（对应题目mislead）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“entertainment”后因为单词拼写较长而手忙脚乱，导致没听清后面解释它如何“误导公众”的验证信息（distorted understanding），平时要注意长词的拼写熟练度。
questions.quote: A further problem is that news is regarded as a type of entertainment. Often, the issues that get a top billing are those that are sensational or controversial. So it's not at all surprising if the public ends up with a rather distorted understanding of food and food safety.

questions.explanation: 录音先是将“food safety”和“nutrition（营养）”并列提出，随后在下一句明确说明很少有（few）电视或广播节目去讨论这些问题。
questions.tip: 题目是把“food safety”和空白处跟在“few programmes”后面，而录音是先说这两个词，再说没有节目报道；你可能会在听到节目时去往后找答案而扑空，要注意听力中并列关系的语序倒置。
questions.quote: On top of that, up till now, food safety and nutrition have never been considered a really interesting topic for the public. Very few TV or radio shows address the issues, and even those shows that are devoted to cooking or eating generally ignore them.

questions.explanation: 录音提到孩子们学到运动的好处后，会回家给他们的“parents（父母）”上课（lecture），这也就是对父母产生了影响（influence）。
questions.tip: 你可能会一直死等“influence”这个词出现，但录音巧妙地用了动词“lecture（说教）”来进行动作画面的同义替换，做题时要根据整体语义去捕捉答案。
questions.quote: I firmly believe in food safety education starting at primary schools. We know that many children who have been taught about the benefits of exercise come home and lecture their parents about it.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about aquaculture and the fishing business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So what I'm going to talk about to you today is something called aquaculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has been responsible for the impressive growth in the supply of fish for human consumption.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also been a slight improvement in the state of certain fish stocks due to improved fishery management.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aquatic food production has transitioned from being primarily based on the capturing of wild fish to the culture of increasing numbers of farmed species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In recent years, a type of genetically modified salmon has been farmed in the New England region, produced by a Massachusetts-based biotech firm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This type of fish is engineered to grow twice as fast as its conventional farm-raised counterpart.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, this increases the speed of the local aquaculture industry development and thus reduces the fishing pressure on wild stock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But local residents have expressed their concerns on the potential negative effects on the ecosystem should those GM fish ever escape into the sea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Stronger, healthier, and faster-growing, these fish might cannibalize others or outcompete wild-type fish for food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Local decision-makers and regulators have thus pushed forward a number of measures making it impossible for most GM fish to mate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A small percentage is able to breed only within confined pools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the economic boom of genetically engineered fish, culturing traditional types of fish is still mainstream among fish farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of them prefer fish with special features, such as tuna.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is a source of high quality protein with almost no fat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It also contains all essential amino acids required by the body for growth and maintenance of lean muscle tissue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With high nutritional value, this kind of fish will always be popular in the fish market.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the fish farming industry, incidents of fish escaping the farms has been a troubling issue over the years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Due to bad weather, nets that used to hold the fish were often destroyed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thousands of salmon worth nearly two hundred and twenty thousand euros escaped from a fish farm in the Norwegian region in July, raising fear that they would breed with wild fish stocks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cages were thus built to withstand storms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The frames of the cages are made of PE, which is dedicated to marine use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This material has trustable strength, resilience, and tenacity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To further strengthen it, strong nets without knots are used to support the cylindrical frame.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A group of small villages on the island of Zanzibar, off the coast of East Africa, have been trying to develop a local aquaculture industry sustainably.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They use a land-based production system that is both economically and ecologically sound.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Land-based recirculation can control ocean temperature and optimize growth for the fish that are used to warmer water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All organic waste from the fish is held on land, with incoming water sterilized to avoid disease, which has historically plagued ocean-based farms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The lack of disease means that no drugs are administered to the fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, one problem facing the villagers is lack of suitable land on the coast for this system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hotels and beaches open to tourists take up most of the coastal area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another problem facing local fishermen is the scarcity of young fish used to breed the species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This predicament stems from overfishing during the previous decades.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The local commercial fishing industry has been reduced by fifty percent for this reason, and the aquaculture industry has yet to thrive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The government has taken a set of initiatives to safeguard native aquaculture and the fishing industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: An open-air seafood market has been launched.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Residents are encouraged to support local fish farming businesses by purchasing marine products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As it turns out, there is a public demand for access to locally produced, sustainable sources of fresh seafood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moreover, local fish farmers are aided to market seaweed and oysters, both of which have additional economic values.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Seaweed is used in various ways in cosmetics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Seaweed extract is often found on the list of ingredients constituting creams, soaps, shampoos, powders, and sprays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is said to be useful in various ways, including the relief of rheumatic pain and the removal of cellulite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oyster is a source of seafood popular among the local hospitality industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Served with caviar and champagne, it is one of the world's ultimate luxury foods, appealing to gourmets with its succulent and delicate flavor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It thus appears to have the greatest potential for commercial culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even though the national and international market has shown demand for marine products in Zanzibar, it is still challenging to survive in the competitive modern fishing industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The government ought to restore the business by encouraging aquaculture, recreation, and shipping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, it could utilize modern fish farming technology to supply more high-quality marine products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tourism is an effective stimulus to boost its sales, and with better shipping capability, more products can be delivered abroad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 录音中提到居民担心这些鱼“escape into the sea”（逃入大海），直接对应题目空格。
questions.tip: 你可能会被前面的 "cannibalise" 或 "out-compete" 干扰，但题目问的是动作，原文用 "should... ever escape" 表示了担心的这种可能性。
questions.quote: But local residents have expressed their concerns on the potential negative effects on the ecosystem should those GM fish ever escape into the sea.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说农民更喜欢具有特殊特征（special features）的鱼，并举例说 "such as tuna"。
questions.tip: 不要填 "protein" 或 "amino acids"，那些是金枪鱼的营养成分，题目要求填的是鱼的种类。
questions.quote: Most of them prefer fish with special features, such as tuna. It is a source of high-quality protein with almost no fat.

questions.explanation: 录音提到建立笼子（cages）是为了 "withstand storms"（抵御风暴），对应题目中的 "prevent... from"。
questions.tip: 你可能想填 "bad weather"，但题目只要求填一个单词，"storms" 是导致鱼逃跑最核心、最具体的因素。
questions.quote: Cages were thus built to withstand storms. The frames of the cages are made of PE, which is dedicated to marine use.

questions.explanation: 录音提到为了加固框架，使用了 "strong nets without knots"（没有结的强韧渔网）。
questions.tip: 注意不要填 "knots"，录音说的是 "without knots"（无结的），空格需要的是形容词修饰 nets。
questions.quote: To further strengthen it, strong nets without knots are used to support the cylindrical frame.

questions.explanation: 录音直说村民面临的问题是缺乏 "suitable land on the coast"（海岸上合适的土地）。
questions.tip: 虽然前面提到了 "Zanzibar" 或 "East Africa"，但那是在交代大背景，具体缺地的地方是 "coast"。
questions.quote: However, one problem facing the villages is lack of suitable land on the coast for this system. Hotels and beaches open to tourists take up most of the coastal area.

questions.explanation: 录音提到另一个问题是缺少用于繁殖的 "young fish"（幼鱼）。
questions.tip: 后面提到的 "overfishing"（过度捕捞）是导致幼鱼短缺的原因，不是短缺的对象本身。
questions.quote: Another problem facing local fishermen is the scarcity of young fish used to breed the species. This predicament stems from overfishing during the previous decades.

questions.explanation: 录音说鼓励居民通过购买产品来 "support local fish farming businesses"。
questions.tip: 不要填 "purchasing"，题目问的是政府鼓励公众对企业的态度/动作，"support" 是动词核心。
questions.quote: Residents are encouraged to support local fish farming businesses by purchasing marine products.

questions.explanation: 录音明确提到海藻（seaweed）被以各种方式用于 "cosmetics"（化妆品）。
questions.tip: 后面列举的 "creams, soaps, shampoos" 都是 cosmetics 的具体例子，题目问的是大类用途。
questions.quote: Seaweed is used in various ways in cosmetics. Seaweed extract is often found on the list of ingredients, constituting creams, soaps, shampoos, powders and sprays.

questions.explanation: 录音说牡蛎在当地的 "hospitality industry"（款待业/餐饮旅游业）中很受欢迎。
questions.tip: 不要填 "luxury foods"，那是对牡蛎的形容，题目问的是它供应给哪一个具体的 "industry"（行业）。
questions.quote: Oyster is a source of seafood popular among the local hospitality industry. It is served with caviar and champagne.

questions.explanation: 在结尾处，录音提到政府通过鼓励水产养殖、娱乐（recreation）和 "shipping"（航运）来恢复商业。
questions.tip: 注意不要填 "tourism"，因为题目中没有对应的空格，且 "tourism" 在录音中被用来解释如何促进销售。
questions.quote: The government ought to restore the business by encouraging aquaculture, recreation and shipping.

31.s: local residents have expressed their concerns

34.q: to support the frames of the cages

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture on the history and importance of ethics in the engineering profession.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today we're starting a series of lectures on ethics in engineering.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is engineering principles relating to right and wrong conduct and the sorts of moral responsibilities that you will have to uphold in your professional lives.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm gonna start by giving you a brief outline of the history of ethics in engineering.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was, of course, only in the nineteenth century that engineering really emerged as a profession.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Initially, ethical issues were considered to be a personal matter, something to be decided in accordance with one's own principles and values.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, things gradually changed as the profession grew and as engineering projects became larger and more complex.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A need began to be felt for a more codified set of principles that all engineers would agree to follow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, it took three major disasters to bring about this change in attitude.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All three of these involved the collapse of bridges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first, known as the Ashtabula River Railroad disaster, happened in eighteen seventy-six in the USA, and we now think it was probably caused by metal fatigue.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then in eighteen seventy-nine, there was a second disaster, this time in Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This occurred because engineers had failed to correctly calculate the effects that wind would have on the structure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The third collapse occurred in nineteen oh seven in Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was also due to an engineering design problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The weight of the structure was so great that it could not support itself, and it collapsed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Public outcry over disasters such as these eventually led to the establishment of professional societies for engineers in most industrializing societies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another different type of disaster also had an impact on the development of professional engineering organizations, and I'd like to talk about this in a little more detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This incident, which happened early in the twentieth century, is known as the Boston Molasses disaster.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the time, molasses was used rather than sugar as the principal sweetener in the USA.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was also used in the manufacture of a number of other important products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One company in the city of Boston had a large amount of molasses waiting to be transferred to another factory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The molasses, more than eight million liters of thick, sticky liquid, was stored in a tank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Suddenly, this collapsed, unleashing a wave of molasses up to five meters high.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nearby buildings were swept off their foundations and crashed to the ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The wave also swept away a considerable stretch of railway track.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many streets round the factory were covered with a thick layer of sticky brown molasses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Local residents were furious as they felt that the company was to blame.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They banded together and succeeded in bringing about a trial, charging the company with negligence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After three years, the company was found responsible for the accident and required to pay out in damages the equivalent of six or seven million dollars in today's money.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even today, no one is absolutely sure about the immediate causes of the accident.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it is certainly clear that not enough safety tests were carried out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Had these been done in accordance with the standards now applicable, then the accident would almost certainly have been prevented.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It seems that the collapse was probably brought about by fermentation of the molasses, which led to an increase in pressure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This increase probably exerted too much force against a fatigue crack or some other weakness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this was one of the main incidents which led to increased legislation in the nineteen twenties to regulate engineers and the engineering profession.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is the reason why we can now only operate if we have gained a license.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This requires us always to be conscientious about doing everything necessary to avoid disasters, however time-consuming or expensive this may sometimes seem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's move on now to another...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We wanted to get some data on what happens to students after they graduate, and also find out how useful they felt their degree course was to them.

transcript.text: We focused on graduates from the course in business management since this is one of the most popular and long-established courses.

transcript.text: We decided to use two different data gathering methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We started off by emailing a brief questionnaire to all last year's graduates from that course, and then we selected a number of those who had replied, and with them, we carried out phone interviews.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'd originally intended to use face-to-face interviews but didn't feel that would be practical.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what did we find?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We were also interested in the attitudes of those who were employed towards their work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The majority said that their expectations had been fulfilled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were generally satisfied in terms of their salary and also happy with their prospects for career development, with very few of them feeling that they were in a dead-end job with no prospects of promotion.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also asked them about which elements of the course had been least valuable to them.

transcript.text: To our surprise, the thing that was mentioned most often here was presentations.

transcript.text: They hadn't enjoyed having to give these as part of their course, nor had they found it useful having to listen to those given by their fellow students.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a presentation about the early history of salt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In my presentation, I'm going to talk about salt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In modern times, when we talk about salt, people may associate it with high blood pressure or increased heart risk, and many health experts warn that we should use less salt in our meals and dishes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, we should not ignore its importance in our cuisine and even in early human history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Salt is one of the oldest, most ubiquitous food seasonings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The taste of salt is one of the basic human tastes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More importantly, salt plays an indispensable role in the health of human beings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, it regulates the body's acid-base balance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of its importance to survival, salt has often been considered a valuable commodity during human history.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This can be tracked all the way back to ancient Greece, ancient Egypt, and ancient Rome, when salt was highly valued and used as a method of trade and currency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In ancient Rome, the busiest road leading to the city was the Via Salaria, which means the salt route in English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A soldier's pay, which partly consisted of salt, was known as salarium argentum in Latin, from which we derived the English word salary.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A soldier's salary was cut if he was not worth his salt, an expression still used today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, salt was not only the first condiment discovered, but also the first preservative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know today that food goes bad because microorganisms in the food multiply in abundance, and a high salt environment is not conducive to microbial reproduction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Extremely high concentrations of salt can even kill microorganisms in the food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The ancients certainly didn't know this, but they did know that salted food can be preserved for a long time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The use of salt as a preservative can be traced to ancient Sweden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, hunting was the principal means of livelihood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this case, meat supplies were unlikely to be frequent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's more, fewer animals were available for hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to ensure the supply of meat, many families in Sweden began to raise animals in the surrounding forests during the summer when the weather was suitable for animals to survive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These animals were fed every day until about three to four months later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's in October, they were ready to be butchered for meat, and that was the only month when ancient Swedish people had fresh meat on their table.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then with the continuous increase in productivity, people finally had some meat left.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, how to store the meat had become a headache until someone invented a whole new way to preserve food, salting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People tried to keep meat from going bad by adding some salt to it, and it could be preserved for several months and even years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was evidence that salt was widely used to preserve meat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Historical documents in fifteen seventy-three recorded the Swedish king's everyday meals, mentioning that one hundred and seventy-five pounds of meat was consumed each year, but over one hundred and fifty pounds was salty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From this, we can clearly see the importance of salt in Sweden at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, the documents also noted the annual sales of beer in Sweden soared during that period, and this must be related to high levels of salt in their food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's turn to the sources of salt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Where is salt from?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, salt is common in nature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has long been found that salt can be extracted from seawater, mineral deposits, saline lakes, brine spring, etc.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among which the two most important ones are oceans and basins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the floor of the latter often lie deserts where traces of salt can be found, such as the Sahara.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, the quality of different salt types varies a lot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, salt from seawater is always mixed with impurities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So after the salt is dried, the sediments and other chemicals need to be purified before eating.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this is not the case with salt from spring water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can hardly find any impurities, and the salt level is much more concentrated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, how did people distribute salt around the world?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, in modern times, we have various ways of transporting goods, but in ancient times it was not the case.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take ancient Sweden we mentioned before as an example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of the heavy use of salt in the diet, Sweden could not feed itself and had to import large amounts of salt from other countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to make sure they could buy enough salt from abroad, the Swedish had to attach great importance to shipping and keep it undamaged, as it was the most crucial way at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While in other ancient countries, in order to distribute salt to other places, groups of men were employed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They put bags of salt on their shoulders or backs and moved them to the surrounding regions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And gradually, these people were considered as a mode of transport in early times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, with the improvement of traffic conditions, salt trade between different regions was boosted, and long-distance food trade was also promoted, making communication between different cultures more frequent and-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about how the discovery of gold in the 1860s transformed New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, today we're focusing on New Zealand in the 1860s, and in particular, how the discovery of gold transformed the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At that time, gold had created great wealth in North America and Australia, and naturally, New Zealand was hoping for the same success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People knew there was gold in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some had been found in 1852, leading to a brief gold rush in which people had come from all parts of the world to see if they could dig up any for themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But now New Zealand needed experienced gold prospectors, people who knew where to look for the stuff to find it in other areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what the local government started doing in the late 1850s was promising a reward if these prospectors discovered gold anywhere in their province.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The man who eventually answered the call was an Australian miner called Gabriel Read, who came to Otago in May 1861.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The story goes that he was walking outside his tent at night when he saw gold shining like stars in a nearby river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It didn't take long for word of his find to spread, and soon thousands were coming to Otago to take part in the gold rush.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Who were these people?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the men that came were predominantly laborers and tradesmen, and often very young, although some were married and left their families back in the countries they came from.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But women did come too, to the towns that suddenly sprang up by the gold fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They made a living by starting up hotels, simple ones, of course, where new arrivals would often stay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then there were businessmen who knew there was money to be made by setting up services like hardware stores that sold mining and camping equipment, and of course, banks where gold could be deposited.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, the businessmen often did better than the miners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as I mentioned before, where there was a gold field, a town began to grow too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At first, the buildings were constructed in a temporary fashion, just made out of materials such as canvas and timber.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But later, once supplies started arriving, it was concrete, so the structures became more permanent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the fact was, the gold fields were often in very isolated areas, so life was very difficult for these people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The miners were often working at the bottom of deep gorges, so they had to cope with freezing temperatures and also sudden flooding when winter ice melted in the mountains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this wasn't bad enough, the miners also had to deal with another problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because they had to carry everything with them, they had a very poor diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They mostly drank tea, and the main thing they had to eat was flour, which they cooked in different ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's all that was available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, some miners were lucky, others not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the gold that was found certainly brought many benefits to the Otago region, and also a couple of problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, the town of Dunedin was suddenly transformed into the biggest city in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of the original residents complained about how the value of land was increasing and about the inadequate sanitation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can imagine how crowded it might have felt with the sudden influx of thousands of immigrants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But overall, the gold brought many positive changes to the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There was immense investment and growth in the shipping industry, just what the region needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another unexpected benefit of this wealth was that it provided the funds for the first university in the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as this, as the industry developed, there was a great demand for workers of all sorts, but most of all, there was a demand for experienced and skilled engineers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They often started their own companies, and many of these companies are still operating today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we will discover next week is that these companies are still-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In Part 4, you will hear about studying dyscalculia, a neurodevelopmental disorder affecting numerical abilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Dyscalculia, a complex neurodevelopmental condition, refers to a learning disorder marked by significant challenges in understanding and manipulating numerical concepts, quantities, and mathematical operations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a condition that affects children's ability to understand and work with numbers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Currently, most schools use the traditional method of teaching mathematics, which may not be effective for children with dyscalculia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These children struggle with grasping mathematical concepts, especially when it comes to understanding the concept of time and sequence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They find it challenging to comprehend the passage of time and the order in which events occur.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the classroom, teachers focus on providing everyday practical examples to help these children overcome their difficulties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They engage the students in activities that involve dealing with money, as this is a common challenge for children with dyscalculia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By incorporating real-life scenarios, teachers aim to make the learning experience more meaningful and relatable for these students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, teachers provide individualized support and interventions tailored to each student's needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To boost their confidence, children with mathematics disorders are encouraged to practice more calculations and problem-solving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This additional practice helps them develop a stronger sense of self-assurance when it comes to dealing with mathematical tasks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teachers also provide positive reinforcement and praise for their efforts and progress.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teachers also implement strategies that encourage children to make educated guesses when they encounter mathematical problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By empowering them to make informed guesses, teachers hope to foster problem-solving skills and reduce anxiety associated with mathematical challenges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, they incorporate various exercises, such as breathing techniques, relaxation exercises, and even walking breaks to promote a conducive learning environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These activities aid in reducing stress and promoting focus during math lessons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teachers also explore alternative teaching methods, such as visual aids and manipulatives, to enhance understanding and engagement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers in this field are particularly interested in finding a potential link between dyscalculia and language learning difficulties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are investigating whether there is a connection between language barriers and the challenges children face in mathematics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Understanding this link could help inform more targeted interventions and support strategies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Children with dyscalculia often struggle with concentration and maintaining focus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teachers are aware of this issue and work to provide additional support and accommodations to help these children stay engaged during lessons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They may use techniques like chunking information, breaking tasks into smaller steps, and providing regular breaks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With this comprehensive approach to teaching children with dyscalculia, the aim is to provide them with the necessary skills and strategies to overcome their mathematical challenges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By implementing these strategies, children may no longer require additional treatment or training specifically focused on their mathematics disorder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ongoing assessment and monitoring of progress are crucial to ensure the effectiveness of interventions and make any necessary adjustments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's important to note that dyscalculia affects not only the children but also their families and teachers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Teachers and families play a crucial role in supporting these children and understanding their unique needs in the classroom and at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Open communication, collaboration, and a supportive environment are key in helping children with dyscalculia thrive academically and emotionally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By recognizing and addressing dyscalculia, we can provide a more inclusive and supportive learning environment for all students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, we'll cover what dormancy is and why organisms become dormant.

transcript.text: To start with, animals can become one and survive conditions that are stressful in environmental terms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, when lakes, ponds, or rivers dry up, aquatic organisms that can enter dormancy can survive the drought, while others who cannot do this will die.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another advantage is that creatures that can become dormant in inhospitable conditions, such as extreme cold, can live in a larger range of places than other organisms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because they can live where other animals can survive when they are active and looking for food, the amount of competition they have to deal with from other regions is greatly reduced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's move on to look at what causes dormancy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are a number of variables, but the ones that are the most significant are temperature changes and the amount of light organisms get.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Availability of food, water, and oxygen is also very important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now we'll explore some specific examples.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let us first look at dormancy in insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Insects experience a reduced metabolism, a form of dormancy called diapause in insects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Diapause is either a reaction to difficult environmental conditions or an unnecessary part of the life cycle, such as with butterflies or certain moths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In terms of environment, it's interesting to know that through dormancy, insects can survive when it's very cold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another creature we'll look at is fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fish share the same main environmental causes for dormancy as other creatures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But as one might imagine, they are particularly sensitive to drought.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, long African fish burrow deep into the mud with low water supply.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It surrounds itself with a cocoon and remains inactive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While dormant faces two dangers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One is the possibility of starvation, which relies on the fat stored in his body to overcome this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other is desiccation or drying up, which is addressed through a reduction in urine production.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Snails are also known to become dormant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some snails seal off their shell, the membrane of dried mucus, after settling at their place of dormancy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other snails do not have this possibility.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They trust the protection of their shell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So when snails have remained outside in their dormancy, they can usually be recognized by a brightly colored shell, reflecting the sunlight and so minimizing evaporation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is why banded snails usually have young shells in open habitats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hibernation is probably the most well-known type of dormancy, which occurs in warm-blooded creatures during the winter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that warm-blooded animals maintain a regular body temperature.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What's really interesting about hibernates is that they can adapt to extreme conditions by turning off their internal thermostats and hibernating until conditions improve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's examine the behavior of a true hibernate, the arctic ground squirrel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This squirrel digs underground and builds a nest that is insulated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once in its nest, it curls into a bowl and tucks in its arms, legs, and tail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its body temperature mirrors the cold of its surroundings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At this point, this squirrel barely breathes and doesn't react to stimulants in a normal way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And during this hibernation period, the squirrel loses nearly forty percent of its weight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The process of awakening for the arctic ground squirrel takes about three hours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When this happens, there is a rapid rise in the heartbeat and circulation is effective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The area around the heart warms faster than the rest of the animal, and despite the strain of hibernation, the squirrel's body processes are normal within twenty-four hours of coming out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a marine biology research student discussing a recent field trip observing dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you know, I recently got back from a field trip in the Northern Territory of Australia, where I was researching two types of dolphin, the Australian snubfin and Indo-Pacific humpback.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The reason for the research is that these two dolphins are among the most threatened mammals worldwide, and our lack of knowledge about them is one of the major obstacles to their effective conservation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Northern Territory is in many ways an ideal place to be searching for dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The coastline there hasn't been developed much, which means the water is clean and it's also rich with sea life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I spent a lot of my field trip on the main river system in this area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is one of the few rivers in the world where hunting is prohibited by law, so the animals that live here are protected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another great reason to be researching there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are disadvantages with the area, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the main problems is that the weather is very extreme, making research difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the huge river mouths where the dolphins love to live are very isolated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, I'll move on now to talk more specifically about the aims of the research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, we need to identify and classify the snubfin and the humpback dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Very little genetic sampling has been done on either dolphin, so we also want to know if they are related.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, we need to determine the exact locations where the dolphins are distributed and study these areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This will help us to find out exactly what kind of environment they need to live in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The next aim of the research is to calculate the size of the population of these dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also need to find out if there's any pattern to the movement of the two dolphin species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, are they affected by the seasons?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, we need to know more about the extent of our own human influence on the dolphins due to our behavior in the areas where they live.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as you can see, there's a lot of research to be done if we're going to help save these dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'll talk about the research techniques we've been using.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We spent a lot of time camping on boats, trying to spot dolphins in order to draw up a map of the hotspot area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This information will be useful in the overall future planning and management for both species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With photo identification techniques, we were able to record the colors and markings we saw on individual dolphins' dorsal fins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This allows us to estimate the number of individuals and also the number of times we're seeing one particular individual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Tissue sampling is also carried out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A small piece of skin is taken, which helps identify the age of the dolphin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If there's enough tissue left, further analysis can be done to determine the amount of pollution the dolphin has been exposed to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it's very early days for the project, but our initial results show that the dolphins occur in small, isolated populations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They live for a long time and breed slowly, only reproducing about once every four years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there is so much more to learn about these dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, I'm interested in going back to find out if exposure to noise has a negative impact on the dolphin populations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, does it lead to beaching, causing dolphins to die when they become stranded on the beach?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So while those waters in the Northern Territory may seem beautiful, there are many threats out there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a biology lecture about dolphins and how views divide over their level of intelligence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In today's lecture, we'll dive into the topic of dolphin intelligence, discussing dolphin behavior and their physical structure in an attempt to shed light on the question: how intelligent are dolphins?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, concerning body size, dolphin brains are among the largest in the animal kingdom, more extensive than chimpanzees, and certain species like bottlenose dolphins have brains even bigger than humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, some current tests suggest that they do not possess the same cognitive abilities as humans, despite having a similar brain size.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, dolphins are often trapped in gill nets originally intended for tuna fishing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These entanglement cases have led to unnecessary injury or deaths of dolphins, gradually depleting their numbers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Clearly, dolphins don't realize that they could just jump over these vertical barriers and swim to safety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People often mistakenly view dolphins' eternal smile as signs of intelligence and joy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Actually, this is not a facial expression at all, but a fixed design of their head.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike human beings with greater than forty facial muscles, dolphins have no such powers with which to form an expression.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, small-brained animals are sometimes underrated for their level of intelligence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pigeons and rats are typical examples of small-brained animals which can perform tasks so complex that most humans would have trouble with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the last few decades, scientists have conducted countless studies on the cognitive abilities of these overlooked animals with quite surprising results.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pigeons are aware of their bodies when they see their reflections in the mirror.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pigeons are also trained under specific conditions and gradually form instinctive reactions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In an experiment in 2009, a group of twelve pigeons was given a reward like food and water every time they pecked a key on a lab table.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All birds successfully performed the trick.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These test results indicate that brain size is probably not the sole factor in determining intelligence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another argument steers the attention to the correlation between intelligence and the constituents of brains rather than their sheer sizes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been found that dolphin brains are comprised chiefly of fatty cells, which serve as a protective barrier between the systemic blood and the extracellular environment of the central nervous system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are also essential components of nerve cell membranes, affecting problem-solving skills performance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the second mainstream view is that dolphins are highly intelligent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research into the behavior of dolphins in the wild and in captivity has yielded incredible data on the intelligence of these marine mammals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Studies show that dolphins not only have the ability to learn as individuals, but those individuals can then pass their new knowledge on to others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's take a look at some typical examples.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among these are tested with Billy, a dolphin trapped in a sea loch and rescued.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Billy spent three weeks in rehabilitation and was released back into the wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There, researchers noticed that Billy had started tail walking, a skill only mastered by captive dolphins who imitated the keepers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Billy had not been trained to tail walk but had learnt the skill simply by observing other dolphins in the rehab center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another study involves a female dolphin named Karen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Karen was given a test in which she was rewarded with a fish for every piece of litter she brought to researchers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To maximize its bounty, she quickly learned to take a newspaper, keep it at the bottom of a tank, and tear off smaller pieces to get more fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the past hundred years, researchers have proven that dolphins are extremely social species and have evolved to have highly developed brains.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These factors are the most significant contributors to their intelligence and become the means of survival for dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In 2008, researchers tracked a group of around four hundred dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One female dolphin in the group was having a lot of trouble swimming and kept flipping upside down or sinking into the water The other dolphins crowded around it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They paddled side by side with the injured female on their backs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By keeping the wounded female above water, they may have helped it to breathe, avoiding drowning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how do they communicate with each other?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, scientists have discovered through observation and meticulous testing that every dolphin has a different sound resembling the whistle that other dolphins recognize as a particular individual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins can emit a wide variety of sounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The frequency levels range ten times beyond what humans can hear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But of course, there are other means of communication for dolphins besides sound.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During mating season, male dolphins stroke females with flippers after a fight to affirm social bonds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture on the behavior of dolphins as a scientific topic of general interest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today's lecture is about the behavior of dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins are mammals closely related to whales and porpoises.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are almost forty species of dolphin, and they vary in size from one point two meters and ninety pounds up to nine and a half meters and ten tons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are found worldwide, mostly in shallower seas of the continental shelves, and they are carnivores, eating mostly fish and squid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins are highly social animals, often living in pods of up to a dozen individuals, though pod sizes and structures vary greatly between species and locations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In places with a high abundance of food, pods can merge temporarily, forming a super pod, which groupings may exceed a thousand dolphins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Membership in pods is not rigid, with interchange being common.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins can, however, establish strong social bonds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They will stay with injured or ill individuals, even helping them to breathe and bringing them to the surface if needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This altruism does not appear to be limited to their own species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A male dolphin called Moko in New Zealand was observed guiding a female pygmy sperm whale together with her calf out of shallow water where they had been stranded several times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins have also been seen protecting swimmers from sharks by swimming circles around the swimmers or charging the sharks to make them leave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins also display culture, something long believed to be unique to humans and possibly other primate species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In May two thousand and five, a discovery in Australia found Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins teaching their young to use tools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They cover their snouts with sponges to protect them while foraging for food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This knowledge is mostly transferred by mothers to daughters, unlike primates, where knowledge is generally passed on to both sexes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Using sponges as mouth protection is a learned behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another learned behavior was discovered among river dolphins in Brazil, where some male dolphins use weeds and sticks as part of a sexual display.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins may also engage in acts of aggression towards each other.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The older a male dolphin is, the more likely his body is to be covered with bite scars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Male dolphins engage in acts of aggression apparently for the same reasons as humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is, disputes between companions and competition for females.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Acts of aggression can become so intense that targeted dolphins sometimes go into exile after losing a fight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Male bottlenose dolphins have also been known to engage in infanticide, which is the killing of their young.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins have also been known to kill porpoises for reasons which are not fully understood, as porpoises generally do not share the same diet as dolphins and are therefore not competitors for food supplies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The main food of dolphins is fish and squid, and various methods of feeding exist among and within species, some apparently exclusive to a single population.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One common feeding method is herding, where a pod squeezes a school of fish into a small volume known as a bait ball.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Individual members then take turns plowing through the ball, feeding on the stunned fish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Corralling is a method where dolphins chase fish into shallow water to catch them more easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Orcas and bottlenose dolphins have also been known to drive their prey onto a beach to feed on it, a behavior known as beach or strand feeding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some species also whack fish with their flukes, stunning them and sometimes knocking them out of the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it comes to playful behavior, dolphins show various types, often including objects, self-made bubble rings, other dolphins or other animals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When playing with objects or small animals, common behavior includes carrying the object or animal along using various parts of the body, passing it along to other members of the group, or, or taking it from another member or throwing it out of the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dolphins have also been observed harassing animals in other ways, for example, by dragging birds underwater without showing any intent to eat them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Playful behavior that involves other animal species with active participation of the other animal can also be observed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Playful human interaction with dolphins being the most obvious example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, playful interactions have been observed in the wild with a number of other species as well as humpback whales and dogs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

questions.quote: Male dolphins engage in acts of aggression apparently for the same reasons as humans, that is disputes between companions and competition for females.

questions.explanation: 题目中 "...... to one population" 的结构，对应录音中的 "...... to a single population"，前面的形容词就是答案。
questions.tip: 不要漏听形容词，这道题考察的是“独有的/排他的”这个特征，而不是捕食方法本身。
questions.quote: The main food of dolphins is fish and squid, and various methods of feeding exist among and within species, some apparently exclusive to a single population.

questions.explanation: 题目中 "...... or strand feeding" 表示两者是别称关系，录音中也在 "strand feeding" 前提到了这个别称。
questions.tip: 不要填 "prey"，虽然它也出现在这句话里，但它不是 feeding 的名称。
questions.quote: Orcas and bottlenose dolphins have also been known to drive their prey onto a beach to feed on it, a behavior known as beach or strand feeding.

questions.tip: 录音中并列了 carrying, passing, taking, throwing 等多个动作，只有 taking 搭配了 "from"。
questions.quote: When playing with objects or small animals, common behavior includes carrying the object or animal along using various parts of the body, passing it along to other members of the group or taking it from another member or throwing it out of the water.

questions.explanation: 听到 "playful behavior may include other animal..." 后，紧跟在 animal 后面的分类名词就是答案。
questions.tip: 不要填 "humans"，虽然 humans 是后面的例子，但空缺处需要填的是 "species" 这个总称。
questions.quote: Playful behavior that involves other animal species with active participation of the other animal can also be observed.
