transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk about the effects of our digital world on young people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on pages seven and eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In this lecture series, we're looking at changes occurring due to the rapid spread of digital technology in the last decades of the twentieth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By digital technology, I include any computer-related devices such as email, the Internet, cell phones, instant messaging, to name but a few.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today's lecture focuses on the ideas of Marc Prensky and what he believes are the major effects that high exposure to digital technology has had on young people today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, what exactly does Prensky believe?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He argues that because today's young people have been born into a digital world and spend hours simply playing with technology, they've changed in fundamental ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He believes they're evolving differently and, as a result, process information differently from previous generations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's even possible that these young people's brains have physically changed, although whether this is literally true isn't yet known, nor does Prensky go quite this far.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Prensky divides people into digital natives and digital immigrants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today's young people are the digital natives, and they belong in this new digital age because they were born into it and grew up as native speakers of the digital language of computer technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Whereas digital immigrants are those born in the generations before the digital age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just as those who learn a second language often retain their foreign accent, the immigrants are usually, in varying degrees, not quite as effective at speaking the digital language as the natives are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, they're more comfortable finding phone numbers using a phone book or looking up information in an encyclopedia rather than using the Internet as a primary source of information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Prensky calls this the digital accent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another example of the digital accent is scanning a manual for a computer program rather than assuming the program itself will teach you how to use it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Basically, people with a digital accent have never really stopped relying on their original non-digital means of sourcing information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They prefer doing things as they've always done them without typing something into a computer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Prensky predicts that due to all this, changes are in store, mainly in the area of education.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what do other educators and theorists such as Thomas Allen, Samuel James, and Peter Vander believe?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Samuel James from Sydney University agrees with Prensky's predictions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He believes that educators are no longer successful in the way they teach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, not surprisingly, Prensky has been criticized by more traditional theorists like Peter Vander and Thomas Allen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They disagree with many of Prensky's assertions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Vander argues that a typical classroom is more varied than Prensky believes, with students coming from a range of backgrounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He maintains that a large percentage of these students are not necessarily proficient with technology, and not all students today fit the one stereotype.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And Allen adds that even though most students today have easy access to technology, some just don't find the digital medium appealing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: James disagrees, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He believes that all today's students do share the same basic interest in and knowledge of digital technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, James believes our younger students can communicate with their digital immigrant teachers and can still learn using methods which have proven to be successful in the past.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: James' theories are taken a step further by Allen, who recognizes that both digital immigrants and natives have to deal with vast amounts of information in today's electronic society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Allen maintains that while most young students are proficient in playing computer games and using the web in quite basic ways, they're not used to using the computer at advanced levels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, to conduct complex information searches which are so necessary for university study today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Irrespective of Allen's research, James believes it's possible for computer games to play a major role in making classroom learning more stimulating, and he cites many instances where this would be possible today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, Vander asserts that rather than focusing on developing games, we should think of better ways to assist teachers because no computer program comes close to doing what a human teacher does every day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.tip: 你可能只听到“游戏”或“网页”，但重点在于他强调了学生缺乏“高级/复杂的搜索能力”。
questions.quote: Alan maintains that while most young students are proficient in playing computer games and using the web in quite basic ways, they're not used to using the computer at advanced levels, for example, to conduct complex information searches, which are so necessary for university study today.

questions.quote: Irrespective of Alan's research, James believes it's possible for computer games to play a major role in making classroom learning more stimulating. And he cites many instances where this would be possible today.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer giving a talk to psychology students about people's sense of smell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So far in this course on perception, we have focused on sight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we're going to move on to consider a sense that has received rather less attention in the literature on human perception.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is our sense of smell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's often said that our ability to sense smells is much less developed than that of animals such as the dog or a fish such as the shark, or of course, the creature which is believed to have the most acute sense of smell of all, the bear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet it seems that this belief that the human sense of smell is weak might actually be a misconception.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to a number of recent studies, our noses are sensitive instruments that influence us in surprising ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Subtle smells can change your mood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Smell can even influence what you go for when you have to make choices, perhaps about whether to buy something or not.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet the power that smell has over us is by and large, not something that we are aware of.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the big mystery is why it is subconscious.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One possible reason is that our noses aren't well-equipped to detect the source of an odor, and so we dismiss it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's look at some practical examples of how smell can influence us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The power of smell will be no news to estate agents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They often suggest that people who want to sell a house arrange things so that there is a smell of newly baked bread on the property to encourage viewers to want to buy it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there are more subtle and surprising effects too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, Dutch researchers carried out a study into the impact of smell in a nightclub.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They discovered, rather to their surprise, that when the aroma of oranges was pumped into the venue, the guests partied harder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They danced more, rated their night as more enjoyable, and even thought the music was better than when there was no added scent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another study found that the hint of a smell wafting out of a hidden bucket of lemon-scented detergent was enough to persuade students to clean the communal kitchen after using it, even though the vast majority of them hadn't actually registered the smell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other work has found that scent can influence our cognitive skills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A study this year gave participants a task to test their decision-making abilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It found that subjecting people to a new smell, either good or bad, let people relying on their emotions to make a decision rather than relying on logic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, these people performed significantly worse than normal when doing the task.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our sense of smell may even help us to pick up on how those around us are feeling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has been shown that certain animals can smell each other's fear.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Is it possible that humans can do the same thing?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To test the idea, one team of scientists took sweat samples from people doing a skydive for the first time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also took sweat samples from the same people after they had worked up their sweat in a gym, a situation where no fear is involved.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They presented the different samples in turn to a series of subjects who did not know the reason for the experiment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As they did this, the scientists observed these subjects' brain activity by means of a scanner, and they saw a much stronger reaction to the skydive sweat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The team of scientists next tested whether the smell of fear sweat, that is the sweat of the skydivers, affected people's responses to various facial expressions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Normally, people pay more attention to angry faces because they pose a threat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, after smelling the fear sweat, the participants gave the same amount of attention to neutral facial expressions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the impact of smell, most people seem totally unaware of how they are being affected by scents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, some psychologists have been trying to train people's noses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They persuaded thirty-two students to wear blindfolds and ear defenders and see whether they could sniff out a trail of chocolate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They found that after three days of practice, the students were all much more accurate in following the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Further evidence of our ability to train our noses comes from a chef who lost her sense of smell after an illness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Knowing that her job depended on her having a good nose, she trained herself gradually by sniffing spices for ten minutes a day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gradually, her ability to smell returned.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's talk on about the...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about a study comparing the teaching methods of Chinese and Scottish teachers.

transcript.text: Welcome to today's lecture on the study of teaching methods of Chinese and Scottish teachers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We will explore several key aspects, including support, collaboration, cultural integration, research, and the evaluation of teaching practices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin with support and collaboration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this study, participants received assistance in navigating their new roles, especially through the manager, who provided guidance on many practical matters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Furthermore, collaboration was encouraged by partnering with a Chinese university teacher, and this connection was initiated through email.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This partnership facilitated the exchange of different educational approaches and cultural understanding.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on to cultural integration, it's essential for overseas students to gain an understanding of the host nation's social norms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One effective way to do this is by watching a video that illustrates the cultural context of the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This method helps students adapt to their new environment more effectively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the research setup, specific classes were selected for observational purposes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, reading classes were chosen as the subject of study, providing a clear window into the instructional methods used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, one of the obstacles encountered throughout the year was the rigid nature of the timetable, which posed challenges for scheduling all the necessary observations and data collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's look at the teaching methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In Scottish classrooms, it was observed that teachers commonly arrange seating in a circle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This setup encourages greater interaction between students and promotes active participation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, it was found that translation played a more significant role in the Scottish classes, likely to assist learners with different language backgrounds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In contrast, the focus in Chinese classrooms was more on spelling, with considerable attention paid to accuracy in written work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lastly, we'll touch on effectiveness and trust.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study evaluated the efficiency of the material chosen for instruction, assessing its appropriateness for the learners' needs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The success of the research, however, depended on the ability of the teachers to build trust with one another.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This mutual confidence was a critical factor in the overall success of the collaborative efforts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In summary, this research sheds light on the differences in teaching methods across cultures and highlights the importance of support, collaboration, and trust in educational settings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.

transcript.text: Welcome, class, to your very first lecture in this series on business in the modern world, conducted by myself, Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Toby Bennett.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we will be looking into the practice of company outsourcing using TCP Technologies as a case study.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, for those of you who are unfamiliar with this practice, I will give you a summative definition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Company outsourcing involves the contracting of various business activities by one company to another.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This practice will sometimes occur from a Western company to a party based in a third world country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The rationale being to make significant financial savings on lower international labor rates and to potentially increase quality.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, our case study for today is TCP Technologies, a party located in India that receives outsourced tasks from Western companies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The manager of TCP Technologies is a man called Manjit Khanna, who has personally developed a series of aims and philosophies by which the company is expected to operate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He claims that the most important of these philosophies is to create a workplace where each individual member has the opportunity to contribute their opinion to the operations of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is to say that he found it important to develop a democratic environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a means of ensuring quality from every individual at TCP Technologies, a grading system has been developed that encourages an ethos of hard work and recognizes accomplishment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This grading of individuals is based upon a series of factors such as turnover, hours worked, and efficiency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Every month, Khanna publishes the grades on an internal website where staff can access not only their own grades, but also compare it to others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A spirit of playful competitiveness has developed through this method, which has resulted in increased efficiency and turnover across the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Khanna also saw it as essential to develop a culturally diverse group of employees as a means of presenting a multifaceted image that would appeal to a host of potential employees from across the globe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This cultural openness has not only increased the quantity of incoming contracted opportunities by seven percent, but has also benefited the company itself significantly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A level of transparency now exists that had not before been apparent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to questionnaires carried out recently, these newly introduced measures have significantly increased the rate of staff satisfaction, which has subsequently led to an increase of thirty-two percent in the company's income.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These figures are truly admirable and serve as a testament to the measures that Khanna has introduced to the workplace at TCP Technologies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In a recent interview published by The Economist, he declared, "The figures speak for themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My system works."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When asked if he had any advice for companies on methods they could employ to streamline workflow and increase turnover, he replied, "It's simple, really.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A company must see itself not as one entity comprised of nameless components, but instead as a living organism composed of cells, each one essential to the functioning of the whole.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I suggest that the motto by which your management operates will be employee first."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many benefits have been reaped from the aforementioned changes in management style, such as a significant decrease in staff turnover.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This improvement alone has solved many problems that had before stunted the growth of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of these improvements came from the realization that the solution does not have to be produced internally, but can come from any other company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The grading system also immeasurably enhanced the dynamics of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The fact that this measuring system is solely produced for staff members and inaccessible by management means that it cannot be used as a judging criterion for promotion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has proven itself a relaxed and informal means of stimulating workflow
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When asked about specific features of his managing style, Kana mentioned that it is important for him to respond personally to any complaints filed by staff members.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Having found the existing complaints process slow and ineffective, he introduced a new online system that created a direct line of communication between Kana and all employees of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The complaint form, dubbed by Kana as a ticket, eradicates the middleman, is easily accessible to all employees online, and has an interface that can be instinctively navigated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Any staff-related complaint, such as those relating to air conditioning and food quality, can be submitted directly to Kana via this online system.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Entitlement to vacation is also a popular issue discussed through this forum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The main benefit of using the system is that staff must include their personal details on the ticket before they are able to submit it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the past, anonymous complaints had been the root of much confusion and caused many wasted work hours, so the new system has put a ban on this form of complaint.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That wraps up the lecture for today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please remember that attendance is mandatory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 4.

questions.explanation: 录音最后直接总结说，经理认为建立一个民主的（democratic）环境很重要，对应题干的“创造一个……环境”。
questions.tip: 你可能听到前面的“workplace”就想填，但题干中已经有了“environment”，而且“workplace”不是形容词，填进去语法不通。
questions.quote: He claims that the most important of these philosophies is to create a workplace where each individual member has the opportunity to contribute their opinion to the operations of the company. That is to say that he found it important to develop a democratic environment.

questions.explanation: 录音中原词重现了每个月公布成绩的地方是在内部网站（internal website）上。
questions.tip: 题干空前是冠词“an”，提示你要填元音发音开头的名词，如果你漏听了“internal”只填了“website”，就会因为不符合语法而丢分。
questions.quote: Every month Khanna publishes the grades on an internal website where staff can access not only their own grades but also compare them to others.

questions.explanation: 录音提到这种文化开放让公司现在具备了一定程度的透明度（transparency），对应题干的“提升了公司的……水平”。
questions.tip: 这个词本身比较长且拼写容易出错，你可能会因为发音不熟悉而写不出全拼，平时需要多积累这种偏商务的词汇。
questions.quote: This cultural openness has not only increased the quantity of incoming contracted opportunities by 7%, but has also benefited the company itself significantly. A level of transparency now exists that had not before been apparent.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说到员工满意度的提高随后带来了公司收入（income）32%的增长。
questions.tip: 卷面上的“growth”在录音里被替换成了“increase”，如果你死盯卷面词，可能会在听到“increase”时没反应过来答案马上就出现了。
questions.quote: According to questionnaires carried out recently, these newly introduced measures have significantly increased the rates of staff satisfaction, which has subsequently led to an increase of 32% in the company’s income.

questions.explanation: 录音里经理直接给出了他的座右铭（motto）是“员工第一（employee first）”。
questions.tip: 前面讲了一大堆关于“细胞（cells）”和“有机体（living organism）”的比喻，你容易被绕进去，做题时必须牢牢抓住题目里“motto”这个原词定位信号。
questions.quote: When asked if he had any advice for companies on methods they could employ to streamline workflow and increase turnover, he replied, it’s simple really, a company must see itself not as one entity comprised of nameless components, but instead as a living organism composed of cells. Each one essential to the functioning of the whole. I suggest that the motto by which your management operates will be, employee first.

questions.explanation: 录音指出很多改善源于一种认识：解决方案（solution）不一定要内部产生，而是可以来自任何其他公司。
questions.tip: 卷面结构是“A ___ can be...”，而录音是“the ___ does not have to... but can come from...”，如果你没跟上句型的转换，很容易抓不到主语。
questions.quote: A lot of these improvements came from the realization that the solution does not have to be produced internally, but can come from any other company.

questions.explanation: 录音说明评分系统不能作为晋升（promotion）的评判标准，完美对应题干的“不被用作……”。
questions.tip: 卷面上的“not used for”在录音里被替换成了“cannot be used as a judging criterion for”，词组拉得比较长，容易在等答案的时候走神。
questions.quote: The grading system also immeasurably enhanced the dynamics of the company. The fact that this measuring system is solely produced for staff members and inaccessible by management means that it cannot be used as a judging criterion for promotion.

questions.explanation: 录音提到投诉表被经理称为“罚单/工单（ticket）”，所有员工都能在线访问。
questions.tip: 卷面上的“known as”在录音中被高级词汇“dubbed by（被戏称为/起绰号为）”替换，如果你不认识这个词，会很难确定填哪个名词。
questions.quote: The complaint form, dubbed by Khanna as a ticket, eradicates the middleman, is easily accessible to all employees online and has an interface that can be instinctively navigated.

questions.explanation: 录音先说了空调和食物质量，紧接着第二句就提到了关于假期（vacation）的权利也是常讨论的问题，填补了并列结构的最后一环。
questions.tip: 录音把卷面上并列的三个事物拆分成了两句话来表达，如果你只在第一句话里找，就会错过下一句以“Entitlement”打头带出的答案。
questions.quote: Any staff related complaint, such as those relating to air conditioning and food quality, can be submitted directly to Khanna via this online system. Entitlement to vacation is also a popular issue discussed through this forum.

questions.explanation: 录音最后提到，新系统对匿名投诉这种形式下达了禁令（ban）。
questions.tip: 答案所在的词组是“put a ban on”，语速快的时候发音会连在一起，你可能听成了某个不认识的单词而不敢下笔。
questions.quote: The main benefit of using this system is that staff must include their personal details on the ticket before they are able to submit it. In the past, anonymous complaints had been the root of much confusion and caused many wasted work hours, so the new system has put a ban on this form of complaint.

33.s: now exists that had not before been apparent

increased the rate of staff satisfaction

35.s: the motto by which your management operates will be

37.s: cannot be used as a judging criterion for

38.s: is easily accessible to all employees online

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk given by a lecturer about cloud science, which is about the origins of studying clouds and other aspects associated with it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, we're exploring the fascinating history and implications of cloud science.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This field has had a profound impact on meteorology, culture, and even human psychology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's start by going back to the early nineteenth century when the first major strides in cloud classification were made.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A British scientist laid the foundation of modern cloud science by introducing a system to categorize clouds based on their shapes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He identified three main types.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of them, which he called cumulus, was noted for its towering vertical appearance and likened to a tower because of its cone-shaped form that stretches high into the atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another type, in contrast, was more spread out and flat, resembling a sheet that blankets the sky.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This innovative classification helped scientists understand atmospheric behavior, but it wasn't without criticism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many scholars questioned the terminology he used as it mixed Latin and English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some critics argued that his language choices were awkward and reflected his challenges as a non-native English speaker.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite these initial hurdles, the scientist became widely celebrated for his work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He even turned to the arts, composing poetry that reflected his admiration for clouds, blending his scientific insights with a deep appreciation for their beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving beyond its scientific origins, the study of clouds began influencing cultural and artistic movements, especially in Britain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The newly established system of cloud classification had a significant impact on Romantic era painters, who started incorporating intricate cloud formations into their landscapes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This was a powerful example of how scientific observation could inspire creativity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Meanwhile, scientists of the time sought practical applications for their newfound knowledge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They experimented with altering weather patterns, attempting to increase rainfall or even create fog in controlled environments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To achieve these goals, they employed innovative methods such as launching rockets filled with substances intended to influence atmospheric conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As we move into the twentieth century, cloud science continued to evolve, but not without challenges.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most notable experiments involved using silver iodide to seed clouds and encourage rainfall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this practice raised environmental concerns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, in Australia, researchers discovered that a lake had been polluted as a direct result of these activities, sparking debates about the sustainability of weather modification.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In response, scientists began exploring alternative approaches.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One promising method involves using salt particles instead of chemicals, which poses less risk to ecosystems while achieving similar results.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lastly, cloud science has shed light on the relationship between weather and human behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Recent studies have revealed that changes in atmospheric conditions can significantly affect cognitive functions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, shifts in humidity or temperature have been shown to influence people's memory, either enhancing or impairing it depending on the circumstances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This underscores the interconnectedness of our environment, our minds, and the skies above.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

Origins
• A British scientist classified clouds into three shapes, with the second type (Cumulus) resembling a cone-shaped {{31}} .
• The third type of cloud was compared to a flat {{32}} .
• The scientist faced criticism for the {{33}} used in naming clouds, as English was not his native language.
• Despite the critiques, he gained fame as a scientific celebrity and even composed {{34}} praising the beauty of clouds.
Cultural and Artistic Impacts
• The {{35}} influenced British art, inspiring artists to incorporate cloud depictions into their works.
• Scientists experimented with altering weather conditions, such as increasing or decreasing rainfall or {{36}} .
• {{37}} were sometimes employed to deliver man-made materials for weather modification.
Modern Weather Science
• The use of silver iodide in weather experiments led to water pollution, as observed in a {{38}} in Australia.
• Today, some research focuses on using {{39}} as a safer alternative for weather manipulation.
• Research into the psychological effects of weather shows that weather changes can significantly impact people’s {{40}} abilities.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到这种云以垂直耸立的外观著称，并因其延伸至大气的锥形形状而被比作 tower（塔）。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "resembling"（像）对应录音中的 "likened to"，不要填 cumulus（云的名字）或 cone（形状修饰词）。
questions.quote: One of them, which he called cumulus, was noted for its towering vertical appearance and likened to a tower because of its cone-shaped form that stretches high into the atmosphere.

questions.explanation: 另一种云更加平坦，像一张覆盖天空的 sheet（床单/薄板）。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "compared to" 对应录音中的 "resembling"，不要填 spread out，那是形容动作而非名词喻体。
questions.quote: Another type in contrast was more spread out and flat, resembling a sheet that blankets the sky.

questions.explanation: 原文明确提到许多学者质疑（即题目中的 criticism）他使用的术语（questioned the terminology he used），因为其中混合了拉丁语和英语。
questions.tip: 不要填 "language"，虽然原文提到了 "language choices"，但 "terminology" 才是直接被质疑的对象，且专门指代“命名所用的术语”。
questions.quote: Many scholars questioned the terminology he used as it mixed Latin and English.

questions.explanation: 这位科学家甚至转向艺术创作，创作了赞美云朵之美的 poetry（诗歌）。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "composed"（创作）对应录音中的 "composing"，填名词 poetry，不要填 poet（诗人）。
questions.quote: He even turned to the arts, composing poetry that reflected his admiration for clouds...

questions.explanation: 新建立的云朵 classification（分类）系统对浪漫主义时期的画家产生了重大影响。
questions.tip: 不要填 system，原文核心词是 classification，system 是修饰它的（system of classification），填 classification 语义更完整。
questions.quote: The newly established system of cloud classification had a significant impact on romantic era painters...

questions.explanation: 科学家们尝试改变天气，比如增加降雨，甚至在受控环境中制造 fog（雾）。
questions.tip: 题目是并列关系 "rainfall or..."，听到 rainfall 后紧跟的名词 fog 即为答案。
questions.quote: They experimented with altering weather patterns, attempting to increase rainfall or even create fog in controlled environments.

questions.explanation: 为了实现这些目标，他们使用了创新方法，例如发射装满物质的 rockets（火箭）。
questions.tip: 题目是被动语态 "were employed"，录音是主动语态 "launching rockets"，注意抓取名词复数。
questions.quote: To achieve these goals, they employed innovative methods such as launching rockets filled with substances intended to influence atmospheric conditions.

questions.explanation: 在澳大利亚，研究人员发现一个 lake（湖泊）因为这些实验活动受到了直接污染。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "observed in a..." 需要填地点名词，不要填 Australia（已在题目中）。
questions.quote: For instance, in Australia, researchers discovered that a lake had been polluted as a direct result of these activities...

questions.explanation: 一种有前景的替代方法是使用 salt（盐）颗粒来代替化学物质，这对生态系统的风险更小。
questions.tip: 不要填 particles（颗粒），它是修饰 salt 的单位词，核心物质是 salt。
questions.quote: One promising method involves using salt particles instead of chemicals, which poses less risk to ecosystems...

questions.explanation: 研究表明大气条件的变化会显著影响人们的 cognitive（认知的）功能或能力。
questions.tip: 不要填 memory，那是 cognitive functions 的一个具体例子（For example... memory），题目需要填概括性的形容词来修饰 abilities。
questions.quote: Recent studies have revealed that changes in atmospheric conditions can significantly affect cognitive functions.

31.s: likened to a tower because of its cone-shaped form
One of them, which he called cumulus

33.q: as English was not his native language
33.s: as it mixed Latin and English

35.q: inspiring artists to incorporate cloud depictions into their works
35.s: painters, who started incorporating intricate cloud formations into their landscapes

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk on the research of architecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome, class, to your very first lecture in this series on architecture, conducted by myself, Dr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Torben Dahl.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we will be looking into the relationship between climate and architecture, where I will be giving you a critical overview of the main climate influences that shape the design of buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Throughout this lecture series, we will be looking at the latest research into climatic design carried out by experts in the field, in addition to case studies and examples drawn from modernist practice, both in cities and rural areas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: acid rain is one of the climatic elements with the most devastating effects on our architecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The chemicals in acid rain can cause paint to peel, corrosion of steel structures such as bridges, and erosion of stone statues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since the nineteen seventies, our government has been making great effort to reduce the release of these chemicals into the atmosphere with positive results.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Private organizations have also been raising awareness and funds and recently received a huge donation from the bank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is interesting to look at the studies that have been carried out into the effects of acid rain at varying altitudes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research has shown that there are lower levels of acid in the damaging pollutants at higher altitudes, meaning that skyscrapers are much less vulnerable to the negative effects as they are exposed to acid rain with far lower levels of damaging pollutants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Recently, the Altar Project was founded to carry out further research into acid rain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This project is directed towards studying the effects of acid rain on old traditional buildings of stone construction that are vulnerable to damage caused by acid rain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Masonry is particularly vulnerable as it is easily corroded and weakened by the acidic chemicals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is imperative that we protect these buildings as they are valuable examples of our history and culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Pollution is one of the main sources of concern in the present day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The construction industry contributes considerably as a source of pollution in its day-to-day processes of creating building materials such as concrete and glass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, more new sustainable methods are being developed to counter this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A recent case study for this is Sky Tower, whose windows have been made from recycled glass to prevent pollution from the glass-making process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Water is the most problematic element to be considered in construction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is imperative that construction elements, such as the insulation, are fitted into the building in dry weather to prevent it from getting wet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This makes winter an undesirable season for construction as the heavy rainfall can have adverse effects on the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another climate type that has an enormous effect on buildings is humidity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Constructions made of steel and stone are largely unaffected by humidity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it can have a serious effect on wooden constructions if the timber has not been correctly treated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moisture from the air can condense in the grain of the wood, which then swells and shrinks in proportion to the magnitude of change in its moisture content.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This variation in size can have disastrous consequences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In areas of the world that are prone to earthquakes, certain design and environmental conditions are preferable for protecting buildings in the event of a tremor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Engineers have come up with numerous building procedures to help minimize shaking in buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, tall buildings have height restrictions and counterweights, and multi-story buildings have reinforced floors and walls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ground conditions are a cause for worry in many constructions, as often the soil is of the wrong density to protect the foundations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Luckily, technology has now been developed that can help to minimize damage by earthquakes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Seismic sensors can give prior warning when an earthquake is about to happen, so that preparations can be made to protect both the people and the buildings from harm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The movement of building structures can now also be measured and monitored over time by architects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has been expressed by architects within the design community that it will be valuable to be given special courses for designing buildings within earthquake zones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Guidelines are also expected to be produced by the government in the near future that will give architects a universal checklist to follow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That wraps up the lecture for today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please remember that attendance is mandatory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.quote: Throughout this lecture series, we will be looking at the latest research into climatic design carried out by experts in the field, in addition to case studies and examples drawn from modernist practice, both in cities and rural areas.

questions.explanation: 录音提到最近从“bank”（银行）那里收到了一笔巨额捐款，对应题目问的从哪里收到了资金。

questions.quote: Research has shown that there are lower levels of acid in the damaging pollutants at higher altitudes, meaning that skyscrapers are much less vulnerable to the negative effects as they are exposed to acid rain with far lower levels of damaging pollutants.

questions.explanation: 录音里介绍Altar项目是为了研究酸雨对传统的“stone construction”（石制建筑/石头）的影响，对应题目里问的建筑是由什么材料制成的（made of）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到“old traditional buildings”就想把traditional buildings填上去，但题目问的是建筑的材质，要填它后面的修饰词“stone”。
questions.quote: Recently, the Altar Project was founded to carry out further research into acid rain. This project is directed towards studying the effects of acid rain on old traditional buildings of stone construction that are vulnerable to damage caused by acid rain.

questions.explanation: 录音明确提到天空塔（Sky Tower）的窗户是用“recycled glass”（回收玻璃）制成的，用来防止污染。

questions.quote: A recent case study for this is Sky Tower, whose windows have been made from recycled glass to prevent pollution from the glass making process.

questions.explanation: 录音里指出冬天不适合施工，因为大量的“rainfall”（降雨）会对建筑产生不利影响，题目的increased对应录音里的heavy。

questions.quote: This makes winter an undesirable season for construction as the heavy rainfall can have adverse effects on the building.

transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about how different building materials are chosen for flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We’ve been talking about choosing building materials in the last week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, a great many factors influence the choice of building materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can’t make a house of cards, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And people who live in glass houses and all that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyhow, today I’d like to say a few words about flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some artificial materials can be used, like plastic for instance, which offer mixed blessings when used as a flooring surface.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the one hand, plastic is cheaper than nearly any other alternative, short of bare ground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Plastic also does not warp like wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the other hand, the best that can be said about plastic is that it looks like wood or stone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it cannot replace the real materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I have mentioned, I’m fixing up a new house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The decorator my wife hired told me plastic does a great job of looking exactly like plastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Besides, it scratches easily, fades or discolors, and starts cracking within a year or two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if you’re fitting out a sleazy hotel or plan to live in a trailer park, go with the plastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Really though, for all intents and purposes, this leaves us with wood or stone as choices for flooring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Stone and wood are alike in at least one respect: both go through processing before they can be put to use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since few of us cut our own lumber or quarry our own stone, this is not perhaps a pressing concern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Still, do-it-yourselfers would do well to remember to buy only properly seasoned wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unseasoned wood warps, and a warped floor quickly becomes firewood, and its owner quickly becomes poorer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Likewise, except for dull-hued materials like slate or sandstone, most stone floors are polished before installation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The choice goes well beyond just wood or stone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Each type requires many further considerations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A few special remarks are called for when considering wood, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As always, aesthetics, personal taste, and layout all play roles, as well as the type of house or room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, and certainly don’t forget the cost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When it comes to cost, a rule of thumb is that the softer and less exotic the wood, the lower the cost.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the US, for instance, pine is both ubiquitous and cheap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mahogany is imported and exorbitantly expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you’re on any kind of budget when remodeling, it’s really helpful to remember to go for the softer woods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from cost, there are still lots of different factors that are important in choosing the best flooring for the job.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Continuing with the example of wood, one must consider the effects of each type of wood on the mood of the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When selecting the best wood to use, particular attention needs to be paid to its grain patterns, texture, and color.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In rooms where relaxation or deep thought is the aim, say bedrooms or the study, dark, strong-grained woods are the rule.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Here, the grain ought to match the furniture for a feeling of homogeneity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In rooms where activity and motion are typical, the dining room or living room, lighter, finer-grained lumber is more suitable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In such a setting, the wood grain might be useful in offering a contrast to the furniture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This leads to a feel of subconscious excitement in keeping with the room’s function.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In either case, though, consult a decorator.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is a decorator’s job to know what materials to use to fit the function of the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though some things about putting together a room are subjective and based on one’s individual taste, materials appropriate to a room’s function are much more straightforward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A decorator takes the needs of the customer and uses a mathematical formula rather than subjective words.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since feelings vary from person to person, verbal descriptions of wood types tend to be ambiguous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You want the wood you select, not something approximate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you do decide to do it yourself, remember that all wood must be treated with preservatives to enhance its appearance and preserve its natural beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the lecture, you have some time to look at questions thirty-eight to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions thirty-eight to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In the case of stone, or quarry tile as flat-cut flooring stone is properly called, a new set of considerations must be weighed up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Simple color aside, the degree of reflection must be kept in mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is called the reflectance rate, which is expressed in a number between zero point zero and one point zero, depending on the amount of light it reflects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At one end of the scale is polished silver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At a rating of one point zero, this shiny surface reflects nearly all of the light directed at it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Numbers closer to zero describe materials that absorb more light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving down the scale a bit, we see that plastic that has been painted white has a rate of zero point eight, which makes sense.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know that the color white reflects all other color, while black absorbs all color, and plastic itself is a relatively reflective material.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Materials that are denser and darker have reflectance rates much closer to zero.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The quarry tile I mentioned a while ago has a rate of zero point one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you may know, quarry tile is generally dark brown and made from clay, so it is quite dense.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there is considerable variation among types of quarry tile because of the hue or treatment of the clay during its creation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Does anyone have any guesses as to what material may have a rate of almost zero point zero?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can guess most of these materials are black in color, but plastic, wood, and even stone reflect some light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One material with a rate of almost zero point zero is black velvet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The texture produces almost no shine at all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Carrera marble, despite its white hue, is actually lower in reflectivity than black onyx.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In any case, the fact that tiles vary somewhat should not be forgotten.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A highly reflective floor would not be suitable in a library.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It would be indispensable in a ballroom, should your home be large enough to feature one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, a rule of thumb is that light means lively.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since form and material follow function, one should only use the more reflective materials in rooms where the cultivation and expression of energy is important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bear in mind, too, that most types of stone cost more than all but the rarest of wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there is no reason why some rooms of a house should not feature wood floors or other stone tiles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can even mix the two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A room with wood panels on the walls can have a beautiful stone floor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My bedroom has white birch walls and a light blue slate floor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The place looks like a Russian hunting lodge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, though, go with what feels right for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good taste and the laws of interior design are the homeowner's servants, not his master.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's only beautiful when you decide it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I mean, you're the one who lives there, not the decorator, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, are there any questions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have 45 seconds to check your answers to Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk on the research of the behavior of chimpanzees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome back to my series of short lectures on apes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today we will examine recent and historical breakthroughs on the behavior of chimpanzees, otherwise known as chimps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The word chimpanzee is an umbrella term for two different species of apes in the genus Pan, which are the common chimpanzee, or Pan troglodytes, found in West and Central Africa, and the bonobo, or Pan paniscus, which are found in the forests of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Chimpanzees belong to the Hominidae family, together with gorillas, orangutans, and indeed humans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Current research tells us that the chimps broke away from the human branch of the Hominidae family approximately six million years ago and remain the closest living relative to humans to this day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More modern researches into chimpanzees have centered on their behavioral characteristics once all biological and genetic factors have been ruled out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this way, scientists have unearthed an unfathomable amount of similarities between human and chimpanzee behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although much of this research has taken place through observation of captive chimps, the results are widely seen as an authoritative reflection of chimps living in the wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Chimps live in large so-called communities comprised of many male and female members, with the social hierarchy determined by an individual chimp's position and influence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Through such research, scientists have found that chimps learn and adapt through observation of others' behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once in power, the alpha male is often seen to alter its body language in order to retain power.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, he might puff himself up in order to intimidate others,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: while lower ranking chimps are noted to behave more submissively and holding out their hands while grunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Female chimpanzees also have a distinct social hierarchy with high social standing inherited by children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not unheard of for dominant females within a community to unite and overthrow the alpha male, backing another in his place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: James Diamond, in his book The Third Chimpanzee, suggests that chimps should now be reclassified in the genus Homo instead of Pan, and there are many arguments still in favor of this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Male common chimpanzees are on average one point seven meters in height, weighing seventy kilograms, with their female counterparts being somewhat smaller.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By comparison, the bonobo is slightly shorter and lighter, but with longer arms and legs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, both species walk on all fours and climb trees with great ease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Jane Goodall made a groundbreaking discovery in 1960 when she observed the use of tools among chimpanzees, including digging for termites with large sticks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A recent study claimed to reveal that common chimpanzees in Senegal have been using spears sharpened with their teeth to hunt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, these reports remain unsubstantiated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have witnessed such tools, namely rocks, being used by chimps to open coconut shells and indeed crushing nuts with stone hammers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As scientific technology has developed, so too has our knowledge of the sheer extent of the chimp's intelligence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Research has now shown that chimps have the capability to learn and use symbols and understand aspects of the human language, including syntax as well as numerical sequences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I mentioned earlier, the umbrella term chimpanzee is comprised of the common chimpanzee and the bonobo.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These two subspecies are divided along the Congo River, with the common chimps living on one side and the bonobos living on the opposite side of the river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the past few decades, both of these subspecies have witnessed an alarming decrease in population density, with animal activists now working harder than ever to protect those remaining and encourage procreation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, next week's episode will focus more closely on how chimpanzees in captivity are able to learn things through imitating the behavior of humans, as well as how chimpanzees behaviors have developed over many generations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you very much for attending this evening's lecture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I hope you found it intellectually stimulating, and I look forward to seeing you again next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a researcher giving a talk about a study on children's humor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We all think we know what makes children laugh, but can we really explain it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And is it useful for educators to be aware of how children's humor works?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, to answer these questions, I'd like to tell you about the large-scale study on the humor of primary school children that I was commissioned to carry out two years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The aim of the study was to find out what children find funny in their everyday lives, both at school and at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We wanted to know how children used humor to interact with each other.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For example, when they were in the playground, we wanted to know what sort of jokes they told one another and which ones were most popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Some research was done in this area about fifty years ago, but it's never been followed up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So that's one area that we wanted to find out more about in our research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And we also wanted to find out about what children find funny when they're at home watching television, since many children spend quite a significant amount of time doing this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So how did we go about finding out this information?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, we interviewed a total of a hundred and fifty children in six different primary schools around the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: We had originally intended to have one-to-one interviews, but we decided that this would be too time-consuming and also might be stressful for the children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So instead, each interviewer had several groups, each consisting of three or four children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They were asked questions like, "What was the last thing that made you laugh?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: and, "Do you know any funny stories?"
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then another method we used to collect information about what makes children laugh was through the use of humor diaries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So we asked the parents of some of the children to keep a diary like this for six months and to describe situations in which their children had laughed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So what were the main findings?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, some of them weren't quite what you'd have expected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You'd think that people laugh when things are funny, but that's not always the case.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One thing we found was that children nearly always laugh if they're in a situation which is unfamiliar to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They're a bit nervous because they're not sure what sort of action it's appropriate for them to take, so they laugh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another type of situation in which we found children often laughed was when people did things which were surprising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If someone's walking down the street with a dog on a lead, that's quite unsurprising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But if someone's got a chicken on a lead, the child will laugh because the usual conventions that govern our behavior aren't being followed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's funny because it's surprising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another interesting area is what sort of person makes children laugh most, and here we found that nearly all primary school children find situations particularly humorous if they involve people looking foolish, and particularly if these are adults.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The children probably find this empowering to see them at a disadvantage for once.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One thing that was observed frequently in the humor diaries was that laughter often erupted spontaneously during pretend games and role-play.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Our research showed there's a strong link between laughter and being creative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's an area that's received little attention to date, maybe because this type of humor isn't often observed in research situations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As well as these, there were other findings that we made during the research process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One quite surprising finding was the fact that when looking at what children find funny, there seems to be hardly any difference between boys and girls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So the children's gender doesn't seem to be significant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Boys sometimes show a slight preference for physical humor, but there's nothing much in it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For educators, as well as for those involved in children's media, it's worth stressing that children still find many of the same things funny as they did in the past.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: There hasn't been much change in what they laugh at over the years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you look at what makes children laugh in the twenty-first century, there's really not much difference from what made their grandparents laugh in the twentieth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They still react positively to the same sort of things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So for example, in the media, they enjoy humor which is non-verbal, where the humor comes from pictures rather than words.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And one of the most striking findings that came out of our research, both the interviews and the diaries, is that just as in their grandparents' generation, what children find incredibly funny is humor that is founded on some kind of danger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The fact that they know it isn't real gives them permission to laugh somehow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So what we can conclude from all this is that humor is incredibly important to children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It plays a crucial role.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture in a business class talking about a global petrol company, Telsa's expansion and its future development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome, ladies and gentlemen, to the second lecture in our series on chain stores in the UK.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Today, I'll be focusing on a very successful global petrol company called Telsa, paying particular attention to their expansion and future development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There will be time for questions at the end, so please refrain from interrupting during the talk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: When it was founded, the company was a family-run organization with only one shop open in a small town in Southern England.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The family was able to compete with other local companies by offering special discounts for returning customers, which resulted in a massive expansion of their client base.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This strategy was so successful that they were able to open petrol stations across the country, subsequently increasing their market share in England.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Within a decade, Telsa was running establishments throughout the UK, including Wales and Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: By comparing the sales income from all of their stores, they were able to collect data that highlighted which areas were the most profitable stations in the south of Scotland.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They discovered that by closing the less useful stations in the south of Scotland, they could increase income from their other more profitable stations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This example demonstrates the importance of continually monitoring and maintaining a clear view of the finances of the company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Once the expertise required to run the company had exceeded the abilities of the family, they needed to hire professional consultants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: After assessing the company's financial statements, the consultants advised that Telsa close the head office of the convenience stores in Oxford.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They deemed the head office unnecessary and identified it as a financial drain on the company as the premises were expensive to run and generated no income.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To avoid firing any employees, they transferred over two hundred staff to other offices and retrained them to carry out their new roles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now that Telsa had conquered the petrol market in the UK, they were able to branch out into other niche areas that offered prospects for profits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They realized that they could establish a new environmentally friendly brand image by selling fresh food in their convenience stores that had been grown by local farmers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This strategy would not only broaden the scope of the company, but also help to strengthen its relationships with local communities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Every year, Telsa holds a meeting in London where all of the consultants and managers meet to discuss plans for development and improvement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: These meetings are essential to the evolution of the company as feedback is heard from all levels of the organization, from the sales staff to the CEOs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They did this by assigning every manager the task of holding staff discussions at which ideas and concerns would be passed on for evaluation at the meeting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Telsa decided to accommodate the individuality of each of their stores instead of forcing them to conform to one overriding company identity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They realized that by increasing the flexibility of the profit-making strategies of each of the retail stores, they subsequently became more commercially successful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The level of staff satisfaction also doubled as a result.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Individuals felt they were not being constrained to one way of thinking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To avoid misunderstandings and mistakes, any future changes were introduced in stages to familiarize the staff with the new regulations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, it's time to conclude the lecture for today, so I will leave you with some food for thought before you go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To run a successful business, one cannot underestimate the importance of maintaining open-mindedness when deciding on strategies for expansion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sometimes it's necessary to employ an independent consultant who can offer an objective and unbiased view on the running of your company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Emotion will only ever cloud your ability to make business-related decisions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Research suitable case studies and look at how department stores, for example, were able to alter their organizational structure while minimizing costs and staff redundancies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Precedents are an essential resource when it comes to making decisions for your own business, so don't undervalue them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, that wraps up our lecture for today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If there are any questions...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to Part four.
