transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My presentation today is about the cave paintings produced by prehistoric artists about thirty thousand years ago, and in particular, the symbols that appear in or near these paintings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These symbols are found deep in caves in many countries around the world, but the ones I'm going to talk about today are mainly European.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, a little about the most common symbols.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The symbols that have been discovered are of different shapes and sizes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some are easily recognizable as they're quite simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most basic are just a series of dots, but they may also include forms such as the triangle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, other symbols are more complex.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A case in point is the wavy line.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is sometimes used on its own, but the same wavy line is also used as part of a larger picture of a horse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we think this is what the wavy line represents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One very important symbol is what's called the hand symbol.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This frequently appears on the walls of caves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll talk about it in a bit more detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, how it was made.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The paint itself was made up from a variety of things that cave artists would have had access to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They had fire, so charcoal was one ingredient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another was the fat from the animals they would have hunted, and lastly, the saliva from their own mouths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there's the question of how they actually applied the runny paint onto the walls of the cave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It certainly wouldn't have been easy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They would have had to use something hollow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's likely to have looked like a straw, you know, like the kind we use for drinking nowadays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They'd have sucked the paint up into it, then blown it out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have recently recreated both the paint and the processes used to make the hand symbols.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The artist would have first put his hand flat against the wall, then blown the paint onto the wall, creating an outline of the hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The researchers who've tried to recreate the process have said that not only is it a difficult technique to master, but also that a strange noise is produced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It also led them to feel light-headed, so we can only imagine that these cave artists felt the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you'll agree that these symbols are really interesting, but they're also of vital importance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have now identified a total of twenty-six symbols commonly used in France and Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We only have this knowledge thanks to a database that's been created and which is being added to all the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It clearly demonstrates that many symbols are often used in particular combinations, even if they're in different places.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is significant as it looks like different tribes of cave people who lived and traveled through the area at that time would have seen these markings as well as adding to them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although researchers don't believe that these symbols are a language as such, they are happy to call them a type of code.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is evidence to support this idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One sequence of five symbols is particularly common in caves in Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Exactly the same sequence of five symbols has been found carved into a necklace made from the teeth of a red deer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it appears that this combination of symbols may have had a special meaning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, many of these explanations are theory as opposed to hard facts, which is why there is disagreement among researchers about the significance of what we are seeing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One theory is called The Great Leap Forward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The idea is that around thirty-five thousand years ago, there was a sudden increase in creativity which led to the invention of the boat, among other things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, not everyone agrees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, many scientists believe that what has been found in Africa seems to indicate that this increase in creativity happened much earlier, around seventy to ninety thousand years ago, and more gradually.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One example of an artifact that is offered to support the idea is the discovery of different sorts of arrows, which would have been used for hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These scientists suggest that the reason more symbols haven't been found from this earlier time is because they would have been painted on things that did not survive, such as wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, we are very lucky that caves have protected these specimens as well as they have, or we might never have known what these artists were capable of.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.explanation: 听到 "include forms such as"（包括诸如……的形状）这个举例信号词后，紧跟在后面的词就是答案。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到前面的 "dots"，但题目中 dots 已经给出了，要注意听 dots 后面那个并列的形状。
questions.quote: The most basic are just a series of dots, but they may also include forms such as the triangle.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到 wavy line（波浪线）是 larger picture of a... 的一部分，紧接着说这就是它 "represents"（代表）的内容，答案就在代表之后。
questions.tip: 不要只听到 "wavy line" 就走神，重点是它依附于哪个更大的图像（part of a larger picture）。
questions.quote: This is sometimes used on its own, but the same wavy line is also used as part of a larger picture of a horse, so we think this is what the wavy line represents.

questions.explanation: 题目问的是混合成分，录音中用 "Another was..." 介绍了除 charcoal 和 saliva 之外的中间那个成分。
questions.tip: 容易听到 "animals"，但 fat 是来自 animals 的提取物，fat 才是具体的配料名称。
questions.quote: They had fire, so charcoal was one ingredient. Another was the fat from the animals they would have hunted, and lastly, the saliva from their own mouths.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "similar to"（像……）对应录音中的 "looked like"，后面的名词就是用来吹颜料的工具。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了 "hollow"（中空的），但那是形容词，题目需要填的是具体的物品名称。
questions.quote: They would have had to use something hollow. In fact, it’s likely to have looked like a straw, you know, like the kind we use for drinking nowadays.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "unusual"（不寻常的）对应录音中的 "strange"，紧跟在其后的名词就是答案。
questions.tip: 不要填 "light-headed"，那是吹颜料导致的身体感觉（result），而不是发出的声音。
questions.quote: The researchers who’ve tried to recreate the process have said that not only is it a difficult technique to master, but also that a strange noise is produced.

questions.explanation: 录音先否定了 symbols 是 language，然后转折说研究者 "happy to call them a type of..."，此处就是正确答案。
questions.tip: 千万别填 "language"，录音中明确说了 "don't believe... are a language"。
questions.quote: Although researchers don’t believe that these symbols are a language as such, they are happy to call them a type of code.

questions.explanation: 听到 "found carved into a..."（被发现刻在……里面），这个介词短语后的物体就是承载符号的东西。
questions.tip: 容易误填 "teeth" 或 "deer"，题目结构是 "on a [object] made from..."，teeth 是制作材料，necklace 才是那个物体。
questions.quote: Exactly the same sequence of five symbols has been found carved into a necklace made from the teeth of a red deer.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "innovations such as"（创新，例如……）对应录音中的 "invention of"，后面的名词即为答案。
questions.tip: 这题定位词 "Great Leap Forward" 出现后要集中注意力听具体的发明物。
questions.quote: The idea is that around 35,000 years ago there was a sudden increase in creativity which led to the invention of the boat among other things.

questions.explanation: 题目中的 "types of" 对应录音中的 "different sorts of"，后面紧跟着的就是在这个早于预期的时间点发现的物品。
questions.tip: 不要填 "hunting"，那是用途（used for hunting），不是物品本身。
questions.quote: One example of an artifact that is offered to support the idea is the discovery of different sorts of arrows, which would have been used for hunting.

questions.explanation: 录音解释了为什么更早期的符号没留下来，因为它们 "painted on things that did not survive, such as..."，例子即答案。
questions.tip: 注意题目问的是 painted on（画在什么上面），不要填成 "survive" 或 "specimens"。
questions.quote: These scientists suggest that the reason more symbols haven’t been found from this earlier time is because they would have been painted on things that did not survive, such as wood.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture on the influence of the car on urban development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, in this second lecture of the series, we turn our attention to transportation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, we're going to take a look at the way the motor car influenced urban development in Australia and changed our lifestyle from the nineteen-forties to the end of the nineteen-nineties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The car is so common nowadays that we all take it for granted, and we barely think about the major effect it has had on our society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But let's go back for a while to the late nineteen-forties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although they had been around since the start of the twentieth century, only one person in eight owned a car in Australia's major cities at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nearly sixty percent of journeys were still made by various means of public transport, and only fifteen percent by car, which is clearly very few compared to statistics now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Buses were very crowded in the days before extensive car use, and they were also considered to be uncomfortable, despite providing a cheap option that most people could afford.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, this wasn't long after the Second World War.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People were tired of living without things, of making do, and to them, cars represented freedom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But even for the wealthy few who did have vehicles, it wasn't easy to run a car at this time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as the expense of buying a car, spare parts were difficult to get, as many were imported.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another problem for car owners was that fuel was still rationed, and car taxes were very high.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Strong public feeling on issues like these from various pressure groups resulted in a change of government in Australia after the general election in nineteen forty-nine, which undoubtedly shaped the future of our nation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the nineteen-sixties, cheaper, more reliable cars became available, and this coincided with the rapid expansion of the suburbs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The car enabled these to grow in all directions, far beyond the train lines laid down in the nineteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the previous one hundred and fifty years, the city center had been a prestigious area, but the addition of cars made the main streets congested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This wasn't the only problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now they were polluted as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since these streets were usually straight, they tempted motorists to speed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the layout of newer streets was affected by this change towards private transport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the newer areas, roads were no longer built straight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, they had curves that were specially designed to force drivers to slow down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This meant they were longer, but this was not a problem because people rarely walked anymore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the nineteen-seventies, the type of roads being built changed, with more lanes in each direction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There were more commuters because now there was faster access to the city where they worked.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By this time, the motor car was affecting many different areas of life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It even, surprisingly, affected relationships.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before this, meeting anyone who lived beyond walking or cycling distance was impractical, if not impossible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The car brought people together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What other effects did the car have?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The increase in car use changed the way we advertise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Previously, advertisements had been designed to attract slow-moving pedestrians, so they were located at eye level and designed on a human scale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the late nineteen-seventies, massive advertisements were designed to attract the notice of the passing motorist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the nineteen-eighties and nineties, even the location of shops began to change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We built shopping malls out in the suburbs, which meant that old town centers did far less business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, we saw the development of drive-in shopping centers, theaters, and even restaurants, which now ensure we get out of our cars as little as possible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'd like to turn your attention to a few statistics related to car ownership over the same period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have one minute to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

questions.tip: 听到 "high" 这个形容词后，紧跟的名词就是答案，注意复数形式。
questions.quote: Another problem for car owners was that fuel was still rationed, and car taxes were very high.

questions.explanation: 来自驾车者的压力导致了1949年澳大利亚 government（政府）的更迭。

questions.explanation: 除了拥堵（congested），主街道现在也变得 polluted（被污染的）了。
questions.tip: 题目结构是 "congested and..."，需要填一个形容词与之并列，不要填名词 pollution。
questions.quote: ...the addition of cars made the main streets congested. This wasn’t the only problem. Now they were polluted as well.

questions.explanation: 到了70年代，道路设计发生了变化，每个方向都有了更多的 lanes（车道）。
questions.tip: 听到 quantifier（数量词）"more" 后，抓取后面的名词，必须用复数 lanes。
questions.quote: By the 1970s, the type of roads being built changed, with more lanes in each direction.

questions.explanation: 演讲者说汽车甚至令人惊讶地影响了人与人之间的 relationships（关系），因为它把住得远的人联系在了一起。
questions.tip: 不要填 advertising，那是汽车影响的下一个领域，注意听 "affected" 后面的直接宾语。
questions.quote: It even, surprisingly, affected relationships. ... The car brought people together.

questions.explanation: 为了吸引过路司机的注意，设计了巨大的新型 advertisements（广告）。
questions.tip: 题目中的 "attract motorists" 是定位点，注意 advertisements 的拼写较长，平时需多练习。
questions.quote: By the late 1970s, massive advertisements were designed to attract the notice of the passing motorist.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the history and technological development of coal mining on Cape Breton Island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about the history and technological development of coal mining on Cape Breton Island, located off the east coast of Canada in Nova Scotia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This area played a critical role in Canada's energy production for over two centuries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Let's begin with the early days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Coal mining in Cape Breton dates back to the 1720s during the French colonial period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These first operations were extremely basic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The miners didn't use machines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They relied on manual labor to gather the coal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In fact, the earliest coal was moved by hand from the base of the cliffs along the island's coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It was a harsh and dangerous task as workers had to navigate slippery rocks while carrying heavy loads of coal in baskets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, as demand for coal increased, it became clear that new systems had to be developed to handle the growing volume.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The ability to transport coal efficiently became one of the biggest challenges facing the industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For production to grow, Cape Breton needed a well-organized transport network.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Initially, they used horse-drawn carts, but as output rose, they introduced railway lines that could carry larger quantities to the port for shipping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This increase in industrial activity also brought about changes in the workforce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Every year, particularly in spring, new groups of laborers would arrive to take advantage of seasonal jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Spring was an ideal time, not just because of the weather, but because mining operations expanded significantly during the warmer months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: By summer, mines would be fully staffed with both local residents and new arrivals from other parts of Canada and abroad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Naturally, this shift in employment patterns had consequences for local demographics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Many people who had lived in remote or agricultural areas began to relocate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Villages near the mines grew while the population in more rural regions started to decline.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Families often moved together and mining towns quickly expanded, sometimes without adequate planning or infrastructure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: By the early twentieth century, Cape Breton had become a major player in the national coal industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At its peak, the island was supplying around forty percent of all coal used in Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This boom not only supported the domestic energy supply, but also provided fuel for export to other countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Let's talk about the workers themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Around the year 1800, the local workforce could no longer meet the demand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: To fill the gap, laborers were recruited from abroad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Most of the early migrants came from Scotland, particularly from mining towns in the central and western regions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These skilled Scottish miners brought valuable knowledge and traditions with them, shaping the way mining was carried out in Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Italian workers also played a key role, especially in the construction of railways and tunnels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, let's look at the technology used in underground mining, specifically how the tunnels were lit before electricity became widespread.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The earliest source of light was a grease torch.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This simple tool burned animal fat to produce a flickering flame.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It was cheap and easy to make, but produced a lot of smoke and posed a serious fire risk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A slightly improved version was to mount a candle in a metal or clay holder.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These holders were usually attached to the timber supports inside the tunnels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: While candles were more manageable than grease torches, they still had open flames and were far from safe in gas-prone environments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The invention of the Davy lamp marked a huge step forward in mine safety.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This device had a flame enclosed in mesh and featured a fitted link sealed by a lock.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The design controlled the airflow and prevented the flame from igniting any methane gas in the air.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Because of this innovation, the number of accidents, such as explosions or fires, dropped significantly across many mining sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Later, carbide lamps were introduced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These worked by combining calcium carbide with water, which created acetylene gas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: When lit, it gave off a steady yellow-white flame that was much brighter than previous sources.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: These lamps were widely used until electric lighting eventually replaced them in the twentieth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

• Mining activity began in the 1720s, when settlers started to extract coal.
• Workers managed to move the first coal from the {{31}} .
• If production was to increase, it depended on the development of the {{32}} system.
• More people came to work in the mines every year from {{33}} .
• The population was reduced in {{34}} areas as people relocated for work.
Growth of the Industry and Immigration
• Coal production gradually increased throughout the 19th century.
• Eventually, the booming mine accounted for {{35}} of Canada’s coal supply.
• A wide range of nationalities were represented in the workforce.
• Around 1800, most miners were from {{36}} , with others from Italy and other European countries.

transcript.text: Section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture on a very popular Canadian food product called maple syrup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Maple syrup can be described as very sweet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Canadians pour it generously over things like pancakes for breakfast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The syrup is produced from the maple tree, and it actually comes from the tree's sap, which is the watery substance that comes out of the trunk of the tree when this is cut.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In order for enough sap to be produced, very special climate conditions are needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In spring, the temperatures need to drop to well below zero at night, but then they need to rise sharply during the day, so they're hugely different over a twenty-four-hour period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And that's exactly what happens in northeastern Canada every spring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The indigenous peoples of North America, known as the First Nations, discovered the maple secret long before the Europeans arrived.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Early folk stories say it was first discovered by a chief who threw his tomahawk, which is similar to an axe, into the trunk of a tree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Clear sap started to run from the cut.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: His wife used this sap to boil meat, and the heat turned it into a sweet syrup, which they found delicious.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Whether or not that story is true, we do know that the maple tree was very important to First Nations peoples for hundreds of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Collecting the sap each spring became a tradition among them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Whole families would migrate to the areas where the maple trees grew and set up camp there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They collected the sap from the trees using buckets.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then they needed to concentrate the sap, removing some of the water from it to create syrup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They had two ways of doing this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One way was to drop hot stones from a fire into the buckets to create steam.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If repeated often enough, this would eventually concentrate the syrup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another method that they used to concentrate the syrup was to leave the sap outside overnight, exposed to freezing temperatures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This would mean that a thick layer of ice would form on top, which could be discarded, leaving the sugary sap below.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Again, this process could be repeated over several days, and eventually a sweet brown syrup was produced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The First Nations people had various uses for the sap and syrup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They drank the sap fresh from the tree as a tonic, knowing that it was an important source of energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But for the most part, they reduced the syrup further and then cooled it so that it crystallized into sugar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This was easy to carry and kept indefinitely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: European settlers who arrived in Canada began to learn about the syrup from First Nations peoples and further expanded its uses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For example, they incorporated it into medicine of different kinds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: They also discovered that by adding yeast to the sap, they could make a maple drink.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And by throwing the hot syrup into the snow, they could make a toffee-like candy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But like the First Nations, they turned most of their sap into maple sugar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For most people, it was the only type of sugar they could afford, since the only alternative was the sugar imported from the Caribbean, which was made from sugarcane.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And this was very expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, after eighteen eighty, the Canadian government decided to stop charging tax on Caribbean sugar, and this made it much cheaper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That meant it was no longer cost-effective to produce maple sugar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And so syrup making became the only viable industry remaining for Canadians, and that's what we've been doing ever since.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: At present, maple syrup is enjoying a boom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In the last two decades, production has doubled in Canada.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, serious threats remain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Like any agricultural product, the harvest is subject to such things as major storms or the arrival of invasive insects, both of which have happened, and these could destroy everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is predicted with some certainty that, in the longer term, climate change will also have an adverse effect on the sap run.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Then there are the social factors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Producing maple syrup is a very labor-intensive process, making it an expensive purchase.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And of equal concern is the fact that nowadays there's a lot of competition from cheaper, artificially flavored brands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Furthermore, we're at a time when obesity is a major issue, making a product that is sixty-seven percent sugar increasingly difficult to sell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Nevertheless, there are reasons to be optimistic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Producers are developing markets abroad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Our syrup is currently being exported to over fifty countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Back here at home, chefs use it enthusiastically.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It's certainly high in calories, but it also contains proteins, minerals, and antioxidants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As such, it is still relatively healthy when you compare it with sugar or corn syrup.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Canadians are proud of maple syrup and its deep roots in our history and geography.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: However, the primary reason for maple syrup's success around the world remains its taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: There's nothing quite like it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That is the end of Section Four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

• Sap collection in spring developed into a First Nations {{33}} .
• The sap was collected in buckets.
• The sap was concentrated into syrup by:
◦ using hot stones to produce {{34}} .
◦ leaving it outside at night and then removing the layer of {{35}} on top.
Uses
• First Nations people drank the fresh sap to give them energy.
• European settlers put the syrup in various types of {{36}} .
• They also used it for drinks and for candy.
• Its use for making sugar declined after 1880, when the {{37}} on Caribbean sugar was removed.

• Natural:
◦ Harvests may be affected by storms and destructive {{38}} .
◦ Climate change may also affect sap production.
• Social:
◦ Maple syrup is expensive and faces considerable {{39}} .
◦ The obesity issue is affecting sales.
Reasons for optimism

questions.quote: In order for enough sap to be produced, very special climate conditions are needed. In spring, the temperatures need to drop to well below zero at night, but then they need to rise sharply during the day, so they're hugely different over a twenty-four-hour period.

questions.quote: Early folk stories say it was first discovered by a chief who threw his tomahawk, which is similar to an ax, into the trunk of a tree. Clear sap started to run from the cut. His wife used this sap to boil meat, and the heat turned it into a sweet syrup, which they found delicious.

questions.quote: Whether or not that story is true, we do know that the maple tree was very important to First Nations peoples for hundreds of years. Collecting the sap each spring became a tradition among them.

questions.tip: 这道题线索很直白，但你可能会因为只顾着听并理解“hot stones”的动作，而漏掉紧跟在句末的答案词“steam”。
questions.quote: They had two ways of doing this. One way was to drop hot stones from a fire into the buckets to create steam.

questions.explanation: 录音提到把树液放在室外过夜，顶部会形成厚厚的“layer of ice”（冰层），并且会被“discarded”（丢弃，同义替换removing），所以填ice。
questions.tip: 你可能听到“freezing temperatures”就想填temperature，但题目问的是顶部的“layer of”什么，注意捕捉具象物质名词。
questions.quote: Another method that they used to concentrate the syrup was to leave the sap outside overnight, exposed to freezing temperatures. This would mean that a thick layer of ice would form on top, which could be discarded, leaving the sugary sap below.

questions.explanation: 录音说欧洲定居者将糖浆混入“medicine of different kinds”（不同种类的药物）中，different kinds替换了题目的various types。

questions.explanation: 录音提到在1880年之后，政府决定停止对加勒比糖征收“tax”（税），stop charging对应了题目里的removed。

questions.explanation: 录音提到收成容易受到重大风暴或入侵“insects”（昆虫）的影响，并且这会破坏一切（对应destructive），所以填insects。

questions.quote: However, serious threats remain. Like any agricultural product, the harvest is subject to such things as major storms or the arrival of invasive insects, both of which have happened, and these could destroy everything.

questions.explanation: 录音在说到枫糖浆很贵之后，引出如今有来自廉价品牌的“competition”（竞争），a lot of替换了considerable。

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about an early form of photography that developed in Britain and France called calotype photography.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome back to this series of lectures on the development of photography.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last week, we looked at a type of photography called daguerreotype,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: the first commercially successful photographic process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we're going to look at how this was gradually replaced by a technique called calotype.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Daguerreotype was a major breakthrough, but there were problems with it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, because the image was produced on a copper sheet, it was expensive to create each photograph.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, during the eighteen forties, a man named William Talbot began looking for an alternative approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Talbot eventually became an influential figure, but he always said he was not a professional photographer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, he trained as an artist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His greatest interest was painting,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: and he only became involved with photography as a secondary interest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Talbot spent many years trying to solve the problems associated with daguerreotype photography.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He tried a number of different approaches, and it took some time to find a successful alternative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in the end, what he did was, instead of producing each photograph on a sheet of copper, he produced them on paper, and at the time, this was a great advance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Talbot's technique, which he called calotype photography, had other advantages as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Maybe the most important was that the pictures themselves weren't as sharp as the ones produced before.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The sharpness had been a problem because it distorted everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this new calotype process produced images that were realistic compared to all earlier photographs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Calotype photography was invented in Britain, but it was also popular with French photographers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The eighteen fifties were a time of rapid development in France, and photography was used to record these changes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One example of how important photography had become occurred in eighteen fifty-one when the French government established a society to promote the interests of photographers, something that hadn't happened before.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To begin with, there were five members, and maybe the most important was a man called Gustave Le Gray.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Le Gray became increasingly fascinated by the calotype process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of all, he wanted to produce different types of image, so began a series of experiments to see how this might be done.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His greatest success was when he designed the first camera that was able to create enlargements, an important step forward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another of Le Gray's innovations was his work on the size of the equipment necessary to take photographs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Originally, it was very heavy and difficult to move about, but Le Gray made it lighter and smaller.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This meant he could take photographs outdoors more easily rather than being limited to the studio, which had sometimes been the case until then.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Le Gray produced numerous photographs during this period and was highly regarded among fellow photographers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But his work also became famous among the general public because he wrote a very popular series of books describing the calotype process and giving examples of his work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The simple fact was that people liked photography.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They thought it was reliable, especially compared to drawing, where the human hand might alter or exaggerate things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This had various consequences,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: one of which was that photography was now often used to record the huge program of renovation work of historical buildings in France during the eighteen fifties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The camera doesn't lie, so people said.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, the calotype process was admired not only by photographers, but increasingly by the government and by mainstream society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, debate still remained about whether photography could truly be called an art form like sculpture or drawing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Certainly, although the public liked it, in the opinion of critics, photography could not be compared to other established forms of art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So in summary, what can we say about calotype photography during this period?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One thing to reemphasize is that the eighteen fifties were a period of great development in Britain and France.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The culture in both countries admired all new technological advances, and photography represented these ideas because it was considered to be a science by most people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, photographers didn't stop experimenting with new materials to improve the quality of their work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of all, they were searching for ways to make images more permanent because calotype photographs tended to fade over time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in the end, they found that if the image was produced on glass, it lasted much longer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So calotype photography was slowly replaced by other techniques which had greater long...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
From Daguerreotype to Calotype
• Daguerreotype was the first commercial photographic process.
• Daguerreotype had a problem: the use of copper made it {{31}}
• William Talbot began looking for an alternative approach in the 1840s.
• Talbot was not originally a photographer but an artist who specialised in {{32}}
• Talbot used paper instead of copper.
• These calotype photographs were more {{33}} because they weren't so sharp.
French Calotype
• In 1851, the first society for photographers was created.
• Gustave Le Gray became fascinated by calotype photography.
• He carried out experiments and produced the first {{34}} using a camera.
• He developed equipment that was easier to use outside the {{35}}
• Calotype became famous because Le Gray produced {{36}} about it.

transcript.text: You will hear a talk on research into music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, we're going to delve into the fascinating history of music in Britain and the evolution that it experienced throughout the duration of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the second half of the eighteenth century, Britain experienced an industrial revolution, during which its manufacturing industry underwent a major transition from hand production methods to the use of machinery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This sudden boom in the industry drew thousands of people into the cities, where they knew they'd be able to find jobs in the factories, working with or maintaining the machinery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This sudden influx of people into the cities did not just come from the surrounding countryside, but also from other poorer nations in search of a better life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Between 1800 and 1900, the population of England increased by four times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This mass immigration from different nations and areas of the country resulted in a variety of cultural influences meeting and mixing to form a new, more diverse culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With this new culture came a new style of music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Prior to the Industrial Revolution, music had originally been written to reflect the hard, labor-intensive life in all kinds of industries when all work had to be done by hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most people resided in small rural communities where their lives revolved around farming.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Life for the average person was difficult, as incomes were meager and malnourishment and disease were common.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the difference in nationalities of the people and the variety of musical genres, all of the music shared one common language: English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As many were unable to write, the songs were a means for the people to give voice to their experiences and feelings about their hard and laborious jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of the music written by the workers during this period has been lost as a result of illiteracy and the wear of time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, you may be asking yourselves how these small musical works were formed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The roots of most of these groups can mostly be traced back to the younger members of the working classes, who were perhaps rebelling against the inferiority of their living and working conditions compared to those of the upper classes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Young performers would often lead these musical trends, usually possessing a great talent for singing or playing particular handmade instruments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As time progressed into the nineteenth century, these musical groups had gained much notoriety and would hold small performances in the street for all to watch.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was perhaps their blind optimism and rebellious spirit that led them to become so popular with their audiences, which were usually made up of the poorest of the poor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite efforts by the upper classes to put an end to these musical traditions, they continued to gain popularity and flourish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the late 1870s, they had evolved past the barrier of the social echelons and gained access to the middle class.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Performances were held in proper establishments such as village halls, and some were even ticketed, with audiences paying a fee for the privilege of watching.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Music produced by these groups were better recorded, and some are still preserved today in museums.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The music of these groups may not exist in the present day, but its influences are still clear if you look closely enough.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In classical culture, for example, many of the themes and theatrical performances are still based on the lives and experiences of the working classes, both prior to and following the Industrial Revolution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The novel entitled Les Misérables by Victor Hugo, for example, is a novel about the French working classes and is still widely popular today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The original recordings of the music written during these periods are now hugely valuable due to the demand from avid collectors and enthusiastic fans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of these recordings are publicly owned and displayed in museum exhibits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, a selection are still privately owned and occasionally appear for sale in auctions, often reaching prices in the hundreds of thousands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, that just about wraps the lecture up for today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if anyone has any questions...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk about the control of wild animals in Europe, given by a speaker to an audience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to thirty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to thirty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name's Jim Robinson, and today we're going to look at the control of wild animals, specifically wild boar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, boar have been natural inhabitants of Western Europe for thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in recent years, there has been a surge in boar activity that poses real threat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Boars are not currently on the protected animals list, which is perhaps why there has been a spike in their breeding activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Boars are an indigenous species and are particularly plentiful in rural France and the Bavarian uplands of Germany.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Boar hunting is a European tradition that goes back to Roman times and became particularly popular among courtiers during the Middle Ages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even during the twentieth century, boar hunting was seen as an integral part of rural life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The decline in boar hunting has obviously led to a rise in the boar populations of Europe, and the situation has reached a critical point, with boar posing a critical threat to the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Proponents of boar hunting cite this factor as a major reason why boar populations should be contained.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Boar also pose a threat to humans too, with countless reports of people being injured during boar attacks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The origins of the wild boar have roots in Germanic, and this perhaps explains their prevalence in Germany.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The problems with the boar population, Germany have ramifications for the rest of Europe as boar packs migrate towards Central and Eastern Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the main issues that is of great concern is the transmission of diseases that infect other species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dairy farmers in France are particularly concerned as many of them have seen their herds depleted by infections.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The methods for containing boar populations have been looked at in great detail and numerous options are available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One is to encourage more boar hunting in wild regions, such as mountains and forests.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hunters would be given licenses to hunt either for food or sport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, boar do pose a threat to human life, so this possibility must be looked at with caution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One method that must be ruled out is poison, as legislation has been introduced prohibiting this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Such methods were tried with rabbits in the 1960s, and this had a disastrous impact on the food chain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The introduction of natural predators into the ecosystem is also an option that can't be considered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only known predators of boar in the world are wild cats, like lions and tigers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Obviously, there's no way such animals can be allowed to roam the mountains and forests of Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Given the threat that boars pose to humans, it is imperative that forest-dwelling boar are kept well away from people in cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is absolutely essential as human safety must be the main priority of policymakers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the eleventh century, boars in several European countries were becoming increasingly rare in Great Britain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: King Charles attempted to reintroduce boars in the New Forest area of the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yet the entire population was almost wiped out during the battles of the English Civil War, when roaming soldiers hunted them for food.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the 1980s, wild boar rearing was encouraged and boar populations began to rise again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By the 1990s, there was a huge rise in the number of boar across England, due in large part to the species no longer forced to live in captivity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many boar have broken free from farms across England and are breeding at a rapid rate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions thirty-seven to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions thirty-seven to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Aside from their environmental threat, boars also pose a problem for farmers growing crops and vegetables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other species such as red deer are a threat to farm produce like grain and potatoes, but boars certainly present the most serious risk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The damage done to the farming industry is estimated to cost millions of pounds and insurance payments as a result of this have spiked in the last decade.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Red deer are predominantly confined to forest areas, and it is unusual to see them outside their habitats during the summer months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, as the weather gets colder, they can be seen looking for food around local villages and fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Red deer have their origins in Asia and are ruminant species, which means they have a stomach that consists of four compartments, much like cows.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are slaughtered for food and their meat is sold as venison and is increasingly popular among consumers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are nine subspecies of red deer, with three of them on the endangered species list.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The deer population doesn't pose the same threat as the boar population, but it certainly needs to be addressed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Forest areas are their main habitats and they are now breeding at a much higher rate than in previous years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, deer are an important part of the food chain and are an important part of the hunting traditions of the UK, so it is important that their population is kept stable for this reason.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Though the real concern is the problems that deer present for farmers who have seen their crops suffer in devastating ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Protection needs to be offered and many farmers report building large perimeter fences around their fields to keep deer out, which costs them a huge amount of money.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Government funding is so far inadequate to offer the protection farmers need, but ways are being looked at to provide subsidies through other means.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part Four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to Part Four.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about research into bird habitats and conservation in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is the third session of the series of lectures on wildlife.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For this lecture, we're going to look at two studies on the habitats of birds and protection measures taken in Australia, including the basic methodology and related areas of research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let me give you some background information about the first research project on birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study was carried out by R.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: B.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cunningham and his team from the Australian National University in nineteen ninety-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The primary goal was to detect the breeding habits and resting sites of some birds, especially those protected species in urban regions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These species included birds like peregrine falcons and kestrels in Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The bird dataset consisted of a total of a hundred and fifty-three species recorded from nine hundred and forty-six sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One might expect that in order to obtain valid data on their distribution patterns and population densities, researchers had to count through binoculars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, they managed to estimate with various standard distance sampling methods like random sampling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, a mapping system was used to study their companionship behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It recorded proposed birds nesting sites to monitor the mating behavior of targeted species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To obtain valid data of birds' whereabouts, researchers attached identity tags to birds' legs transmitting radio signals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The tagging process was done when the birds were between five and seven days of age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After the initial tagging, data was collected from subsets of radio-tagged birds, making it possible to assess the trends of birds over fifteen months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what did they find?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, as it turned out, many of the birds tagged had the tendency to nest in the same habitat where they grew up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their nesting sites were quite varied and included freshwater reed beds, tidal reed beds, agricultural crops, and man-made sites.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even though naturally occurring nests were common, birds sometimes accidentally nested in man-made devices like power towers, chimneys, and tunnels.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This research also studied the impact of humans on bird communities and found out that pollution had contributed greatly to the declining birth rates of some species, which were considered to be extinct or threatened to vanish from the study area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These species are dependent on natural forests because of their breeding holes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They will become extinct when local natural forests continue to be polluted heavily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A number of measures were thus taken by members from local animal conservation organizations to boost their alarming survival rates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, breeding boxes were placed in trees taking on the role of breeding holes that were contaminated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Protection guidelines were also introduced strictly prohibiting killing, disturbance, and habitat destruction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A further measure was taken to ensure the safety of birds from wind farms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, birds are sometimes shedded by wind turbine blades.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A great deal of work was done on how to prevent them from colliding with turbines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A case in point was protecting space for bird migration by ensuring that migratory routes were kept free.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Falcons generally cope well with wind turbines, but not in weather conditions where visibility is bad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So with knowledge of how fast falcons fly, bird stations in northern Australia can notify wind farms further south of the falcon's approach so that turbines can be shut down as they pass by.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then another piece of research was done a couple of years later by Conway in two thousand and six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His team detected the calling frequency of seabirds flying at night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Acoustic signals are important communication tools for birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These signals can indicate social cohesion, prey location, and breeding behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Courtship songs are common among various species during mating seasons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Males produce calling songs that attract distant females, and then courtship songs will induce nearby females to respond.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Surveyors also took recordings of the sounds of all the individual birds detected.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A tablet PC was used to process detailed information like sound pitch, spectrum, length, and timing of surveys.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To minimize the disturbance on the bird community, all the sounds were recorded from a distance using microphones to detect noise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They found that the probability of call events was much higher for solitary birds communicating early and late in the day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer talking to a group of environmental science students about fuel made from biomass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty on page seven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this course, we've been discussing the principles of sustainable development, and now we're going to look at some of the ways in which these principles are being put into practice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'm going to talk about the use of biomass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And for those of you who don't know what biomass is, it's plant material, usually agricultural waste, such as sawdust or straw.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And briquettes made out of biomass are used as fuel, either in the home or in industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll start with the benefits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Using briquettes has a financial benefit because they make use of waste products as raw materials, so there isn't any cost involved for that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another advantage is convenience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Handling briquettes is cleaner than handling materials like wood or charcoal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, briquettes are less trouble to store because they're a uniform size and shape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's look briefly now at how these briquettes are made.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are two basic methods of manufacture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first method uses machinery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the initial stage, all the loose plant material is ground into a powder and then mixed with other materials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, a machine compresses the biomass mixture, and that process raises the temperature and causes it to melt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The machine forces the biomass mixture out through rectangular or circular holes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, as the pressure decreases, the mixture cools and becomes solid again, and that's how the briquettes are formed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's important to point out that with this method, electricity is essential to operate the machinery, and the exact amount you need depends on the type of biomass you use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But generally, the amount required is only three percent to nine percent of the energy that's produced by the briquettes when they are burnt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second method involves making briquettes by hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This method is suitable when the biomass is mainly composed of material that doesn't melt, like paper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The biomass is made into a paste by adding water, and in addition, something sticky, such as starch.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This mixture is then shaped using either a simple metal press or bare hands.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So where is biomass fuel used and how extensively?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it's difficult to obtain detailed figures, but it's been used for several years in Europe and the USA, mainly for agriculture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And since two thousand, there's been a rapid increase in the production and use of briquettes made out of wood waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I can give you a ballpark figure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In two thousand and ten, about five million tons were used in Europe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of these had to be imported from the USA.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving further east, both India and China have been producing biomass briquettes since the nineteen-nineties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Detailed figures are hard to come by, but in China in two thousand and two, the number of factories producing biomass briquettes had increased to approximately six hundred, and production is still growing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I don't have information about Africa in general, but I can give you an example of one company in Uganda which is producing briquettes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of the company's customers are public institutions like schools and universities that provide hot meals for their students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other main users are businesses that need a source of heat for producing their products.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, how viable are biomass fuels like these in economic terms, and what is likely to happen in the future?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the answer depends partly on the price of the fuels that they replace, and that varies from place to place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in general, the demand for biomass fuels is almost certain to grow, and that can only benefit the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's turn now to another facet of sustain...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section four.

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecture about behavioral economics and energy use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions thirty-one to forty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Today, we're looking at how behavioral economics can help explain the way people use energy at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This is useful because many governments and energy companies want households to reduce consumption, but simply giving people information does not always work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Traditional economists often imagine consumers as careful decision-makers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: In this view, people compare costs and benefits, think through the available evidence, and choose rationally, as if every decision were based on logic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Behavioral economics takes a different view.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It suggests that many everyday choices are made quickly and almost automatically.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Instead of analyzing every detail, people are often guided by habit, emotion, or instinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A simple example comes from a savings program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Participants were attracted by the chance of winning a prize, even though the mathematical probability was very low.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What mattered to them was the possibility of gaining something, not the actual likelihood of success.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now let's turn to an energy project involving household customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Researchers expected that giving people advice would make them use less energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: But in some cases, the figures moved in the opposite direction and showed an increase.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This was surprising because the scheme had been designed to reduce consumption.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The customers were divided into four groups.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Each group received a different message about why they should cut down on energy use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One message focused on saving money.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another emphasized environmental protection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: A third said that using less energy would help people living nearby, especially their neighbors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: The final group was told that many other households in the local area were already using less energy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Only this group actually changed its behavior.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So what can be done to encourage change?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: One lesson is that facts alone are often not enough.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: People may respond better when there is some form of reward, even a small one, such as a discount or positive feedback.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Another useful tool is technology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Smart meters, phone apps, and reminders can make energy use easier to notice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: It is also important to remember that progress does not always require major action.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Small changes in routine can still produce useful results, such as reducing heating or switching off unused lights.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: There is also a role for the government, especially in funding schemes that help households improve energy efficiency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: For example, a family may use much less energy if an old heating system is replaced with a modern boiler.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

Behavioral Economics and Energy Consumption
Introduction
• Behavioural economics studies human behaviour to influence the decisions people make.
• Traditional economists assume that people act {{31}} and make their own decisions.
• Behavioural economics recognises the human tendency to rely on {{32}} , as well as habit and emotion.
• As shown by a savings scheme, people value the possibility of gaining more than the {{33}} of success.
Scheme for energy customers
• An energy-saving scheme led to an unexpected {{34}} .
• Energy customers were given information about consumption for different reasons.
• They were divided into four groups.
• Each group was told about a different benefit, such as:
- financial savings
- benefits to the environment
- benefits to their {{35}}
• Only the last group actually changed their behaviour.
Ways to encourage change
• People want a {{36}} .
• {{37}} might be an efficient way to encourage change.
• Even minor {{38}} can have an effect.
• The {{39}} should spend money on this.
• For example, people could change a {{40}} .

questions.explanation: 录音里提到的“choose rationally”对应了题目里的“act rationally”，意思就是凭逻辑理性地做决定。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到上一句很清晰的“decision-makers”，但要注意题目空格前是动词“act”，需要填一个副词，所以只能填“rationally”。
questions.quote: Traditional economists often imagine consumers as careful decision-makers. In this view, people compare costs and benefits, think through the available evidence, and choose rationally, as if every decision were based on logic.

questions.explanation: 录音中的“guided by... instinct”直接表明被本能引导，完美替换了题目里的“rely on instinct”。
questions.tip: 录音并列给出了“habit, emotion, or instinct”三个词，只需要填入题干缺少的 instinct 即可。
questions.quote: Behavioral economics takes a different view. It suggests that many everyday choices are made quickly and almost automatically. Instead of analyzing every detail, people are often guided by habit, emotion, or instinct.

questions.explanation: 题目意思是“看重获得的可能而不是成功的...”，刚好对应录音最后对比部分指出的“not the actual likelihood of success”。
questions.tip: 前面提到了一个意思相近的干扰词“probability”，但它修饰的是获奖几率，而只有“likelihood”紧跟着题目要求的“of success”。
questions.quote: A simple example comes from a savings program. Participants were attracted by the chance of winning a prize, even though the mathematical probability was very low. What mattered to them was the possibility of gaining something, not the actual likelihood of success.

questions.explanation: 题目说导致了一个出乎意料的结果，录音里的“showed an increase”对应结果，紧接着的“surprising”刚好替换了“unexpected”。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到“opposite direction”并试图自己去拼凑答案，但填空题只能填录音里实实在在读出来的那个明确结果“increase”。
questions.quote: Researchers expected that giving people advice would make them use less energy. But in some cases, the figures moved in the opposite direction and showed an increase. This was surprising because the scheme had been designed to reduce consumption.

questions.explanation: 录音中的动词“help”直接同义替换了题目里的“benefits to（对...有好处）”，明确指出了对象是他们的“neighbors”。
questions.tip: 刚听到“people”时你可能就想填了，但录音紧跟着用“especially”强调了更具体精准的受众群，所以答案必须是“neighbors”。
questions.quote: A third said that using less energy would help people living nearby, especially their neighbors.

questions.explanation: 题目问人们想要什么，录音说人们在有某种“reward”的时候反应更好，直接对应了题目想要表达的诉求。
questions.tip: 录音马上跟了具体的例子“discount”或“feedback”，你可能很容易被细节干扰，错过了前面起统领作用的核心词“reward”。
questions.quote: So what can be done to encourage change? One lesson is that facts alone are often not enough. People may respond better when there is some form of reward, even a small one, such as a discount or positive feedback.

questions.explanation: 录音直接用“Another useful tool”引出新方法，“tool”在这里就是“way”的替换，直接锁定核心词“technology”。
questions.tip: 紧接着录音举例了“Smart meters”和“phone apps”，你可能顺手填了这些具体的应用词，而忽略了这一整段的大方向总起词。
questions.quote: Another useful tool is technology. Smart meters, phone apps, and reminders can make energy use easier to notice.

questions.explanation: 录音里的“Small”替换了题目的“minor”，所以直接填后面的名词“changes”，而“produce useful results”就是“have an effect”的同义表达。

questions.quote: It is also important to remember that progress does not always require major action. Small changes in routine can still produce useful results, such as reducing heating or switching off unused lights.

questions.tip: 你可能会听到前面的“heating system”，但那是原本就被淘汰的旧东西，题目需要你填的是更新后的物件，所以必须是“boiler”。
