transcript.text: Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a lecturer discussing the use of fumigants in food storage and the conservation of historical objects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In today's lecture, I'm gonna discuss a case study on fumigants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fumigants are chemicals, usually gases, that destroy insects, bacteria, and other organisms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're commonly used to protect stored food, but they can also be used in museums to prevent damage to paintings, furniture, and other historical objects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll begin by looking at some of the problems associated with traditional chemical fumigants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then I'll describe a safer method that was tested on a museum object.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, we'll consider a possible biological alternative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's begin with the environmental effects of chemical fumigation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although chemical fumigants can be highly effective, their use may have serious consequences for the atmosphere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, some of the chemicals released during the process can affect the ozone layer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is important because the ozone layer protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, the use of traditional fumigants has now been restricted in many countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most common fumigants used in the past was methyl bromide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was popular because it killed a wide range of insects in a relatively short time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it was later discovered that the chemical could cause damage to certain museum pieces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, if methyl bromide was used on a painting, it could reduce the strength of its color.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In some cases, pigments became noticeably less bright after treatment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There were also health and safety concerns.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because the gas was dangerous to breathe, both the object and the chemical had to be completely contained.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the food industry, for example, food could be kept inside a sealed bag while the fumigant was introduced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This prevented the gas from escaping.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the effectiveness and cost of fumigation depend on time and setting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Climate is crucial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In humid countries, extra equipment may be required to control the treatment conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That can make the process slower and more expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's turn to an alternative method.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead of using methyl bromide, researchers created an environment with almost no oxygen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The goal was to kill the insects without harming the objects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The total exposure time was 14 days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's longer than some chemical treatments, but it was much safer, both for the objects and for the people carrying out the treatment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The object was placed in a sealed environment where air was removed and replaced with nitrogen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since insects need oxygen, they eventually died.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The method was tested on an old wooden sculpture that had been badly infested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the end of the 14 days, the insects had been destroyed and the wood was unharmed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The study showed that nitrogen could be an effective alternative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the process requires careful control.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even a small leak could reduce its effectiveness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, a different approach has been proposed by scientists.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some are studying chemicals found in the skins of certain frogs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These substances help protect the animals from infection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Researchers have found that they can destroy harmful microorganisms, so they act like natural pesticides, killing bacteria before they cause an infection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Scientists hope that similar compounds could one day protect food or artifacts without the environmental damage caused by traditional fumigants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, they're not very effective in the presence of moisture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Water may dilute them or break them down, so more research is needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To conclude, traditional fumigants work, but may harm the environment or the objects treated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Nitrogen treatment is safer, though slower, and natural chemicals could offer a new direction if we solve the moisture problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 4.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.content:
A CASE STUDY ON FUMIGANTS
Problems with traditional fumigation
• Some chemicals released during fumigation may damage the Earth’s {{31}} layer.
• After methyl bromide treatment, paintings may lose some of their original {{32}} .
• To prevent dangerous gas from escaping, food can be placed inside a sealed {{33}} .
• In countries with humid conditions, the treatment is often more {{34}} because additional equipment is required.
An alternative treatment
• Researchers created an environment containing almost no oxygen.
• The total {{35}} period used in the experiment lasted fourteen days.
• Air was removed from the sealed space and replaced with {{36}} .
• The new method was tested on an old wooden {{37}} that had been attacked by insects.
• The treatment killed the insects without causing visible damage to the object.
A possible biological solution
• Scientists have examined protective substances found in the skin of certain {{38}} .
• These natural chemicals behave in a similar way to {{39}} , as they destroy harmful organisms.
• One current limitation is that the substances become less effective when exposed to {{40}} .

questions.explanation: 录音中提到释放的化学物质会影响（affect对应题目中的damage）ozone layer（臭氧层），所以答案是 ozone。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到前面第12句的 atmosphere（大气），但这里题目明确问的是具体破坏了什么“layer（层）”，所以应该填 ozone。
questions.quote: In particular, some of the chemicals released during the process can affect the ozone layer. This is important because the ozone layer protects the Earth from harmful ultraviolet radiation.

questions.explanation: 录音指出使用溴甲烷会降低画作 color（颜色）的强度（reduce the strength对应题目中的lose some of their original），因此填 colour 或 color。
questions.tip: 你可能会想填 strength（强度）或 pigments（颜料），但这里修饰的是画作“失去了原有的某样东西”，根据录音语境，失去的是颜色的强度，核心名词是 color。
questions.quote: For example, if methyl bromide was used on a painting, it could reduce the strength of its color. In some cases, pigments became noticeably less bright after treatment.

questions.explanation: 录音明确说到为了防止气体泄漏（prevented the gas from escaping），食物会被放在一个 sealed bag（密封袋）里，直接对应题目内容。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到 contained 或是 environment 并被干扰，但题目中空前有非常明确的修饰词 sealed（密封的），这直接对应录音里听到的 sealed bag。
questions.quote: Because the gas was dangerous to breathe, both the object and the chemical had to be completely contained. In the food industry, for example, food could be kept inside a sealed bag while the fumigant was introduced. This prevented the gas from escaping.

questions.explanation: 录音里提到在潮湿的国家需要额外设备（extra equipment对应题目中的additional equipment），这会让过程变得更缓慢且更 expensive（昂贵）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到 slower 就直接当答案填了，但题目空前有 more 修饰，英语中比较级不会说 more slower，只能和 expensive 搭配。
questions.quote: In humid countries, extra equipment may be required to control the treatment conditions. That can make the process slower and more expensive.

questions.explanation: 题目寻找总计14天的什么“时期（period）”，录音中的原话是 total exposure time（总暴露时间），time 对应了 period，因此填 exposure。
questions.tip: 你可能会想填 treatment，但忽略了整体语义，录音里明确和“14天”直接连用且作定语修饰时间的是 exposure。
questions.quote: The total exposure time was 14 days. That's longer than some chemical treatments, but it was much safer, both for the objects and for the people carrying out the treatment.

questions.explanation: 录音原句直白地说明密封空间里的空气被移除，并且被替换成了（replaced with）nitrogen（氮气）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到紧接着出现的 oxygen（氧气）就填上去了，但那是用来解释昆虫需要氧气所以死掉的原因，并不是用来替换空气的气体。
questions.quote: The object was placed in a sealed environment where air was removed and replaced with nitrogen. Since insects need oxygen, they eventually died.

questions.explanation: 题目问这种方法在什么古老的木制物品上做测试，录音直接给出了 tested on an old wooden sculpture（雕塑）。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没跟上 sculpture 或者忽略了具体名词而想填 object 或 wood，但填空题一定要做好预判，紧跟形容词后面的核心名词才是关键。
questions.quote: The method was tested on an old wooden sculpture that had been badly infested. At the end of the 14 days, the insects had been destroyed and the wood was unharmed.

questions.explanation: 录音提到科学家们在某些 frogs（青蛙）的皮肤（skins对应题目中的skin）中发现了保护性化学物质，直接对应填空。
questions.tip: 你可能会被后面一句总结性的 animals（动物）干扰，但题目中有 certain（某些）作为限定修饰词，必须填入录音里具体的物种 frogs。
questions.quote: Some are studying chemicals found in the skins of certain frogs. These substances help protect the animals from infection.

questions.explanation: 题目说这些自然化学物质的作用方式类似于什么，录音中 act like（表现得像，对应题目behave in a similar way to）后面紧跟着的就是 natural pesticides（天然杀虫剂）。
questions.tip: 你可能听到 bacteria 或者 microorganisms 就急着填，但这俩是被化学物质“消灭”的有害生物，而不是它们“起效方式的同类物”。
questions.quote: Researchers have found that they can destroy harmful microorganisms, so they act like natural pesticides, killing bacteria before they cause an infection.

questions.explanation: 录音提到在有 moisture（水分）存在的情况下（in the presence of对应题目exposed to），这些物质变得不那么有效（not very effective对应become less effective）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到下一句解释原理的 water，虽然意思大体相近，但紧跟在“存在导致无效”这一直接条件短语后的原词是 moisture。

transcript.text: Part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a lecture about the history of architecture in New Zealand given by an architectural historian.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions thirty-one to forty.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Architects in New Zealand in the early twentieth century were big fans of traditional styles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At that time, they often looked to European models for inspiration and perceived building design from a traditional perspective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The climate, for example, was the top concern when designing the roof.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Weather conditions across the country can vary significantly, and regions with frequent rain needed special attention.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In areas where the annual precipitation is high, ensuring water could drain efficiently was essential for protecting the structure and longevity of the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Therefore, proper drainage systems had to be considered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Wood was the most popular choice for house building, mainly due to its availability, cost-effectiveness, and ease of use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other materials either weren't affordable or simply weren't accessible in rural parts of the country at the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The majority of traditional buildings are square in shape, and this wasn't by accident.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was a strategic choice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Straight lines and right angles are easier to construct and more space efficient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Architects believed this approach helped to maximize utilization of interior space, especially in areas where plots of land were relatively small.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Additionally, avoiding unusual shapes like curves and diagonal corners made furnishing the interiors much more straightforward.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Complex forms not only wasted valuable room, but also posed problems when arranging furniture or installing fixtures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the country progressed, there were several changes New Zealand architects embraced in the 1960s.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These changes reflected not only a shift in design philosophy, but also improvements in technology and construction methods.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first was a shift to concrete as a material, which gradually replaced timber in many modern buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This transition was made possible by construction techniques introduced by immigrants from Europe and Japan, who brought with them advanced machinery and engineering knowledge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time, New Zealand, like many other nations, was dealing with financial constraints following global events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because of the economic impact of the Second World War, resources had to be used wisely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, both private developers and government-backed construction projects were focused on the cost of construction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Minimizing expense while maximizing utility became the dominant goal during this period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's one of the key factors they considered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They pursued economical designs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sir Miles Warren's architecture offers a classic example of this country's architectural styles at that time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He became well known for modernizing the traditional aesthetic and for using geometric forms in innovative ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In many of his works, he integrated repetitive block-like shapes into his works, a feature that became a hallmark of his style.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This approach came to be associated with a trend in architecture called brutalism, which emphasized raw materials and strong, bold structures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the same time, the use of natural materials was changing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He, like others, abandoned some expensive materials such as stone, not just for economic reasons, but also for practicality in mass construction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Meanwhile, car ownership was on the rise and families were becoming increasingly reliant on private vehicles for commuting and daily tasks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, equipping each new house with a garage gradually became trendy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This change was seen not just as a convenience, but as a necessity that architects needed to incorporate into every design for suburban homes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Among other modern housing styles, Lockwood homes, which featured identical walls, stood out for their uniformity and efficient production.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These homes were mass-produced and became popular for their quick assembly and affordability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also gained in popularity, especially among working-class families.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the design was not without its critics.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some architects and homeowners felt it lacked variety and personal expression, and the buildings were also criticized for this characteristic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A sameness that didn't allow much room for individuality or creativity in layout.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Still, few people would have doubts about the architectural changes of this era, especially considering how widespread and influential they became.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In urban centers, industrial or business complexes have been designed to resemble towers, a departure from earlier, more horizontal layouts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These tall structures helped maximize space in crowded city districts and symbolized economic development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This has happened elsewhere in some industrialized countries, following similar trends seen in places like the UK and Japan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition to the overall shape, which served a functional purpose, architects also concentrated on the visual appeal of some detailed designs, such as shadow and colors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These finer aesthetic elements helped modern buildings feel less sterile and more engaging to the eye, improving both their beauty and their emotional impact on residents and visitors alike.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear two students called Aria and John discussing the research on water hyacinths.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Farmers cannot travel in boats on the water and thus cannot fish in it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, heavy free-floating mats of water hyacinth are clogging the dam at the power station in West Africa.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Dams often cease to function as a result, severely restricting the electricity generation.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later, it was introduced into Europe and Africa as an ornamental garden pond plant due to its beauty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Flowers of this plant were being sold in local markets in African countries as a source of income for women.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since the nineteen hundreds, this weed has infested lakes, rivers, and creeks of the delta areas in West Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

questions.tip: 录音中间大段描述了看孩子们怎么玩耍（play）和相处（peer relationships），你如果不往后听到最后一句的转折强调，就会选错成 A 或 B。
questions.quote: Anyway, I'd also like to make a short film about a few children. A good idea, but it will depend on building up a relationship with one or 2 health visitors willing to introduce you to a family. An opportunity like that would allow you to look at how young children begin to form words, for example. And peer relationships between children, as well as the ways in which they relate and play with each other, especially when they are around 2 to 3 years old, although early use of language is my main interest.

options.text: to watch how they play.
to look at their relationships.
to study their language.

questions.prompt: According to Dr. Harris, how might the arrival of a new baby affect a family?
questions.explanation: 导师指出新生儿会给父母带来影响，尤其是额外的经济花销会成为一种担忧（expense could be a worry），这对应的就是父母承受的压力（pressure），对应选项 B。
questions.tip: 你可能会凭生活经验脑补新生儿会让其他孩子嫉妒（jealous），但录音里明确列举的例子是给父母带来的“经济环境”烦恼，做题绝不能靠常识瞎猜。
questions.quote: An equally important area is the child's home environment and the effect of a newborn baby. Right. You need to consider the impact of this on the parents, particularly if the family lives in poor economic circumstances. Of course, the additional expense could be a worry, especially if there are other children.

options.text: Other children may feel jealous.
Parents may be put under pressure.
Sufficient support may not be available.

questions.prompt: Dr. Harris agrees with Lisa that she needs to find out about
questions.explanation: 你问是不是要熟悉家庭法，导师不仅大力赞同，还强调必须参考法律（refer to the law）来界定干预的程度，完全对应选项 A 中的法律限制。
questions.tip: 导师中间故意抛出了医疗条件（medical conditions）和社会实践（social practice）来做干扰，如果你没跟上最后用 But 引出的关于法律（law）的核心结论，就会踩坑。
questions.quote: This is the area where I will need to be familiar with family law, isn't it? Very much so. By all means, be aware of the medical conditions, and you also need to consider social practice. But you'll find that in most circumstances, you will have to refer to the law to understand how far a health visitor can intervene. Yes, I appreciate that.

options.text: legal constraints.
family considerations.
medical circumstances.

groups.instructions:
What features are suitable for each of the following textbooks?
Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter from A-G next to questions 26–30.

options.text: global coverage but sometimes inaccurate
interesting but rather unrealistic
practical and full of thoughtful tips
up-to-date with an international approach
wide ranging but poorly organized
good value despite some omissions
extremely costly but comprehensive

questions.explanation: 你提到这书是新版所以信息很新（current），导师补充说能借此了解其他国家（other countries）的发展，两者结合就是“更新及时且有国际视野”，对应选项 D。
questions.tip: 导师说书里有些内容“可能不相关（may not be relevant）”，你千万别把它当成了“不准确（inaccurate）”而误选了 A。
questions.quote: Now, your book list. I'm glad to see Worldwide Health Care Policies tops your list. Well, I wasn't sure how relevant it would be, but it's a new edition, so the information is current. Yes, some of it may not be relevant, but it's important to keep abreast of developments in other countries which may inform our own government's legislation.

questions.explanation: 导师明确夸这本书考虑到价格的话非常划算（excellent buy），尽管它确实遗漏了一些东西（leave a few things out），对应选项 F 的性价比高且有疏漏。
questions.tip: 你听到“遗漏（leave out）”这个缺点时，不能只看带贬义的选项，必须结合前面的“不那么贵/买得值（not as costly / excellent buy）”做正负向的综合判断。
questions.quote: I understand. What about Supporting Vulnerable Families? It's not as costly as some of the other books on my list. It's an excellent buy considering the price, even though it does leave a few things out.

questions.explanation: 导师直言这本书非常昂贵（very expensive），但没有几本书能像它一样涵盖这么多的细节（cover as much detail as this），精准对应选项 G。
questions.tip: 导师最后随口吐槽了一句文风偶尔无聊（boring），如果你注意力被带偏去选带负面评价的干扰项，就漏掉了“投资很值且内容详尽”的核心结论。
questions.quote: I've already ordered Health Visitors and Child Protection. I hope that was right. Well, it's very expensive, but it's a sound investment, and there aren't many textbooks which cover as much detail as this. It will be a valuable reference, even if the style is occasionally boring.

questions.explanation: 导师觉得这本书很有启发性（stimulating），但探讨的都是基于“完美世界”和“钱不是问题”这种不太现实（unrealistic）的假设，对应选项 B。
questions.tip: 你听到“不具备实用价值（Probably not useful）”可能会直接找纯负面选项，但忽略了后面紧跟着的正面词“启发思考（stimulating）”，要找正负结合的选项。
questions.quote: And what about The Future of Health Visiting? I'm unsure how useful it will be. Useful in a utilitarian sense? Probably not. But it's stimulating in the way the writer considers what health visiting could be like in a perfect world. I'd suggest dipping into it to discover the improvements which could be made if money were no object.

questions.explanation: 导师肯定了这本书内容丰富（huge variety），但立刻批评它呈现方式杂乱无章（haphazard way），连索引都没啥用，对应选项 E 的范围广但组织混乱。
questions.tip: 即使你在考场上没听懂 haphazard（杂乱的）这个难词，只要抓住了转折词 but 以及后面跟着的具体例子“索引没用（index isn't much use）”，也能推断出是排版组织出了问题。
questions.quote: And Resources for Health Visitors? Strangely enough, it's not as helpful as the title suggested. It offers a huge variety of activities and strategies which are great when working with young children, but they're presented in a rather haphazard way, and the index isn't much use either. Be very careful when using it.

23.s: make a short film about a few children

24.s: impact of this on the parents

24.q: Parents may be put under pressure.
24.s: the additional expense could be a worry

25.s: will need to be familiar with

26.s: developments in other countries which may inform our own government's legislation

29.s: what health visiting could be like in a perfect world

30.s: huge variety of activities and strategies

transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear two students talking about the Moa with the lecturer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Thank you all for coming here today to hear about the Moa, a kind of animal which has been extinct for a long time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, first of all, we look at what the Moa are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Moa are nine species of flightless birds endemic to New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were the dominant herbivores in New Zealand's forest, shrubland, and subalpine ecosystems for thousands of years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But around five hundred years ago, they all went extinct.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When I mention extinct animals during ancient times, you may immediately think of dinosaurs, which disappeared around sixty-six million years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fossils of dinosaurs, which we use to study, are large in number, but not many of those of Moa remain, though both animals appeal to people today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the Moa sound more mysterious now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But Sir, I've got a question about these flightless birds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How can we distinguish them from other birds?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's a good question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds are commonly characterized by being warm-blooded, having feathers and wings, usually capable of flight, and laying eggs, while the flightless Moa, until their extinction, were the largest birds in the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their heads are relatively small in relation to their bodies, and they are the only wingless birds lacking even the vestigial wings and substantial tailbones in their family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's impressive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But were they born to be like that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I mean, when they were chicks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, absolutely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's move on to the chicks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The eggs of Moa were laid in nests and incubated for about two months.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The chicks would be well-developed upon hatching and probably would be able to leave the nests to feed on their own almost immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've heard that the male Moa are thought to have incubated the eggs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Is that true?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think there is a possibility for that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've read somewhere that the sex-specific DNA recovered from the outer surfaces of eggshells suggested that these eggs were likely to have been hatched by the male, but we still need to consult more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I have a question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There has been some occasional speculation that the Moa were still alive because someone said they had caught sight of them in New Zealand in the late nineteenth century or even the twentieth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Do you think it's possible?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm not amazed by that, since that kind of thing has been claimed several times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But I find it funny because no reliable evidence of Moa tracks has ever been found, and experts still contend that Moa survival is extremely unlikely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: So what was the reason for the Moa's extinction?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I wonder if it was global warming or some other factors related to their living environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, before the arrival of human settlers in New Zealand, the Moa's only predator was the massive Haas eagle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then the Maori arrived sometime before CE thirteen hundred, and all Moa genera were soon driven to extinction by hunting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What a horrible thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's look at the features of some species of Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The South Island giant Moa may have been the tallest birds ever known, and the second tallest of the nine Moa species is the North Island giant Moa, with the females being markedly larger than males, both in weight and height.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I've heard that the smallest of the Moa birds are the coastal Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Is that right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, you are right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And have you heard about any other kind of Moa before?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know the crested Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The eggs they laid may be larger than others.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As they mainly lived in the remote interior of the Southern Island, their fossils are rare or absent in archaeological sites, and no egg remains have yet been identified.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Are there any species of Moa that have got more fossils?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A considerable amount of remains of the stout-legged Moa exist due to the well-preserved properties of their habitat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their skulls reveal relatively bad vision, a good sense of smell, and a very short bill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there is the eastern Moa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were remarkable in having very long and narrow windpipes, which probably enabled them to make louder, more resonant calls than those of other Moa and had the greatest vocal abilities, so they could communicate when they could not see each other in the forest or at night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They used a range of senses apart from sound in their search for food, such as their sense of smell and vision.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter A, B or C

questions.prompt: What is the thing that makes the Moa similar to dinosaur?
questions.explanation: 讲师提到虽然恐鸟化石不多，但恐鸟和恐龙这两种动物如今都吸引着人们（appeal to people today），对应选项 A 的“公众感兴趣”。
questions.tip: 不要听到 dinosaur 就选 B（灭绝时间），录音明确说了恐龙灭绝于6600万年前，而恐鸟是500年前，两者时间完全不同；也不要选 C，录音说恐鸟的化石并不多（not many）。
questions.quote: Lecturer: Fossils of dinosaurs which we use to study are large in number but not many of those of Moa remain, though both animals appeal to people today so the Moas sound more mysterious now.

options.text: Both are of interest to the public.
Both are extinct at a similar time.
Both left lots of fossil remains.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Moa and other birds?
questions.explanation: 讲师强调恐鸟是唯一一种连退化翅膀（vestigial wings）都没有的无翼鸟，也就是完全没有翅膀骨头。
questions.tip: 虽然提到了头比较小（relatively small），但这是描述特征，不是与其他鸟类区分的“唯一（only）”决定性差异，区分点在于完全无翅。
questions.quote: Lecturer: Their heads are relatively small in relation to their bodies and they are the only wingless birds lacking even the vestigial wings and substantial tailbones in their family.

options.text: no wing bones
a long tail
a smaller head

questions.prompt: What’s the special feature of their chicks?
questions.explanation: 讲师说小恐鸟孵化后发育良好，几乎可以立刻离开巢穴去自己觅食（feed on their own），对应选项 C。
questions.tip: 听到 "leave the nests" 不要想当然选 A（从不回巢），录音只说了离巢觅食，没说不回来；B 选项的“两个月”是孵化期，不是存活期。
questions.quote: Lecturer: The eggs of Moa were laid in nests and incubated for about 2 months. The chicks would be well-developed upon hatching and probably would be able to leave the nests to feed on their own almost immediately.

options.text: They never return to the nests.
Most of them die within two months after birth.
They can find food by themselves.

questions.prompt: What is the tutor’s opinion on male hatching the eggs?
questions.explanation: 针对雄性孵蛋的说法，讲师说“认为有这个可能性”（think there is a possibility），并且 DNA 证据也表明“likely”（很可能）。
questions.tip: 讲师最后补充说“还需要参考更多资料（still need to consult more）”，说明还没有达到 C 选项那样“完全确定（certainty）”的程度，但也绝不是 A 选项的“怀疑”。
questions.quote: Student: I've heard that the male Moa are thought to have incubated the eggs, is that true? Lecturer: I think there is a possibility for that. ...suggested that these eggs were likely to have been hatched by the male, but we still need to consult more.

options.text: He doubts whether it is true or possible.
He thinks it may be true.
He can say with certainty that it is true.

questions.prompt: What is the male student’s response after hearing some people see a Moa recently?
questions.explanation: 注意：题目问的是 male student 的反应，但根据答案 C 和录音内容，这里实际考查的是讲师（回答者）对“有人目击恐鸟”这件事的态度。 讲师说他觉得这事“很滑稽/好笑”（I find it funny），因为没有可靠证据，专家认为不可能。
questions.tip: 听到 "I'm not amazed" 就可以排除 A（惊讶），讲师的态度是觉得这种传闻很可笑，而不是担心或惊讶。
questions.quote: Student: ...Do you think it's possible? Lecturer: I'm not amazed by that since that kind of thing has been claimed several times, but I find it funny because no reliable evidence of Moa tracks has ever been found...

options.text: He is surprised.
He is worried.
He is amused.

questions.prompt: Why did the Moa become extinct?
questions.explanation: 讲师说毛利人（Maori）到达新西兰后，恐鸟很快因为狩猎（hunting）而灭绝，狩猎属于人类干预。
questions.tip: 讲师提到了“arrival of human settlers”，所以不是 A（气候变化）或 C（与其他动物竞争），虽然提到了鹰（Eagle），那是人类到来之前的捕食者，不是灭绝原因。
questions.quote: Lecturer: Well before the arrival of human settlers in New Zealand... Then the Maori arrived sometime before CE 1300 and all Moa were soon driven to extinction by hunting.

options.text: climate change
human interference
competitions with other animals

groups.instructions: Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A-F.

options.text: the much taller female
less fossils left
the biggest eggs
feeding at night
better vocal sound
poor eyesight

questions.prompt: the North Island Giant Moa
questions.explanation: 录音中提到该物种的雌性在体重和身高上都明显比雄性大（markedly larger than males），对应选项 A。
questions.tip: 听到 "tallest birds" 确定是关于身高的描述，重点在于后面提到的性别差异（females larger）。
questions.quote: Lecturer: ...the second tallest of the nine Moa species is the North Island Giant Moa, with the females being markedly larger than males both in weight and height.

questions.prompt: the Crested Moa
questions.explanation: 录音说这种恐鸟的化石很稀少或在遗址中缺失（fossils are rare or absent），对应选项 B（留下的化石较少）。
questions.tip: 不要听到 eggs 就选 C，这里说的是 "no egg remains have yet been identified"（没发现蛋的遗骸），而不是蛋很大。
questions.quote: Student: I know the Crested Moa... Their fossils are rare or absent in archaeological sites and no egg remains have yet been identified.

questions.prompt: the Stout-legged Moa
questions.explanation: 录音提到它们的头骨显示视力相对较差（relatively bad vision），直接对应选项 F。
questions.tip: 这一题是直接的同义替换，bad vision = poor eyesight，只要抓住了 vision 这个词就不容易错。
questions.quote: Lecturer: A considerable amount of remains of the Stout-legged Moa exist... Their skulls reveal relatively bad vision, a good sense of smell and a very short bill.

questions.prompt: the Eastern Moa
questions.explanation: 录音说这种恐鸟有很长很窄的气管，能发出更响亮、更共鸣的叫声（louder, more resonant calls），拥有最强的发声能力（greatest vocal abilities）。
questions.tip: 虽然录音后面提到了 communication（交流）和 smell/vision（嗅觉/视觉），但最突出、描述最多的特征是它的声音能力。
questions.quote: Lecturer: Then there is the Eastern Moa. They were remarkable in having very long and narrow windpipes which probably enabled them to make louder, more resonant calls than those of other Moa and had the greatest vocal abilities.

21.q: Both are of interest to the public.
21.s: both animals appeal to people today.

22.s: wingless birds lacking even the vestigial wings

22.q: What is the difference between Moa and other birds?
22.s: How can we distinguish them from other birds?

23.q: They can find food by themselves.
23.s: able to leave the nests to feed on their own

24.q: He thinks it may be true.
24.s: I think there is a possibility for that.

25.q: some people see a Moa recently

26.q: Why did the Moa become extinct?

transcript.text: You will hear a business student called Ron getting feedback from his tutor on his presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Thanks, Ron, for coming to my office to discuss the presentation you gave yesterday to the Business Management Seminar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll go over what you did with the aim of helping you improve your next presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the topic was the just-in-time, or JIT, supply system used by a lot of manufacturers, 1st in Japan and then in the West, I think.

transcript.text: But actually, one thing I should have made clearer and talked about was the fact that the Americans actually pioneered the idea of just-in-time, though it wasn't called that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Henry Ford and his cars, in fact, at the turn of the 20th century.

transcript.text: And later, a big US supermarket chain used it, and this was where Toyota in Japan got the idea for its car making.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a discussion between two students, Liz from New Zealand and Scott from the UK, who are working on a presentation about a key historical site in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, Scott.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's sort this presentation out then.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The first thing I found out about Stone Point is it's an extinct volcanic cone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You probably know that already, being a New Zealander.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think the tutor allocated us this topic, though, because of Stone Point's significant historical role.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been used by both Māori and European settlers as a place to shelter from attack or launch an attack for centuries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah, and the fact it was an ideal place for building a village, it would have been quite a sheltered spot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I suppose the Māori settled there because they thought the volcanic soil would help their crops grow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, they would have realized the benefits of the soil after a few good harvests, but initially, the fishing opportunities would have been the attraction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You're right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Actually, I also read that Māori regard Stone Point as taonga.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I believe that means a treasured thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Wow, [chuckles] your Māori vocabulary is improving, Scott.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We do have to deal with Stone Point's cultural value for Māori.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's still part of its historical significance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But we need to keep most Māori terminology out of the presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Otherwise, a lot of the international students won't be able to follow us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's a shame.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'm sure they'd be interested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, I am, but yeah, we wouldn't be able to explain it in the time allowed, so I guess we have to stick to English.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Anyway, European migrants turned Stone Point into a lookout point for ships.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then it became a fort, an army base in the late eighteen-eighties, and then during the world wars, the fort was modernized again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's also been a public park sometimes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'd prefer to devote more of the presentation to the military use of Stone Point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There are some great websites about the engines they installed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sorry, I wouldn't go into the technical side if I were you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you start describing mechanical stuff, people will switch off.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think it's more interesting to look at the impact Stone Point had on the people's lives at the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I mean, for example, there were about twenty-five years when they used local prisoners to build the tunnels and the underground rooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They lived there too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah, I guess, if we can find some first-hand accounts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, so let's make a checklist of things to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the early Māori inhabitation section, we have to look at the material we've used again and make sure we know who the writers were and when they wrote it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, that needs work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And for the part about Stone Point being used as a lookout point, I'm sure we can locate some drawings of how Stone Point looked then and the kind of ships coming in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Nice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And what else?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We haven't got a lot of detail for the reconstruction of the fort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We should add some more information about what it was the prisoners were adding to it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll do that bit too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So I'll deal with the section regarding the modernization that happened in the nineteen-thirties and forties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great.

questions.prompt: According to Liz, Stone Point played a key role in local history because

questions.tip: 不要看到 "settlers" 就选 B（登陆点），录音说的是毛利人是在火山爆发几千年后航行到这里的，并未强调这里是唯一的“登陆点”，重点在于它的军事用途。
questions.quote: I think the tutor allocated us this topic, though, (21) because of Stone Point's significant historical role, it's been used by both Maori and European settlers as a place to shelter from attack, or launch an attack, for centuries.

it was developed as a commercial port.

questions.prompt: Scott and Liz agree that Maori originally chose to inhabit Stone Point because of

questions.quote: Well, they would have realised the benefits of the soil after a few good harvests. But initially the fishing opportunities would have been the attraction. You're right.

options.text: its rich soil.
the supply of fish.
available building materials.

questions.prompt: Scott and Liz agree that using Maori terminology in their presentation
questions.explanation: Liz 提议必须避免（keep... out）在演讲中使用大部分毛利语术语，因为国际学生听不懂，Scott 虽然觉得遗憾但也同意了。
questions.tip: Scott 确实说了 "I'm sure they'd be interested"（A选项干扰），但这只是他的愿望，最终结论是为了让人听懂必须 "stick to English"（只用英语）。
questions.quote: But we need to keep most Maori terminology out of the presentation. Otherwise, a lot of the international students won't be able to follow us.

options.text: will be of interest to international students.
is required as a component of their research.
would be best avoided.

questions.tip: 不要听到 "technical side" 就以为要解释它（C选项），Liz 说的是 "I wouldn't go into..."（我不会深入讲...），即建议避开。
questions.quote: Sorry, I wouldn't go into the technical side if I were you. ... (24) I think it's more interesting to look at the impact Stone Point had on the people's lives at the time.

options.text: focus on the human aspect instead.
check the accuracy of specific dates.
explain complex technical language.

questions.explanation: 关于作为公园（public park）的部分，Scott 问边界究竟在哪里（Where is the boundary exactly），并表示要去查实，对应选项中的“核实具体位置”。

questions.prompt: Understanding is Essential
questions.explanation: 录音提到学会了“有效表达自己（express myself）”和“做清晰的汇报（presenting clear reports）”，对应职场沟通（Workplace communication）。
questions.tip: 不要只看课程名字瞎猜，要听课程内容的实际描述（表达、汇报）。
questions.quote: "...taught me how to express myself much more effectively... I also learned a lot about presenting clear reports to my supervisors..."

questions.prompt: Foundations
questions.explanation: 录音强调要理解我们如何“融入整个系统（fit into the overall system）”，对应 PSW 在医疗体系中的角色。
questions.tip: "System" 这个词很大，在这里指代的就是整个 Health Care 体系。
questions.quote: "...we absolutely have to understand how we fit into the overall system."

questions.prompt: The Way We Work
questions.explanation: 录音解释说课程涵盖了“维持身体运作的功能（functions that keep our bodies operating）”，对应生物学方面（Biological aspects）。
questions.tip: 录音先提到了 "psychology"（心理学），但紧接着男生纠正说主要是关于 body operating 的，所以排除心理相关选项。
questions.quote: "...covers the functions that keep our bodies operating well. Even if you're not a PSW, the course is really interesting."

questions.prompt: Residence Care
questions.explanation: 录音提到改造家庭环境让人们能“待在家里（stay there）”并“自助（help themselves）”，对应独立生活（Independent living）。
questions.tip: 听到 "toilets" 或 "equipment" 不要困惑，这些都是为了支持独立生活而举的例子。
questions.quote: "...changes people can make to their homes so they can stay there. Like installing higher toilets... special equipment people can get to help themselves..."

questions.prompt: Dynamics
questions.explanation: 关键词是“缓解焦虑和压力（relieve anxiety and strain）”，直接对应选项 F（处理压力）。
questions.tip: 这里的 "family" 指的是客户的家庭，重点在于解决由此产生的压力，而不是家庭本身。
questions.quote: "You'll learn different strategies to help relieve some of the anxiety and strain that happens within the family."

questions.prompt: The Power With in
questions.explanation: 录音目的是“保持大脑活跃（keep the mind active）”以防“健忘（forgetful）”，对应记忆刺激活动（Memory stimulation）。
questions.tip: 听到 "mind" 容易联想到心理学，但落实到 "not so forgetful" 就锁定了记忆（Memory）。
questions.quote: "...help clients keep the mind active so they're not so forgetful."

25.s: dealing in a better way with people in general

26.s: how we fit into the overall system

27.s: the functions that keep our bodies operating well

28.s: changes people can make to their homes
specialized equipment people can get to help themselves

questions.prompt: Samoa

questions.quote: I think Samoa is the obvious place. It's famous for its very fine cloth called siapo, which is hand-painted with representations of the ancestors. Still today, at the most profound events in life, such as births, funerals, weddings, and the investiture of chiefs, Samoans wear siapo robes to add significance and meaning to the ceremony.

questions.prompt: Tonga
questions.explanation: 汤加的布做起来又快又简单，主要用于做床罩、蚊帐和窗帘等各种家庭日常功能，非常注重实际应用（practical）。

questions.prompt: Cook Islands

questions.quote: Good point. Now, what about Cook Islands tapa? Well, the soil there is poor quality, so the breadfruit tree is often used. One type of thick cloth called tikoru was wrapped around the poles and used to mark the entrances to places of worship, so it was highly regarded in local culture.

questions.prompt: Fiji
questions.explanation: 斐济人曾经把tapa布当成货币（currency）来使用，用来交换其他商品，这是最典型的商业（commercial）功能。
questions.tip: 听到“独木舟”或“猪”千万别脑补成休闲或者单纯的实用，前面的“货币（currency）”和“交换（exchange）”才是判定商业用途的题眼。

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear part of a seminar on ocean research given by a climate scientist.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Thanks to all of you for coming along today to hear about how the robotic float project is helping with ocean research.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, first of all, we'll look at what a robotic float does and its use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's start with the device itself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It looks a bit like a cigar, and it's about one and a half meters long.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More importantly, it's full of equipment that's designed to collect data, so it can help us in building up a profile of different factors which work together within the world's oceans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sounds like a big project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Isn't it too big for one country to undertake?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's quite true.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But this project is a really good example of international cooperation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Over the last five years, scientists from thirteen countries have been taking part in the project and launching floats in their area of ocean control.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And next year, this number will rise to fourteen when Indonesia joins the project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's impressive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But let's move on to how floats work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The operational cycle goes like this: Each of the floats is dropped in the ocean from a boat at a set point and activated from a satellite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then the float immediately sinks about two thousand meters.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's two whole kilometers down in the water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It stays at this depth for about ten days and is carried around by the currents which operate in the ocean at this level.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During this time, it's possible for it to cover quite large distances, but the average is fifty kilometers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what is it actually recording?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Well, at this stage, nothing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But as it rises to the surface, it collects all sorts of data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most importantly, variations in salinity, that's salt levels, and the changes in temperature, a bit like underwater weather balloons.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then when it gets back to the surface, all the data it's collected is beamed up to the satellite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After about five hours on the surface, the float automatically sinks, beginning the whole process again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What happens to the data?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the information is transferred direct to onshore meteorological stations like our one in Hobart, and within four hours, the findings can be on computers, and they can be mapped and analyzed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the seminar, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You say you're building models of the world's ocean systems, but how are they going to be used, and more importantly, when?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Some of the data has already helped in completing projects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, our understanding of the underlying causes of El Niño events is being confirmed by float data.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, another way we're using float data is to help us to understand the mechanics of climate change, like global warming and ozone depletion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's part of an ongoing variability study, but the results are still a long way off.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, this is not the case with our ocean weather forecasting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because we know from the floats what the prevailing weather conditions will be in certain parts of the ocean, we can advise the Navy on search and rescue missions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's happening right now, and many yachtsmen owe their lives to the success of this project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, the float data can help us to look at the biological implications of ocean processes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Would that help with preserving fish stocks?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, and advising governments on fisheries legislation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're well on the way to completing a project on this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We hope it will help to bring about more sustainable fishing practices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be seeing the results of that quite soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It sounds like the data from floats has lots of applications.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yes, it does.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's also a powerful agricultural tool.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If we were aware of what the weather would be like, say, uh, next year, we could make sure that the farmers planted appropriate grain varieties to produce the best yield from the available rainfall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That sounds a bit like science fiction, [laughs] especially when now we can't even tell them when a drought will break.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I agree that this concept is still a long way in the future, but it will come eventually, and the float data will have made a contribution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.

transcript.text: You will hear two students called Jeannie and Dan discussing some research on the effects of music on consumer behavior.

transcript.text: Yes, it's all done.

transcript.text: Congratulations.

transcript.text: Well, at first, I didn't have a specific purpose until one day I read a report that said if appropriate music is played while people are eating, it may cause some changes in their behavior.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So I wanted to carry out a thorough investigation into this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: That's quite unique.

transcript.text: I started by looking for five different restaurants and then went to each of the restaurants to order some food and observe other people.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Oh, you're so lucky.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Subjects are also asked why they choose to dine at a particular restaurant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.text: It's really interesting.

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty.

transcript.text: Great.

transcript.text: I've learned a lot from your research.

transcript.text: I think it's meaningful and innovative.

transcript.text: Thanks for telling me, Jeannie.

transcript.text: You're welcome, Dan.

questions.quote: Well, at first I didn't have a specific purpose until one day I read a report that said if appropriate music is played while people are eating, it may cause some changes in their behaviour, but the report didn't illustrate the changes in detail. So, I wanted to carry out a thorough investigation into this.

the effect of music on eating
the effect of music on the price of food

the music is played at a uniform volume level.
the music is played at a certain time.

a professional dictionary

questions.prompt: Choose TWO are the main reasons given for choosing a restaurant?
questions.explanation:
录音提到人们会在网上对比邻近的餐厅，如果一家店比“竞争对手（rivals）”出色就会被选中。
录音明确指出大多数人选择餐厅取决于“有多少空位（available seats）”，对应选项中的座位容量。
questions.tip:
你可能听到 location（位置）就想选 C，但录音随后反驳说现在大家有私家车，不再担心交通问题了。
你可能听到 service（服务）就选 D，但女生紧接着说只有 12% 的人选这个，并不是“主要”原因。
questions.quote:
What I find interesting, however, is that a large percentage of people say they will compare different restaurants in the neighbourhood on the internet first. If one of them stands out from its rivals, they will choose it.
I thought people would put service first, but that's not the case. Only about 12% of them have chosen this reason. While the majority of respondents think whether they will pick this restaurant depends on how many available seats it has. They think it's terrible to eat in a crowded place.

people don't even notice the music
people will come back again

questions.prompt: nomusic
questions.explanation: 录音说如果没有音乐，人们会觉得餐厅收费太高（charges too much），对应选项 D 的“不值这个价”。
questions.tip: 不要因为听到 too much 就联想到钱多，这里的逻辑是没音乐会让顾客心理平衡感缺失。
questions.quote: The result shows that music has become an indispensable part of restaurants. If people find there isn't any music during the meal, they will think the restaurant charges too much.

questions.prompt: jazz
questions.explanation: 录音提到播爵士乐时，人们倾向于待更久并“点更多的菜（order more food）”，这意味着会花更多钱。
questions.tip: 注意听 stay longer 后面的行为，点更多食物是直接导致“花钱多”的原因。
questions.quote: Yes, most people think that if jazz is being played when eating, they tend to stay at the restaurant longer and order more food to enjoy the music.

questions.prompt: classical music
questions.explanation: 录音说播古典乐时顾客连一分钟都不想多待，会赶紧吃完跑路（hurry away），对应“吃完就走”。
questions.tip: 虽然录音说了 don't like this type of music，但选项 E 的具体行为描述比选项 F 的纯情感描述更贴合语境。
questions.quote: Many customers think if the restaurant plays classical music, they wouldn't like to stay there for another minute, but finish the food quickly and hurry away, because they don't like this type of music at all.

questions.prompt: popmusic
questions.explanation: 录音提到流行乐会增加顾客再次光顾同一家店的可能性（presence at the same restaurant），即“会再回来”。
questions.tip: 听到 popular 不要只联想到选项 F 的喜欢，要听到最后关于 presence（出现/光顾）的结论。
questions.quote: And last, about pop music, it's very popular these days, especially among young people, as I've noticed in restaurants. They like listening to this type of music during their meals. As a result, this greatly increases the possibility of their presence at the same restaurant.

questions.prompt: What skills does Peter want to learn?
questions.explanation: Peter 明确表示，为了未来的职业生涯，他缺乏且需要针对性训练的技能是处理统计数据（dealing with statistics）。

questions.quote: Peter: I still need a lot of practical training in dealing with statistics.

options.text: how to organise ideas
how to handle data
how to write a business proposal

questions.prompt: What is Peter's main strength?
questions.explanation: 文中彼得（Peter）提到自己在“时间紧迫”（pushed for time）时表现更好，且肖娜（Shona）确信他能在一家“压力大”（stressful）、“要求高”（demanding）且有“严格截止日期”（strict deadline）的公司表现出色，这对应了能承受高压/长时间工作的能力。
questions.tip: 选项 A 是最大的干扰项，原文中彼得说“I thought I was a good team leader”（我原以为我是个好领导），但紧接着用“But... mentioned something else”（但是别人指出了其他的）进行了自我否定。
questions.quote: Peter: ...I thought I was a good team leader. But many people I’ve worked with for various projects mentioned something else. They admired that I could stick to the schedule... and indeed, I’m more focused and perform better when I’m pushed for time. Shona: ...Although many employees say it’s stressful working there... I’m sure you’ll excel at this.

options.text: He is a good leader.
He can work long hours.
He can communicate well with many people.

questions.prompt: What will the careers officer help Peter with?
questions.explanation: Peter 决定去找职业官员看他的**个人陈述（personal statement）**并寻求润色建议。
questions.tip: C 选项（Application form）Peter 原本想去，但 Shona 说是非必须的（unnecessary）；A 选项（CV）Peter 说已经在课上学过了，不需要帮忙。
questions.quote: Peter: Then I’ll ask the careers officer to look at my personal statement, and give me some tips on polishing it up.

options.text: CV
personal statement
school application form

questions.prompt: Why did Peter choose the IT business?

questions.quote: Peter: I’m prepared to work in an IT company to keep up with the latest trends.

options.text: to update his knowledge in the area
to be good at presentations
to prepare himself for lectures

questions.prompt: What will Peter do for the next term?

change to another language
discontinue the language course

questions.prompt: According to Dominic, what is surprising about the supermarket garden project?

The cost could be too high.
There may not be enough room.

questions.explanation: 录音中提到男生以前从未考虑过（never considered before）的因素是，由于栖息地没被打断，当地物种的基因多样性得到了改善（genetic diversity... has improved），对应选项B。

questions.quote: It's not surprising that the data reveals a huge drop in the number of road accidents in areas where there are wildlife crossings. That's one of the predicted outcomes. Something I read about in the research, which I'd never considered before, was how the animal populations in these areas are affected. Naturally, more of them survive, but because their habitat is not interrupted too much by the roads, the genetic diversity of local species has improved. That's true.

Animal populations become more genetically diverse.

questions.tip: 你可能会因为听到 only a few countries 去选A，但录音原话是在强调参与的国家“并不多（not so much the size... only a few...）”，以此来衬托重点其实是官方给予社区的帮助大。

how fast cities can convert to 100% renewable energy
how much help is given to participating communities

questions.quote: So, they stop buying products that aren't eco-friendly, like a boycott? No. Actually, it's the opposite of that. It allows businesses to fund initiatives to help protect the environment by boosting their profiles.

options.text: It helps businesses undertake eco-friendly projects.
It encourages people to buy sustainable products.
It creates a sense of community in the people who participate.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Following instructions from their tutor, you will hear two economic students called James and Anna discussing a recent survey about the cost of buying a house in New Zealand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five on page six.

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.

transcript.text: Okay, for this week's assignment, you're going to assess the value survey on house prices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What were the survey's findings?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Was it a reliable survey?

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Sure, James.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, um, first, how did the value survey actually measure the cost of houses?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because there are lots of ways of calculating it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it looked at all houses, didn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: New and old.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So it started with average incomes across the whole workforce and then worked out house prices in relation to that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No, that's a limitation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, what's different about the value survey?

transcript.text: Yeah, there's lots of these surveys every year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Value is actually one of the newer ones, but it stands out because it gives figures for a range of the largest urban centers, which none of the others do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, good point.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then one finding was that New Zealand houses are relatively expensive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Why is that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Because most of them are built of wood, and that's quite cheap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the problem is there are too many regulations and restrictions about where you can build.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if more building sites were created for housing, the costs would come down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's it, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, um, what else?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, what about transport?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I mean, it's all very well to talk about new housing, but how are people going to get there?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Is the survey proposing new roads, new rail networks?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It should be a coordinated approach.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, but the survey didn't mention it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a missed opportunity because a commitment to funding public transport from the outset would improve air quality in our cities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: True.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay then, the next survey, what can we expect?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It'll look at all the same places, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Exactly the same.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the next one will give an idea of the way prices are moving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The government may have to think about how house prices are affecting society.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty on page seven.

transcript.text: Then in the assignment, we need to evaluate how reliable the survey was.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we should look at some of the criticism made by commentators.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So there's the economist Andrew Coleman.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He actually questioned whether the survey was money well spent because it only looked at a single year in isolation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A year when it was difficult to borrow money to buy a house, pushing up costs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So he thought the survey should consider a longer timeframe.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Did you get that article by Professor Massey?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, interesting.

transcript.text: He realized the method used to calculate how much money people had didn't take savings into account.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then Richard Bernard, his criticism was original.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He found out they were using quite outdated software to process all the information they gathered, which was crazy because they actually had the money available for an upgrade.

transcript.text: So even though it was a highly regarded team of people, the way the statistics were interpreted was open to question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then Professor Lowndes, he thought the report was just badly written.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.text: No, it wasn't that.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But she thought the actual properties used should have been revealed, you know.

transcript.text: The process should have been transparent if the people are going to have full confidence in the survey.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So a lot of criticism.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, but this sort of research is often controversial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

questions.tip: A 选项（建造新房的总价）被 James 否定，因为他说调查看了所有房子（New and old）；B 选项（典型家庭能买多大的房子）Anna 明确说 "There’s no information about the size..."。
questions.quote: James: So it started with average incomes across the whole workforce and then worked out house prices in relation to that, I mean to what people were earning.

options.text: the total price of building a new house.
the size of house a typical family can afford.
the price of houses compared to average income.

questions.prompt: Anna says the Value Survey is unusual because
questions.explanation: Anna 指出这项调查之所以独特（stands out），是因为它提供了各大城市中心（urban centres）的数据，这是其他调查没有的。
questions.tip: B 选项说它是最老的（oldest），但原文说它是 "one of the newer ones"；C 选项说每年发布，原文只说每年有很多其他调查，没强调这个频率是它的独特之处。
questions.quote: Anna: ...but it stands out because it gives figures for a range of the largest urban centres, which none of the others do.

options.text: it compares prices in different cities.
it is the oldest survey of its kind.
it publishes its results annually.

questions.prompt: The students decide that New Zealand house prices are high because of
questions.explanation: 两人讨论新西兰房价高的原因，认为是关于在哪里可以建房的规章制度（regulations and restrictions）太多了。
questions.tip: A 选项（建筑材料）被否定，因为木材其实很便宜（quite cheap）；B 选项（建筑工短缺）也被否定，因为有大量的承包商（plenty of contractors）。
questions.quote: James: ...the problem is there are too many regulations and restrictions about where you can build.

options.text: the cost of construction materials.
the shortage of builders.
the rules concerning land use.

questions.prompt: When the students talk about transport, they are
questions.explanation: James 质疑调查是否提议了新路或铁路网，Anna 确认调查根本没有提及（didn’t mention it），这是一个错失的机会。
questions.tip: 两人是觉得调查缺乏协调的交通规划（co-ordinated approach），而不是担心成本（B）或拥堵（C）。
questions.quote: James: Is the survey proposing new roads, new rail networks?... Anna: Yeah, but the survey didn’t mention it.

options.text: concerned there is no plan.
worried about rising costs.
alarmed by increasing congestion.

questions.prompt: The students agree that the next Value Survey will
questions.explanation: James 说下一次调查将会给出价格变动方向（way prices are moving）的概念，即趋势。
questions.tip: A 选项（比较更多地点）被否定，原文说 "It’ll look at all the same places"。
questions.quote: James: But the next one will give an idea of the way prices are moving.

options.text: compare a wider number of locations.
indicate a future trend in house prices.
advise against regulation of house prices.

questions.prompt: Andrew Coleman
questions.explanation: Andrew Coleman 批评调查只孤立地看了一年（single year），他认为应该考虑更长的时间框架。
questions.tip: "Single year" 和 "longer time frame" 对应的就是调查覆盖的时期（Period）。
questions.quote: Anna: ...because it only looked at a single year in isolation... So he thought the survey should consider a longer time frame.

questions.prompt: Professor Massey
questions.explanation: Professor Massey 指出计算人们有多少钱的方法（method used to calculate how much money people had）没有把存款算进去。
questions.tip: "How much money people had" 对应选项中的 "wealth"（财富）。
questions.quote: James: He realised the method used to calculate how much money people had didn’t take savings into account.

questions.prompt: Richard Bernard
questions.explanation: Richard Bernard 发现他们用来处理信息的软件非常过时（outdated software）。
questions.tip: "Outdated software" 对应选项中的 "old-fashioned systems"。(注：你提供的题目选项中写的是 date analysis，应为 data analysis 的笔误，但不影响做题)
questions.quote: Anna: He found out they were using quite outdated software to process all the information...

questions.prompt: Professor Lowndes
questions.explanation: Professor Lowndes 认为报告写得很烂，太长且结构松散（weakly structured）。
questions.tip: "Weakly structured" 直接对应选项中的 "organization of final text"。
questions.quote: Anna: ...the finished report was just too long and weakly structured.

questions.prompt: Maria Darling
questions.explanation: Maria Darling 批评被评估的房产从未被公开身份（never identified），她认为过程应该是透明的，实际房产应该被披露。
questions.tip: "Should have been revealed" 和 "Transparent" 对应选项中的 "access to full information"（公众无法获知完整信息）。
questions.quote: Anna: But she thought the actual properties used should have been revealed...

transcript.text: Okay, shall we now have a look at the projects that different researchers and organizations are working on?

transcript.text: Definitely.
