transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear two law students called Eleanor and Jamie discussing their work on whether the evidence given by people who witness crimes is reliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-six on page five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, Jamie.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've just been reading this book about eyewitness testimonies.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It really goes into how much we can actually rely on what the people who witness crimes actually say and what things influence eyewitness reliability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, I've read a couple of case studies on that too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Can we compare notes?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's fascinating to learn that eyewitness identification is such compelling evidence in both civil and criminal trials.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You mean if a witness says something, generally they're believed?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And reading between the lines, I'd say that when a witness gives evidence in a very self-assured way, everyone takes them at their word, whether they're a doctor who speaks with an assumed authority or the average person in the street.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It doesn't seem to matter as much as their manner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So is that textbook worth reading?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, it's a good book, divided into user-friendly sections.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It refers to case studies, and the conclusions are clearly underlined.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But actually, some of the cases are more than ten years old now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it's the same problem with the survey reports our tutor gave us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But at least they draw on a representative sample.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All the books point out that eyewitness statements are very often unreliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But there can be good reasons for that, like an incident may happen at night in the dark.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Or it happens some way away.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But it's the fact that it can happen in just a split second that makes the witness's account so unreliable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That point's made very strongly in what I've read, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Have you read anything about photo identifications?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, about the procedure and the reliability of witnesses looking at photos of different people and picking out the suspect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The case studies all clearly show how easy it is to sway a witness's choice of photo, even just by the flicker of an eye.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But steps have been taken now to avoid this happening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And are the witnesses told exactly what they have to do?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mostly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But the trouble is, most people focus on the photos and choose the most likely suspect from the bunch and forget about the actual incident and who they saw at the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And I read something about a naive observer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Do you know what that is?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Is it a witness who's never been in a court before?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, I understood it to mean someone who's had nothing to do with the event, and they're asked to look at the photos and pick out the potential suspect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That figures.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then they can see if the photos are a good set and make sure one person doesn't stand out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another thing I read was that witnesses don't like to change their minds once they've made a particular statement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I thought people might worry about the fact that they told a lie in court and think they might be punished in some way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But it's simply that they're afraid of seeming unintelligent or lightweight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: People are reluctant to lose face.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Imagine if a case had been going on for weeks and you suddenly realized you'd got something wrong right at the beginning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-seven to thirty on page six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-seven to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Changing the topic slightly, can I just check with you what you've understood about the problems of interviewing child witnesses when they've witnessed, for example, a robbery?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Did you get the handout about the stages that should be followed when children are interviewed?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The rapport stage, when a relationship between the child and the interviewer is built up, seems to be crucial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But many children fail to say anything that provides any real information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It must be hard for them not to feel a bit scared about being in a formal setting like a court building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Still, it's a good lead-in to open-ended questions where the interviewer carefully sticks to their prepared questions in order to remain neutral.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I can see the point of that, but the handout discusses the issue of children simply not understanding the specialist language used, so the whole interview just gets more puzzling for them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think the stage called closed questions is easier for children to handle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They just have to answer yes or no.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But everything's not so clear cut in a child's world, and abstract concepts such as honesty haven't been fully grasped by young children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You mean they make things up?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Apparently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And in the final stage, closure, where the interviewer has to check anything that hasn't been made clear to them by repeating previous questions, children often become suspicious of the questioner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It must require lots of training to be able to interview children successfully.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, I think...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.tip: 你可能会听到 music 和 running 的干扰，但录音明确否定了听音乐（Nothing like that），并表示很惊讶他们“没有（didn't）”拿跑步来做对比，千万别漏听否定词。
questions.quote: Well, in the experiments, the researchers tested participants' creativity by comparing how many ideas they thought of while they were walking compared to while they were doing other activities. What, like listening to music? Nothing like that. But they did analyze the ideas participants came up with when sitting, both outdoors and inside. What I found surprising was that they didn't compare walking to other forms of exercise, like running, for example.

options.text: sitting.
running.
listening to music.

questions.prompt: Daniel says that in each experiment, there was a different
questions.explanation: 当被问到实验之间有什么不同时，Daniel直接回答说每项实验中“活动的组合方式不同（activities were put together in different ways）”，对应选项中的活动模式（pattern of activities）。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没跟上 activities 这个词的同义转述而陷入犹豫，注意识别 put together in different ways 其实就是在表达 pattern（模式/组合）。
questions.quote: Right. So what was the difference between the experiments? Well, in each one, the activities were put together in different ways.

options.text: type of control group.
pattern of activities.
way of selecting participants.

questions.prompt: Daniel thinks the experiment with words is
questions.explanation: Daniel认为这个文字实验中，学过语言的人会“更有优势（at an advantage）”，说明实验本身是偏向特定人群的（biased in favour of certain people）。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到Katie质疑基于研究者观点的公平性而想选C，但题目问的是“Daniel”的看法，做题时一定要分清说话人的身份。
questions.quote: I just don't see how the experiment is fair. Why? Because the conclusions are based only on the researcher's opinion? I think it's more that anyone who'd studied language would be at an advantage.

options.text: biased in favour of certain people.
a good indicator of creativity.
open to personal interpretation.

questions.prompt: What is Katie and Daniel’s attitude to the experiment on focused thinking?
questions.explanation: 两人都认为没有足够的证据来支持实验结论（conclusions），并且对做出这样的论断感到犹豫（hesitate），说明他们对结论持极其谨慎的态度。
questions.tip: 录音中Daniel特意提到即使他们的方法（methods）是合理的（sound），这直接帮你排除了对实验方法感到困惑的B选项。
questions.quote: What evidence did they have? Well, that's it. I don't think there was enough evidence to support their conclusions, even if their methods were sound. Well, I'd certainly hesitate before making such a bold statement.

options.text: they are doubtful about its aims.
they are confused by its methods.
they are cautious about its conclusions.

questions.prompt: Katie thinks that the best way forward is to consider
questions.explanation: 面对未来的研究方向，Katie明确强调她个人最想了解的是影响创造力的“根本原因（fundamental reason）”，完美对应选项中的 cause。
questions.tip: A选项（测试其他运动）和C选项（应用到工作中）都是Daniel提出的建议，且C选项更是被Katie当场反驳为“次要的（secondary）”，审题时要死死盯住问的是“Katie”的观点。
questions.quote: I suppose to move forward with this, they'll need to test other ways people keep fit, like swimming. That would be useful, but personally, I'd like to know more about the fundamental reason for the effect on people's creativity. That would be good. Then it could be applied more widely in work, for example. Again, that's secondary, really.

options.text: whether other types of exercise affect creativity.
the cause of the improvement in creativity.
how the results can be applied to creativity in real life.

questions.quote: What about the effect of footwear? Hmm, hadn't thought of that. Well, I've read that shoes with thinner soles were found to be better for people's joints. It even made the skeletal structure tougher.

questions.quote: And what about the effect that walking has for elderly people? Better balance, by any chance? More than that. It had a positive effect by helping them maintain their body clock's natural rhythm, both when going to bed and waking up.

questions.explanation: 录音提到老师写完单词后，会做一些模仿动作（mime）来传达意思（convey the sense），完美对应选项D的“展示含义（Demonstrate meaning）”。
questions.tip: 你可能会把录音举例的“run on the spot（原地跑步）”当成一项单纯的体育活动，而没理解这只是为了“convey the sense（表达意思）”。
questions.quote: I thought I'd introduce the topic by writing the word energy on the board and reinforcing the spelling and the pronunciation. Then I'll do a little mime, you know, run on the spot or something to convey the sense.

questions.explanation: 录音顺着教学流程说到，老师接下来准备了一组简单的陈述句（a set of simple statements），对应选项G的“展示句子（Present sentences）”。
questions.tip: 这里的教学步骤比较长，你可能会把前面提到的写出问题（write the question）误当成这一步的答案而选错。
questions.quote: Yes, that's what I was going to do. Then I've produced a set of simple statements like, energy makes cars move along the road, and energy makes our bodies grow.

questions.explanation: 老师说明会把句子写在黑板上，然后让学生抄写到他们的笔记本上（copy them out in their notebooks），动作要求直接对应选项C。
questions.tip: 你可能会听到老师要“read them out loud（大声读出来）”就去选项里找听或读的动作，而漏听了紧接着针对学生的指令是“copy（抄写）”。
questions.quote: Are you going to give them out as a handout or write them up on the board? First, put them up on the board, and then I'll read them out loud, and I'll get the pupils to copy them out in their notebooks. I'll also ask them to think up one more similar statement by themselves and add it to the list.

questions.explanation: 贴出图片后，老师明确会让学生弄清楚这些图片应该以什么顺序出现（work out what order the pictures should come in），“order（顺序）”对应选项A的sequence。
questions.tip: 录音里罗列了一大堆图片内容（太阳、植物、食物等），你可能会陷入这些名词细节里，而没抓住动词短语“work out what order”才是任务核心。
questions.quote: After that, I thought I'd vary things a bit by sticking some pictures up of things like the sun, and plants, and food, and petrol, and a running child. And I'll get the pupils to work out what order the pictures should come in in terms of the energy chain.

questions.explanation: 录音提到最后老师做了一个填空练习来分发给学生（give out），“give out”是选项E“Distribute（分发）”的同义替换。
questions.tip: 你可能会因为没听懂“gap fill exercise（填空练习）”其实就是“worksheet（工作纸/练习卷）”的具体形式而不敢选E。
questions.quote: Yes, I think they'd enjoy that. And to finish off, I've made a gap fill exercise to give out. They'll be doing that individually, and while they're writing, I'll walk around and check their work.

questions.tip: 听到 "on the right" 就要把目光移到最右边，不要被中间复杂的结构干扰。
questions.quote: Eve: That's the overflow tank. That container on the right.

groups.instructions: Label the diagram below

options.text: A
B
C
D
E
F

questions.prompt: inlet pipe
questions.explanation: 进水管（inlet pipe）位于系统最后端的地面低处（low to the ground right at the back），对应图中最后面的管口 D。
questions.tip: 一定要找准方位 "at the back"（在后面），不要跟前面的出水管 C 弄反了。
questions.quote: Speaker: First, the inlet pipe... You'll find it positioned low to the ground right at the back end of the system.

questions.prompt: treadle
questions.explanation: 踏板（treadle）是沿着机器顶部（top of the machine）延伸的长条踏板，对应图中顶部的长木梁 E。
questions.tip: 不要看下面的支撑结构，录音强调是 "runs along the top"（沿着顶部走）的部件。
questions.quote: Speaker: Next, we have the treadle. This is the long pedal that runs along the top of the machine...

questions.prompt: cylinder
questions.explanation: 气缸（cylinder）是中间两个垂直的腔体之一，形状像高高的管子（tall tube），对应图中的圆柱体 B。
questions.tip: B 是外面的管子，A 是里面的杆子，听到 "vertical chambers"（垂直腔体）选 B。
questions.quote: Speaker: Now let's look at the cylinder. This is one of the two vertical chambers... shaped like a tall tube.

questions.prompt: piston
questions.explanation: 录音明确说活塞（piston）在气缸里面（Inside the cylinder），并且能够上下移动（moves up and down），对应A。
questions.tip: 你可能会在听到“moves up and down”这种动作描写时才反应过来去找，一定要注意前置的方位词“Inside the cylinder”才是锁定答案的最快关键。
questions.quote: Inside the cylinder, we find the piston. This part moves up and down rapidly to create the suction needed to pull water into the cylinder and then push it out. It's a rod-like device connected to the treadle by a series of levers.

questions.prompt: discharge pipe
questions.explanation: 录音提到排放管（discharge pipe）位于机器靠近底部（near the base）的侧面（on the side），对应C。
questions.tip: 这里的排放管容易和前面的进水管混淆，你必须盯紧“on the side”和“near the base”这两个决定性的空间特征。
questions.quote: Finally, the discharge pipe. This pipe is located on the side near the base of the machine. Once the water is pressurized, it exits through the discharge pipe and flows into channels that carry it to the fields.

21.s: container on the left is where you put the waste

29.s: part moves up and down rapidly

questions.explanation: 教授明确指出，除了 classical history（古典历史） 之外，考古学可以和任何学科结合。
questions.tip: Anthropology（人类学）是 Paul 问能否结合的学科，教授说是可以的（Yes），所以不能填；只有 classical history 是不行（apart from）的例外。
questions.quote: Professor: You can combine it with any other subject apart from classical history.

questions.explanation: 教授解释说第一学期有三个模块，所有的都是 compulsory（必修的）。
questions.tip: Optional（选修）是干扰项，教授说要到明年（next year）才会有选修模块。
questions.quote: Professor: All of them are compulsory. We don’t offer optional modules till next year.

questions.explanation: 第一个模块主要关注从特定文物中学到什么，它的名字叫 Object Matters。
questions.tip: 注意首字母大写，且 Matters 是复数形式（或动词第三人称单数形式作为标题），需完整听写。
questions.quote: Professor: It’s called Object Matters and it’s taught by Dr Morris.

questions.explanation: 教授列举了该模块涉及的流程：记录材料，然后是 classification（分类），接着是解释数据。
questions.tip: 注意词性，前后 Recording, Interpretation 都是名词性质，所以中间也要填名词 Classification。
questions.quote: Professor: First of all, recording material, then classification, then interpretation of the data.

questions.explanation: Paul 问是否有考试，教授回答说没有，全部分数基于 coursework（平时作业/课程作业）。
questions.tip: 题目问 Assessment by...，Exam 是干扰项，教授明确说了 "No"（不是考试）。
questions.quote: Professor: No, it’s all based on coursework.

questions.explanation: 第二个模块的名字叫 Towns and Cities（城镇与都市）。
questions.tip: 听到 "called" 后面紧跟的就是模块名称，注意首字母大写和复数形式。
questions.quote: Professor: ...that's the one called Towns and Cities, is taught by our department head Professor Elliott.

questions.explanation: 教授介绍该模块是关于建筑环境的 origins（起源） 以及它们是如何发展的。
questions.tip: 注意 plural（复数）形式，录音中 origins 带有清晰的 's' 尾音。
questions.quote: Professor: ...the module's about the origins of built environments and how they developed.

questions.explanation: 虽然是通过考试评估，但教授强调这是一个 oral（口头） 考试而不是笔试。
questions.tip: Written（笔试）是干扰项，注意转折词 "rather than"（而不是），重心在前面的 oral。
questions.quote: Professor: But you may be pleased to know it's an oral rather than a written exam.

questions.tip: Lectures 是干扰项，教授明确说 "There aren't any lectures"；题目中 "50%" 对应原文的 "half"。
questions.quote: Professor: Oh, it's half lab work and half seminars.

transcript.text: Section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear two archeology students, called May and Thomas, talking about the excavations they have been involved in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi, Thomas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Did you have a good time in Turkey?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hi, May.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I had a great time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But I have to say, although I've always been keen on being an archeologist, before I went on an excavation, I used to find some of the things we did in class totally mystifying.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Me too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before I did my trip to Egypt, I was often irritated at not being able to picture exactly what the lecturers meant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were always so excited about everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We did a lot of practical stuff on the excavation, which I really needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Was it harder than you expected?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, mostly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I learned a lot more about the rules of archeology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I was really taken aback by how precise you have to be with your data collection and recording.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I took loads of photographs, and they proved very useful, and the drawing went well too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, I think I'm quite good with the camera.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I minded about the recording though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I had no idea it would take so much time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Did you find anything particularly interesting when you were digging?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I did, actually.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I had to dig a trench in part of the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Interestingly, there weren't any bits of pottery there like you would expect to find, but I did get out some pieces of cloth and what looked like one or two silver beads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But our team leader said that they weren't.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They were probably lead weights for weaving.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What about you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I didn't find anything myself, but quite a few of the other students did.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What I enjoyed was trying to identify what crops the people who had once lived in the area had grown.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They seemed to have had a much better diet than I expected: fish and wheat, as well as oats, honey, and fruit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Lots of different things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes, it's amazing, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And from measuring the bones in one of the sites, we found that the people were actually taller and had better teeth than the people who live in the area today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Probably due to less carbohydrates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How were the people you had to work with?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: My team was great.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They were made up of people my age from all over the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It was good to work with them, lots of fun, and they taught me a lot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It was tough for us all, though, getting up at dawn every day and being out until late afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Oh, that's true enough.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We were all exhausted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I'd like to have an international team next time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mine was mainly made up of English and Americans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I enjoyed the field school, but everyone was much more experienced and older than I was.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was a bit scary.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: You know, there's gonna be a question about the excavation projects in our test next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Should we just run through it for practice?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our team leader was very strict about following the right procedure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He used to say, "Never excavate anything if you're not sure it's worth excavating."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I think that when you've decided where to excavate, you go to the site hut and get whatever tools you need, then clean the area so you know exactly how big it's going to be.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And you need to make sure you can remember what the site looks like before you begin digging.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think photos are probably best for that rather than drawings at this stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I agree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You then attach them to a record sheet, which you get from the team leader, remembering to put in the site code, unit number, and time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So much red tape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You seem to spend half the time marking rather than digging.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's true.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think you then have to draw up a detailed plan of where you're digging and then measure the limits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And this is all before you actually start digging.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so far so good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now you can start with the trowel, but first you have to get soil samples, and you keep them for further analysis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anything that you don't think is useful, you leave in place on the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, and if you make any finds, that is any object you retrieve, including animal bone, stone, as well as artifacts, they should all be registered and labeled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And then you put them in a plastic bag and return them to the site hut.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And remember to leave the tools and site hut as you would expect to find them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Ha.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Looks like we've learned something after all.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a conversation between an art history student called Terence and his tutor about the student's plan for a class presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, Terence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I've looked through your preliminary outline and notes for the presentation on the art of the Ife region in Africa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's in Nigeria, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'm concentrating on Ife sculptures from the twelfth to the fifteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How did you get interested in that?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know there have been some recent articles in the journals about African sculpture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I've read most of those now, but initially, I got my introduction to this at a special display at the City Museum a few years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I just happened to be there and saw these works and thought they were fantastic, and I even went to Nigeria last summer to see more of them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I've seen the photos for your presentation, and I must say the sculptures are gorgeous portrayals of what appear to be kings and queens.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I decided to concentrate on those as they're the most typical.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They're interesting because they're so naturalistic, unlike the abstract figures we often associate with African art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There's also a lovely sculpture of a mudfish and one of the scaly crocodile, but I didn't get very good pictures of those, so I won't spend long on them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what was the city of Ife like when these works were made?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It, it's on the Niger River, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The boat traffic's what made it a center of commerce then, as it still is today, but nowadays it's better known as the home of a big university.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Speaking of modern day Ife, tell me about your trip.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: [chuckles]
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I was incredibly lucky to be able to get enough money to go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: My parents encouraged me, but they couldn't afford to send me.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I applied for a grant from the Arts Council, and in the end, I got it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I also wrote a series of articles about my trip for the local newspaper, but I didn't get any money for that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I was just pleased to get them published.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the highlight of the trip?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That had to be meeting a professor working on the site in Ife who had been a young boy when they first discovered the sculptures by accident at a building site in nineteen thirty-eight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He had been working at the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Of course, I also got to talk to lots of artists who are working there today, and I got to try my hand at making a little sculpture myself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions twenty-five to thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, let's see what you might do to improve what you're planning for your presentation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: About the sculptures themselves, I think I need to add as much as possible about the details of the way they were made.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Of course, I can't add anything about the artists who made them because nobody really knows anything about them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: All good points, and you've certainly said enough about what the sculptures depict, uh, what the subjects are.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's well covered.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I'd make some bigger photos of them so you can clearly see the fine detail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And I would limit my personal reactions to these works of art if I were you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I know you think they're fantastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: [chuckles] You're right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'll contain my enthusiasm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: [chuckles]
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What about the section of the presentation which I call history?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'd like to go into more depth about the history of that whole area, you know, in the countries around Nigeria.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That would make the presentation stronger, but I think you've covered the situation regarding the rulers of the country quite well, and you've got plenty already about what the Ife people were doing then and the way their society was structured.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And in fact, I think you could cut out the bit about modern Nigerian history because it's not relevant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I agree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That doesn't fit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But perhaps I should concentrate more on the religious beliefs since all these sculptures do seem to have some kind of religious association.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I can lend you a book on that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, probably the part the class will find most interesting is the report of your trip to Nigeria and the research you did there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, so I gather you managed to use the university library in Ife.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As soon as I'd explained why I wanted the information, that was no problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They couldn't have been more helpful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There were some interesting accounts of how the first sculptures were found and what happened to them, which I want to include.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What struck me when I saw the sculptures in Nigeria is the extent to which twentieth-century European artists were influenced by them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But that's beyond the scope of my presentation, I think.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What about the sources of the materials they used?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You don't mention that anywhere.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I didn't manage to find out much about that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I want to cover the theories about who the original sculptors were, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The idea that a lot of them may have been made by the same person.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's very interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is, isn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, thanks for all the advice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now I think I need to work-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part three.

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a woman who helps run a program called Young Explorer talking to participants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to read questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: All right, shall we start?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's good to see so many people keen to participate in our Young Explorer Program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I think that at this meeting we have groups from twelve different high schools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I can promise you that while it's challenging, it's also going to be a lot of fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Young Explorer Program offers some unique opportunities to participants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the program, you'll be trekking through forests or maybe mountain tracks or perhaps kayaking along the coastline.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It can be a tough few days, but this part of the program really gives your group an occasion to work as a team.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some kind words and encouragement can go a long way, whether it's convincing someone they can walk the last five miles or helping them fit everything back inside their backpack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No one's in charge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's all about cooperation, and please don't see it as a race.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are going to be moments when there is disagreement about which way to go or where to camp for the night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But here's the chance to listen properly to the opinions of others and reach a decision that's best for everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's an opportunity not many other programs provide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later this morning, you need to choose a weekend when you can attend some preliminary training.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A number of practical subjects will be covered to ensure you get the most out of your four-day trek.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, everything you eat and drink you'll have to take with you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll also have to use a portable stove and the fuel it requires.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll make sure you know how to use that safely during the training session.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We don't want you or the food to get burnt or for you to accidentally set light to any trees.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Training will also include learning how to read a map and use a compass, so you can head in the right direction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll also need to know how to put up a tent and where to put it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, putting it next to a river or stream might seem like a good idea, but there are plenty of reasons not to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, there are six tracks on your list, and your group can decide which track it wants to take.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Each of them are about the same distance, but very different in other respects.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first one, North Face, that's one of my favorite tracks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It takes you high up into the mountains and the view is stunning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But we've just heard that some maintenance work is taking place, unfortunately, and so people aren't allowed to use it at the moment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the other tracks are very interesting too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You've got Blue River, which I'd thoroughly recommend, but you need to keep an eye out when you're walking that track.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's easy to slip on the rocks when you're crossing the river, and you do have to cross it several times.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there's Pioneer Track, which takes you through some native forest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You follow the track for about a day and a half, and then it comes to an end at a town called Richmond.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It starts up again on the other side of town, and the rest of the route is along the coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You might also consider Edgewater.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You get to see some beautiful lakes and birdlife.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only thing I'd say, though, is that it's very popular and you'll probably come across a number of other groups out walking on the way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Number five on the list is the Murray Track.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That one is certainly quite challenging.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are some very steep sections, and at some points you'd be walking right next to the cliff edge on a very narrow path.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's definitely a track where caution needs to be taken.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great views, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And last but not least is Lakeside Track, which, as the name suggests, takes you along one of our biggest lakes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has some terrific camping spots, but that also means it's a bit of a tourist attraction and you could well be sharing the track with many other visitors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, it's up to you which track you decide to take.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers to Part two.

transcript.text: Well, thank you all for coming along to this talk about our new waterfront development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The council has developed the old boat harbor to provide a new area of leisure facilities right here on the city's waterfront, and we want to encourage local people to visit the new development.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, I'll start with some background.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Long before the harbor was built, the 1st building on the site was put up by Sir Michael Grayson.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He'd been working in Asia for a time, and when he came home, he began developing the city along this part of the coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, there was a problem with the site.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Because the land was low-lying, whenever there was a storm, large waves would break on the shore, which could be destructive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So Grayson built a wall along the beach to protect the land behind it, and that solved the problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, in 1915, the land here became more valuable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some companies were not doing very well financially, so the government wanted to increase local business activity, and they did this by constructing a better road connecting this site to the city center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That had an important impact, and later on, over the following years, it led to additional migration to this part of the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One obvious change came in the 1920s when the 1st boat harbor was built here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The water was too shallow for large ocean liners carrying people, so these continued to use the main wharf further south.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the smaller boats that went out each day to catch snapper, tuna, and other species to feed the city started to use this as their port.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Defense Force ships, of course, already had their own base further up the coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, in the 1930s, warehouses were built around the harbor, and it was made deeper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's because international trade was increasing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's true that some parts of the economy, like sheep farming, were in decline, but forestry was a major growth sector.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The timber was brought here by train, kept in the new buildings, then shipped to foreign countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, why do we need this latest redevelopment?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, over the years, the harbor had become run-down.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They talked about doing something for 10 years before anything actually happened.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, the project started when a team of designers began work and a consultation plan was drawn up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And now, 14 years after the project started, the new waterfront area is open to the public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We hope that nothing will need to be done now for another 25 years when the harbor wall will need upgrading.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have to say, some parts of the redevelopment were quite difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We were lucky with the steamship because it had already been restored.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we really wanted were some traditional trams, so we bought some from another city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it turned out to be a long process, and they needed a lot of modification for our system, the hardest thing we had to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We decided against renovating the old bridge and instead replaced it with a modern one, which was very simple in comparison.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 17 to 20.

transcript.text: So, the open-air cinema.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They show movies on a big outdoor screen, after dark, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a lot of fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it's up on North Wharf.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look in the northwest corner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a circular enclosure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can't miss it.

transcript.text: It's close to South Gate.

transcript.text: Find Pier One, and it's right down at the end of that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the Maritime Museum is well worth a visit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's the only one of its sort in the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk given at a community meeting about local waste collection services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to read questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Hi folks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name is Loretta Johnston, and I’m here from the Baltimore Department of Public Waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for coming out to our community meeting tonight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I’ve got a few words to say about the waste collection here in Baltimore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, there’s the sorted collection bins themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They’re made of sturdy, solid material, so none of your trash can seep out or puncture the bin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, since these things sit out on the curb overnight, rain or shine, they have to be waterproof.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can’t have water getting up in it and filling up the bin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember to pay attention to which bin is which and sort your waste accordingly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You should have a blue or green bin for recyclable garbage, a yellow bin for unrecyclable garbage, and a red bin for toxic waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our citywide waste management is divided into two services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first is commercial waste collection, or trash collection from buildings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The majority of building waste is paper, which goes in the blue or green bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You’ll notice in your office buildings there are signs that warn you not to overfill these bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: All that paper adds up, and an overflowing bin is infinitely harder for collectors to carry to the truck and empty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Aside from paper, another large source of building waste is metals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Metals such as tin and aluminum can be put in the yellow recycle bins, but metals like lead and copper should be disposed of in the red bins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These heavy metals are harmful to the environment and exacerbate our city’s existing pollution problem.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That’s about all the information you need for building waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on to the second service, household waste collection is probably what you primarily think of when you think of what we do here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of the same guidelines apply: the sorting is the same, etc.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please remember to keep garbage like kitchen waste in a plastic bag.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It makes collection easier and lessens the abominable rotten trash smell.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So, after we take your trash away, what happens to it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We take all the garbage to one of a number of garbage disposal plants, each of which is located in the middle of an open space of some sort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No one wants to have their home or office right next door to a waste disposal plant, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Waste is collected and then disposed of once every four weeks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of trash can build up in that time, so we’re in the process of developing a plan to fund collection more frequently.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Ideally, it would be collected weekly, but we will likely have to settle for biweekly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The garbage trucks make their rounds to clear the bins at night in order to avoid traffic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I’m sure you’ve seen how much waste your own household produces in a given week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now imagine all the trash produced by all the households in Baltimore.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It’s a lot, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It may surprise you that this amount is only marginal compared to commercial waste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yep, the main waste producers are actually businesses, industrial facilities, retail, and offices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Hard to believe humans produce that much waste, right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No wonder we have pollution problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, after all incoming waste is sorted, recyclables are sent to a recycling plant, while garbage and toxic waste are transported to their respective areas of the plant for treatment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Items such as stones, which should not be disposed of in our bins, are separated out and discarded.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once the trash has undergone the treatment process, it is compacted and disposed of with all the other trash.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And finally, when the landfill space is full, it is buried deep underground, and in time, something new is built on the land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That’s everything about waste collection.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for listening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Are there any questions?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Section 2.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a tour guide talking to some tourists who are going on a walking holiday in Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen on page three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Well, good evening, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name's Gary Payne, and I'll be the leader for your walking holiday in Spain.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the purpose of this evening's meeting is for us all to get to know each other in advance and for you to ask any questions you may have about the holiday.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I'll begin by telling you a little bit about what to expect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the ferry crossing from England to Santander in Spain takes about twenty-four hours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be sailing on the Prince Regent, which was first launched in the 1980s.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As well as the crew of one hundred and sixty, it can accommodate about two thousand people and six hundred cars, and it sails at an average speed of thirty-seven kilometers an hour.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There'll be an onboard map on one of the decks which charts the ship's progress during the voyage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although our minibus will be on one of the vehicle decks in the boat, access to these decks is prohibited during the crossing, so when you leave our bus, you'll have to take everything that you're likely to need with you, like toiletries or books and magazines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In fact, it's probably a good idea to put these things in a separate bag beforehand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You shouldn't need snacks on board as meals are provided and they're quite substantial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you don't feel well or get a headache, you can get tablets from me.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I always carry an adequate supply.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, once we're in Spain, we'll be based at a hostel in a small village called La Vega de Lebana, about a hundred and twenty kilometers from Santander.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a very picturesque area that's retained a lot of its traditional industry and culture.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The hostel accommodation's fairly simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are bunk beds, and each room holds four to eight people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the bathrooms and showers are of a high standard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The hostel residents have the use of tennis courts nearby if you feel like a game.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be given breakfast and an evening meal at the hostel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In general, the hostel is relaxed, but there are a few rules which the owners enforce strictly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Smoking is not allowed anywhere inside the building, and food and drink is banned in the dormitories.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Any chairs or tables which you take outside into the gardens must be returned every evening to their original place.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, and finally, the doors are locked after midnight out of consideration for other guests who are trying to sleep.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, that's enough about travel and accommodation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But before I move on, I should say something briefly about equipment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a list in the guidebook you've been sent, but I'll just elaborate on one or two items.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, boots.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Make sure that the ones you bring have thick soles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the most important thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Don't bring trainers for walking in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Apart from anything else, they're dangerous because they slip.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's important to bring spare socks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then about waterproofs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'd strongly advise you not to come with anything heavy, you know, with a thick lining.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The ideal things are those lightweight ones because they fold up small, and although they do keep the wind out, they don't make you too hot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Next, sun cream.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is absolutely essential.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And regarding the strength, make sure you get what's known as total block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Even factor twenty-five isn't good enough for those latitudes in July.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, uh, let's see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bring a folder to keep your map and other papers in, you know, one of those plastic ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's not very likely to rain, but if it does, [chuckles] you'll find it soaks everything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So that's the practicalities over.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let me tell you a little bit about the area in Spain where we'll be walking, the Picos de Europa.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a very popular area for tourists because of its spectacular peaks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although they're only twenty-five kilometers from the sea, the highest peaks are more than two thousand six hundred meters high and have year-round snow caps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the highest peaks, you've got alpine plants that are only free of their snow cover for a few months a year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then you've got meadows that are full of wildflowers at certain times of the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then the northern slopes are covered by woodlands, giving homes to rare species such as wolves and bears.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And because of the variety of plant life which survives in that part of Europe, due to the traditional way of life there, you-
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.

transcript.text: Welcome to Student Life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's spring, and many of you may be thinking about arranging work for the long vacation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So on today's program, Roger Anwell reports on a survey we conducted into the pleasures and problems of vacation jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Roger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you, Sarah.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, the first thing to say is that by far, the majority of students we surveyed did just three types of jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: All of these obviously had their advantages and disadvantages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Starting with stocktaking in supermarkets,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: the thing that students said they enjoyed most about this job was the traveling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They were often required to go to branches to do their stock takes, and this was regarded as an interesting plus.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The main negative, however, was that they tended to find the job tiring with long hours spent on their feet and climbing high shelves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, one thing we did ask the students in our survey was whether they had any recommendations for other people taking on their job, and they said, perhaps not surprisingly, "Get good shoes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That's the only way you can keep going."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another job which lots of students did was office work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And the positive feature of this actually rather surprised me, until I remembered what a hot summer it was last year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Lots of students named air conditioning as the best thing about office work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The downside, which many talked about, was wearing formal clothes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Obviously, this didn't go down too well with students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The advice most people gave was to select a large office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That way, you have more variety of social contacts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Otherwise, the work can get very boring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The third job, which had attracted large numbers of students, was as a theme park attendant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And again, I got a surprise here because the big plus people talked about was good pay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, [chuckles] it must have improved since my day, I must say.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Anyway, the downside I did recognize: having to deal with difficult customers, especially in the heat when tempers get frayed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Not easy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And people said that it was a good idea to live nearby 'cause there's a lot of shift work, and you don't have to worry about transport at difficult times of the day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty on page five.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So those were the findings from the survey on the most common student jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But not all student jobs have to be mundane and boring.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: One of the students who responded in our survey spoke at length about his amazing job as a zoo attendant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Peter Marshall had read about work opportunities on the zoo website and just went along with a friend to talk to someone in personnel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He was offered a job there and then, as easy as that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In previous years, he'd done singularly unexciting shop work, so he was very pleased to be doing such original work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He ended up working for just under three months, which was actually slightly more than he'd anticipated and meant that he had to miss part of university term time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But he said it was well worth it because he thinks he's found his future career path as a result of this experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He loved working on the educational side, in particular, helping young kids understand about the animals in their natural environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He said it was the most intriguing thing he'd ever done.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: He tells us, though, that with final exams coming up, he won't be able to do any paid work this coming vacation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So why don't you apply?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: [chuckles] If you're interested in getting further information about the findings of the survey...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk about a summer sports camp for people who are interested in working there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome to this talk about the UK Summer Sports Camp.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm going to tell you about our summer sports camp for children and something about the children who come.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Later on, I'll tell you how to apply if you'd like to work with us this year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So please be patient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Feel free to interrupt if there's anything you don't understand about the way the camp is administered, though if you could save any questions about the work itself until the end, that would be good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The UK Summer Sports Camp offers courses for kids aged six to sixteen, which focus on a wide range of sports and activities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our aim is to provide a fun, safe experience for kids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The reason we're successful is because parents trust us and send their children to us summer after summer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We aren't the cheapest camp around, uh, which might put some people off, but we make sure our team are caring and enthusiastic, and that's why parents want their children to keep coming back rather than because of the facilities on offer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great as they are, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We think our summer camp is special in a number of ways.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have students from all over the country, not just the local area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We run all the activities you'd expect in a summer camp, arts and music as well as sports, but we also have special coaching for those who might be able to make a career in their chosen sport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What will your role be if you come and work with us then?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We need lots of people who are willing to teach the activities, but we also have non-coaching roles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What we particularly like this summer are people who are willing to be in charge of looking after our younger kids, making sure they're happy and have someone to go to if they have any problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We usually need a few cooks too, though we don't need anyone extra for our office at the moment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This year, I'm very pleased to introduce a new role at the camp: camera person.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We need someone with great video and photography skills to record the fun everyone has.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll supply first-class equipment, but we need you to supply your creative abilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're interested in this role, come and talk to me at the end.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, you probably want to know about working conditions, hours, and pay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Um, this depends on your role.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can choose to work daytimes, evenings, or weekends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Daytime coaching roles pay the highest wages because of the sports skills required and the longer hours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you choose to work in the kitchen, your hours of work will be either at breakfast and lunch or at dinner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cleaners work in the mornings before the camp activities start at ten AM, so not too early.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you do work with us, there are lots of benefits in addition to the money.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Whether you're teaching a sport or not, you'll be given access to all our facilities, which means you can have a swim or play a football match without having to pay anything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have an Internet cafe where there's a small charge for access, and, uh, we also provide discounted meals in our canteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll give everyone UK summer camp T-shirts, which we'll expect you to wear when working, and if you wish, we also have some cool sports bags which are available for a small fee.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what do we expect from you?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll be glad to hear that we don't need to see any formal certificates.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you've worked with kids before, that would be an advantage, but it isn't essential.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, you need to be sociable and enjoy meeting people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There'll always be a supervisor available who you should talk to before making any important decisions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We can't accept applications from people under the age of eighteen, I'm afraid.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But if you haven't got there yet, don't worry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's always next time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

title: The Mc.Fadden Hiking And Nature Trail

transcript.text: Part 2.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear the warden of a nature trail talking to a group of people who are interested in hiking on the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: 1st, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm Susan Meyer, trail warden for the McFadden Hiking and Nature Trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me tell you a bit about the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The trail is 25 miles long, running roughly east to west.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To hike it, you may start at either end of the trail or in between.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can hike the whole length of the trail or just a couple of miles, because there are 20 entry points along the trail, each connected to public roads by short paths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For hikers coming from Johnson City, there's a shuttle bus to each of the 2 end points every morning and evening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And 4 of the entry points have a free car park with television camera surveillance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At one-mile intervals along the trail, there are rest stations providing picnic areas, water, toilets, and places where you can recharge your electronic devices.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In response to a poll of walkers last year, we've recently installed kiosks at each rest station with clear, easy-to-follow maps and other trail information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are several distinct sections of trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Red Rock Walk offers a superb opportunity to study a huge variety of vegetation along the way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's lots to look at, though you can't see great distances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Birds are actually hard to spot,
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: but with a pair of binoculars and at certain times of day, you may see some rare varieties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The River Walk comprises about 5 miles of trail winding along the bank of the Mulder River.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Personally, I prefer this section of the trail in winter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The river does freeze over, and the snow can accumulate, but that doesn't always discourage visitors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Sometimes, though, if the weather conditions are really unsuitable, we might have to close this walk to the public.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But often, it can get crowded with hikers who've discovered the attraction of the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now let me tell you about the Halfway Hostel, located approximately midway along the trail.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has a range of facilities available to help make your walking experience memorable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me give you some information about the various facilities available there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there are beds in dormitories for use at a very reasonable 7 dollars per person, weekdays or weekends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, we found that pre-booking beds just didn't work, so now we allocate them as people arrive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But we have extra cots and sleeping bags to help with any overflow.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are 2 family rooms accommodating 6 people each with private bathrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're 35 dollars per room, and for them, you will need to make arrangements ahead of time as they're very popular, especially at the weekends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A popular facility that we've recently added is coin-operated washing machines for your clothes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can get awfully wet and dirty if you're walking the trail in bad weather, and since we got these machines, you can put on clean gear when you set out in the morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The hostel serves 2 meals a day, breakfast at 4 dollars and dinner at 8 dollars, the same for adults and kids.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's always a vegetarian and a non-vegetarian option, depending on your preferences.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We do ask you to give a hand with serving and cleaning up after meals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have plenty of showers and unlimited hot water available, so you can have this luxury at no charge, and you can enjoy it as long as you like.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, some people like to spend time on the trail on mountain bikes and maybe take a bit of a rest from all that walking, and that's permitted as long as you observe basic safety rules.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The hostel's in the process of creating a bike rental scheme, which should be up and running next year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So, if you think that...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of Part 2.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have 30 seconds to check your answers to Part 2.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0
