transcript.text: Hello.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've been asked to talk to you today about Connect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Connect is a club for people who have retired from full-time work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first Connect club began back in nineteen sixty in Brisbane, Australia.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll concentrate on Frankston Connect, the club where I'm a member.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It services the communities around the suburb of Frankston here in Melbourne.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so what are our club aims?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're not a fitness club or anything like that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some Connect branches do charity work, but that's not for us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our objective is to provide social contact with others who have similar interests and ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, meetings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have monthly club meetings where the usual club business is discussed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, at the last meeting, we talked about how much money was spent that month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, at that meeting, someone had just returned from an overseas trip, and he spoke about that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then we looked at entries for our photography competition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The winner will be announced soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Up until now, we've used the school hall for our meetings, but that's about to be renovated, so we needed to find an alternative.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been a great venue because of its size, and it's so easy to get to, but I'm sure historical Frankston Hall will suit us just fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our social committee plans and organizes club trips from time to time, and they're always looking for suggestions from members for new places to go to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you join, you should check the activities list that's posted on our website each month and attend anything that interests you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come and make friends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're just one big happy family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how do you join, and what about membership fees?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's simple.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just fill in the form and give it to me before you leave this morning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are a few payment options.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some members prefer to make an annual payment, which is a slightly cheaper option, or you can pay monthly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Why don't you get a group together?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It makes the activities more fun.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: If you still haven't decided whether to join or not, let me try to tempt you with some of our upcoming events.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our Moonlight Wildlife Walk was previously available to members' immediate families as well, but this wonderful activity has become so popular that it's now limited to just members.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although it's free, we do ask our members to pay something to the wildlife fund so it can continue its good work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Everyone makes their way to the wildlife park independently, arriving at dusk, where a guide walks with the group and tells us about all the animals we encounter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, Theater in the Park.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We see a different play every month.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The park's on the train line and easy to access, so we don't organize buses or anything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Come along and recline on a blanket on the grass.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although some members prefer to take along their own seat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No need to make a reservation, there's plenty of space.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The City Botanical Gardens walk is a popular activity that occurs a couple of times a year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Members make their own way there and usually meet up outside the gates at eight forty-five AM, setting off for the hour's walk with the volunteer guide by nine AM.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many members bring a friend or relative, and this is fine.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a speaker talking on a radio program about a new cycle route.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to read questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome to our holiday special.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, I'll be talking about a new cycle route in this area called the Amsden Way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's well signposted, so you can see exactly where to go, and it's an easy route with no steep hills.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's thirty-five kilometers long from Amsden to Lowington and consists partly of cycle paths and partly roads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me outline the route briefly starting at Amsden Railway Station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first part is a cycle path running eastwards, roughly parallel to the rail track.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Almost immediately, the railway curves away and goes around the southern side of a little lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the cycle path takes the northern route around the lake.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Keep your eyes open for the swans that nest there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The path then joins the road, and the next landmark is a group of massive rocks which tower over the countryside.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will see them to the east of the road just before the road goes under the railway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're very impressive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Soon, you'll come to a fork in the road where you're going to leave the road and head off toward the river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But if you want to make a detour to Colleen Nature Reserve, go straight on instead of leaving the road here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Continuing along the cycle path, you'll reach the River Cleave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The cycle path follows the river southwards.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After a bit, you'll see the Ashington China Factory, which closed in nineteen sixty-two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When you get there, there's a bridge over the river, and you carry on with Langton Forest to the south and farmland to the north.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The route ends at Langton Village, where you'll find a railway station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So you can either catch the train here or cycle back to Amsden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: One point to remember when you're cycling on the Amsden Way is that you should keep your eyes open for sheep which occasionally stray onto the cycle path from adjoining fields.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So be careful to avoid accidents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The path is well constructed, so it's not affected by wet or muddy conditions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There might be the odd car or tractor when you're cycling on roads, but most traffic has been diverted to the main road that bypasses the whole area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, a bit more about some of the places you'll see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The starting point, Amsden Station, was quite busy in the early twentieth century with services to several major cities, but it was closed in the nineteen fifties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And actually, a small company was set up to turn it into a sort of railway museum, maintaining it in the style of the nineteen fifties.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And the station was ready for trains to start using it again earlier this year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's only used by a few local trains, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's a visitor center at the station which has a small exhibition about the history of railway transport all over the world and a facility for hiring bikes if you don't have one of your own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's also a small shop just across the road from the station that sells refreshments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As I said, you can cycle to Langton and return to Amsden by train or the other way around because you can take your cycle on the train.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's no need to book.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's plenty of room and no extra charge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, the service is very limited, and the trains between these two places don't run on weekdays.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you want to see the River Elm, there's a footpath from Amsden Station, and you can safely leave your bike in the car park there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Leave yourself plenty of time, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Going down's easy, but the climb up is very steep, so the walk back up to the top can take quite a while.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it's worth the effort.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The scenery is wonderful, and the footpath runs right next to the river, down to a waterfall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, if you'd like to do some more cycling in the area, there are lots of other cycle paths.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll be talking on the radio about them, and you'll be able to get full details in the Saturday edition of the local paper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The National Cycle Network also has some details on their website, although I have to say they don't have many local ones yet, but that may change.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we'll be telling you more about...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

transcript.text: Section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You'll hear a coordinator for the annual ski and snowboard exhibition talking to the audience about some practical information for the whole event.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the annual ski and snowboard exhibition held from April the eighth to seventeenth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am Mary Granger, coordinator of the event this year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The ten-day event features many highlights.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a snow sports lover, I know you are looking forward to a great time here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'd like to offer you some practical information about the whole event and what to expect from it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This might be the first time coming here for some of you, so for those who are still wondering about the right accommodation, I recommend Sky Hotel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It has its own health and sports clubs, just like most of the hotels here, but I love it because of its incredibly cozy beds, which guarantees good rest after an exhausting day of exploration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you haven't brought your own equipment like poles, boots, and skis, they are available for purchase or rent at Ski Set or Snow Rental.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The exhibition this year provides a colorful look into the history of skiing and an inspiring peek into the future prospects of the sport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Apart from the fascinating photo exhibitions and the most up-to-date skiing gear like always, this year we have added four computers which can imitate the process of skiing, ensuring the same physical activity and sensations that appear during the skiing process on downhill slopes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I have to warn you that it might be quite time-consuming to line up for the free trial experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many have posed the question as to how to enter the skiing and snowboarding competition.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, rather than filling out the back of the entrance ticket or bombarding the committee with emails, the most effective method is by checking out the exhibition newsletter delivered every month for availability.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As the most beloved local event, the exhibition has also drawn attention from the press.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last year, massive media coverage was on the worrisome amount of snowfalls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to avoid the same predicament, several artificial skiing slopes have been built.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: With more participants this year, we have lowered the entrance fee, which has been widely reported to local newspapers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A bonus for our participants is the ski program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It offers a wide variety of lessons and sessions with qualified instructors, ensuring that all ages and abilities are catered to, from the first-timers to seasoned amateurs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I strongly advise you to sign up for the program as it is offering an unprecedented thirty percent discount.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's mainly because we are cooperating with the program organizer who promises affordable prices only for the participants of the festival this year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, I would like to introduce you to the list of presentations during the following week so that you can better plan your schedule.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first presenter, Simon, is one of our best ski instructors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As an experienced instructor, he will inform you about the dangers that face skiers and snowboarders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Accidents happen mostly to those who are careless or ignorant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good risk management involves considering both the probability and consequences of an accident.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The next speech, titled Solution, is given by Jamie Kurt.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A list of problems may occur to novice skiers and snowboarders, so he is going to offer useful information for first-timers on choosing the appropriate gears, the right dress code, and ways of protecting your skin.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, some of you may have rented the skiing equipment, but rental footwear is notoriously uncomfortable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then Jamie will provide instructions to help make your footwear fit better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The third speech is about a documentary introducing skiing and snowboarding and the difference between the two sports.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It also depicts a group of snow lovers exploring new slopes with breathtaking views.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The director, Andy Fisher, will be there addressing the whole shooting experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The fourth talk is about the tricks of skiing presented by Harry Tyson.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is most useful for those who have already tried skiing, yet still need more practice to master the sport.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Harry will teach you how to turn more skillfully.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of people can keep their skis roughly parallel, but there's no point if you make it hard to work with and slide around out of control.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Useful exercises will also be suggested to improve your parallel skiing technique so that you can tackle steeper slopes and enjoy yourself more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Jason Smith will be the last presenter, mainly addressing towards advanced skiers.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Climbing in soft snow, you are floundering around.

transcript.text: Walking becomes harder, so a good trick during climbing is to maintain a wider gait, approximately shoulder width, so that you are more stable while walking.

transcript.text: This works for skiing as well.

transcript.text: Today, we're pleased to welcome Peter Gentle, who is organizing this year's famous Tavy Point Walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Can you tell us about the walk, Peter?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, it's an organized group walk which takes place every year on one day in October across some of the most beautiful scenery in the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Just about anyone with normal fitness can do it, but we have lots of volunteer stewards who are posted at regular intervals along the way to offer help if needed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The walk is mainly aimed at families.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We want to help people to walk with their children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's healthy exercise, and it helps people get to know their local area better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, for those of your listeners who might be interested in doing the walk, it takes place this year on Sunday, the twenty-seventh of October.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's eighty miles in length, so quite long, but we ensure walkers are very well looked after.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We like to involve as many people as possible, and it's getting busier every year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For most of the walk's history, we set a maximum of two hundred and twenty walkers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But this year, we've been able to expand to two hundred and eighty because we've got a total of fifty volunteers to help us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You provide a lot of support then.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have to be pretty strict about arrangements, but we do what we can to help people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If someone arrives without proper clothing, we can help out from our stocks of waterproofs, for example.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We don't just turn them away [chuckles] .
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The only time we do that is if people behave badly at the start.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We also spend a lot of time fielding walkers' questions about safety, both before the walk and while it's going on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Do you ever cancel the walk for very bad weather?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Yes, but it hasn't happened for several years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: However, a couple of years ago, the organizers made a decision to cancel because we didn't get as many volunteers as we needed to act as stewards on the walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The team felt really awful about it, but these things happen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If something does go amiss, we try to inform all walkers well in advance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, if any of your listeners are interested in joining the walk, they should go to our website at www.tavywalk.org and give us their details.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It costs four pounds fifty each to enter, and that covers a bottle of juice and a hot pie.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It also helps towards maintaining the twelve staff checkpoints at different parts on the route.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: About ninety percent of our walkers do complete the whole eighty-mile route.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But if you're not well or feel you can't go any further, just inform the stewards when you get to the checkpoint, and they'll organize transport to get you where you need to go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If you do complete the course, you are entitled to receive a badge.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, unfortunately, we can't give those to you immediately on finishing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: If you want one, you have to order it one week before the walk, and you'll get it by post two weeks after the walk, as long as you finish, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It may seem a strange system, but we found it works because only those walkers who really want a badge get one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: What do walkers need to take with them?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good question.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: When you register for the walk, we send you a booklet with all the key information.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But basically, we do say that you should be properly dressed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now, it must be emphasized that this doesn't mean that you wear thick trousers like jeans.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Lighter, waterproof apparel is better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Some people like to bring their mobile phones, but there isn't always a good signal.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And remember, the checkpoints are there, so you can always rely on those.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Some people asked if they should bring a torch, but frankly, they're a waste of space and weight.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's a relatively gentle, straightforward walk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Another thing people ask about is refreshments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Whether you carry things like high-energy drinks is up to you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And finally, we say it's a very good idea to bring a rucksack, but what size is up to the individual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But as I say, there's full information in the walkers' booklet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Well, thank you very much, Peter.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear part of a radio travel program about a tourist resort called Stanley Island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome once again to the show where we give you travel tips on popular tourist destinations in the Pacific region.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And today, our focus is on beautiful Stanley Island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, before we get started, a word of warning.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The seaplane service to the island was discontinued last week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for the next month at least, the sole link to the island is provided by the old ferry service, since plans to run a hovercraft service to the island have been delayed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So what is there to see and do on Stanley Island?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the main tourist areas are on the north, south, and east coasts of the island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As far as recreation goes, in the south, you'll find several leisure parklands, such as Waterworld and Fantasy Island, which seem well-equipped and reasonably priced.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If it's golf you're after, the eighteen-hole course in the south of the island is currently being turned into a conference center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But don't despair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are two excellent courses just thirty minutes away on the east coast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The south of the island has many large resorts and hotels with plenty of children's activities and clubs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This part of the island caters mainly for those seeking luxury to medium-class accommodation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But the east coast has basic apartment complexes with fully equipped kitchens so that at least you can cook for yourself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For those who like to get back to nature, you'll probably find the south coast rather overdeveloped.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The rainforest areas on the west coast are largely inaccessible because of the surrounding mountains, but those on the north coast are within easy reach, and a local agency runs guided treks through the jungle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're into water sports, all of the areas have something to offer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, here are a few bits of advice for those visiting the island for the first time to make your stay safer and more enjoyable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The island is generally safe, but it's as well to take a few precautions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're on any medication, bring this with you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It may not be available on the island.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And it's also a good idea for everyone to pack some insect spray in their luggage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're thinking of going into the more mountainous region in the west of the island, let someone know where you're going.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And remember, the reception for your mobile phone may be unreliable, so don't depend on that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Take your own water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Don't drink out of rivers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You're likely to come across lots of monkeys.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're cute, but watch out as they can bite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, when you're back in the more inhabited areas, take a break from steak and do try the local seafood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's fresh and very good value.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a teacher giving a talk about a junior school to a group of parents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you will have some time to look at questions eleven to seventeen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to seventeen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, can everybody hear me?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Good.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I'd like to welcome all the new parents to Springdown Junior School.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name is Anne Rawson, and I'm the assistant head teacher.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What I'd like to do is tell you about the school day and show you around the school, and perhaps you can ask me any questions you may have at the end.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, let me start by telling you a little bit about what happens here and what's on offer.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Children are expected to arrive at school between eight forty-five and eight fifty, and the bell is rung for everybody to go to their classrooms at eight fifty-five so that we can take the register.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We then have assembly at nine o'clock when the whole school meets in the hall for the head to talk to the children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He may discuss what's happened in the news or something that is important for the school.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lessons run until four PM with an hour for lunch.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lunch is served in the canteen, and children can bring their own packed lunch or a hot meal is available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They also have time to play outside and get some fresh air.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the middle of the morning and the middle of the afternoon, there are two breaks of fifteen minutes when the children also generally go outside, unless it's wet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we encourage the children to do as much as they can, and we offer them several ways of achieving this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, on Thursday afternoons, rather than continuing with lessons, we expect the whole school to do sports.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We vary these between summer and winter, and everything is supervised by the teachers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, we like the children to work on something artistic over a long period of time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for each of the three terms, they are expected to produce a poster.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This will normally be on something particular that they have studied that term, such as the environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also make sure we keep a close eye on how each child is doing in their schoolwork.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And every month, rather than the teacher giving the children a report, as I know some schools do, they have to do tests, and we record their performance over the year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're very proud of our school and of the very good results we achieve.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our teachers are all very committed to the school.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And at the end of the school day, many of them have set up clubs that the children go to for an extra hour to learn a new skill, such as music.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions eighteen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions eighteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Okay, I'll quickly show you where everything is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're here at the main entrance and on the right, where you would normally expect to find reception, you'll see the head's office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He likes to see visitors personally, and his door is always open.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Opposite this are two of the classrooms, but most of the classrooms are down the long corridor.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The library then is situated between those two classrooms, and we are hoping that we will be able to create a computer room within that so that the children can have somewhere quiet to work on their own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On the left of the classrooms, we have converted one of the old cloak rooms to create a music room, and children can go in there at lunchtime if they want to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if you come with me through the main hall here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, as you can probably see, this main hall is a new addition this year, and we are very pleased with it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We used to be squashed into the old assembly hall next door, which, as you can see, has now been turned into a gym for the children, and we have weekly lessons here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Do feel free to go and look around the classrooms, and I'll be waiting here to answer your questions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have forty-five seconds to check your answers to part two.

transcript.text: Hello, ladies and gentlemen, and thanks for tuning in to Action Radio, where we discuss current affairs and global issues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My name is Jill, and today I'll be discussing the very relevant issue of the importance of saving water and how you can do this at home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The most common type of wasted energy in the domestic environment is heat.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, since the walls of my home are very well insulated, I am lucky to have no issue with this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've discovered, however, that I waste a lot of water as a result of my lifestyle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I've researched ways to minimize my water usage online and have been pleasantly surprised to find that there are specialists in the area who can make some changes to my home immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The only downside is that the works are quite expensive and there are no means of getting financial assistance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if any of you listeners are interested in reducing your energy usage, here are a couple of easy and positive changes you can make immediately.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A lot of the magazines will recommend that you change your bulbs for those with energy-saving capabilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, I have found that these make little difference to your electricity bills, and they also severely reduce the light levels in your home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, simply switch off all plug sockets and appliances to make an immediate saving on your electricity consumption.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If this doesn't make enough of a saving for you, you could later try turning down the thermostat as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the discount that my energy provider gave me for prompt payment, my monthly bills were very expensive for the amount of energy that I was using, so I decided to change providers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Not only did I make a huge monthly saving, but the company also offered me other perks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am now able to pay my monthly bills online, for example, which I am thrilled about because it means that I no longer have to drive to the bank.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Once I have been a customer with them for a year, they will also offer a deduction for all of the energy-saving appliances I use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, many of you will have an electricity meter at home, so I'm sure you'll all understand the issues associated with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They occupy a lot of space in your home and can be unsightly if you're unable to tuck them away in a cupboard.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Mine is quite large as it measures both my gas and electricity, but I was luckily able to hide it in the coat cupboard where I can keep it hidden but also access it easily.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Having said that, whenever I have to take a meter reading, I have to use a torch because the screen is too dark to read the numbers correctly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have recently had an extension built on my house to make room for a new bathroom complete with a low-energy boiler so I can take long showers guilt-free.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The walls are nice and thick and well-insulated, but unfortunately, the window is a little drafty, so I'm going to have to invest in upgrading it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Speaking of renewable energy, I initially considered installing solar panels on the roof instead of using a low-energy boiler, which was the less expensive option.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the end, I decided that the panels would look too ugly on my house despite that they were technically easy to operate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, if you're a fan of taking long showers like I am, then switching from baths to showers will not help to reduce your water usage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Instead, here are some small but effective changes you can make.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When making a cup of tea, for example, measure out the amount of water that you need before boiling it, and when brushing your teeth, use a cup of water instead of a running tap.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I tried filling up my washing machine before switching it on, but I found that the clothes were not thoroughly cleaned, so I would not recommend this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If your tap drips when it is turned off, then you should call a plumber to fix it as this can result in a lot of water being wasted.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before finishing today's show, I'd like to address two questions that we often get asked by listeners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We had some great feedback about our answer to last week's question on how to calculate the price involved in powering domestic appliances.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So let's see how we do this week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our most commonly asked questions this week was which device is the lowest energy option for watching films?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The simplest answer is that the smaller the screen, the lower the energy used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of our listeners wrote in with a question that made me chuckle, and the answer is yes, solar panels only work when the sun is out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, on a more serious note, a number of you wanted to know what the most efficient temperature is to set the thermostat to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The answer is that the closer you set it to room temperature, the lower the energy used.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before I say goodbye until next week, I'll leave you with one last tip: Turn off the lights when you leave the room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.

transcript.text: You will hear part of a talk at a public meeting about a road and rail improvement project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Welcome, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thanks for coming to this information evening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The purpose of this meeting is to give you a chance to learn more about the road and rail improvement project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We've identified several problem areas, and we've come up with some changes that we think will improve the local environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the shared access paths, by those I mean the paths shared by both bikes and pedestrians, we plan to turn these into open areas with grass around them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cyclists and pedestrians need to be able to see each other clearly to avoid any accidents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we've decided to remove the large native trees from the area for that reason.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, along the highway, we want to put trees that are native to this area to add shade and make it more attractive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We thought possibly the spotted gum, which grows naturally here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I know those of you who live in the housing estate are disturbed by the sound of traffic nearby.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're aiming to solve this problem by constructing a wall between the estate and the road, and possibly in the future, we might consider adding some artwork to it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We think this will be quite an effective solution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on now to the local roads, we want to encourage more public transport use and solve some of our traffic problems, so we're going to add a considerable number of stops to the bus routes that run along those roads.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Just finally, as a way of thanking the community for their cooperation, we plan to make the picnic area in the park near the bus terminal more attractive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we're adding some colorful new rose beds that our gardeners will be putting in at the completion of the project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now I'd like to give you more information about the renovations to Richland's train station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Can you all see a copy of the plan?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We envisage Richland Station as more than just a train station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It'll be a transport hub linking all forms of transport in the area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To this end, we're building an underground park-and-ride car park so commuters can drive to the station, park, and then ride to work on the train.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the entrance to it on the corner of Progress and Garden Road.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can drive into it from Progress Road.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, on the Progress Road side of the site, on the top left of your map is where we plan to put the bus interchange.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Commuters will have direct access to the platform from the bus interchange via a covered walkway.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cycling is an important part of our city's transport plan, so cyclists will also be fully catered for with eighty new bicycle lockers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can see where they are on the plan in the bottom left-hand corner next to the bike path.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cyclists can ride to the station, store their bikes in the lockers, and board the train.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, and I forgot the most important thing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll even be able to shower at the station after your bike ride, as we're installing showers between the toilets and the platform.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll also install a fountain at the station to make the area more attractive.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can see it in the center of the plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And between the fountain and the ticket machine, we're putting in a lift for our elderly and disabled passengers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They will be able to buy their ticket, then pass directly to the platform via the lift.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I hope that gives you a much better idea of the new facilities that'll be available at Richland Station.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we would like your feedback about the project.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So-

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk by a volunteer who has been taking part in a project to find out what everyday life was like two thousand five hundred years ago in Britain during the time known as the Iron Age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Jim Stevens has been taking part in an experiment to find out what everyday life was like in Britain over two thousand five hundred years ago in the period of history we call the Iron Age.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He is one of a group of volunteers who have been living for the last six months in the sort of village that people inhabited in those days and following the sort of daily routine that ordinary people followed then.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So Jim, tell us what you do on a typical day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A typical day in the Iron Age village begins with rising at first light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I occasionally did that when I was at home because I loved having time to myself before the family got up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But here I do it every day because it's so light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Others also get up early because they find the straw beds rather cold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We start work immediately, usually tending to our fires which have died down in the night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I feed the cattle before starting to get breakfast ready, usually porridge that's been soaked the night before.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It sounds horrid, doesn't it?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But it's not so bad.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: As it takes such a long time to cook anything, we end up eating only twice a day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We have a late breakfast after a morning's work, and then in the evening we gather together as a community.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Although the evening meal provides a chance for us to chat about the day, it can be quite chilly, so we go to bed pretty early.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I think we're always hungry because we use much more energy than usual.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's all the physical exertion.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A lot of time is spent just trying to get enough to eat, looking for berries and fruit and things like that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: There are lots of other jobs to be done, like cooking, finding wood, and keeping the fires going.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The biggest priority for the blacksmiths working the forge is to tend the fire and to get it nice and hot so they can carry out their tasks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They've got various things to make: tools, cooking implements, and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So life here is about looking after the animals and looking after ourselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Everybody's always doing something round the fire as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's not as if we're just sitting there chatting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Just living, surviving takes up most of our time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And actually, it's quite difficult to fit in other things around it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For example, you might be breaking hazelnuts, spinning some wool, or just doing things like straining milk.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Here, you're finding out how to do different things every day, which keeps you on your toes and keeps you interested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And I understand that you even built your own houses to live in.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Roundhouses built in just the same way that archaeologists think that Iron Age people constructed them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So tell us exactly how you build an Iron Age roundhouse.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a bit like putting up a tent at first, but without the benefit of ready-made metal poles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You mark the center of your house with a wooden peg.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: What you do then is loop a length of rope around it and mark out the circle to give you the outer boundary of your building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Once you've got this, you then have to dig out the ground ready for the wall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And in Iron Age times, people didn't have shovels or diggers like we do today, but used tools which they fashioned from animal bone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It must have been quite hard work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Next, you have to start on the wall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Although there were several native trees around, like the ash and the elm, the ancients preferred oak for the wall posts, which they knocked into the circle they had dug.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Don't forget to leave room for the entrance, otherwise you won't be able to get into the house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now you can begin to see the wall of the house developing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To create the framework for the final wall, the stakes were not nailed or glued onto each other as they might be today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Instead, ones with holes cut into each end are slotted over the upright posts, making what to us looks like a fence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This procedure creates a very firm structure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To support the large roof, first you need to put up a good-sized center post, which is secured with ropes and pegs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But it's not only this which is relied upon to hold up the roof.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So the next thing you have to do is build around the post a timber scaffold tower, similar to the metal ones used in Britain today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: This temporary structure of wooden poles enables you to put up the main supporting beams, which are then tied together with rope and fixed to the wall plate at the bottom of the fence.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The top part of this tent-like construction is strengthened with two ring beams.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now the framework for the roof has to be completed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Rather like weaving a basket using rods from the willow tree, hazel wood rods are linked to the beams in parallel hoops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Now you can see the house in skeletal form.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The tricky bit is thatching the roof because it requires great skill.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I find this very difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: First, you take reed bundles and cut them so that each is of equal length.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then you must fix them firmly so they won't blow away in heavy winds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The final part of the process is the daubing, which in effect is like modern-day plastering.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Whereas today we use plaster and paint or wallpaper, the Iron Age people had a mixture of clay, cow dung, and straw, which they daubed all over the inside and outside to give the house a smooth finish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a radio talk on horse riding for disabled people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen on page three.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: This week, our slot is A Life in the Day of Joan Gilbert, local organizer for Riding for the Disabled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Joan, would you like to tell us about this?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I always have the very best intentions of starting the day at five thirty to give the horses a really good muck out, but reality intervenes, and I finally wake at about six thirty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That probably still sounds very early to you, but for a farm worker, which is what my son is at the moment, that's cutting things pretty fine.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Once I've managed to get him safely on his way at about seven AM, I can start turning my attention to the other important tasks of the day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For about five years, we've been taking overseas students from the international center at our local college, and I have to give them a proper breakfast.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Most of our students used to be from the Middle East, but they're no longer coming, so we tend to have Malaysian girls, and they like to have a cooked breakfast much more than any Europeans we've had, including me, and I don't have anything these days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: After cooking, I finally get round to the poor horses.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's only after this that I can start thinking about what I regard as my most important task, work for Riding for the Disabled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I've been involved with this organization on and off for over twenty years, but I've only recently taken on the job of chairperson.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Most of the work seems more secretarial, but that's how charities get organized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In our immediate district, we have had as many as thirty riders, but currently, we've only got twenty-two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The number of helpers who have volunteered is actually forty, but we can rely on twenty-five to come regularly to help in the different groups.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We now have four separate groups which cater for disabled children and adults from six to forty years old.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As I say, I feel that although I no longer have any proper full-time paid employment, I do have a full and busy life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I'm a housewife, which I don't mind because I don't really object to doing things like washing and cooking.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then there's my own horses, which I adore, even the revolting stuff like cleaning out the stables.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The official RDA stuff is a mixed bag really.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I don't have major problems with all the letter writing and correspondence which it entails.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But like lots of shy people, I find the fundraising horrendous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Other regular RDA duties, such as ringing round the riders to fix times, et cetera, is one of the pleasantest aspects of the work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: After all, that's why I'm involved with charity work, the contact with people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: My working day ends with the least enjoyable job of all, sorting the accounts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I got involved with RDA because I've always loved horses, and I can see disabled people gaining so much.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I know all the medical evidence that shows that it does wonders for muscle building and so on, which is important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But from talking to the riders, they say it is the confidence they gain and also the opportunity to be part of a new and exciting environment which gives them the greatest benefit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: In terms of the RDA organization itself, I feel it works very well, but we're always striving to make it better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I wish, for example, our helpers and the organizers in the various centers could really rationalize the fundraising efforts, which sometimes are very inefficient.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And it also saddens me how unaware some of the stables can be about the difficulties faced by people who are disabled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Anyway, I feel very privileged to work with our riders and to see such tangible benefits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It sends me to sleep with a feeling that though the day has been hard, it has been worthwhile.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a principal of a school talking to a group of parents about a three-day trip for pupils to an outdoor education center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to sixteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to sixteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good evening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's good to see so many parents here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me begin by explaining why we go to the outdoor education center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, by age ten, we feel the children are ready for a trip away from home, but still in a safe environment and under the guidance of a familiar adult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the school, we strongly believe children should be encouraged to try different things and not give up when it gets difficult.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And that's what the center is all about, having a go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyway, to start with, the sleeping arrangements.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For some children, this will be their first time in a tent and away from home, so please prepare them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can do this just by making sure they have some early nights before we go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another thing, there's space for three children per tent, so we can't guarantee your child will be in with their best friends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So do make them aware of this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, you should have received a list with the clothing the children will need in their backpack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But there are some extras.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Please provide a packet of biscuits or maybe fruit bars, but these need to go in the box in the school hall, not with the children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Actually, what we do need in the backpacks are bags for cleaning up and for wet clothing, so plastic ones, please.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: A torch is a good idea, but don't worry about putting money in because there's nothing to buy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While we're on the subject, let's talk about some other items.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Cell phones are permitted, but they must be switched off at night and also off during the teaching sessions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, for wood carving activities, knives will be provided by the center, so children shouldn't bring them from home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Electronic games are banned, so rather than bring one of these, children should bring quiet board games.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turning to the question of parent attendance, in the past, we've had too many volunteers, so we have written names on bits of paper and pulled them out of the box.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But then some parents have changed their minds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if you're absolutely sure you can come, put your name down on the sign-up form, and the first ten will be asked to come.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Experience isn't required.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We just want you to lend a hand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I'm afraid the fee for the trip needs to be paid by the fifteenth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Payment to the center is made by school, not by parents.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And your teacher will be given your child a form with the school's bank account details if you want to use them to make payments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Otherwise, please leave payment in an envelope in the box at the school office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let's have a look the center.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I hope you all have leaflet with a map on the back, and we'd like you to show this to your children before they go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if you look at the map, you will see the entrance at the bottom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so just through the entrance, you'll see reception.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now the wood carving studio.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: See the building marked kayaks on right side riverbank?

transcript.text: When our graphic design company was established with just the two of us ten years ago, this space was ideal and the rent is very reasonable.

transcript.text: But we've just outgrown the space since we took on six new staff last year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So we've decided to cut short our lease.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you're going to like the new office.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, it's important that you're all aware of your responsibilities so that the move goes smoothly.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Remember, things you're currently working on should stay in the office due to our privacy laws.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the day of the move itself will be a Saturday when we are closed for business.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We'll leave it all to the professionals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So just go directly to the new building on the Monday, and by then, hopefully, all the hard work will have been done.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You'll see some desks there drawn on the plan.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For the sales staff, we've asked the builders to put in a partition between your area and the rest of the staff.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're aware that you're on the phone a lot talking to clients, and you'll need some privacy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So that's your area in the top left corner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if you look at the very top of the plan, opposite the doorway, you'll see the designer's desks.

transcript.text: We didn't want to put you too close to the entrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

questions.prompt: jam
questions.explanation: 因为果酱（jam）是用蓝莓做的，所以产品相当贵（quite dear），你得多花点钱。
questions.tip: "Dear" 在英式英语中常指 "昂贵的"，对应 "Expensive"。文中虽然说了 "delicious"，但选项中没有这个干扰项，只有 B 最贴切。
questions.quote: Guide: Although because it’s made from blueberries, this product is quite dear, so you’ll have to spend a little more than usual.

questions.prompt: soaps
questions.explanation: 肥皂（soaps）没有香精或色素，没有任何人工添加，是彻头彻尾的纯净肥皂（simple soap）。
questions.tip: "Nothing artificial added" 和 "just simple soap" 对应选项 A "Pure"。原文提到 "not perfumed or coloured"，排除了 C 和 I。
questions.quote: Guide: ...just simple soap through and through, made by hand the old-fashioned way with nothing artificial added.

questions.prompt: candles
questions.explanation: 如果你想让你的每一分钱都花得最值（dollar to stretch as far as possible），蜡烛（candles）是最佳购买选择（top buy）。
questions.tip: "Top buy" 和 "dollar to stretch" 意为性价比最高，对应 D。文中提到 "colour of wax... not too exciting"，排除了 I（Coloured）。

questions.prompt: ice cream

questions.tip: "Awarded the gold medal" 直接对应选项 H "Prize-winning"。
questions.quote: Guide: In fact, it’s so good that it’s classified export grade and was awarded the gold medal at this year’s food fair.

questions.prompt: shampoo

transcript.text: Well, first of all, I'll give you a bit of background to the museum and then tell you about some of the galleries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You probably won't have time to see everything today, so what I recommend you do is go to the Egyptian room first, because it's everyone's favorite place, and it gets very crowded with the school parties later in the day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Oh, and I should mention that the photography gallery's undergoing refurbishment at the moment, so while that's definitely worth seeing, it'll have to wait for another time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the actual museum building itself is quite interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was designed by a local architect called William Craven in the nineteenth century at a time when the city was developing rapidly with new factories to cope with the expansion of the textile industry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The museum's built in a very similar style to the railway station, which was constructed at around the same time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That was designed by another architect, but William Craven did also provide the plans for the town hall, which was built just a few years later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Construction of the museum began in eighteen eighty-eight with a large team of carpenters, stonemasons, and builders.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then in recent years, it's been extensively refurbished.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The lovely big windows have been retained to let the daylight flood in, but the award-winning part of the project was the restoration of the area around the central hall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In particular, the beautiful wrought iron staircase, which was brought back to its former glory.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unfortunately, the museum's original tiled floor had to be replaced with new tiles of a similar design.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was a very expensive project, and since we don't charge admission fees, we had to find other ways of funding it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We did get some money from the Department of Culture at national level, but we had even more generous support from companies and industries here in the city, who were our main benefactors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, we do also depend on donations from people living in the area for the ongoing maintenance of the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So how will the museum mainly be spending its money in the next five years?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We already work with schools and colleges, helping people get a better understanding of all the creative disciplines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We consider the most important part of our work the restoration of the valuable historical objects we are lucky enough to have in our possession, and this will continue to be where the most funding is allocated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, it would be wonderful to purchase new objects for the museum, but we simply don't have the space at the moment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we do hope you enjoy your day today, but if you would like to learn more about our exhibits on display here, I suggest you come to one of the Saturday morning lectures, which are given every month by one of our team of experts.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, you can pick up leaflets about the exhibits in most of the galleries too, but you'll only get a basic introduction from those.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're also working to update our website so that it provides more background on the exhibits, but that's still at the planning stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.text: Now let me just tell you a bit about what's on at the moment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, we're very well known for our collection of eighteenth-century paintings, both oils and watercolors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some of these are English landscapes and portraits, but we also have paintings by other European artists who were working during this period.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you're interested in art, that's a bit nearer home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The Farnley collection is a set of drawings by Paul Farnley.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He was born in Ireland, but he came to work here in the city in the early twentieth century and then made it his home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He worked in a factory but spent his spare time drawing the buildings and urban landscape of the city, and his work has now been collected and displayed here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On a more practical note, we have a display of kitchen appliances, which might interest you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: These are the sorts of things you wouldn't normally expect to see in a museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's an electric potato peeler from the nineteen seventies, which sold really well at the time, but no one's got one now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are lots of other similar appliances, which must have seemed like great ideas at the time, but which never took off.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You might also like to visit the fashion gallery.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is an exhibition which is running for the next few weeks only and shows men's and women's fashion from nineteen hundred to two thousand, including some of the famous designers of the time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay, so if anyone's got any questions, follow me over...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1
