transcript.text: I’m Hazel, the guide from Travelite Agency.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since we mentioned the trip to Muna Island in the last program, we’ve received several online messages from those who have been there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, we’ve collected some helpful do’s and don’ts for new visitors, which will hopefully help you to know the island better and enjoy your stay to the fullest.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first suggestion is about tips.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although tipping is required in most circumstances in Muna Island, the amount you should give differs significantly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you take a taxi, there is no set rate on how much you should leave to the driver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Someone may give a generous tip if he thinks the service is fantastic.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It’s up to you entirely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, if you go to the hairdresser’s or enjoy a meal in the restaurant and the bill comes with no service charge, a ten percent tip is advisable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Muna Island has got relatively good medical service.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you get sick, the quickest way is to ask the hotel to arrange an English-speaking doctor for you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But remember, it’s not a complimentary service.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other alternative is to visit the local clinic, and you have to prepare for the charge as well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I should remind you that the medical service on the island can be pricey, so it’s better to buy your insurance before you leave.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When you visit Muna Island, you’ll see the notice nearly everywhere: Tap water is safe to drink, but you might not get used to its weird taste because it contains minerals.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this case, you can buy bottled water sold in every shop, but you’d better make sure the sealed lid is untouched as the locals often put tap water into the bottle.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although there aren’t many bus lines, they’re always on time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, some people complained that the road was so bumpy that they even got nausea and dizziness.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a result, it’s not a good choice if you want to sit peacefully and relax on the way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And another thing is before you jump on the bus, inquire of the driver about where the bus will go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Unlike most cities, here in Muna Island, you cannot find the destination shown in front of the bus or at the bus stop.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Maybe you found the bus service is not so enjoyable.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In that case, you can always rent a car.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you choose this way, I advise you to prepare well beforehand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although some taxi companies provide car rental services, many visitors sometimes find nobody answering the phone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So leave this way when you are in a hurry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It’s wise to compare several car rental companies online beforehand as the price may vary a lot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: More importantly, don’t forget to check with the company what the price covers in detail, like daily rental expenses, car insurance, commission, etc.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It usually includes unlimited mileage, too, but fuel is excluded.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you don’t want to drive, a taxi is the quickest and most comfortable way.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm Chris Butler, and I'm the chairperson of the Middletown Urban Farming Scheme, or MUFS for short, a highly successful program which encourages city dwellers to grow their own fruit and vegetables, to become city farmers, if you will.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Who started MUFS?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, the idea of urban farming has been around for quite a while, particularly among town planners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But it was actually a group of Middletown business people, including myself, who decided to create what became MUFS.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: University agriculture specialists got involved later.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, initially, the aim was not some eco-friendly goal of reducing CO two emissions caused by the transport of food from farm to dinner plate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was simply to maximize the utilization of the vacant or idle land that lies within the city.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, later we realized that an additional benefit might be a healthier diet for local people.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me tell you a bit about the groups that have joined the scheme.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We've got any number of schools involved and loads of corporate employees, so our message seems to have been well received there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But for next year, we're gonna concentrate on getting various community centers, like those for senior citizens to join, because so far they've been somewhat slow to take up the scheme.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, the core committee of the MUFS is a group of dedicated gardeners.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They probably won't be familiar with your specific plot of land.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're mostly amateurs, but they are the people who know the ins and outs of gardening, and they will be happy to sit down with any MUFS member and make some hands-on suggestions about gardening.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But don't expect them to know the answers to technical questions like the Latin names of plants.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The MUFS are keen to support members who are physically disabled.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're looking at the possibility providing specially adapted gardening tools on loan to members who can't cope with regular tools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's not happening yet, but we do have some window boxes as well as larger containers which we can distribute free of charge to these members, although they will have to provide their own soil and compost themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm especially proud of the work we've done with the local schools, both grade school level and high schools.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The teachers say that they knew the scheme would be of some practical use in science classes like biology.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Despite the original hopes of some, the fruit and vegetable plots haven't provided cheaper lunches for their students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But what they didn't anticipate was the change in attitude that the scheme has created amongst their students.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They say the students have become much more conscious of their surrounding environment.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They want to keep it neat and tidy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, a number of local organizations and businesses provide our members with free goods and services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me go through some of them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The city hospital, as you might expect, has to provide thousands of meals for its patients.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So the manager of its kitchen runs a course for our members on how to use vegetables in a huge variety of dishes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The local government found it had a large glass building which the parks department used to start off flower seeds and young plants during the winter, and they agreed to allow our members to use this free of charge to get their own little seedlings off to a good start.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Another thing, the university has agreed that if members send them a sample of their soil, they will do a series of tests on it to indicate what kind of plants will grow best and what types of fertilizer and nutrients would be best to use.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And just to make sure our members know what's good for them, a supermarket is offering a series of classes on how to lose weight and stay healthy by having a sensible diet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's talk about the practicalities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.

questions.prompt: What is the key to feeding kangaroos?

The kangaroos may interpret you bending over as a sign of aggression, so please be careful. Also, no matter how cute the babies are, any physical contact should be avoided. The adults are quite protective of their young while they are still in the pouch, so please refrain from the urge to give them a pat. transcript.text: Section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a talk by a wildlife specialist on a type of bird called a kiwi.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As you listen to the first part of the talk, answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Ladies and gentlemen, welcome to Auckland Zoo on this sunny Sunday afternoon and to our special kiwi fundraising event.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: My job is to tell you all about the amazing little kiwi, and your job, hopefully, is to dig deep in your pockets [laughing] .
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, for the benefit of our overseas visitors here today, I should explain first of all that the kiwi is the national bird of New Zealand, and sometimes New Zealanders themselves are known as Kiwis.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, while kiwis in the wild are a rare sight, the kiwi as a symbol is far more visible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Apart from being in toy stores and airport shops all over the world, you'll find them on our stamps and coins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The kiwi is the smallest member of the genus Apteryx, which also includes ostriches and emu.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It gets its name from its shrill call, which sounds very much like this, "Kiwi, kiwi."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Kiwis live in forests or swamps and feed on insects, worms, snails, and berries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a nocturnal bird with limited sight, and therefore it has to rely on its very keen sense of smell to find food and to sense danger.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Its nostrils are actually right on the end of its long beak, which is one-third of the body length.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, here's an interesting fact.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although kiwis have wings, they serve little purpose because the kiwi is a flightless bird.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Since white settlement of the islands, kiwi numbers have dropped from twelve million to less than seventy thousand, and our national bird is rapidly becoming an endangered species.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is because they're being threatened by what we call introduced animals, animals which were brought to New Zealand, such as cats and ferrets, which eat kiwi eggs and their chicks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: As the talk continues, answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: And so we have launched the Kiwi Recovery Program in an all-out effort to save our national bird from extinction.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are three stages to this program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, we have the scientific research stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This involves research to find out more about what kiwis need to survive in the wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then secondly, we have the action stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is where we go into the field and actually put our knowledge to work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We call this putting science into practice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And then we come to the third stage, the global education stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: By working with schools and groups like yourself, as well as through our award-winning kiwi website, we're hoping to educate people about the plight of the kiwi.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As part of the action stage, which I just mentioned, we've introduced Operation Nest Egg, and this is where your money will be going.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It works like this.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a three-stage process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First of all, we go out to the kiwi's natural habitat, and we collect kiwi eggs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is the tricky part because it can be very difficult to find the eggs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then, in safe surroundings, away from predators, the chicks are reared.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, this can be done on predator-free islands or in captivity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They're reared until they're about nine months old, at which stage the chicks are returned to the wild.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So far, it's proving successful, and since we started the program, some thirty-four chicks have been successfully raised this year, and their chances of survival have increased from five to eighty-five percent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, it's not time to celebrate kiwi survival just yet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: About ninety-five percent of kiwi chicks still don't make it to six months of age without protection, which is why Operation Nest Egg is so important.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And we ask you to give generously today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear a school principal talking to a group of parents who are volunteering at a school fair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good evening, and thank you for coming to the Kenvale School Fair volunteers meeting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you know, this is the biggest fundraising event in the school year, and as usual, we're expecting lots of people to come, which is why we're starting to prepare now, six months before the big day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll begin tonight by talking about the different volunteer roles so you can decide what you'd like to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The entertainment coordinator position involves deciding what kinds of rides and activities will be at the fair and making sure there's a good variety of things to do.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From past experience, this role involves a lot of liaising with other helpers and the entertainers, which means that most of the work is done after office hours.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We need an advertising and promotion coordinator to make sure that people hear about the fair and lots of people come.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We know this is a big job, so we've decided to have a couple of people doing it to share the load.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The parent who did this role last year has just been offered a job which starts next month, so she won't be able to lend us the benefit of her experience, sadly.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The technical coordinator makes sure that there is a suitable stage for the performers and that there are enough speakers, and people can hear them, and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, this may sound like a technical background is required, but it's not, as you don't actually have to set up or fix anything yourself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Having a car is essential, though, because in the week leading up to the event, you'll need to be able to get to the school early in the mornings and occasionally later at night.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We also need a staffing coordinator.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This person will be required to look after the many helpers on the day of the fair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This role has just been created based on our experience of last year's event.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We found that our volunteers felt a bit overworked, and so we're hoping that this role will make things easier.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It will help to reduce stress if you organize the helpers about a month before the fair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, moving on to the map of the school fair, I'll point out some of the more important areas that you'll need to know about so you can help direct the visitors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can see that we'll be using the large grounds just behind the school, and we'll set up temporary areas and pathways there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first thing I'll show you are the fairground rides, which are always popular with the children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you look at the map, you'll see the fair entrance at the bottom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: From there, follow the main path in the direction of the river, and it's the third area on the left, the large rectangular area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The entertainment stage is a big feature of the fair, and this is where everyone will be able to see all the performers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To find this, go straight along the main path until you get to the river.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Turn right and follow the path to the end, and there it is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's not much shade here, so we should remind parents to bring hats for their children.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If anyone wants a cold drink or a snack, then they'll ask you where the cafe is.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Originally, we were going to put it opposite the toilets, but we've decided to put it near the river to take advantage of the views and breezes.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can see it on the map.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's a circular area surrounded by trees near the playground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first aid tent is always an important part of the fair.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We wanted to put that in an area that was easily accessible and a bit separated from the other attractions, but near the entrance.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you look at the map, you'll see it south of the toilets, not far from the school fence line.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The market stalls are where visitors will be able to pick up a bargain or some homemade produce.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last year, these were located just south of the meeting area, but the stallholders complained that it was too exposed and hot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So this year, we've moved them to the north of the meeting area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lots of good shelter provided by the trees here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, there'll be the ever-popular pony rides.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To reach these, direct visitors to follow the main path from the entrance until they reach the L-shaped area on the left next to the playground.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, as I was saying...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.

transcript.text: You will hear an interview with the organizer of a town's cultural festival called International Week.

transcript.text: Next week is our town's International Week, which has been going on annually for several years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Today, we have George Johnson, the organizer of International Week, to talk about it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: George, how did it all begin?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Well, I was with a group of businessmen in town one February day five years ago, and we were discussing what we could do for livening things up in August when the weather's good, and the kids are out of school till September.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And someone said, "Hey, we've got people from all over the world living here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's have an international celebration and get people to show off things about their home country."
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And we all agreed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The first year, the celebration lasted just one day, and it featured three countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It was a great success and was written about in our local newspaper.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And so the next year, even though it cost more, the organizers expanded it to an International Week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And so many people were eager to feature their countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: On each of the first six days of the week, one country is designated to star.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: And then on the seventh day, weather permitting, we have a street party near the town hall with music provided by the radio station and food and games.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Everyone has a ball.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Of course, we move it to the school gym if it rains like last year, but nobody minds.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Our year starts in January when we ask for applications.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: To apply to have a day for their country, people don't need to belong to a particular country association.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They can just be a group who identify themselves with a particular country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They submit a formal plan to us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They don't need to worry at this stage about funding, but some grants are available.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The organizing committee has to select the ones with the best ideas.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The organizing committee arranges for places for the country to do whatever they want.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Unfortunately, for large outdoor activities, we aren't allowed to use the local stadium because they've got other commitments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: But the community center lets us use its parking lot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The hall is kind of small, but it has been kind enough to permit us to make use of its classrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Local people have been very generous.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: A lot of business people let us have things like tables and amplifiers for the week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The organizing committee handles all the administration, and the town library has been great about featuring books about the countries.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now, for each country's day, we ask them to have one special event like a show or exhibition or demonstration.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: For example, some people could show how they make traditional handicrafts, or it might just be an exhibition, say, photographs of the country.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, [beep] what are the special events this year?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Fantastic things.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: [beep] Monday is Mexico Day, and these ladies and gentlemen are going to put on a show that's hotter than those chili peppers they're famous for eating.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They'll be singing and playing songs, and those drums will make you want to get up and move around.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Then Tuesday is South Africa Day, and they've got an exhibition of dresses and robes used in traditional ceremonies and dances, and they are magnificent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Apparently, some of them are worth more than their weight in gold.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Next, Wednesday is Indonesia Day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: They have an exhibition where you'll definitely get your money's worth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Two ladies will put on their chef's hat to demonstrate how they prepare those dishes and sauces they're famous for.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Let's see.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That brings us to Thursday, Canada Day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: We think of them as fit outdoorsmen and ice hockey players, but they've arranged to have some of their countrymen show us how they use just a knife and blocks of wood from Native American trees to make absolutely lovely statues of birds and bears and other animals famous in local legends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: So next is Friday, Italy Day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

questions.prompt: What makes the Home Improve Store special?
questions.explanation: 录音提到这家店与竞争对手不同的主要优势是规模大，因此能降低成本并提供最划算的价格（cut our costs and offer the best deals），完美对应A选项的价格低。
questions.tip: 你可能听到了优质的客户服务（great service）和丰富的商品选择（excellent choice of goods）想选B或C，但紧接着录音就强调了“这些并不是我们独有的（isn't unique to us）”，通过识别这些干扰信息可以帮你迅速排错。
questions.quote: The first thing staff need to know is what makes us different to our competitors. Our main advantage, due to our size, is that we can cut our costs and offer the best deals. Of course, we are proud of the great service we provide to our customers, especially through our help desk. We also have an excellent choice of goods so that we can provide plenty of options to our customers. But of course, that isn't unique to us.

options.text: their low prices
their wide range of products
their customer service

questions.prompt: What should staff promote to customers?
questions.explanation: 录音要求员工必须确保发给每位顾客（given to every customer）的是商店杂志（store magazine），对应B选项。
questions.tip: 你极易被A和C的并列信息干扰：录音明确说产品目录（catalog）“仅限员工使用（staff use only）”，而网站（website）“正在重建，顾客现在上不去（can't access it right now）”，理清这些限定条件就能排除干扰项。
questions.quote: First, there's our catalog, which lists all our items. It's been around for years, but we still have a policy of staff use only. The most important marketing material, and the one you want to ensure is given to every customer, is our store magazine, showing the latest products, workshops, and offers. The website is being redeveloped at the moment, so customers can't access it right now.

options.text: the catalogue
the magazine
the website

questions.prompt: What do the current staff like best about working in the store?
questions.explanation: 录音说大多数员工最欣赏的一点是，你可以自由选择工作时间（choose your hours）来配合你的生活，对应C选项的弹性工作时间。

questions.quote: Like most of the staff, I'm sure you'll appreciate the fact that you can choose your hours to fit your lifestyle, family, or study. transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have been able to do some work and have come up with two options that I think should fit what you are looking for.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first house is situated on Allen Street, and the owner told me that he bought the house largely because of where it is located.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The house was decorated a few years ago, but I think it still looks new to a large extent.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Anyways, you might dislike the old-fashioned design of the house, which was modeled to the original owner's taste.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, you can arrange decorations of your own.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I just have to inform you beforehand.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I looked through your profile, and it said that you have a large family of six.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I felt this house could be more appropriate for you with children than just young couples, as it has eight rooms, including four bedrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: According to your budget, although the house is a bit pricey, the price hasn't exceeded your limit yet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's very reasonable, though, for a house on Allen Street.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The owner had initially fixed every afternoon for potential buyers to visit.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then he shifted it to all weekends.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But by yesterday, he informed me that he would be allowing only Wednesdays during lunchtime for visits.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So it means we have to go either tomorrow or next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions fourteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fourteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Okay, on to the next house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I was able to get the layout of this building to help you understand it better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The house is situated on Pearl Street, just around the corner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is a well-planned and designed house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the southeast of the house, you can see the master room, whereas the dining room is in the northwestern corner.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There is a bathroom in the southwestern corner of the house that is modern and well-equipped.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It provides adequate storage for the whole family.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As for the bedroom, which is kept especially for visitors, it is in the direct south of the house, just between the bathroom and the master room.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will see the kitchen to your left when you just step in the house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, I should give as much information as I can so as to help you in the decision-making process.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The second house has both advantages and disadvantages, and you should know well about them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: First, the premises are quite lovely, and there is a small garden just behind the main building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, you do not have to manage space with other neighbors since there is a big parking lot, unlike the first house.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As you can see, north of the house, you have a lot of banks, and to the east and west, there are a good number of companies and malls.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is very compact and easily accessible due to its central location.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Again, in contrast to the first house, there are only two bedrooms, and this would have been good for a young couple with a small family size.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: However, for a family size like yours, I really am not sure.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But if necessary, perhaps you could turn the storeroom into a bedroom.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then there will be three bedrooms.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The last problem is that it lacks a garage, which is a very important feature for residents here, as every household has at least one car, and there are few public car parks in this area.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is all I have for now, and...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.

transcript.text: So, what will you be doing?

transcript.text: Well, we're open Monday through Sunday, so you'll need to be able to work weekends as well as irregular weekday shifts.

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Your duties will include checking and unpacking lorry deliveries, as well as working on the shop floor, stocking shelves and so on.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you'll only be required to do manual lifting if the goods are light.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When the store is very busy, you'll also have to assess changing priorities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For example, if there's a queue at the tills, you'll jump on a spare one to help.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you notice something's been spilt and the surface is a little bit wet, you'll get a mop to clean it up.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: No need to check with a manager first.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Similarly, if bakery items are selling quickly, you'll help cook some more.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you'll still get time off to relax too, of course.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We pride ourselves on a positive attitude here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And always smile.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It forces you to stay positive, and being generally upbeat makes your whole team happy too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This increases efficiency and gives a good impression to customers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If it's quiet, help someone pack their bags.

transcript.text: Staying calm is also a necessity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Occasionally, when working tills, you'll find yourself waiting for someone to extract their wallet from the bottom of a cluttered bag while a long queue of annoyed customers builds up.

transcript.text: Part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: How to make a guitar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear a man being interviewed on the radio about his work as a musician and a guitar maker.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you listen, you have thirty seconds to read questions eleven to fourteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Great to have you here today, Hamish.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I've been a fan of yours for ages.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The very first rock concert I went to when I was thirteen, your band was playing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Gosh, I'd like to thank this station too, Juliet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: If I remember rightly, Ray Rogers' interest in Sound Hole's second album put us on the map.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Good old Ray.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Alas, who could forget when Sound Hole broke up and Ray wept live on his show?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: [clears throat] But to set the record straight, Sound Hole isn't getting back together despite rumors on social networks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: My performing days are over.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Even solo?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Especially solo.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Frankly, solo gigs were a nightmare.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I was so anxious every time I went out onto a stage.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Live audiences seriously scare me.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Yet you've got such a rapport with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You look so relaxed in those clips on YouTube.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Yeah, well, one thing the social networks did get right is the reason I quit performing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Oh?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: I was manic when I was on the road with the band.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Crazy.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I'd stay up days on end.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Back home, I was horribly depressed.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I'd sleep for a week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: My life was a mess.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: My first wife left me, and my second wife left me.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I've got three children I hardly know.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: My son sent me a card just before Sound Hole split up, in which he'd written he'd seen more of me on TV than in the flesh.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Before you listen to the rest of the talk, you have thirty seconds to read questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions fifteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: So how long have you been making acoustic guitars, Hamish?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Full time for about three years.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: My sister and I work together.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: She sources the materials and does the books.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I build the instruments.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I checked on the Internet last night, and it's a long process to make a guitar.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: You bet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: There's at least fifteen steps.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I won't go into them all now, but sourcing the wood, the first step, is crucial.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Cheap guitars use softer wood, which equates with poorer sound quality.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: But harder wood is scarce these days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: For instance, the back of a great guitar, historically, was made from Brazilian rosewood, but the supply is minuscule now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I use East Indian rosewood, which will also disappear soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Likewise, spruce was once preferred for the top of a guitar, but I use cedar, which is more plentiful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I thought guitars were mainly mahogany.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Cheap guitars, yes, but only the necks of good ones.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: The neck must resist distortion when pulled by the strings, and it mustn't swell or contract with changes in temperature and humidity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Mahogany's perfect for the neck.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I like that wavy pattern you get on the tops and backs of guitars.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How's that done?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: That pattern is called book matching.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: A thickish block of wood about half the size of the body is sliced horizontally.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: The two pieces are laid together with the grain continuous before they're glued.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: The next two steps are to saw the top of the guitar into that sensual shape and cut out the sound hole.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: What's inside the guitar to control its vibration and improve its tone?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Braces.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Narrow little bits of wood glued in an X pattern.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: The process is known as strutting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: The back also has strutting to reflect sound waves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: Interesting.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: How's the neck made?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: It's carved from a single piece of mahogany, and a metal rod is driven up into it for reinforcement.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: How'd you get those lovely curved sides?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Strips are cut, sanded, and soaked in water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: They're molded until they're set in that shape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: When everything's been glued together, the back, the sides, the top, and the neck, the guitar is put into clamps for several days.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: There are some other reinforcements too, like end blocks and bindings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I guess precision is the key to much of this work.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Absolutely.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: In fact, guitar making has improved my mental health because everything's nice and slow and precise.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I'm alone in my workshop dealing with wood.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: It has a calming effect.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: It seems as though you sound whole again.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 2

transcript.text: Please.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: No more silly puns on the name of our band.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: I spent fourteen years explaining that Hole was spelt with a W.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 3

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

Stage 1:
• Mahogany is used for the neck as it can endure changes in {{15}} and humidity.
Stage 2:

Stage 5:
• The back, sides, top, and neck are glued and clamped together for {{18}} .

transcript.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to this orientation session prior to our camp next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you for coming along to find out what you and your children will be doing on this year's camp.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: To start off with, let's tell you a bit about the campsite itself so that you'll be able to find your way around once you get there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, we'll be arriving by bus into the car park, which if you look at the plan you have in front of you, you'll see at the top of the picture on the left-hand side.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, if you cross the road from the car park, the first building you'll come to is the toilet block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's been recently upgraded, so it's very nice and clean in there now with plenty of facilities.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And built onto that, so this is across the road from the community hall, is the new shower block.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The hot water does run out occasionally, but usually there's enough to cope with a group your size.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If you now move to the bottom left of your map among the pine trees, there is a special flat site set up for pitching tents with power points and outdoor taps for water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, let's go back and move along the top of your map.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There's another area of pine forest, and then over on the far right-hand side, there's a block of small cabins.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Note that this is different from the main accommodation block, which doesn't appear on this map, but is further over again to the right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's look down from there over the road, so we're moving clockwise round your map, okay?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In this next block beside the flower beds, we have a lovely place for barbecues where you can cook in the open air.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: What else to tell you about?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Um, below the flower bed and across Lakeside Drive, you'll see a trail for mountain biking, which is always a popular activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Moving on now, in the middle of the campsite, you'll see the lake where you can canoe, and above that again, the community hall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So that completes your introduction to the campsite.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I hope you found that useful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty on page four.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now let's think about what you need to bring with you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'm sure you're all wondering what you need to pack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The lake is a bit cold for swimming at this time of year, so you can leave your togs out of the suitcase.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: While we're on the subject of weather too, usually, I recommend that campers bring sunblock with them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I guess now that we're into April, that too can be left behind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Uh, let me think.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some campers like a torch, but actually the days are still so long that it's light outside till quite late, and the blocks all have outside lighting now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So I'd say that a pair of earplugs are more useful, as in my experience, a lot of talking goes on after lights out.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in April, if it's wet, it can get muddy around the campsite, so to bring boots isn't a bad idea.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, can you all please prepare something for the final night concert?
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Bring your musical instruments or whatever else you need.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You can't have a camp without a good singalong.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's our favorite activity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Maybe you could recite a poem, act out a skit or charades for us if you're brave enough to try that, or failing that, perhaps you can tell a joke or a funny story.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But actually, people much prefer to see some good dancing.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I'll look forward to seeing you all perform next week.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You will hear a man introducing a charity to a group of listeners.

transcript.text: Hello, everyone.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thanks for attending tonight's event.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me start with the early history of our charity, Eye Saver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Eye Saver was founded by a retired optometrist, Timothy Gaines.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I have spent much of my working life at Eye Saver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am sixty years old now, and I started working for this organization fifteen years ago when I left a corporate position to help people with eye problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now our charity has been helping people for three decades.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may know that we are now doing various other things to help people with eye problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That includes medications for children with eye diseases and operational help to those in the public who have eye problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But when Mr.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Gaines just founded Eye Saver, he wanted the program to be able to offer common eye equipment to those who needed it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We receive occasional donations from corporations and charity groups.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now we have over one thousand five hundred volunteers who work on the streets with the little red donation boxes, which many of you are familiar with, and this is the main source of funding for us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Besides, we are planning to work to secure donations from wealthy benefactors.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many people are passionate about charity cause and have been inquiring how to donate money to us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I really appreciate that.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But our main need is to collect glasses for our patients.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Many of you have multiple pairs of old glasses in your possession, and we encourage you to gather these pairs which you no longer need and donate them to our cause.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In doing this, you'll be able to make sure that someone else can see better.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Most of us cannot imagine a life in which we are unable to see well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This is why your eyeglass donations are so critical to our mission.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And as a side note, we offer full-time positions.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Let me know if you are interested.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our goal is to make people aware that even the smallest of donations can help change a person's life.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So your donation can be a turning point for them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The other day, when I was talking to some people on the street, they were surprised to find out how easily some eye problems can be cured.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And I am proud to say that our next program will aim at educating people about common eye diseases.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We are able to prevent many fatal eye problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In order to publicize our charity program, we surely need to do some advertising.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When we first started our program, we used computers to create awareness for our cause.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: For instance, promoting seminars in which we informed people as to how they could help us to solve eye problems.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But in recent years, the main means of advertising our program is through audio recordings.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have found it cost-efficient and effective.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's good to know that many of our staff are recommending our program to their friends and colleagues.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But I am afraid that our training cannot show people the whole picture of our program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Finally, I would like to tell you about some organizations which have played important roles in the development and success of Eye Saver.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our affiliation with the National Vision Funding Group has allowed us to gain fame and to become even more significant.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So many people around the country are coming for our services.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our association with the Eye for the Future organization has allowed us to run cooperative ads by which we seek producers of equipment to work with us.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Meanwhile, some of our staff has been sent to this organization for some special training.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Their skills should be improved very soon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, we have had a long time cooperation with Sam's Eye Care Institution.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our relationship with it has given us the opportunity to link with many different academic institutions, including colleges and universities with good reputation.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And we have a similar friendship with a group called Youth Health.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Our connection with that group allows us to link directly with young kids since this is a crucial stage in their growth.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We plan to contact with some colleges and hope that with their help, more college students could get to know our program.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So as you can see, we have all bases covered in linking with students as we have affiliations directly with both administrators and the students themselves.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Thank you so much for your attention today.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As we try to stamp out eye problems, we will appreciate your donations, no matter how large or how small.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We believe with our efforts, the world will be a brighter and more beautiful...
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's the end of section two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You now have half a minute to check your answers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So for those of you who don't know very much about the company, let me start by giving you some basic information about it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Earn and Learn started nearly twenty years ago.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It is not a charity, but a for-profit company that enables promising entrepreneurs to make money while traveling.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: During the past ten years, it has grown rapidly and has gained great influence in most countries of the world.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We have a partnership with the school and take a large number of recent graduates from the business school.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So if you are a recent graduate, I'd say you can consider applying to our company.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before your application, you might be curious about what sort of places you could go to.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: There are four main locations, but you also have the freedom to submit a different location, and if they can make the necessary arrangements, you can go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first country Earn and Learn and Learn established locations was the US, where you may choose from multiple locations as long as you can commit to their more rigid schedule of August to December.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Also, you could do the Australia internship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That one is really cool.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You work at a wildlife shelter and learn about the business practices of nonprofit organizations.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You do have to be willing to commit eight months for that one, though.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Perhaps that's a long time to be so far away, but I would say it is really an amazing opportunity.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I don't know whether some of you are in decent physical shape.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: If so, the South Africa internship is another exciting one.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You learn a lot about sustainable farming, but you would be doing some of the manual labor involved in maintaining a farm.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Indeed, it's hard work, but I think you would definitely be able to do it.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It may be wise to wait until after their summer is over, so it's not so terribly hot.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In addition, there is a most recently established location in India.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: This one gives you more of a study abroad feel, given that they arrange a host family for you to stay with.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: In the other locations, you live in an apartment with other interns, so this is definitely a unique experience.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions seventeen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Some students may want to know whether this is a paid internship.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But you have the opportunity to create your own small business, which could earn you money if it's successful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: So basically, you pay for it all up front.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But when you're there, you can find ways to make money.

transcript.text: You'll meet everyone you'll be working with once you get there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Okay.

questions.quote: The most popular cooking tour is in the early summer in Northern California, which is famous for its cheeses. This four-day tour is special because each student receives one-on-one classes with a master chef. Then you'll take part in visits to the great cheese producers of the region, and you'll taste cheeses and see how they are made.

questions.prompt: Italy

transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: You will hear the manager of a bookshop called Bibliostack talking to a group of young people about the way the bookshop is organized.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: First, you have some time to look at questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions eleven to fifteen.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone, and a big welcome to Bibliostack.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Firstly, I'll explain the plan of the store to you.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The building is on seven floors and is circular, as you can see, and we're here on the ground floor in its entrance hall.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Right in the center of this floor, but behind the bookshelf, so you can't see it very well from here, is our main seating area, where people are encouraged to sit and read for as long as they like.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they're under no pressure to buy what they're reading.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's not how we operate.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And if you look to your immediate left, past the first double row of shelves, you'll see piles of colored cushions in front of the window there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We provide those so that people can sit wherever they want.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Lots of people like to sit close to the bookshelves, and if they want to sit on the floor there, we want them to be as comfortable as possible.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: On your right, between the two larger bookshelves, you'll see the computer bench, where our visitors can search through our entire catalog.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We pride ourselves in being the largest bookshop in the country, so our sales assistants can't possibly know all the available titles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although the room in front of you is dominated by the bookshelves, at the far end, just in front of the lift, you'll see that we provide a small café bar here, too.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: And just to your right, there's a door to the cloakroom, where people can leave their coats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Then after that, there's a stand where we keep a selection of local and national newspapers.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Customers are welcome to browse through them, and we also have some for sale.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We really want people to feel as though they're browsing through books in the comfort of their own home.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Now listen and answer questions sixteen to twenty.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, I suggest we walk slowly up through the building, and I'll give you more information as we go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We're open twelve hours a day.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We don't mind if people spend the whole day here, but leave without buying anything.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, we hope they'll buy something, but our purpose is to draw people in, to provide the kind of environment which makes them want to stay and read.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Look at how busy each floor is, but how quiet.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: You may be wondering whether there are any children in the building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We debated about locating children's books on the ground floor or halfway up the building, like the third or fourth floor, but in the end, we decided to put them on the very top level, and I can assure you, it's not the least bit quiet up there.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Of course, many parents would prefer to spend time on other floors, and so we provide a supervised area for children under two in the basement, so parents can wander around the shop for a few hours and not worry.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: But they do have to pay for this service, because although we thought about using some of our own assistants, we decided to employ qualified nursery staff for parents' complete peace of mind.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now, we're just passing the fiction section, and you've probably noticed a small crowd of people beginning to gather.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That's because a well-known author is going to read from her latest novel.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We try to hold events like this at least once or twice a week, and as you can imagine, they're very popular.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: We don't make a charge for people to attend, but we obviously hope that some of them will want to purchase the book after listening to part of it being read aloud.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Other events which are proving to be very popular are our workshops.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Last week, we held a poetry workshop, and people came along with poems that they'd written.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the country's best-known poets ran the workshop, and the participants read their poems aloud to him.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He was kind and encouraging, and many people felt inspired by his advice.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It's extremely difficult to earn your living as a professional poet, and even published poets have other jobs.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Now we're going to take a look at our section on audiobooks.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: That is the end of part two.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 0

transcript.text: Good afternoon.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Welcome to Barton Museum.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I am Carly, and I am your tour guide.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: I would be taking you through all the places of interest in this museum before we actually set out to go.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The first building we stop at is the Barton House, which was built by the man himself, Barton.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: When he first came to this area, it was largely uninhabited, and as a matter of fact, this place was a vast expanse of land where an abandoned farm was situated.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: After he bought it, he began building, and in about three years, the basic structure was complete.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although he never really stopped building.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: As a man who loved the arts, Barton spent a good fortune on them.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He had several paintings from all over the world, and his gallery is still considered one of the best in town.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: One of the most notable of his collection is the Chinese wallpaper, which was painted in the eighteenth century.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Rumor has it that he paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for the piece of art.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Barton kept adding some features to his house every year.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He did this until the night he died.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He was building a new bird room in which he collapsed and never came to himself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: His dining room is also beautifully adorned with antiquity, from the tables to the stools to the mats.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: The chairs were bought from some Japanese merchants in the area then.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Looking at the location of his house, which sits some feet higher than surrounding lands, it is possible to see areas of just green, lush vegetation that run for miles.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: At the backyard, there is a garden which he started himself.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He used to care for the plants there personally and made sure they never lacked water.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He detested fertilizers as he believed that it would spoil the cycle of growth of the plants in the garden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: He had some trees in the garden.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are not ordinary trees, but some rare ones, and they have been alive for decades now.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Under one of those trees was his favorite spot, and history tells us that he used to sing and pray under the tree.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Recently, the government brought in some flamingos here as the environment supports their growth and development well.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They are believed to make the scenery livelier and more beautiful.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: Although there are many exotic animals in the garden, swans are still the most popular animal here.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: They seem to be everywhere, and it was said that Barton thought that they were a gift from the heaven.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

transcript.text: It was forbidden to kill or hurt any of these animals in his time.
transcript.speaker: Speaker 1

questions.explanation: 最著名的收藏之一是中国壁纸，它是在 18th（18）世纪绘制的。
questions.tip: 注意听 "century" 前面的数字，虽然录音中提到了钱数 "hundreds of thousands"，但那是价格，不是年份世纪。
questions.quote: One of the most notable of his collection is the Chinese wallpaper, which was painted in the 18th century.

questions.explanation: Barton 是在一间他正在建造的新 bird（鸟）房里倒下并去世的。
questions.tip: 题目问的是 "died in the ... room"，原文对应 "collapsed and never came to himself"（倒下且再没醒来），发生的地点是 bird room。

questions.explanation: 餐厅里有很多古董，其中 chairs（椅子）是从当地的日本商人那里买来的。

questions.explanation: 花园里有一些并不普通的树，而是一些 rare（稀有的）植物，且已经存活了几十年。
questions.tip: 题目中是 "____ plants"，录音中说的是 "trees... not ordinary... but some rare ones"，树属于植物，核心形容词是 rare。
questions.quote: He had some trees in the garden, they are not ordinary trees, but some rare ones, and they have been alive for decades now.

questions.explanation: 录音直接陈述，政府（government）引进了火烈鸟（flamingos）。

questions.quote: Recently, the government brought in some flamingos here as the environment supports their growth and development well. They are believed to make the scenery livelier and more beautiful.

questions.explanation: 虽然有很多外来动物，但 swans（天鹅）仍然是这里最受欢迎的动物。
questions.tip: 题目关键词是 "most popular"，录音中明确说 "swans are still the most popular"，不要被前面的 exotic animals 干扰。
questions.quote: Although there are many exotic animals in the garden, swans are still the most popular animals here.

transcript.text: You will hear an electronic toy company manager talking to a small group of new temporary staff who are starting work at the company.

transcript.text: Good morning, everyone.
